questions.text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta \left(\alpha \;<\; \beta\right)$ are the roots of the equation $\left(-2 \;+\; \sqrt{3}\right)\left(\left\lvert \sqrt{x} \;-\; 3 \right\rvert\right) \;+\; \left(x \;-\; 6\sqrt{x}\right) \;+\; \left(9 \;-\; 2\sqrt{3}\right) \;=\; 0, \; x \;\ge\; 0$, then $\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{\alpha}} \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha\beta}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Group $x \;-\; 6\sqrt{x} \;+\; 9$ as $\left\lvert \sqrt{x} \;-\; 3 \right\rvert^2$ and substitute $u \;=\; \left\lvert \sqrt{x} \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;\ge\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Let $t \;=\; \sqrt{x} \;\ge\; 0$. Since $t^2 \;-\; 6t \;+\; 9 \;=\; \left(t \;-\; 3\right)^2 \;=\; \left\lvert t \;-\; 3 \right\rvert^2$, the equation becomes $\left\lvert t \;-\; 3 \right\rvert^2 \;+\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;-\; 2\right)\left\lvert t \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;-\; 2\sqrt{3} \;=\; 0$. Let $u \;=\; \left\lvert t \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;\ge\; 0$; factoring $u^2 \;+\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;-\; 2\right) u \;-\; 2\sqrt{3} \;=\; 0$ gives $\left(u \;-\; 2\right)\left(u \;+\; \sqrt{3}\right) \;=\; 0$. Since $u \;\ge\; 0$, we have $u \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \left\lvert \sqrt{x} \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \sqrt{x} \;-\; 3 \;=\; \pm 2 \;\implies\; \sqrt{x} \;=\; 1$ or $\sqrt{x} \;=\; 5 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 1$ or $x \;=\; 25$. Since $\alpha \;<\; \beta$, $\alpha \;=\; 1$ and $\beta \;=\; 25$. Therefore, $\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{\alpha}} \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha\beta} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{25}{1}} \;+\; \sqrt{25} \;=\; 5 \;+\; 5 \;=\; 10$.

questions.text: Two dice are thrown independently. Let $A$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is less than the number appeared on the $2^{\text{nd}}$ die, $B$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is even and that on the second die is odd, and $C$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is odd and that on the $2^{\text{nd}}$ is even. Then

options.text: the number of favourable cases of the event $\left(A \;\cup\; B\right) \;\cap\; C$ is $6$
The number of favourable cases of the events $A, \;B$ and $C$ are $15, \;6$ and $6$ respectively

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the distributive law $\left(A \;\cup\; B\right) \;\cap\; C \;=\; \left(A \;\cap\; C\right) \;\cup\; \left(B \;\cap\; C\right)$ and note that $B \;\cap\; C \;=\; \phi$. // 📝 Solution: Here $n\left(A\right) \;=\; 5 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 3 \;+\; 2 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 15$, $n\left(B\right) \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 3 \;=\; 9$, and $n\left(C\right) \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 3 \;=\; 9$. Also, $B$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive, so $B \;\cap\; C \;=\; \phi$. Therefore, $\left(A \;\cup\; B\right) \;\cap\; C \;=\; \left(A \;\cap\; C\right) \;\cup\; \left(B \;\cap\; C\right) \;=\; A \;\cap\; C$. The outcomes in $A \;\cap\; C$ have an odd number on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die and a larger even number on the $2^{\text{nd}}$ die: $\left(1, \;2\right), \;\left(1, \;4\right), \;\left(1, \;6\right), \;\left(3, \;4\right), \;\left(3, \;6\right), \;\left(5, \;6\right)$, which gives $6$ favourable cases.

💡 Hint: Express the polynomial in factored form $4\prod_{k=1}^4 \left(x \;-\; x_k\right)$ and substitute $x \;=\; 2i$ and $x \;=\; -2i$. // 📝 Solution: Using the factor theorem, $4 x^4 \;+\; 8 x^3 \;-\; 17 x^2 \;-\; 12 x \;+\; 9 \;=\; 4\left(x \;-\; x_1\right)\left(x \;-\; x_2\right)\left(x \;-\; x_3\right)\left(x \;-\; x_4\right)$. Substituting $x \;=\; 2i$ gives $4\left(2i\right)^4 \;+\; 8\left(2i\right)^3 \;-\; 17\left(2i\right)^2 \;-\; 12\left(2i\right) \;+\; 9 \;=\; 64 \;-\; 64i \;+\; 68 \;-\; 24i \;+\; 9 \;=\; 141 \;-\; 88i \;=\; 4\left(2i \;-\; x_1\right)\left(2i \;-\; x_2\right)\left(2i \;-\; x_3\right)\left(2i \;-\; x_4\right)$. Similarly, substituting $x \;=\; -2i$ gives $141 \;+\; 88i \;=\; 4\left(-2i \;-\; x_1\right)\left(-2i \;-\; x_2\right)\left(-2i \;-\; x_3\right)\left(-2i \;-\; x_4\right)$. Multiplying these two equations yields $141^2 \;+\; 88^2 \;=\; 16\left(4 \;+\; x_1^2\right)\left(4 \;+\; x_2^2\right)\left(4 \;+\; x_3^2\right)\left(4 \;+\; x_4^2\right) \;\implies\; \frac{125}{16} m \;=\; \frac{19881 \;+\; 7744}{16} \;=\; \frac{27625}{16} \;\implies\; m \;=\; \frac{27625}{125} \;=\; 221$.

questions.text: If $\alpha, \;\beta$ are the roots of the equation, $x^2 \;-\; x \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ and $S_n \;=\; 2023 \alpha^n \;+\; 2024 \beta^n$, then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Any linear combination $S_n \;=\; A\alpha^n \;+\; B\beta^n$ of the roots of $x^2 \;-\; x \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ satisfies $S_n \;=\; S_{n-1} \;+\; S_{n-2}$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of $x^2 \;-\; x \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$, we have $\alpha^2 \;=\; \alpha \;+\; 1$ and $\beta^2 \;=\; \beta \;+\; 1$. Now consider $S_{n-1} \;+\; S_{n-2} \;=\; 2023\alpha^{n-2}\left(\alpha \;+\; 1\right) \;+\; 2024\beta^{n-2}\left(\beta \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 2023\alpha^{n-2}\left(\alpha^2\right) \;+\; 2024\beta^{n-2}\left(\beta^2\right) \;=\; 2023\alpha^n \;+\; 2024\beta^n \;=\; S_n$. Substituting $n \;=\; 12$, we obtain $S_{12} \;=\; S_{11} \;+\; S_{10}$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be the distinct roots of the equation $x^2 \;-\; \left(t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6\right) x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0, \; t \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ and $a_n \;=\; \alpha^n \;+\; \beta^n$. Then the minimum value of $\frac{a_{2023} \;+\; a_{2025}}{a_{2024}}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Newton's sum formula $a_{n+2} \;-\; \left(t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6\right) a_{n+1} \;+\; a_n \;=\; 0$ and complete the square in $t$. // 📝 Solution: By Newton's identity for the quadratic equation $x^2 \;-\; \left(t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6\right) x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$, we have $a_{n+2} \;-\; \left(t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6\right) a_{n+1} \;+\; a_n \;=\; 0$. Substituting $n \;=\; 2023$, we get $a_{2025} \;+\; a_{2023} \;=\; \left(t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6\right) a_{2024} \;\implies\; \frac{a_{2023} \;+\; a_{2025}}{a_{2024}} \;=\; t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6$. Completing the square gives $t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6 \;=\; \left(t \;-\; \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 \;-\; \frac{1}{4}$. Therefore, the minimum value is $-\frac{1}{4}$.

questions.text: Let $\lambda \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ and let the equation $E$ be $\left\lvert x \right\rvert^2 \;-\; 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; \left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 0$. Then the largest element in the set $S \;=\; \left\{x \;+\; \lambda \;:\; x \text{ is an integer solution of } E\right\}$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Complete the square as $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;+\; \left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 1$ and analyze possible integer values of $x$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting equation $E$ by completing the square gives $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;+\; \left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 1$. Since $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;\ge\; 0$ and $\left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;\ge\; 0$, and $x$ is an integer, $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2$ can only be $0$ or $1$. Case 1: $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \pm 1$, and $\left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 2$ or $4$. Here, the maximum value of $x \;+\; \lambda$ is $1 \;+\; 4 \;=\; 5$. Case 2: $\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; 0$ or $2 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 0, \;\pm 2$, and $\left\lvert \lambda \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 3$. Here, the maximum value of $x \;+\; \lambda$ is $2 \;+\; 3 \;=\; 5$. Thus, the largest element in $S$ is $5$.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{\alpha \;:\; \log_2\left(9^{2\alpha \;-\; 4} \;+\; 13\right) \;-\; \log_2\left(\frac{5}{2} \;\cdot\; 3^{2\alpha \;-\; 4} \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 2\right\}$. Then the maximum value of $\beta$ for which the equation $x^2 \;-\; 2\left(\sum_{\alpha \;\in\; S} \alpha\right)^2 x \;+\; \sum_{\alpha \;\in\; S} \left(\alpha \;+\; 1\right)^2 \beta \;=\; 0$ has real roots, is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the logarithmic equation by setting $t \;=\; 3^{2\alpha \;-\; 4}$, then apply the discriminant condition $D \;\ge\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: From the logarithmic equation, $\frac{9^{2\alpha \;-\; 4} \;+\; 13}{\frac{5}{2} \;\cdot\; 3^{2\alpha \;-\; 4} \;+\; 1} \;=\; 2^2 \;=\; 4$. Let $t \;=\; 3^{2\alpha \;-\; 4}$. Then $t^2 \;+\; 13 \;=\; 10t \;+\; 4 \;\implies\; t^2 \;-\; 10t \;+\; 9 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 1$ or $t \;=\; 9$. Thus $3^{2\alpha \;-\; 4} \;=\; 3^0$ or $3^2 \;\implies\; 2\alpha \;-\; 4 \;=\; 0$ or $2 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 2$ or $3$. Hence $S \;=\; \left\{2, \;3\right\}$, so $\sum_{\alpha \;\in\; S} \alpha \;=\; 2 \;+\; 3 \;=\; 5$ and $\sum_{\alpha \;\in\; S} \left(\alpha \;+\; 1\right)^2 \;=\; 3^2 \;+\; 4^2 \;=\; 25$. The quadratic equation becomes $x^2 \;-\; 50 x \;+\; 25\beta \;=\; 0$. For real roots, $D \;=\; 50^2 \;-\; 4\left(1\right)\left(25\beta\right) \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; 2500 \;-\; 100\beta \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; \beta \;\le\; 25$. Therefore, the maximum value of $\beta$ is $25$.

questions.text: The number of real solutions of the equation $3\left(x^2 \;+\; \frac{1}{x^2}\right) \;-\; 2\left(x \;+\; \frac{1}{x}\right) \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0$, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; x \;+\; \frac{1}{x}$ and recall that $\left\lvert t \right\rvert \;\ge\; 2$ for all real $x \;\ne\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Let $t \;=\; x \;+\; \frac{1}{x}$. Then $x^2 \;+\; \frac{1}{x^2} \;=\; t^2 \;-\; 2$. Substituting into the given equation gives $3\left(t^2 \;-\; 2\right) \;-\; 2t \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 3t^2 \;-\; 2t \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 1\right)\left(3t \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 1$ or $t \;=\; -\frac{1}{3}$. However, for any real $x \;\ne\; 0$, $\left\lvert x \;+\; \frac{1}{x} \right\rvert \;\ge\; 2$, so neither $t \;=\; 1$ nor $t \;=\; -\frac{1}{3}$ yields a real solution. Hence, the number of real solutions is $0$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta; \; \alpha \;>\; \beta$, be the roots of the equation $x^2 \;-\; \sqrt{2} x \;-\; \sqrt{3} \;=\; 0$. Let $P_n \;=\; \alpha^n \;-\; \beta^n, \; n \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. Then $\left(11\sqrt{3} \;-\; 10\sqrt{2}\right) P_{10} \;+\; \left(11\sqrt{2} \;+\; 10\right) P_{11} \;-\; 11 P_{12}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the recurrence relation $P_{n+2} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{n+1} \;-\; \sqrt{3} P_n \;=\; 0$ for $n \;=\; 10$ and $n \;=\; 9$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of $x^2 \;-\; \sqrt{2} x \;-\; \sqrt{3} \;=\; 0$, Newton's formula gives $P_{n+2} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{n+1} \;-\; \sqrt{3} P_n \;=\; 0$. For $n \;=\; 10$, we get $P_{12} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{11} \;-\; \sqrt{3} P_{10} \;=\; 0$. For $n \;=\; 9$, we get $P_{11} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{10} \;-\; \sqrt{3} P_9 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; P_{11} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{10} \;=\; \sqrt{3} P_9$. Rearranging the given expression: $\left(11\sqrt{3} \;-\; 10\sqrt{2}\right) P_{10} \;+\; \left(11\sqrt{2} \;+\; 10\right) P_{11} \;-\; 11 P_{12} \;=\; -11\left(P_{12} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{11} \;-\; \sqrt{3} P_{10}\right) \;+\; 10\left(P_{11} \;-\; \sqrt{2} P_{10}\right) \;=\; -11\left(0\right) \;+\; 10\left(\sqrt{3} P_9\right) \;=\; 10\sqrt{3} P_9$.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{x \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;:\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)^x \;+\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;-\; \sqrt{2}\right)^x \;=\; 10\right\}$. Then the number of elements in $S$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Note that $\sqrt{3} \;-\; \sqrt{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}}$ and substitute $t \;=\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)^x$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)\left(\sqrt{3} \;-\; \sqrt{2}\right) \;=\; 3 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 1$, let $\left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)^x \;=\; t \;>\; 0$. Then the equation becomes $t \;+\; \frac{1}{t} \;=\; 10 \;\implies\; t^2 \;-\; 10 t \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; \frac{10 \;\pm\; \sqrt{100 \;-\; 4}}{2} \;=\; 5 \;\pm\; 2\sqrt{6} \;=\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;\pm\; \sqrt{2}\right)^2$. Thus, $\left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)^x \;=\; \left(\sqrt{3} \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)^{\pm 2} \;\implies\; x \;=\; 2$ or $x \;=\; -2$. Hence, the number of elements in $S$ is $2$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the equation $p x^2 \;+\; q x \;-\; r \;=\; 0$, where $p \;\ne\; 0$. If $p, \;q$ and $r$ be the consecutive terms of a non-constant G.P and $\frac{1}{\alpha} \;+\; \frac{1}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$, then the value of $\left(\alpha \;-\; \beta\right)^2$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $p \;=\; A, \; q \;=\; A R, \; r \;=\; A R^2$ to express the sum and product of roots solely in terms of the common ratio $R$. // 📝 Solution: Let $p \;=\; A, \; q \;=\; A R, \; r \;=\; A R^2$. Substituting into $p x^2 \;+\; q x \;-\; r \;=\; 0$ and dividing by $A \;\ne\; 0$ gives $x^2 \;+\; R x \;-\; R^2 \;=\; 0$. Thus, $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; -R$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; -R^2$. Given $\frac{1}{\alpha} \;+\; \frac{1}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{3}{4} \;\implies\; \frac{\alpha \;+\; \beta}{\alpha\beta} \;=\; \frac{-R}{-R^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{R} \;=\; \frac{3}{4} \;\implies\; R \;=\; \frac{4}{3}$. Therefore, $\left(\alpha \;-\; \beta\right)^2 \;=\; \left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)^2 \;-\; 4\alpha\beta \;=\; R^2 \;-\; 4\left(-R^2\right) \;=\; 5 R^2 \;=\; 5\left(\frac{16}{9}\right) \;=\; \frac{80}{9}$.

questions.text: The number of solutions, of the equation $e^{\sin x} \;-\; 2 e^{-\sin x} \;=\; 2$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; e^{\sin x}$ and compare the roots with the range $\left[e^{-1}, \;e^1\right]$ of $e^{\sin x}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $e^{\sin x} \;=\; t \;>\; 0$. The equation becomes $t \;-\; \frac{2}{t} \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; t^2 \;-\; 2t \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 1 \;\pm\; \sqrt{3}$. Since $t \;>\; 0$, we reject $1 \;-\; \sqrt{3}$ and get $e^{\sin x} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \sqrt{3} \;\approx\; 2.732$. However, for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, $-1 \;\le\; \sin x \;\le\; 1 \;\implies\; e^{\sin x} \;\le\; e^1 \;\approx\; 2.718 \;<\; 1 \;+\; \sqrt{3}$. Therefore, no real solution exists.

questions.text: The sum of all the real solutions of the equation $\log_{\left(x \;+\; 3\right)}\left(6 x^2 \;+\; 28 x \;+\; 30\right) \;=\; 5 \;-\; 2\log_{\left(6 x \;+\; 10\right)}\left(x^2 \;+\; 6 x \;+\; 9\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor $6 x^2 \;+\; 28 x \;+\; 30 \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)\left(6 x \;+\; 10\right)$ and $x^2 \;+\; 6 x \;+\; 9 \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)^2$, then use logarithm base-change properties. // 📝 Solution: Domain requires $x \;+\; 3 \;>\; 0, \; x \;+\; 3 \;\ne\; 1, \; 6 x \;+\; 10 \;>\; 0, \; 6 x \;+\; 10 \;\ne\; 1$. Note that $6 x^2 \;+\; 28 x \;+\; 30 \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)\left(6 x \;+\; 10\right)$ and $x^2 \;+\; 6 x \;+\; 9 \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)^2$. Let $a \;=\; \log_{\left(x \;+\; 3\right)}\left(6 x \;+\; 10\right)$. Then $\text{LHS} \;=\; 1 \;+\; a$ and $\text{RHS} \;=\; 5 \;-\; \frac{4}{a}$. Thus, $1 \;+\; a \;=\; 5 \;-\; \frac{4}{a} \;\implies\; a^2 \;-\; 4a \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 2$. Hence, $\log_{\left(x \;+\; 3\right)}\left(6 x \;+\; 10\right) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)^2 \;=\; 6 x \;+\; 10 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 6 x \;+\; 9 \;=\; 6 x \;+\; 10 \;\implies\; x^2 \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 1$ or $x \;=\; -1$. Both satisfy the domain constraints, so the sum of solutions is $1 \;+\; \left(-1\right) \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let the set $C \;=\; \left\{\left(x, \;y\right) \;\mid\; x^2 \;-\; 2^y \;=\; 2023, \; x, \;y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}\right\}$. Then $\sum_{\left(x, \;y\right) \;\in\; C} \left(x \;+\; y\right)$ is equal to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check $y \;=\; 1$ directly and analyze the equation modulo $4$ for $y \;\ge\; 2$. // 📝 Solution: We are given $x^2 \;=\; 2023 \;+\; 2^y$ where $x, \;y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. For $y \;=\; 1$, $x^2 \;=\; 2023 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 2025 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 45 \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. For $y \;\ge\; 2$, $2^y$ is divisible by $4$, so $x^2 \;=\; 2023 \;+\; 2^y \;\equiv\; 3 \;+\; 0 \;\equiv\; 3 \pmod{4}$. However, the square of any integer is congruent to $0$ or $1 \pmod{4}$, so no solution exists for $y \;\ge\; 2$. Thus, the only element in $C$ is $\left(45, \;1\right)$, and $\sum_{\left(x, \;y\right) \;\in\; C} \left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; 45 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 46$.

questions.text: The number of real solutions of the equation $x \left(x^2 \;+\; 3\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 5\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; 6\left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert\right) \;=\; 0$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the sign of the expression inside the parentheses for all real $x$. // 📝 Solution: The given equation holds if either $x \;=\; 0$ or $x^2 \;+\; 3\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 5\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; 6\left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert \;=\; 0$. Since each term inside the parentheses is non-negative for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ and they cannot vanish simultaneously, $x^2 \;+\; 3\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 5\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; 6\left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert \;>\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Therefore, $x \;=\; 0$ is the only real solution, so the number of real solutions is $1$.

questions.text: A building construction work can be completed by two masons A and B together in $22.5$ days. Mason A alone can complete the construction work in $24$ days less than mason B alone. Then mason A alone will complete the construction work in :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Let mason A take $a$ days and mason B take $a \;+\; 24$ days, then equate their combined daily work rate to $\frac{1}{22.5}$. // 📝 Solution: Let mason A alone take $a$ days to complete the work; then mason B alone takes $\left(a \;+\; 24\right)$ days. Their combined daily work rate gives $\frac{1}{a} \;+\; \frac{1}{a \;+\; 24} \;=\; \frac{1}{22.5} \;=\; \frac{2}{45} \;\implies\; \frac{2a \;+\; 24}{a\left(a \;+\; 24\right)} \;=\; \frac{2}{45} \;\implies\; 45\left(2a \;+\; 24\right) \;=\; 2a\left(a \;+\; 24\right) \;\implies\; 90a \;+\; 1080 \;=\; 2a^2 \;+\; 48a \;\implies\; a^2 \;-\; 21a \;-\; 540 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(a \;-\; 36\right)\left(a \;+\; 15\right) \;=\; 0$. Since $a \;>\; 0$, we get $a \;=\; 36$ days.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ be roots of equation $x^2 \;-\; 70 x \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 0$, where $\frac{\lambda}{2}, \;\frac{\lambda}{3} \;\notin\; \mathbb{N}$. If $\lambda$ assumes the minimum possible value, then $\frac{\left(\sqrt{\alpha \;-\; 1} \;+\; \sqrt{\beta \;-\; 1}\right)\left(\lambda \;+\; 35\right)}{\left\lvert \alpha \;-\; \beta \right\rvert}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; 70$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; \lambda$, ensuring neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ is a multiple of $2$ or $3$ to minimize $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: From $x^2 \;-\; 70 x \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 0$, we have $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; 70$ and $\lambda \;=\; \alpha\beta$. Since $\lambda$ is not divisible by $2$ or $3$, neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ can be a multiple of $2$ or $3$. To minimize $\lambda \;=\; \alpha\left(70 \;-\; \alpha\right)$ for $\alpha \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, we test the smallest possible values of $\alpha$: $\alpha \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 69$ (divisible by $3$, rejected); $\alpha \;=\; 2, \;3, \;4$ are rejected; $\alpha \;=\; 5 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 65$ (neither is divisible by $2$ or $3$, valid). Thus, $\alpha \;=\; 5, \;\beta \;=\; 65$, and $\lambda \;=\; 5 \;\times\; 65 \;=\; 325$. Substituting these values into the expression gives $\frac{\left(\sqrt{5 \;-\; 1} \;+\; \sqrt{65 \;-\; 1}\right)\left(325 \;+\; 35\right)}{\left\lvert 5 \;-\; 65 \right\rvert} \;=\; \frac{\left(2 \;+\; 8\right) \;\times\; 360}{60} \;=\; 60$.

questions.text: The smallest positive integral value of $a$, for which all the roots of $x^4 \;-\; a x^2 \;+\; 9 \;=\; 0$ are real and distinct, is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; x^2$ and require the resulting quadratic in $t$ to have two distinct positive roots. // 📝 Solution: Let $t \;=\; x^2$. Then the biquadratic equation becomes $t^2 \;-\; a t \;+\; 9 \;=\; 0$. For $x^4 \;-\; a x^2 \;+\; 9 \;=\; 0$ to have four real and distinct roots, the quadratic in $t$ must have two distinct positive roots. Hence: 1) Discriminant $D \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; a^2 \;-\; 36 \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; \left\lvert a \right\rvert \;>\; 6$, 2) Sum of roots $= \; a \;>\; 0$, and 3) Product of roots $= \; 9 \;>\; 0$. Combining these gives $a \;>\; 6$, so the smallest positive integral value of $a$ is $7$.

questions.text: The number of distinct real roots of the equation $\left\lvert x \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \left\lvert x \;+\; 3 \right\rvert \;-\; 4 \left\lvert x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0$, is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; \left\lvert x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert$ and observe that $\left\lvert x \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \left\lvert x \;+\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert \left(x \;+\; 2\right)^2 \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$. // 📝 Solution: Let $y \;=\; x \;+\; 2$. The equation becomes $\left\lvert y \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \left\lvert y \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \;-\; 4\left\lvert y \right\rvert \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left\lvert y^2 \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;-\; 4\left\lvert y \right\rvert \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0$. Let $t \;=\; \left\lvert y \right\rvert \;\ge\; 0$. Case 1: $0 \;\le\; t \;<\; 1$. Then $1 \;-\; t^2 \;-\; 4t \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t^2 \;+\; 4t \;-\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; -2 \;\pm\; \sqrt{10}$. Neither value lies in $\left[0, \;1\right)$. Case 2: $t \;\ge\; 1$. Then $t^2 \;-\; 1 \;-\; 4t \;+\; 5 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t^2 \;-\; 4t \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 2\right)^2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 2 \;\ge\; 1$. Thus, $\left\lvert x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; x \;+\; 2 \;=\; \pm 2 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 0$ or $x \;=\; -4$. Hence, there are $2$ distinct real roots.

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ be a root of the equation $\left(a \;-\; c\right) x^2 \;+\; \left(b \;-\; a\right) x \;+\; \left(c \;-\; b\right) \;=\; 0$ where $a, \;b, \;c$ are distinct real numbers such that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \alpha^2 & \alpha & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \end{bmatrix}$ is singular. Then the value of $\frac{\left(a \;-\; c\right)^2}{\left(b \;-\; a\right)\left(c \;-\; b\right)} \;+\; \frac{\left(b \;-\; a\right)^2}{\left(a \;-\; c\right)\left(c \;-\; b\right)} \;+\; \frac{\left(c \;-\; b\right)^2}{\left(a \;-\; c\right)\left(b \;-\; a\right)}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the identity $x^3 \;+\; y^3 \;+\; z^3 \;=\; 3xyz$ when $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Since the matrix is singular, its determinant is zero: $\alpha^2\left(c \;-\; b\right) \;-\; \alpha\left(c \;-\; a\right) \;+\; \left(b \;-\; a\right) \;=\; 0$, which holds for $\alpha \;=\; 1$ (since $a, \;b, \;c$ are distinct). Notice that the given expression can be written with a common denominator as $\frac{\left(a \;-\; c\right)^3 \;+\; \left(b \;-\; a\right)^3 \;+\; \left(c \;-\; b\right)^3}{\left(a \;-\; c\right)\left(b \;-\; a\right)\left(c \;-\; b\right)}$. Since $\left(a \;-\; c\right) \;+\; \left(b \;-\; a\right) \;+\; \left(c \;-\; b\right) \;=\; 0$, we use the identity $X^3 \;+\; Y^3 \;+\; Z^3 \;=\; 3XYZ$ to get $\frac{3\left(a \;-\; c\right)\left(b \;-\; a\right)\left(c \;-\; b\right)}{\left(a \;-\; c\right)\left(b \;-\; a\right)\left(c \;-\; b\right)} \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: The sum of all the roots of the equation $\left(x \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;-\; 5\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; 6 \;=\; 0$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; \left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$ or use symmetry of the roots about $x \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Let $t \;=\; \left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;\ge\; 0$. The equation becomes $t^2 \;-\; 5t \;+\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 2\right)\left(t \;-\; 3\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 2$ or $t \;=\; 3$. For $\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; 2$, we get $x \;=\; 3$ or $x \;=\; -1$. For $\left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; 3$, we get $x \;=\; 4$ or $x \;=\; -2$. Therefore, the sum of all the roots is $3 \;+\; \left(-1\right) \;+\; 4 \;+\; \left(-2\right) \;=\; 4$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be the roots of the quadratic equation $12 x^2 \;-\; 20 x \;+\; 3\lambda \;=\; 0, \; \lambda \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$. If $\frac{1}{2} \;\le\; \left\lvert \beta \;-\; \alpha \right\rvert \;\le\; \frac{3}{2}$, then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express $\left\lvert \beta \;-\; \alpha \right\rvert \;=\; \sqrt{\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)^2 \;-\; 4\alpha\beta}$ in terms of $\lambda$ and solve the double inequality for integer $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: For $12 x^2 \;-\; 20 x \;+\; 3\lambda \;=\; 0$, we have $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; \frac{20}{12} \;=\; \frac{5}{3}$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; \frac{3\lambda}{12} \;=\; \frac{\lambda}{4}$. Thus, $\left\lvert \beta \;-\; \alpha \right\rvert \;=\; \sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2 \;-\; 4\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)} \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{25 \;-\; 9\lambda}}{3}$. Given $\frac{1}{2} \;\le\; \frac{\sqrt{25 \;-\; 9\lambda}}{3} \;\le\; \frac{3}{2} \;\implies\; \frac{3}{2} \;\le\; \sqrt{25 \;-\; 9\lambda} \;\le\; \frac{9}{2}$. Squaring throughout gives $\frac{9}{4} \;\le\; 25 \;-\; 9\lambda \;\le\; \frac{81}{4} \;\implies\; \frac{19}{36} \;\le\; \lambda \;\le\; \frac{91}{36}$. Since $\lambda \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$, the possible values are $\lambda \;=\; 1, \;2$. Their sum is $1 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: If $2$ and $6$ are the roots of the equation $a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$, then the quadratic equation, whose roots are $\frac{1}{2a \;+\; b}$ and $\frac{1}{6a \;+\; b}$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the sum and product of roots of $a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$ to find $a$ and $b$, then form the new quadratic equation. // 📝 Solution: Given that $2$ and $6$ are the roots of $a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$, we have: Sum of roots $= \; 2 \;+\; 6 \;=\; 8 \;=\; -\frac{b}{a}$ and Product of roots $= \; 2 \;\times\; 6 \;=\; 12 \;=\; \frac{1}{a} \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{1}{12}$. Substituting $a$, we get $b \;=\; -8a \;=\; -\frac{8}{12} \;=\; -\frac{2}{3}$. Now, evaluate the new roots: $2a \;+\; b \;=\; \frac{2}{12} \;-\; \frac{2}{3} \;=\; -\frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; \frac{1}{2a \;+\; b} \;=\; -2$, and $6a \;+\; b \;=\; \frac{6}{12} \;-\; \frac{2}{3} \;=\; -\frac{1}{6} \;\implies\; \frac{1}{6a \;+\; b} \;=\; -6$. For the required quadratic equation, Sum of roots $\left(S\right) \;=\; \left(-2\right) \;+\; \left(-6\right) \;=\; -8$ and Product of roots $\left(P\right) \;=\; \left(-2\right)\left(-6\right) \;=\; 12$. Hence, the equation is $x^2 \;-\; S x \;+\; P \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 8 x \;+\; 12 \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: The number of real roots of the equation $\sqrt{x^2 \;-\; 4 x \;+\; 3} \;+\; \sqrt{x^2 \;-\; 9} \;=\; \sqrt{4 x^2 \;-\; 14 x \;+\; 6}$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor the expressions under all three square roots to extract the common factor $\sqrt{x \;-\; 3}$. // 📝 Solution: Factoring each quadratic gives $\sqrt{\left(x \;-\; 1\right)\left(x \;-\; 3\right)} \;+\; \sqrt{\left(x \;-\; 3\right)\left(x \;+\; 3\right)} \;=\; \sqrt{\left(x \;-\; 3\right)\left(4 x \;-\; 2\right)}$. For real roots, either $x \;-\; 3 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 3$ (which satisfies the domain of all radicals since each radicand becomes $0$), or for $x \;>\; 3$ we can divide by $\sqrt{x \;-\; 3}$ to get $\sqrt{x \;-\; 1} \;+\; \sqrt{x \;+\; 3} \;=\; \sqrt{4 x \;-\; 2}$. Squaring both sides gives $\left(x \;-\; 1\right) \;+\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right) \;+\; 2\sqrt{x^2 \;+\; 2 x \;-\; 3} \;=\; 4 x \;-\; 2 \;\implies\; 2\sqrt{x^2 \;+\; 2 x \;-\; 3} \;=\; 2 x \;-\; 4 \;\implies\; \sqrt{x^2 \;+\; 2 x \;-\; 3} \;=\; x \;-\; 2$. Squaring again gives $x^2 \;+\; 2 x \;-\; 3 \;=\; x^2 \;-\; 4 x \;+\; 4 \;\implies\; 6 x \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{7}{6}$, which is rejected as $x \;>\; 3$ is required. Thus, $x \;=\; 3$ is the only real root.

questions.text: If the value of real number $a \;>\; 0$ for which $x^2 \;-\; 5a x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$ and $x^2 \;-\; a x \;-\; 5 \;=\; 0$ have a common real root is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2\beta}}$ then $\beta$ is equal to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Eliminate $x^2$ between the two equations to find the common root in terms of $a$, then substitute it back. // 📝 Solution: Let $\alpha$ be the common root. Subtracting $\alpha^2 \;-\; a\alpha \;-\; 5 \;=\; 0$ from $\alpha^2 \;-\; 5a\alpha \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$ gives $-4a\alpha \;+\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{3}{2a}$. Substituting $\alpha \;=\; \frac{3}{2a}$ into $\alpha^2 \;-\; a\alpha \;-\; 5 \;=\; 0$ yields $\frac{9}{4a^2} \;-\; \frac{3}{2} \;-\; 5 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{9}{4a^2} \;=\; \frac{13}{2} \;\implies\; a^2 \;=\; \frac{9}{26} \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{3}{\sqrt{26}}$ (since $a \;>\; 0$). Comparing with $a \;=\; \frac{3}{\sqrt{2\beta}}$, we obtain $2\beta \;=\; 26 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 13$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 \;+\; 2a x \;+\; \left(3a \;+\; 10\right) \;=\; 0$ such that $\alpha \;<\; 1 \;<\; \beta$. Then the set of all possible values of $a$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $1$ to lie strictly between the roots of $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 0$ with a positive leading coefficient, apply the condition $f\left(1\right) \;<\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; x^2 \;+\; 2a x \;+\; \left(3a \;+\; 10\right)$. Since the coefficient of $x^2$ is $1 \;>\; 0$ and $\alpha \;<\; 1 \;<\; \beta$, $x \;=\; 1$ lies strictly between the roots if and only if $f\left(1\right) \;<\; 0$. Substituting $x \;=\; 1$, we get $1 \;+\; 2a \;+\; 3a \;+\; 10 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; 5a \;+\; 11 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; a \;<\; -\frac{11}{5}$. Thus, $a \;\in\; \left(-\infty, \;-\frac{11}{5}\right)$.

questions.text: For $0 \;<\; c \;<\; b \;<\; a$, let $\left(a \;+\; b \;-\; 2c\right) x^2 \;+\; \left(b \;+\; c \;-\; 2a\right) x \;+\; \left(c \;+\; a \;-\; 2b\right) \;=\; 0$ and $\alpha \;\ne\; 1$ be one of its root. Then, among the two statements (I) If $\alpha \;\in\; \left(-1, \;0\right)$, then $b$ cannot be the geometric mean of $a$ and $c$ (II) If $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \;1\right)$, then $b$ may be the geometric mean of $a$ and $c$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Notice that $x \;=\; 1$ is a root because the sum of coefficients is zero, then use the product of roots to find $\alpha$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\left(a \;+\; b \;-\; 2c\right) \;+\; \left(b \;+\; c \;-\; 2a\right) \;+\; \left(c \;+\; a \;-\; 2b\right) \;=\; 0$, the roots are $1$ and $\alpha \;=\; \frac{c \;+\; a \;-\; 2b}{a \;+\; b \;-\; 2c}$. Given $0 \;<\; c \;<\; b \;<\; a$, the denominator $a \;+\; b \;-\; 2c \;>\; 0$. For Statement (I): If $\alpha \;\in\; \left(-1, \;0\right)$, then $c \;+\; a \;-\; 2b \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; b \;>\; \frac{a \;+\; c}{2} \;>\; \sqrt{ac}$ (by AM-GM inequality), so $b$ cannot be the G.M. of $a$ and $c$. Thus (I) is true. For Statement (II): If $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \;1\right)$, then $0 \;<\; \frac{c \;+\; a \;-\; 2b}{a \;+\; b \;-\; 2c} \;<\; 1 \;\implies\; c \;<\; b \;<\; \frac{a \;+\; c}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{ac} \;\in\; \left(c, \;\frac{a \;+\; c}{2}\right)$, $b$ may be the G.M. of $a$ and $c$. Thus Both (I) and (II) are true.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be roots of $x^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2} x \;-\; 8 \;=\; 0$. If $U_n \;=\; \alpha^n \;+\; \beta^n$, then $\frac{U_{10} \;+\; \sqrt{2} U_9}{2 U_8}$ is equal to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Newton's recurrence relation $U_n \;+\; \sqrt{2} U_{n-1} \;-\; 8 U_{n-2} \;=\; 0$ for $n \;=\; 10$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $x^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2} x \;-\; 8 \;=\; 0$, they satisfy $\alpha^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\alpha \;=\; 8$ and $\beta^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\beta \;=\; 8$. Thus, $U_{10} \;+\; \sqrt{2} U_9 \;=\; \left(\alpha^{10} \;+\; \beta^{10}\right) \;+\; \sqrt{2}\left(\alpha^9 \;+\; \beta^9\right) \;=\; \alpha^8\left(\alpha^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\alpha\right) \;+\; \beta^8\left(\beta^2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\beta\right) \;=\; 8\left(\alpha^8 \;+\; \beta^8\right) \;=\; 8 U_8$. Therefore, $\frac{U_{10} \;+\; \sqrt{2} U_9}{2 U_8} \;=\; \frac{8 U_8}{2 U_8} \;=\; 4$.
questions.topic: Newton's Theorem on Symmetric Sums of Roots

questions.text: Let $a, \;b, \;c$ be the length of three sides of a triangle satisfying the condition $\left(a^2 \;+\; b^2\right) x^2 \;-\; 2b\left(a \;+\; c\right) x \;+\; \left(b^2 \;+\; c^2\right) \;=\; 0$. If the set of all possible values of $x$ is the interval $\left(\alpha, \;\beta\right)$, then $12\left(\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2\right)$ is equal to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite the equation as a sum of two squares $\left(a x \;-\; b\right)^2 \;+\; \left(b x \;-\; c\right)^2 \;=\; 0$ and apply the triangle inequality. // 📝 Solution: Rearranging the given equation gives $\left(a x \;-\; b\right)^2 \;+\; \left(b x \;-\; c\right)^2 \;=\; 0$. Since $a, \;b, \;c, \;x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, we must have $a x \;-\; b \;=\; 0$ and $b x \;-\; c \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; b \;=\; a x$ and $c \;=\; b x \;=\; a x^2$ (with $x \;>\; 0$). Since $a, \;b, \;c$ are the sides of a triangle, $a \;+\; b \;>\; c$ and $b \;+\; c \;>\; a$: 1) $a \;+\; a x \;>\; a x^2 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; x \;-\; 1 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(\frac{1 \;-\; \sqrt{5}}{2}, \;\frac{1 \;+\; \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$. 2) $a x \;+\; a x^2 \;>\; a \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; x \;-\; 1 \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;>\; \frac{\sqrt{5} \;-\; 1}{2}$ (since $x \;>\; 0$). Combining these, $x \;\in\; \left(\frac{\sqrt{5} \;-\; 1}{2}, \;\frac{\sqrt{5} \;+\; 1}{2}\right) \;=\; \left(\alpha, \;\beta\right)$. Thus, $12\left(\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2\right) \;=\; 12\left[\left(\frac{\sqrt{5} \;-\; 1}{2}\right)^2 \;+\; \left(\frac{\sqrt{5} \;+\; 1}{2}\right)^2\right] \;=\; 12\left(\frac{6 \;-\; 2\sqrt{5} \;+\; 6 \;+\; 2\sqrt{5}}{4}\right) \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 12 \;=\; 36$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 \;+\; 2\sqrt{2} x \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$. The quadratic equation, whose roots are $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4$ and $\frac{1}{10}\left(\alpha^6 \;+\; \beta^6\right)$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use algebraic identities to compute $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4$ and $\alpha^6 \;+\; \beta^6$ from $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; -2\sqrt{2}$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; -1$. // 📝 Solution: From $x^2 \;+\; 2\sqrt{2} x \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$, we have $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; -2\sqrt{2}$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; -1$. First, $\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2 \;=\; \left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)^2 \;-\; 2\alpha\beta \;=\; \left(-2\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \;-\; 2\left(-1\right) \;=\; 8 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 10$. Next, $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4 \;=\; \left(\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2\right)^2 \;-\; 2\left(\alpha\beta\right)^2 \;=\; 10^2 \;-\; 2\left(1\right) \;=\; 98$. Also, $\alpha^6 \;+\; \beta^6 \;=\; \left(\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2\right)\left(\alpha^4 \;-\; \alpha^2\beta^2 \;+\; \beta^4\right) \;=\; 10\left(98 \;-\; 1\right) \;=\; 970 \;\implies\; \frac{1}{10}\left(\alpha^6 \;+\; \beta^6\right) \;=\; 97$. Thus, the required quadratic equation with roots $98$ and $97$ is $x^2 \;-\; \left(98 \;+\; 97\right) x \;+\; \left(98 \;\times\; 97\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 195 x \;+\; 9506 \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let $a \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ and let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 \;+\; 60^{\frac{1}{4}} x \;+\; a \;=\; 0$. If $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4 \;=\; -30$, then the product of all possible values of $a$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the identity $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4 \;=\; \left[\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)^2 \;-\; 2\alpha\beta\right]^2 \;-\; 2\left(\alpha\beta\right)^2$ to form a quadratic equation in $a$. // 📝 Solution: Here, $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; -60^{\frac{1}{4}}$ and $\alpha\beta \;=\; a$. Given $\alpha^4 \;+\; \beta^4 \;=\; -30 \;\implies\; \left[\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)^2 \;-\; 2\alpha\beta\right]^2 \;-\; 2\alpha^2\beta^2 \;=\; -30 \;\implies\; \left(\sqrt{60} \;-\; 2a\right)^2 \;-\; 2a^2 \;=\; -30 \;\implies\; 60 \;-\; 4\sqrt{60} a \;+\; 4a^2 \;-\; 2a^2 \;=\; -30 \;\implies\; 2a^2 \;-\; 4\sqrt{60} a \;+\; 90 \;=\; 0$. Since the discriminant of this quadratic in $a$ is $D \;=\; 16\left(60\right) \;-\; 4\left(2\right)\left(90\right) \;=\; 960 \;-\; 720 \;=\; 240 \;>\; 0$, both roots are real, and the product of all possible values of $a$ is $\frac{90}{2} \;=\; 45$.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{x^3 \;+\; a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; c \;:\; a, \;b, \;c \;\in\; \mathbb{N} \text{ and } a, \;b, \;c \;\le\; 20\right\}$ be a set of polynomials. Then the number of polynomials in $S$, which are divisible by $x^2 \;+\; 2$, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $x^3 \;+\; a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; c \;=\; \left(x^2 \;+\; 2\right)\left(x \;+\; k\right)$ and compare coefficients. // 📝 Solution: If $x^2 \;+\; 2$ divides $x^3 \;+\; a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; c$, we can write $x^3 \;+\; a x^2 \;+\; b x \;+\; c \;=\; \left(x^2 \;+\; 2\right)\left(x \;+\; k\right) \;=\; x^3 \;+\; k x^2 \;+\; 2 x \;+\; 2k$. Comparing coefficients gives $a \;=\; k, \; b \;=\; 2$, and $c \;=\; 2k \;=\; 2a$. Since $a, \;b, \;c \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ and $a, \;b, \;c \;\le\; 20$, we require $c \;=\; 2a \;\le\; 20 \;\implies\; a \;\le\; 10$. Thus $a \;\in\; \left\{1, \;2, \;\dots, \;10\right\}$ and $b \;=\; 2$ is fixed, giving $10$ such polynomials in $S$.

questions.text: The number of real solutions of the equation $x \left\lvert x \;+\; 5 \right\rvert \;+\; 2 \left\lvert x \;+\; 7 \right\rvert \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the real line into three intervals around the critical points $x \;=\; -5$ and $x \;=\; -7$ of the modulus terms. // 📝 Solution: Case I: $x \;\ge\; -5$. The equation becomes $x\left(x \;+\; 5\right) \;+\; 2\left(x \;+\; 7\right) \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7 x \;+\; 12 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(x \;+\; 3\right)\left(x \;+\; 4\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; -3, \;-4$. Both satisfy $x \;\ge\; -5$. Case II: $-7 \;<\; x \;<\; -5$. The equation becomes $-x\left(x \;+\; 5\right) \;+\; 2\left(x \;+\; 7\right) \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -x^2 \;-\; 3 x \;+\; 12 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 3 x \;-\; 12 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{-3 \;\pm\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; 48}}{2} \;=\; \frac{-3 \;\pm\; \sqrt{57}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{57} \;\approx\; 7.55$, $x \;=\; \frac{-3 \;-\; \sqrt{57}}{2} \;\approx\; -5.27 \;\in\; \left(-7, \;-5\right)$ is accepted, while $\frac{-3 \;+\; \sqrt{57}}{2}$ is rejected. Case III: $x \;\le\; -7$. The equation becomes $-x\left(x \;+\; 5\right) \;-\; 2\left(x \;+\; 7\right) \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7 x \;+\; 16 \;=\; 0$. Here, discriminant $D \;=\; 49 \;-\; 64 \;=\; -15 \;<\; 0$, giving no real roots. Thus, the total number of real solutions is $2 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 0 \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: The sum of all the solutions of the equation $\left(8\right)^{2x} \;-\; 16 \;\cdot\; \left(8\right)^x \;+\; 48 \;=\; 0$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; 8^x$ to form a quadratic equation in $t$ and use logarithm properties. // 📝 Solution: Let $8^x \;=\; t \;>\; 0$. The given equation becomes $t^2 \;-\; 16 t \;+\; 48 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 4\right)\left(t \;-\; 12\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 4$ or $t \;=\; 12$. Substituting back $8^x \;=\; t$, we have $8^x \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; x_1 \;=\; \log_8\left(4\right)$ and $8^x \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; x_2 \;=\; \log_8\left(12\right)$. Therefore, the sum of all solutions is $x_1 \;+\; x_2 \;=\; \log_8\left(4\right) \;+\; \log_8\left(12\right) \;=\; \log_8\left(48\right) \;=\; \log_8\left(8 \;\times\; 6\right) \;=\; \log_8\left(8\right) \;+\; \log_8\left(6\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \log_8\left(6\right)$.

questions.text: Let $\lambda \;\ne\; 0$ be a real number. Let $\alpha, \;\beta$ be the roots of the equation $14 x^2 \;-\; 31 x \;+\; 3\lambda \;=\; 0$ and $\alpha, \;\gamma$ be the roots of the equation $35 x^2 \;-\; 53 x \;+\; 4\lambda \;=\; 0$. Then $\frac{3\alpha}{\beta}$ and $\frac{4\alpha}{\gamma}$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the sum and product of roots of both equations to eliminate $\beta, \;\gamma$ and find $\alpha$ and $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: From the given equations, $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; \frac{31}{14}, \;\alpha\beta \;=\; \frac{3\lambda}{14}$ and $\alpha \;+\; \gamma \;=\; \frac{53}{35}, \;\alpha\gamma \;=\; \frac{4\lambda}{35}$. Dividing the products gives $\frac{\beta}{\gamma} \;=\; \frac{3\lambda / 14}{4\lambda / 35} \;=\; \frac{15}{8} \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; \frac{15}{8}\gamma$. Subtracting the sums gives $\beta \;-\; \gamma \;=\; \frac{31}{14} \;-\; \frac{53}{35} \;=\; \frac{7}{10} \;\implies\; \frac{7}{8}\gamma \;=\; \frac{7}{10} \;\implies\; \gamma \;=\; \frac{4}{5}$, so $\beta \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$, $\alpha \;=\; \frac{31}{14} \;-\; \frac{3}{2} \;=\; \frac{5}{7}$, and $\lambda \;=\; \frac{14}{3}\alpha\beta \;=\; 5$. Thus, the new roots are $\frac{3\alpha}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{3\left(5/7\right)}{3/2} \;=\; \frac{10}{7}$ and $\frac{4\alpha}{\gamma} \;=\; \frac{4\left(5/7\right)}{4/5} \;=\; \frac{25}{7}$. Their sum is $\frac{35}{7} \;=\; 5$ and product is $\frac{250}{49}$, giving $x^2 \;-\; 5 x \;+\; \frac{250}{49} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 49 x^2 \;-\; 245 x \;+\; 250 \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let $S$ be the set of positive integral values of $a$ for which $\frac{a x^2 \;+\; 2\left(a \;+\; 1\right) x \;+\; 9a \;+\; 4}{x^2 \;-\; 8 x \;+\; 32} \;<\; 0, \;\forall x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Then, the number of elements in $S$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the sign of the denominator $x^2 \;-\; 8 x \;+\; 32$ and apply the condition for a quadratic to be negative for all real $x$. // 📝 Solution: The denominator is $x^2 \;-\; 8 x \;+\; 32 \;=\; \left(x \;-\; 4\right)^2 \;+\; 16 \;>\; 0, \;\forall x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Thus, the given inequality requires the numerator to be strictly negative for all real $x$: $a x^2 \;+\; 2\left(a \;+\; 1\right) x \;+\; 9a \;+\; 4 \;<\; 0, \;\forall x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. This holds only if the leading coefficient $a \;<\; 0$ and discriminant $D \;<\; 0$. Since $a$ must be negative, there are no positive integral values of $a$. Hence, the number of elements in $S$ is $0$.

options.text: two solutions and both are negative
four solutions two of which are negative
two solutions and only one of them is negative

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \;=\; e^x \;>\; 0$, divide the reciprocal equation by $t^2$, and set $z \;=\; t \;-\; \frac{1}{t}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $t \;=\; e^x \;>\; 0$. Then $t^4 \;+\; 8t^3 \;+\; 13t^2 \;-\; 8t \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. Dividing by $t^2$ gives $\left(t^2 \;+\; \frac{1}{t^2}\right) \;+\; 8\left(t \;-\; \frac{1}{t}\right) \;+\; 13 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; \frac{1}{t}\right)^2 \;+\; 8\left(t \;-\; \frac{1}{t}\right) \;+\; 15 \;=\; 0$. Let $z \;=\; t \;-\; \frac{1}{t}$. Then $z^2 \;+\; 8z \;+\; 15 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; z \;=\; -3$ or $z \;=\; -5$. Thus $t \;-\; \frac{1}{t} \;=\; -3 \;\implies\; t^2 \;+\; 3t \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{13} \;-\; 3}{2}$ (since $t \;>\; 0$), or $t \;-\; \frac{1}{t} \;=\; -5 \;\implies\; t^2 \;+\; 5t \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{29} \;-\; 5}{2}$ (since $t \;>\; 0$). Since both values of $t$ lie in $\left(0, \;1\right)$, $x \;=\; \ln t \;<\; 0$ in both cases. Hence, there are two solutions and both are negative.

questions.text: If $\alpha, \;\beta$, where $\alpha \;<\; \beta$, are the roots of the equation $\lambda x^2 \;-\; \left(\lambda \;+\; 3\right) x \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0$ such that $\frac{1}{\alpha} \;-\; \frac{1}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{1}{3}$, then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor the quadratic equation directly as $\left(\lambda x \;-\; 3\right)\left(x \;-\; 1\right) \;=\; 0$ to find the roots $1$ and $\frac{3}{\lambda}$. // 📝 Solution: The given equation $\lambda x^2 \;-\; \left(\lambda \;+\; 3\right) x \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0$ factors as $\left(\lambda x \;-\; 3\right)\left(x \;-\; 1\right) \;=\; 0$, so its roots are $1$ and $\frac{3}{\lambda}$. Since $\alpha \;<\; \beta$ and $\frac{1}{\alpha} \;-\; \frac{1}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{1}{3} \;>\; 0$, both roots must have the same sign (positive, as $\lambda \;>\; 0$), so $\frac{1}{\alpha} \;>\; \frac{1}{\beta}$. The reciprocals of the roots are $1$ and $\frac{\lambda}{3}$. Thus, $\left\lvert \frac{\lambda}{3} \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{3} \;\implies\; \frac{\lambda}{3} \;-\; 1 \;=\; \pm\frac{1}{3} \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 4$ or $\lambda \;=\; 2$. Both values yield distinct roots satisfying $\alpha \;<\; \beta$, so the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is $4 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 6$.

questions.text: Let $n$ be the number obtained on rolling a fair die. If the probability that the system $x \;-\; ny \;+\; z \;=\; 6$, $x \;+\; \left(n \;-\; 2\right)y \;+\; \left(n \;+\; 1\right)z \;=\; 8$, $\left(n \;-\; 1\right)y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$ has a unique solution is $\frac{k}{6}$, then the sum of $k$ and all possible values of $n$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A system of linear equations has a unique solution when the determinant of the coefficient matrix is non-zero. // 📝 Solution: The determinant of the coefficient matrix is $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -n & 1 \\ 1 & n - 2 & n + 1 \\ 0 & n - 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 1\left[\left(n \;-\; 2\right) \;-\; \left(n^2 \;-\; 1\right)\right] \;-\; 1\left[-n \;-\; \left(n \;-\; 1\right)\right] \;=\; -n^2 \;+\; 3n \;-\; 2 \;=\; -\left(n \;-\; 1\right)\left(n \;-\; 2\right)$. For a unique solution, $\Delta \;\neq\; 0 \;\implies\; n \;\neq\; 1, \; 2$. Since $n \;\in\; \left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6\right\}$, the favorable values are $n \;\in\; \left\{3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6\right\}$. The probability is $\frac{4}{6} \;=\; \frac{k}{6} \;\implies\; k \;=\; 4$. Required sum $= 4 \;+\; \left(3 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 5 \;+\; 6\right) \;=\; 22$.

questions.text: Among the statements : I : If $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos \alpha & \cos \beta \\ \cos \alpha & 1 & \cos \gamma \\ \cos \beta & \cos \gamma & 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & \cos \alpha & \cos \beta \\ \cos \alpha & 0 & \cos \gamma \\ \cos \beta & \cos \gamma & 0 \end{vmatrix}$, then $\cos^2 \alpha \;+\; \cos^2 \beta \;+\; \cos^2 \gamma \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$, and II : If $\begin{vmatrix} x^2 + x & x + 1 & x - 2 \\ 2x^2 + 3x - 1 & 3x & 3x - 3 \\ x^2 + 2x + 3 & 2x - 1 & 2x - 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; px \;+\; q$, then $p^2 \;=\; 196q^2$,
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand both determinants in Statement I to find $\cos^2 \alpha \;+\; \cos^2 \beta \;+\; \cos^2 \gamma$, and substitute $x \;=\; 0, \; 1$ in Statement II to find $p$ and $q$. // 📝 Solution: Statement I: Expanding the left determinant gives $D_1 \;=\; 1 \;-\; \cos^2 \alpha \;-\; \cos^2 \beta \;-\; \cos^2 \gamma \;+\; 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma$, and the right determinant gives $D_2 \;=\; 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma$. Equating $D_1 \;=\; D_2 \;\implies\; \cos^2 \alpha \;+\; \cos^2 \beta \;+\; \cos^2 \gamma \;=\; 1 \;\neq\; \frac{3}{2}$, so Statement I is false. Statement II: Putting $x \;=\; 0$ in the determinant gives $q \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; -1\left(1 \;+\; 9\right) \;-\; 2\left(1 \;-\; 0\right) \;=\; -12$. Putting $x \;=\; 1$ gives $p \;+\; q \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 2\left(3\right) \;-\; 2\left(4\right) \;-\; 1\left(-14\right) \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; p \;=\; 24$. Thus $p^2 \;=\; 576$ and $196q^2 \;=\; 196 \;\times\; 144 \;=\; 28224$, so $p^2 \;\neq\; 196q^2$ and Statement II is also false. Hence, both are false.

questions.text: Let for any three distinct consecutive terms $a, \; b, \; c$ of an A.P., the lines $ax \;+\; by \;+\; c \;=\; 0$ be concurrent at the point $P$ and $Q\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right)$ be a point such that the system of equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 6$, $2x \;+\; 5y \;+\; \alpha z \;=\; \beta$ and $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 4$, has infinitely many solutions. Then $\left(PQ\right)^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the A.P. relation $a \;-\; 2b \;+\; c \;=\; 0$ to find the fixed point $P$, and apply $\Delta \;=\; \Delta_x \;=\; 0$ for infinitely many solutions to find $Q\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a, \; b, \; c$ are in A.P., $2b \;=\; a \;+\; c \;\implies\; a\left(1\right) \;+\; b\left(-2\right) \;+\; c \;=\; 0$. Comparing with $ax \;+\; by \;+\; c \;=\; 0$, the point of concurrency is $P\left(1, \; -2\right)$. For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta \;=\; 0$ and $\Delta_x \;=\; 0$. Now, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & \alpha \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(15 \;-\; 2\alpha\right) \;-\; 1\left(6 \;-\; \alpha\right) \;+\; 1\left(4 \;-\; 5\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 8 \;-\; \alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 8$. Also, $\Delta_x \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 6 & 1 & 1 \\ \beta & 5 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 6\left(15 \;-\; 16\right) \;-\; 1\left(3\beta \;-\; 32\right) \;+\; 1\left(2\beta \;-\; 20\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 6$. Thus $Q\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right) \;=\; \left(8, \; 6\right)$, and $\left(PQ\right)^2 \;=\; \left(8 \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;+\; \left(6 \;+\; 2\right)^2 \;=\; 49 \;+\; 64 \;=\; 113$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $2x+\lambda y+3z=5$, $3x+2y-z=7$, $4x+5y+\mu z=9$ has infinitely many solutions, then $(\lambda^2+\mu^2)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\Delta_3=0$ to get $\lambda$ and $\Delta=0$ to get $\mu$. // 📝 Solution: $\Delta_3=\begin{vmatrix}2&\lambda&5\\3&2&7\\4&5&9\end{vmatrix}=\lambda+1=0 \implies \lambda=-1$; $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}2&-1&3\\3&2&-1\\4&5&\mu\end{vmatrix}=7\mu+35=0 \implies \mu=-5$; $\lambda^2+\mu^2=26$

questions.text: For the system of linear equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 6$, $\alpha x \;+\; \beta y \;+\; 7z \;=\; 3$, $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 14$, which of the following is NOT true ?

options.text: If $\alpha \;=\; \beta \;=\; 7$, then the system has no solution
If $\alpha \;=\; \beta$ and $\alpha \;\neq\; 7$ then the system has a unique solution
There is a unique point $\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right)$ on the line $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 18 \;=\; 0$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions
For every point $\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right) \;\neq\; \left(7, \; 7\right)$ on the line $x \;-\; 2y \;+\; 7 \;=\; 0$, the system has infinitely many solutions.

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z$ from the first and third equations, then substitute into the second equation. // 📝 Solution: Subtracting equation (1) from equation (3) gives $y \;+\; 2z \;=\; 8 \;\implies\; y \;=\; 8 \;-\; 2z$, and substituting into (1) gives $x \;=\; z \;-\; 2$. Putting $x$ and $y$ into the second equation gives $\alpha\left(z \;-\; 2\right) \;+\; \beta\left(8 \;-\; 2z\right) \;+\; 7z \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \left(\alpha \;-\; 2\beta \;+\; 7\right)z \;=\; 2\alpha \;-\; 8\beta \;+\; 3$. For infinitely many solutions, we need both $\alpha \;-\; 2\beta \;+\; 7 \;=\; 0$ and $2\alpha \;-\; 8\beta \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0$, which yields a single unique point $\left(\alpha, \; \beta\right) \;=\; \left(-\frac{25}{2}, \; -\frac{11}{4}\right)$, not every point on the line $x \;-\; 2y \;+\; 7 \;=\; 0$. Thus, option D is NOT true.
questions.topic: Consistency of System of Linear Equations

questions.text: If $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 2\cos^4 x & 2\sin^4 x & 3 + \sin^2 2x \\ 3 + 2\cos^4 x & 2\sin^4 x & \sin^2 2x \\ 2\cos^4 x & 3 + 2\sin^4 x & \sin^2 2x \end{vmatrix}$, then $\frac{1}{5}f'\left(0\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply row operations $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; R_1$ and $R_3 \;\to\; R_3 \;-\; R_1$ to simplify the determinant before differentiating. // 📝 Solution: Applying $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; R_1$ and $R_3 \;\to\; R_3 \;-\; R_1$, we get $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 2\cos^4 x & 2\sin^4 x & 3 + \sin^2 2x \\ 3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding along the first row gives $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 2\cos^4 x\left(9\right) \;-\; 2\sin^4 x\left(-9\right) \;+\; \left(3 \;+\; \sin^2 2x\right)\left(9\right) \;=\; 9\left[2\left(\cos^4 x \;+\; \sin^4 x\right) \;+\; 3 \;+\; \sin^2 2x\right]$. Using $\cos^4 x \;+\; \sin^4 x \;=\; 1 \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\sin^2 2x$, we obtain $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 9\left[2 \;-\; \sin^2 2x \;+\; 3 \;+\; \sin^2 2x\right] \;=\; 45$. Since $f\left(x\right)$ is constant, $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{1}{5}f'\left(0\right) \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $11x \;+\; y \;+\; \lambda z \;=\; -5$, $2x \;+\; 3y \;+\; 5z \;=\; 3$, $8x \;-\; 19y \;-\; 39z \;=\; \mu$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda^4 \;-\; \mu$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the conditions $D \;=\; 0$ and $D_1 \;=\; 0$ for infinitely many solutions to find $\lambda$ and $\mu$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $D \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 11 & 1 & \lambda \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 8 & -19 & -39 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 11\left(-117 \;+\; 95\right) \;-\; 1\left(-78 \;-\; 40\right) \;+\; \lambda\left(-38 \;-\; 24\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -242 \;+\; 118 \;-\; 62\lambda \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -2$. Also, $D_1 \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} -5 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 3 & 5 \\ \mu & -19 & -39 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -5\left(-22\right) \;-\; 1\left(-117 \;-\; 5\mu\right) \;-\; 2\left(-57 \;-\; 3\mu\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 110 \;+\; 117 \;+\; 5\mu \;+\; 114 \;+\; 6\mu \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 11\mu \;=\; -341 \;\implies\; \mu \;=\; -31$. Therefore, $\lambda^4 \;-\; \mu \;=\; \left(-2\right)^4 \;-\; \left(-31\right) \;=\; 16 \;+\; 31 \;=\; 47$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $x \;+\; 4y \;-\; z \;=\; \lambda, \; 7x \;+\; 9y \;+\; \mu z \;=\; -3, \; 5x \;+\; y \;+\; 2z \;=\; -1$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\left(2\mu \;+\; 3\lambda\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\Delta \;=\; 0$ to find $\mu$ and $\Delta_x \;=\; 0$ to find $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 & -1 \\ 7 & 9 & \mu \\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(18 \;-\; \mu\right) \;-\; 4\left(14 \;-\; 5\mu\right) \;-\; 1\left(7 \;-\; 45\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 18 \;-\; \mu \;-\; 56 \;+\; 20\mu \;+\; 38 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 19\mu \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \mu \;=\; 0$. Next, $\Delta_x \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} \lambda & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 9 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda\left(18\right) \;-\; 4\left(-6\right) \;-\; 1\left(6\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 18\lambda \;+\; 18 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -1$. Thus, $2\mu \;+\; 3\lambda \;=\; 2\left(0\right) \;+\; 3\left(-1\right) \;=\; -3$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha\beta\gamma \;=\; 45; \; \alpha, \; \beta, \; \gamma \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $x\left(\alpha, \; 1, \; 2\right) \;+\; y\left(1, \; \beta, \; 2\right) \;+\; z\left(2, \; 3, \; \gamma\right) \;=\; \left(0, \; 0, \; 0\right)$ for some $x, \; y, \; z \;\in\; \mathbb{R}, \; xyz \;\neq\; 0$, then $6\alpha \;+\; 4\beta \;+\; \gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the vector equation as a homogeneous linear system in $x, \; y, \; z$ and set its determinant to zero since $xyz \;\neq\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: The given condition gives the homogeneous system $\alpha x \;+\; y \;+\; 2z \;=\; 0$, $x \;+\; \beta y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 0$, $2x \;+\; 2y \;+\; \gamma z \;=\; 0$. Since $xyz \;\neq\; 0$, the system has a non-trivial solution, so $\begin{vmatrix} \alpha & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & \beta & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & \gamma \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha\left(\beta\gamma \;-\; 6\right) \;-\; 1\left(\gamma \;-\; 6\right) \;+\; 2\left(2 \;-\; 2\beta\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha\beta\gamma \;-\; 6\alpha \;-\; \gamma \;+\; 6 \;+\; 4 \;-\; 4\beta \;=\; 0$. Substituting $\alpha\beta\gamma \;=\; 45$ gives $45 \;+\; 10 \;=\; 6\alpha \;+\; 4\beta \;+\; \gamma \;\implies\; 6\alpha \;+\; 4\beta \;+\; \gamma \;=\; 55$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \beta \left(\alpha \ne \beta\right)$ be the values of $m$ for which the equations $x + y + z \; = \; 1$, $x + 2y + 4z \; = \; m$ and $x + 4y + 10z \; = \; m^2$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the value of $\sum_{n=1}^{10}\left(n^{\alpha} + n^{\beta}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Eliminate variables to get a consistency condition in $m$, then use the sum formulas. // 📝 Solution: $y + 3z \; = \; m - 1 \;,\; 3y + 9z \; = \; m^2 - 1 \implies m^2 - 3m + 2 \; = \; 0 \implies \alpha \; = \; 1 \;,\; \beta \; = \; 2 \implies \sum n + \sum n^2 \; = \; 55 + 385 \; = \; 440$
questions.topic: Infinitely Many Solutions and Power Sums

questions.text: For $\alpha, \; \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, suppose the system of linear equations $x \;-\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 5$, $2x \;+\; 2y \;+\; \alpha z \;=\; 8$, $3x \;-\; y \;+\; 4z \;=\; \beta$ has infinitely many solutions. Then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\Delta \;=\; 0$ and $\Delta_z \;=\; 0$ to find $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then form the quadratic equation $x^2 \;-\; \left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)x \;+\; \alpha\beta \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & \alpha \\ 3 & -1 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(8 \;+\; \alpha\right) \;+\; 1\left(8 \;-\; 3\alpha\right) \;+\; 1\left(-2 \;-\; 6\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 8 \;-\; 2\alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 4$. Also, $\Delta_z \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & -1 & \beta \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(2\beta \;+\; 8\right) \;+\; 1\left(2\beta \;-\; 24\right) \;+\; 5\left(-2 \;-\; 6\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 4\beta \;-\; 56 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 14$. The quadratic equation with roots $4$ and $14$ is $x^2 \;-\; \left(4 \;+\; 14\right)x \;+\; 4 \;\times\; 14 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 18x \;+\; 56 \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: The values of $m, \; n$, for which the system of equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 4$, $2x \;+\; 5y \;+\; 5z \;=\; 17$, $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; mz \;=\; n$ has infinitely many solutions, satisfy the equation :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $D \;=\; 0$ and $D_3 \;=\; 0$ to find $m$ and $n$, then test which equation they satisfy. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $D \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & m \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(5m \;-\; 10\right) \;-\; 1\left(2m \;-\; 5\right) \;+\; 1\left(4 \;-\; 5\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 3m \;-\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; m \;=\; 2$. Also, $D_3 \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 & 17 \\ 1 & 2 & n \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(5n \;-\; 34\right) \;-\; 1\left(2n \;-\; 17\right) \;+\; 4\left(4 \;-\; 5\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 3n \;-\; 21 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; n \;=\; 7$. Checking option A: $m^2 \;+\; n^2 \;-\; mn \;=\; 2^2 \;+\; 7^2 \;-\; 2\left(7\right) \;=\; 4 \;+\; 49 \;-\; 14 \;=\; 39$.

💡 Hint: Apply row operations $R_1 \;\to\; R_1 \;-\; R_2$ and $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; R_3$ and divide the expanded equation by $\left(\alpha \;-\; a\right)\left(\beta \;-\; b\right)\left(\gamma \;-\; c\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Applying $R_1 \;\to\; R_1 \;-\; R_2$ and $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; R_3$ gives $\begin{vmatrix} \alpha - a & b - \beta & 0 \\ 0 & \beta - b & c - \gamma \\ a & b & \gamma \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0$. Expanding along the first row: $\left(\alpha \;-\; a\right)\left[\gamma\left(\beta \;-\; b\right) \;-\; b\left(c \;-\; \gamma\right)\right] \;-\; \left(b \;-\; \beta\right)\left[-a\left(c \;-\; \gamma\right)\right] \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \gamma\left(\alpha \;-\; a\right)\left(\beta \;-\; b\right) \;+\; b\left(\alpha \;-\; a\right)\left(\gamma \;-\; c\right) \;+\; a\left(\beta \;-\; b\right)\left(\gamma \;-\; c\right) \;=\; 0$. Dividing throughout by $\left(\alpha \;-\; a\right)\left(\beta \;-\; b\right)\left(\gamma \;-\; c\right)$ yields $\frac{a}{\alpha \;-\; a} \;+\; \frac{b}{\beta \;-\; b} \;+\; \frac{\gamma}{\gamma \;-\; c} \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $x \;+\; \left(\sqrt{2}\sin\alpha\right)y \;+\; \left(\sqrt{2}\cos\alpha\right)z \;=\; 0$, $x \;+\; \left(\cos\alpha\right)y \;+\; \left(\sin\alpha\right)z \;=\; 0$, $x \;+\; \left(\sin\alpha\right)y \;-\; \left(\cos\alpha\right)z \;=\; 0$ has a non-trivial solution, then $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A homogeneous system of linear equations has a non-trivial solution if and only if its coefficient determinant is zero. // 📝 Solution: Setting the determinant of coefficients to zero: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \sqrt{2}\sin\alpha & \sqrt{2}\cos\alpha \\ 1 & \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ 1 & \sin\alpha & -\cos\alpha \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(-\cos^2\alpha \;-\; \sin^2\alpha\right) \;-\; \sqrt{2}\sin\alpha\left(-\cos\alpha \;-\; \sin\alpha\right) \;+\; \sqrt{2}\cos\alpha\left(\sin\alpha \;-\; \cos\alpha\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -1 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\sin 2\alpha \;-\; \sqrt{2}\cos 2\alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \cos 2\alpha \;-\; \sin 2\alpha \;=\; -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. Dividing by $\sqrt{2}$ gives $\cos\left(2\alpha \;+\; \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \;=\; -\frac{1}{2} \;=\; \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$. For $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $2\alpha \;+\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{3} \;\implies\; 2\alpha \;=\; \frac{5\pi}{12} \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{5\pi}{24}$.

questions.text: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be respectively the sets of all $a \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0\right\}$ for which the system of linear equations $ax \;+\; 2ay \;-\; 3az \;=\; 1$, $\left(2a \;+\; 1\right)x \;+\; \left(2a \;+\; 3\right)y \;+\; \left(a \;+\; 1\right)z \;=\; 2$, $\left(3a \;+\; 5\right)x \;+\; \left(a \;+\; 5\right)y \;+\; \left(a \;+\; 2\right)z \;=\; 3$ has unique solution and infinitely many solutions. Then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute the determinant $\Delta$ of the coefficient matrix and check its real roots in $\mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0\right\}$. // 📝 Solution: The determinant of the coefficient matrix is $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} a & 2a & -3a \\ 2a + 1 & 2a + 3 & a + 1 \\ 3a + 5 & a + 5 & a + 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; a \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2a + 1 & 2a + 3 & a + 1 \\ 3a + 5 & a + 5 & a + 2 \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding and simplifying gives $\Delta \;=\; a\left(15a^2 \;+\; 31a \;+\; 36\right)$. For the quadratic $15a^2 \;+\; 31a \;+\; 36$, the discriminant is $D \;=\; 31^2 \;-\; 4\left(15\right)\left(36\right) \;=\; 961 \;-\; 2160 \;<\; 0$, so $15a^2 \;+\; 31a \;+\; 36 \;>\; 0$ for all $a \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Since $a \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0\right\}$, we have $\Delta \;\neq\; 0$ for all $a \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0\right\}$. Hence $S_1 \;=\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0\right\}$ and $S_2 \;=\; \Phi$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $x + 2y - 3z \; = \; 2$, $2x + \lambda y + 5z \; = \; 5$, $14x + 3y + \mu z \; = \; 33$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda + \mu$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Infinitely many solutions need $D \; = \; 0$ along with consistency of the equations. // 📝 Solution: $D \; = \; \lambda\mu - 4\mu + 42\lambda + 107 \; = \; 0 \text{ with consistency} \implies \lambda \; = \; -1 \;,\; \mu \; = \; 13 \implies \lambda + \mu \; = \; 12$

questions.text: If the system of linear equations $x \;-\; 2y \;+\; z \;=\; -4, \; 2x \;+\; \alpha y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 5, \; 3x \;-\; y \;+\; \beta z \;=\; 3$ has infinitely many solutions, then $12\alpha \;+\; 13\beta$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate $\Delta_y \;=\; 0$ and $\Delta \;=\; 0$ for infinitely many solutions to determine $\beta$ and $\alpha$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta \;=\; \Delta_x \;=\; \Delta_y \;=\; \Delta_z \;=\; 0$. First, $\Delta_y \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & \beta \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(5\beta \;-\; 9\right) \;+\; 4\left(2\beta \;-\; 9\right) \;+\; 1\left(6 \;-\; 15\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 13\beta \;-\; 54 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; \frac{54}{13}$. Next, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & \alpha & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & \beta \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(\alpha\beta \;+\; 3\right) \;+\; 2\left(2\beta \;-\; 9\right) \;+\; 1\left(-2 \;-\; 3\alpha\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha\beta \;-\; 3\alpha \;+\; 4\beta \;=\; 17$. Substituting $\beta \;=\; \frac{54}{13}$ gives $\frac{54}{13}\alpha \;-\; 3\alpha \;+\; 4\left(\frac{54}{13}\right) \;=\; 17 \;\implies\; 15\alpha \;+\; 216 \;=\; 221 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{1}{3}$. Therefore, $12\alpha \;+\; 13\beta \;=\; 12\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \;+\; 13\left(\frac{54}{13}\right) \;=\; 4 \;+\; 54 \;=\; 58$.

questions.text: For $\alpha, \; \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ and a natural number $n$, let $A_r \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} r & 1 & \frac{n^2}{2} + \alpha \\ 2r & 2 & n^2 - \beta \\ 3r - 2 & 3 & \frac{n\left(3n - 1\right)}{2} \end{vmatrix}$. Then $2A_{10} \;-\; A_8$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply row operations $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; 2R_1$ and $R_3 \;\to\; R_3 \;-\; 3R_1$ to simplify $A_r$ first. // 📝 Solution: In $A_r$, applying $R_2 \;\to\; R_2 \;-\; 2R_1$ and $R_3 \;\to\; R_3 \;-\; 3R_1$ gives $A_r \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} r & 1 & \frac{n^2}{2} + \alpha \\ 0 & 0 & -\beta - 2\alpha \\ -2 & 0 & -\frac{n}{2} - 3\alpha \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding along the second column gives $A_r \;=\; -1\left[0 \;-\; \left(-2\right)\left(-\beta \;-\; 2\alpha\right)\right] \;=\; 2\left(2\alpha \;+\; \beta\right) \;=\; 4\alpha \;+\; 2\beta$, which is independent of $r$ and $n$. Therefore, $2A_{10} \;-\; A_8 \;=\; 2\left(4\alpha \;+\; 2\beta\right) \;-\; \left(4\alpha \;+\; 2\beta\right) \;=\; 4\alpha \;+\; 2\beta$.

questions.text: For the system of linear equations $\alpha x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $x \;+\; \alpha y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $x \;+\; y \;+\; \alpha z \;=\; \beta$, which one of the following statements is NOT correct ?

options.text: It has infinitely many solutions if $\alpha \;=\; 2$ and $\beta \;=\; -1$
It has no solution if $\alpha \;=\; -2$ and $\beta \;=\; 1$
It has infinitely many solutions if $\alpha \;=\; 1$ and $\beta \;=\; 1$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the roots of $\Delta \;=\; 0$; when $\Delta \;\neq\; 0$, the system always has a unique solution. // 📝 Solution: The coefficient determinant is $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} \alpha & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \alpha & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \alpha \end{vmatrix} \;=\; \left(\alpha \;+\; 2\right)\left(\alpha \;-\; 1\right)^2$. For $\alpha \;=\; 2$, $\Delta \;=\; \left(4\right)\left(1\right)^2 \;=\; 4 \;\neq\; 0$, which means the system has a unique solution regardless of $\beta$. Therefore, it cannot have infinitely many solutions for $\alpha \;=\; 2$ and $\beta \;=\; -1$, making statement A NOT correct.

questions.text: If the system of equations $2x - y + z \; = \; 4$, $5x + \lambda y + 3z \; = \; 12$, $100x - 47y + \mu z \; = \; 212$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\mu - 2\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set the coefficient determinant to zero and require the system to stay consistent. // 📝 Solution: $D \; = \; 2\lambda\mu + 5\mu - 100\lambda - 253 \; = \; 0 \text{ with consistency} \implies \lambda \; = \; -2 \;,\; \mu \; = \; 53 \implies \mu - 2\lambda \; = \; 53 + 4 \; = \; 57$

questions.text: If $y(x)=\begin{vmatrix}\sin x&\cos x&\sin x+\cos x+1\\27&28&27\\1&1&1\end{vmatrix}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply $C_3\to C_3-C_1$ and expand along the new column. // 📝 Solution: $y=-(1+\cos x) \implies y'=\sin x,\ y''=\cos x \implies y''+y=-1$

questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; B \;=\; \left[B_1, \; B_2, \; B_3\right]$, where $B_1, \; B_2, \; B_3$ are column matrices, and $AB_1 \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; AB_2 \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; AB_3 \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $\alpha \;=\; \left\lvert B \right\rvert$ and $\beta$ is the sum of all the diagonal elements of $B$, then $\alpha^3 \;+\; \beta^3$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Combine the column equations into the matrix equation $AB \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ to find $\left\lvert B \right\rvert$ and the diagonal elements of $B$. // 📝 Solution: Since $B \;=\; \left[B_1, \; B_2, \; B_3\right]$, we have $AB \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Solving for the columns $B_1, \; B_2, \; B_3$ (or multiplying by $A^{-1} \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$) gives $B \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$. Also, $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 1$ and $\left\lvert AB \right\rvert \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \left\lvert B \right\rvert \;=\; 3$. The sum of diagonal elements of $B$ is $\beta \;=\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 1$. Therefore, $\alpha^3 \;+\; \beta^3 \;=\; 3^3 \;+\; 1^3 \;=\; 28$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 3$, $4x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 4z \;=\; 4$, $8x \;+\; 4y \;-\; \lambda z \;=\; 9 \;+\; \mu$ has infinitely many solutions, then the ordered pair $\left(\lambda, \; \mu\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Eliminate $x$ from the three equations and equate the ratios of coefficients of $y, \; z$ and constant terms for infinitely many solutions. // 📝 Solution: Let the equations be (i), (ii), and (iii). Operating $4 \;\times\; \text{(i)} \;-\; \text{(ii)}$ gives $5y \;+\; 16z \;=\; 8$ ...(iv). Operating $2 \;\times\; \text{(ii)} \;-\; \text{(iii)}$ gives $2y \;+\; \left(\lambda \;-\; 8\right)z \;=\; -1 \;-\; \mu$ ...(v). For infinitely many solutions, equations (iv) and (v) must represent the same line: $\frac{5}{2} \;=\; \frac{16}{\lambda \;-\; 8} \;=\; \frac{8}{-1 \;-\; \mu}$. Thus, $5\left(\lambda \;-\; 8\right) \;=\; 32 \;\implies\; 5\lambda \;=\; 72 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; \frac{72}{5}$, and $-5 \;-\; 5\mu \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; 5\mu \;=\; -21 \;\implies\; \mu \;=\; \frac{-21}{5}$.

questions.text: The system of equations $x + y + z \; = \; 6$, $x + 2y + 5z \; = \; 9$, $x + 5y + \lambda z \; = \; \mu$ has no solution if:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: No solution needs $D \; = \; 0$ and at least one of $D_x, D_y, D_z$ non-zero. // 📝 Solution: $D \; = \; \lambda - 17 \; = \; 0 \implies \lambda \; = \; 17 \implies \text{eliminating gives } 4y + 16z \; = \; \mu - 6 \text{ against } 4y + 16z \; = \; 12 \implies \mu \ne 18$

questions.text: Consider the system of linear equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 4\mu, \; x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 2\lambda z \;=\; 10\mu, \; x \;+\; 3y \;+\; 4\lambda^2 z \;=\; \mu^2 \;+\; 15$, where $\lambda, \; \mu \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: The system has unique solution if $\lambda \;\neq\; \frac{1}{2}$ and $\mu \;\neq\; 1, \; 15$
The system is inconsistent if $\lambda \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$ and $\mu \;\neq\; 1$
The system has infinite number of solutions if $\lambda \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$ and $\mu \;=\; 15$

questions.text: The system of linear equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 6$, $2x \;+\; 5y \;+\; az \;=\; 36$, $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3z \;=\; b$ has
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the coefficient determinant $\Delta$ at $a \;=\; 8$ and use row elimination to find the condition on $b$ for consistency. // 📝 Solution: The coefficient determinant is $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & a \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 1\left(15 \;-\; 2a\right) \;-\; 1\left(6 \;-\; a\right) \;+\; 1\left(4 \;-\; 5\right) \;=\; 8 \;-\; a$. For $a \;=\; 8$, $\Delta \;=\; 0$, so a unique solution is not possible. Applying $R_2 \;-\; 2R_1$ for $a \;=\; 8$ gives $3y \;+\; 6z \;=\; 24 \;\implies\; y \;+\; 2z \;=\; 8$. Applying $R_3 \;-\; R_1$ gives $y \;+\; 2z \;=\; b \;-\; 6$. For infinitely many solutions, $b \;-\; 6 \;=\; 8 \;\implies\; b \;=\; 14$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; z \;=\; 5$, $x \;+\; \alpha y \;+\; 3z \;=\; -4$, $3x \;-\; y \;+\; \beta z \;=\; 7$ has infinitely many solutions, then $13\alpha\beta$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express one plane as a linear combination of the other two planes to find $\alpha$ and $\beta$. // 📝 Solution: Using the family of planes for infinitely many solutions: $2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; z \;-\; 5 \;=\; k_1\left(x \;+\; \alpha y \;+\; 3z \;+\; 4\right) \;+\; k_2\left(3x \;-\; y \;+\; \beta z \;-\; 7\right)$. Comparing coefficients of $x$ and constant terms: $k_1 \;+\; 3k_2 \;=\; 2$ and $4k_1 \;-\; 7k_2 \;=\; -5$. Solving these gives $k_1 \;=\; -\frac{1}{19}$ and $k_2 \;=\; \frac{13}{19}$. Comparing coefficients of $y$ and $z$: $k_1\alpha \;-\; k_2 \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; -\frac{\alpha}{19} \;-\; \frac{13}{19} \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; -70$, and $3k_1 \;+\; \beta k_2 \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; -\frac{3}{19} \;+\; \frac{13\beta}{19} \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; -\frac{16}{13}$. Hence, $13\alpha\beta \;=\; 13\left(-70\right)\left(-\frac{16}{13}\right) \;=\; 1120$.

questions.text: Let the system of equations $x+5y-z=1$, $4x+3y-3z=7$, $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$, where $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}$, have infinitely many solutions. Then the number of solutions of this system, if $x,y,z$ are integers satisfying $7\le x+y+z\le77$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Infinitely many solutions need $\Delta=\Delta_1=0$; then parametrise and impose integrality. // 📝 Solution: $\Delta=0 \implies \lambda=-17$; $\Delta_1=0 \implies \mu=45$; the parametrised integer solutions with $7\le x+y+z\le77$ occur for exactly three parameter values $\implies$ count $=3$

questions.text: Consider the following system of equations $\alpha x \;+\; 2y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $2\alpha x \;+\; 3y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $3x \;+\; \alpha y \;+\; 2z \;=\; \beta$, for some $\alpha, \; \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Then which of the following is NOT correct.

options.text: It has no solution if $\alpha \;=\; -1$ and $\beta \;\neq\; 2$
It has no solution for $\alpha \;=\; -1$ and for all $\beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$
It has no solution for $\alpha \;=\; 3$ and for all $\beta \;\neq\; 2$
It has a solution for all $\alpha \;\neq\; -1$ and $\beta \;=\; 2$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the values of $\alpha$ where $D \;=\; 0$ and examine $D_x, \; D_y, \; D_z$ for consistency. // 📝 Solution: Here $D \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} \alpha & 2 & 1 \\ 2\alpha & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & \alpha & 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; \alpha\left(6 \;-\; \alpha\right) \;-\; 2\left(4\alpha \;-\; 3\right) \;+\; 1\left(2\alpha^2 \;-\; 9\right) \;=\; \alpha^2 \;-\; 2\alpha \;-\; 3 \;=\; \left(\alpha \;-\; 3\right)\left(\alpha \;+\; 1\right)$. Also, $D_x \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ \beta & \alpha & 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; \left(2 \;-\; \alpha\right) \;+\; \left(\alpha \;-\; \beta\right) \;=\; 2 \;-\; \beta$, $D_y \;=\; \alpha\left(\beta \;-\; 2\right)$, and $D_z \;=\; \alpha\left(2 \;-\; \beta\right)$. When $\alpha \;=\; -1$ and $\beta \;=\; 2$, we have $D \;=\; D_x \;=\; D_y \;=\; D_z \;=\; 0$, and the system reduces to $-x \;+\; 2y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$ and $-2x \;+\; 3y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, which has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, statement B is NOT correct.

questions.text: Let the system of equations $x + y + 2z \; = \; 6$, $2x + 3y + az \; = \; a + 1$, $-x - 3y + bz \; = \; 2b$, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, have infinitely many solutions. Then $7a + 3b$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Infinitely many solutions require $D \; = \; D_1 \; = \; D_2 \; = \; D_3 \; = \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: $D \; = \; 2a + b - 6 \; = \; 0 \text{ and consistency of the system} \implies a \; = \; -2 \;,\; b \; = \; 10 \implies 7a + 3b \; = \; -14 + 30 \; = \; 16$

questions.text: If $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} x^3 & 2x^2 + 1 & 1 + 3x \\ 3x^2 + 2 & 2x & x^3 + 6 \\ x^3 - x & 4 & x^2 - 2 \end{vmatrix}$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, then $2f\left(0\right) \;+\; f'\left(0\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute $f\left(0\right)$ directly and differentiate the determinant row by row to evaluate $f'\left(0\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $x \;=\; 0$, we get $f\left(0\right) \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; -2\left(-2 \;-\; 4\right) \;=\; 12$. Differentiating $f\left(x\right)$ row by row and setting $x \;=\; 0$ gives $f'\left(0\right) \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \;+\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \;+\; \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 6 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 3\left(8 \;-\; 0\right) \;+\; 0 \;-\; 1\left(6 \;-\; 0\right) \;=\; 24 \;-\; 6 \;=\; 18$. Hence, $2f\left(0\right) \;+\; f'\left(0\right) \;=\; 2\left(12\right) \;+\; 18 \;=\; 42$.

questions.text: The values of $\alpha$, for which $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \frac{3}{2} & \alpha + \frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{3} & \alpha + \frac{1}{3} \\ 2\alpha + 3 & 3\alpha + 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0$, lie in the interval
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand the determinant along the third row to form a quadratic equation in $\alpha$. // 📝 Solution: Expanding the determinant along the third row, we get $\left(2\alpha \;+\; 3\right) \left[\frac{3}{2}\left(\alpha \;+\; \frac{1}{3}\right) \;-\; \frac{1}{3}\left(\alpha \;+\; \frac{3}{2}\right)\right] \;-\; \left(3\alpha \;+\; 1\right) \left[\left(\alpha \;+\; \frac{1}{3}\right) \;-\; \left(\alpha \;+\; \frac{3}{2}\right)\right] \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(2\alpha \;+\; 3\right)\left(\frac{7\alpha}{6}\right) \;-\; \left(3\alpha \;+\; 1\right)\left(-\frac{7}{6}\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{7}{6}\left(2\alpha^2 \;+\; 6\alpha \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 2\alpha^2 \;+\; 6\alpha \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. Solving for $\alpha$ gives $\alpha \;=\; \frac{-6 \;\pm\; \sqrt{36 \;-\; 8}}{4} \;=\; \frac{-3 \;\pm\; \sqrt{7}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{7} \;\approx\; 2.64$, the roots are approximately $-0.18$ and $-2.82$, which lie in the interval $\left(-3, \; 0\right)$.

questions.text: Consider the matrices : $A \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 3 & m \end{bmatrix}, \; B \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 20 \\ m \end{bmatrix}$ and $X \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$. Let the set of all $m$, for which the system of equations $AX \;=\; B$ has a negative solution (i.e., $x \;<\; 0$ and $y \;<\; 0$), be the interval $\left(a, \; b\right)$. Then $8\int_a^b \left\lvert A \right\rvert \, dm$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve $AX \;=\; B$ for $x$ and $y$ in terms of $m$, impose $x \;<\; 0$ and $y \;<\; 0$ to find $\left(a, \; b\right)$, and integrate $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2m \;+\; 15$. // 📝 Solution: The system is $2x \;-\; 5y \;=\; 20$ and $3x \;+\; my \;=\; m$, with $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2m \;+\; 15$. By Cramer's Rule, $x \;=\; \frac{25m}{2m \;+\; 15}$ and $y \;=\; \frac{2m \;-\; 60}{2m \;+\; 15}$. For $x \;<\; 0$, we get $m \;\in\; \left(-\frac{15}{2}, \; 0\right)$, and for $y \;<\; 0$, we get $m \;\in\; \left(-\frac{15}{2}, \; 30\right)$. Taking the intersection gives $m \;\in\; \left(-\frac{15}{2}, \; 0\right) \;=\; \left(a, \; b\right)$. For $m \;\in\; \left(-\frac{15}{2}, \; 0\right)$, $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2m \;+\; 15 \;>\; 0$. Thus, $8\int_{-15/2}^0 \left(2m \;+\; 15\right) \, dm \;=\; 8\left[m^2 \;+\; 15m\right]_{-15/2}^0 \;=\; -8\left(\frac{225}{4} \;-\; \frac{225}{2}\right) \;=\; 8 \;\times\; \frac{225}{4} \;=\; 450$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $\left(\lambda - 1\right)x + \left(\lambda - 4\right)y + \lambda z \; = \; 5$, $\lambda x + \left(\lambda - 1\right)y + \left(\lambda - 4\right)z \; = \; 7$, $\left(\lambda + 1\right)x + \left(\lambda + 2\right)y - \left(\lambda + 2\right)z \; = \; 9$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda^2 + \lambda$ is equal to:
