questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $D \; = \; 0$ and $D_x \; = \; 0$ and find the common $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: $D \; = \; \left(\lambda - 3\right)\left(2\lambda + 1\right) \; = \; 0 \;,\; D_x \; = \; 2\left(3 - \lambda\right)\left(23 - 2\lambda\right) \; = \; 0 \implies \lambda \; = \; 3 \implies \lambda^2 + \lambda \; = \; 12$

questions.text: Let $\lambda, \; \mu \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If the system of equations $3x \;+\; 5y \;+\; \lambda z \;=\; 3$, $7x \;+\; 11y \;-\; 9z \;=\; 2$, $97x \;+\; 155y \;-\; 189z \;=\; \mu$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\mu \;+\; 2\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the third equation as a linear combination of the first two equations to find $\lambda$ and $\mu$ quickly. // 📝 Solution: Let $97x \;+\; 155y \;-\; 189z \;=\; p\left(3x \;+\; 5y \;+\; \lambda z\right) \;+\; q\left(7x \;+\; 11y \;-\; 9z\right)$. Comparing coefficients of $x$ and $y$: $3p \;+\; 7q \;=\; 97$ and $5p \;+\; 11q \;=\; 155$. Solving these gives $p \;=\; 9$ and $q \;=\; 10$. Now, comparing the $z$-coefficient and constant term for infinitely many solutions: $9\lambda \;+\; 10\left(-9\right) \;=\; -189 \;\implies\; 9\lambda \;=\; -99 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -11$, and $\mu \;=\; 9\left(3\right) \;+\; 10\left(2\right) \;=\; 27 \;+\; 20 \;=\; 47$. Therefore, $\mu \;+\; 2\lambda \;=\; 47 \;+\; 2\left(-11\right) \;=\; 25$.

questions.text: Let $S$ denote the set of all real values of $\lambda$ such that the system of equations $\lambda x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $x \;+\; \lambda y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, $x \;+\; y \;+\; \lambda z \;=\; 1$ is inconsistent, then $\sum_{\lambda \in S} \left(\left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert^2 \;+\; \left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set the coefficient determinant $\Delta \;=\; 0$ and check which values of $\lambda$ make the system inconsistent. // 📝 Solution: Here $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} \lambda & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} \;=\; \left(\lambda \;+\; 2\right)\left(\lambda \;-\; 1\right)^2$. Setting $\Delta \;=\; 0$ gives $\lambda \;=\; 1, \; -2$. For $\lambda \;=\; 1$, all three equations become $x \;+\; y \;+\; z \;=\; 1$, so the system has infinitely many solutions. For $\lambda \;=\; -2$, adding the three equations gives $0 \;=\; 3$, so the system is inconsistent. Thus $S \;=\; \left\{-2\right\}$, and $\sum_{\lambda \in S} \left(\left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert^2 \;+\; \left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert\right) \;=\; \left\lvert -2 \right\rvert^2 \;+\; \left\lvert -2 \right\rvert \;=\; 4 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 6$.
questions.topic: Consistency of System of Linear Equations

questions.text: If the system of linear equations $3x+y+\beta z=3$, $2x+\alpha y-z=-3$, $x+2y+z=4$ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $22\beta-9\alpha$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $\Delta=0$ and $\Delta_3=0$ and solve for $\alpha,\beta$. // 📝 Solution: $\Delta_3=\begin{vmatrix}3&1&3\\2&\alpha&-3\\1&2&4\end{vmatrix}=9\alpha+19=0 \implies \alpha=-\tfrac{19}{9}$; $\Delta=0 \implies \beta=\tfrac{6}{11}$; $22\beta-9\alpha=12+19=31$

questions.text: Let the system of equations $2x+3y+5z=9$, $7x+3y-2z=8$, $12x+3y-(4+\lambda)z=16-\mu$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the radius of the circle centred at $(\lambda,\mu)$ and touching the line $4x=3y$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Infinitely many solutions force the determinants to vanish; then use the distance from a point to a line. // 📝 Solution: $\lambda=5,\ \mu=9$; radius $=\dfrac{\lvert 4(5)-3(9)\rvert}{\sqrt{4^2+3^2}}=\dfrac{7}{5}$
questions.topic: Consistency of system and circle radius

questions.text: Let the system of equations $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3z \;=\; 5, \; 2x \;+\; 3y \;+\; z \;=\; 9, \; 4x \;+\; 3y \;+\; \lambda z \;=\; \mu$ have infinite number of solutions. Then $\lambda \;+\; 2\mu$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply $\Delta \;=\; 0$ and $\Delta_1 \;=\; 0$ for infinitely many solutions to determine $\lambda$ and $\mu$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(3\lambda \;-\; 3\right) \;-\; 2\left(2\lambda \;-\; 4\right) \;+\; 3\left(6 \;-\; 12\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -\lambda \;-\; 13 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -13$. Next, $\Delta_1 \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 5 & 2 & 3 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & -13 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 5\left(-39 \;-\; 3\right) \;-\; 2\left(-117 \;-\; \mu\right) \;+\; 3\left(27 \;-\; 3\mu\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -210 \;+\; 234 \;+\; 2\mu \;+\; 81 \;-\; 9\mu \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 7\mu \;=\; 105 \;\implies\; \mu \;=\; 15$. Thus, $\lambda \;+\; 2\mu \;=\; -13 \;+\; 2\left(15\right) \;=\; 17$.

questions.text: If the system of equations $2x \;+\; 7y \;+\; \lambda z \;=\; 3$, $3x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 5z \;=\; 4$, $x \;+\; \mu y \;+\; 32z \;=\; -1$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\left(\lambda \;-\; \mu\right)$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For infinitely many solutions, set $D_3 \;=\; 0$ to find $\mu$ and then set $D \;=\; 0$ to find $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions, $D \;=\; D_1 \;=\; D_2 \;=\; D_3 \;=\; 0$. First, $D_3 \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 7 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & \mu & -1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 2\left(-2 \;-\; 4\mu\right) \;-\; 7\left(-3 \;-\; 4\right) \;+\; 3\left(3\mu \;-\; 2\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -4 \;-\; 8\mu \;+\; 49 \;+\; 9\mu \;-\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \mu \;=\; -39$. Next, $D \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 7 & \lambda \\ 3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & -39 & 32 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 2\left(64 \;+\; 195\right) \;-\; 7\left(96 \;-\; 5\right) \;+\; \lambda\left(-117 \;-\; 2\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 518 \;-\; 637 \;-\; 119\lambda \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 119\lambda \;=\; -119 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -1$. Hence, $\lambda \;-\; \mu \;=\; -1 \;-\; \left(-39\right) \;=\; 38$.

questions.text: Let $M$ and $m$ be the maximum and minimum values of $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \begin{vmatrix} 1 + \sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & 4\sin 4x \\ \sin^2 x & 1 + \cos^2 x & 4\sin 4x \\ \sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & 1 + 4\sin 4x \end{vmatrix}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $M^4 - m^4$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply $R_1 \to R_1 + R_2 + R_3$-type simplification to reduce the determinant to a single-variable expression. // 📝 Solution: $f\left(x\right) \; = \; 2 + 4\sin 4x \implies M \; = \; 6 \;,\; m \; = \; -2 \implies M^4 - m^4 \; = \; 1296 - 16 \; = \; 1280$
questions.topic: Evaluation of Determinants with Trigonometric Entries

questions.text: Let $A$ be a $3 \;\times\; 3$ real matrix such that $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; 2\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \; A\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; 4\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \; A\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; 2\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then, the system $\left(A \;-\; 3I\right)\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ has
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use linearity of matrix multiplication on the given relations to construct matrix $A$ and check $\det\left(A \;-\; 3I\right)$. // 📝 Solution: From $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$, adding and subtracting gives $A\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Also, $A\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Thus, $A \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A \;-\; 3I \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det\left(A \;-\; 3I\right) \;=\; -1 \;\neq\; 0$, the matrix $\left(A \;-\; 3I\right)$ is non-singular, so the system has a unique solution ($x \;=\; -3, \; y \;=\; -2, \; z \;=\; -1$).
questions.topic: Matrix Equations and System of Linear Equations

questions.text: If the system of equations $3x \;+\; y \;+\; 4z \;=\; 3$, $2x \;+\; \alpha y \;-\; z \;=\; -3$, $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; z \;=\; 4$ has no solution, then the value of $\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A system of linear equations has no solution if the coefficient determinant $\Delta \;=\; 0$ and at least one of $\Delta_x, \; \Delta_y, \; \Delta_z$ is non-zero. // 📝 Solution: For no solution, we set $\Delta \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & \alpha & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0$. Expanding along the first row gives $3\left(\alpha \;+\; 2\right) \;-\; 1\left(2 \;+\; 1\right) \;+\; 4\left(4 \;-\; \alpha\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 3\alpha \;+\; 6 \;-\; 3 \;+\; 16 \;-\; 4\alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 19 \;-\; \alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 19$. For $\alpha \;=\; 19$, $\Delta_x \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \\ -3 & 19 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 3\left(21\right) \;-\; 1\left(1\right) \;+\; 4\left(-82\right) \;=\; -266 \;\neq\; 0$. Thus, the system has no solution for $\alpha \;=\; 19$.

questions.text: Let the system of linear equations $x \;+\; y \;+\; kz \;=\; 2$, $2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; z \;=\; 1$, $3x \;+\; 4y \;+\; 2z \;=\; k$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the system $\left(k \;+\; 1\right)x \;+\; \left(2k \;-\; 1\right)y \;=\; 7$, $\left(2k \;+\; 1\right)x \;+\; \left(k \;+\; 5\right)y \;=\; 10$ has :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set the coefficient determinant of the first system to zero to find $k$, then solve the second system of equations. // 📝 Solution: For infinitely many solutions of the first system, $\Delta \;=\; \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & k \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1\left(6 \;+\; 4\right) \;-\; 1\left(4 \;+\; 3\right) \;+\; k\left(8 \;-\; 9\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 10 \;-\; 7 \;-\; k \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; k \;=\; 3$. Substituting $k \;=\; 3$ into the second system gives $4x \;+\; 5y \;=\; 7$ ...(1) and $7x \;+\; 8y \;=\; 10$ ...(2). These two lines have a unique solution since $\frac{4}{7} \;\neq\; \frac{5}{8}$. Subtracting (1) from (2) gives $3x \;+\; 3y \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; x \;+\; y \;=\; 1$.

questions.text: The value of $\frac{8}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\left( \cos x \right)^{2023}}{\left( \sin x \right)^{2023} \;+\; \left( \cos x \right)^{2023}} dx$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the property $\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx \;=\; \int_{0}^{a} f(a \;-\; x) \, dx$ and add the two integrals. // 📝 Solution: Let $I \;=\; \frac{8}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\left( \cos x \right)^{2023}}{\left( \sin x \right)^{2023} \;+\; \left( \cos x \right)^{2023}} dx \quad \text{...(1)}$. Using the property $\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx \;=\; \int_{0}^{a} f(a \;-\; x) \, dx$ with $a \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, we get $I \;=\; \frac{8}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\left( \sin x \right)^{2023}}{\left( \cos x \right)^{2023} \;+\; \left( \sin x \right)^{2023}} dx \quad \text{...(2)}$. Adding equations (1) and (2) gives $2I \;=\; \frac{8}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 1 \, dx \;=\; \frac{8}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; I \;=\; 2$.

questions.text: The value of the integral $\int_{1}^{2} \left( \frac{t^4 \;+\; 1}{t^6 \;+\; 1} \right) dt$ is
The value of $\sum_{r=1}^{20} \left( \left\lvert \sqrt{\pi \left( \int_{0}^{r} x \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx \right)} \right\rvert \right)$ is ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use King's property $\int_{0}^{r} f\left( x \right) dx \; = \; \int_{0}^{r} f\left( r \; - \; x \right) dx$ and the periodicity of $\left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert$. // 📝 Solution: Let $I_r \; = \; \int_{0}^{r} x \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx$. By King's property, $I_r \; = \; \int_{0}^{r} \left( r \; - \; x \right) \left\lvert \sin \pi \left( r \; - \; x \right) \right\rvert dx \; = \; \int_{0}^{r} \left( r \; - \; x \right) \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx$. Adding the two expressions gives $2I_r \; = \; r \int_{0}^{r} \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx \; \implies \; I_r \; = \; \frac{r}{2} \int_{0}^{r} \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx$. Since $\left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert$ has period $1$, $\int_{0}^{r} \left\lvert \sin \pi x \right\rvert dx \; = \; r \int_{0}^{1} \sin \pi x \, dx \; = \; \frac{2r}{\pi}$. Thus, $I_r \; = \; \frac{r}{2} \; \cdot \; \frac{2r}{\pi} \; = \; \frac{r^2}{\pi}$. Substituting into the summation gives $\sum_{r=1}^{20} \sqrt{\pi \; \cdot \; \frac{r^2}{\pi}} \; = \; \sum_{r=1}^{20} r \; = \; \frac{20 \; \times \; 21}{2} \; = \; 210$.

questions.text: If $\int \left( \frac{1 \; - \; 5\cos^2 x}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} \right) dx \; = \; f\left( x \right) \; + \; C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration, then $f\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \; - \; f\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the numerator as $1 \; - \; 5\cos^2 x$ and apply integration by parts to $\int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\sin^5 x} \, dx$. // 📝 Solution: Rewrite the integral as $\int \frac{1 \; - \; 5\cos^2 x}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} \, dx \; = \; \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\sin^5 x} \, dx \; - \; 5 \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$. Applying integration by parts to the first integral with first function $\frac{1}{\sin^5 x}$ and second function $\sec^2 x$: $\int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\sin^5 x} \, dx \; = \; \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} \; - \; \int \left( -\frac{5\cos x}{\sin^6 x} \right) \tan x \, dx \; = \; \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} \; + \; 5 \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$. Substituting this back cancels $5 \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$, giving $f\left( x \right) \; = \; \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x}$. Therefore, $f\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \; - \; f\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^5} \; - \; \frac{1}{\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^5} \; = \; \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}} \; - \; 4\sqrt{2} \; = \; \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}} \left( 8 \; - \; \sqrt{6} \right)$.

questions.text: The value of the integral $\int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{x} dx$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \;=\; \frac{1}{t}$ and add the resulting integral to the original integral using $\tan^{-1} x \;+\; \cot^{-1} x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $I \;=\; \int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{x} dx \quad \text{...(1)}$. Substitute $x \;=\; \frac{1}{t} \;\implies\; dx \;=\; -\frac{1}{t^2} dt$. When $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$, $t \;=\; 2$; when $x \;=\; 2$, $t \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, $I \;=\; -\int_{2}^{1/2} \frac{\tan^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{t} \right)}{\frac{1}{t}} \cdot \frac{dt}{t^2} \;=\; \int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{\cot^{-1} t}{t} dt \;=\; \int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{\cot^{-1} x}{x} dx \quad \text{...(2)}$. Adding equations (1) and (2): $2I \;=\; \int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{\tan^{-1} x \;+\; \cot^{-1} x}{x} dx \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \int_{1/2}^{2} \frac{dx}{x} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \ln x \right]_{1/2}^{2} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \left( \ln 2 \;-\; \ln\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \right) \;=\; \pi \ln 2 \;\implies\; I \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \log_e 2$.

questions.text: Let $f$ be a differentiable function defined on $\left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right]$ such that $f(x) \;>\; 0$ and $f(x) \;+\; \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \sqrt{1 \;-\; \left( \log_e f(t) \right)^2} \, dt \;=\; e$, $\forall \; x \;\in\; \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right]$. Then $\left( 6 \log_e f\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \right)^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate the given integral equation with respect to $x$ using Leibnitz's rule and solve the resulting separable differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Putting $x \;=\; 0$ in the given equation gives $f(0) \;=\; e$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using Leibnitz's rule: $f'(x) \;+\; f(x) \sqrt{1 \;-\; \left( \ln f(x) \right)^2} \;=\; 0$. Let $y \;=\; f(x)$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; -y \sqrt{1 \;-\; \left( \ln y \right)^2} \;\implies\; \int \frac{dy}{y \sqrt{1 \;-\; \left( \ln y \right)^2}} \;=\; -\int dx$. Let $\ln y \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dy}{y} \;=\; dt$, which gives $\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1 \;-\; t^2}} \;=\; -x \;+\; C \;\implies\; \sin^{-1}\left( \ln f(x) \right) \;=\; -x \;+\; C$. Using $f(0) \;=\; e$, we have $\sin^{-1}(1) \;=\; 0 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$. Thus, $\sin^{-1}\left( \ln f(x) \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; x \;\implies\; \ln f(x) \;=\; \cos x$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6}$, $\log_e f\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; \cos\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Therefore, $\left( 6 \log_e f\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \right)^2 \;=\; \left( 6 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)^2 \;=\; \left( 3\sqrt{3} \right)^2 \;=\; 27$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha \;\in\; \left( 0, 1 \right)$ and $\beta \;=\; \log_e \left( 1 \;-\; \alpha \right)$. Let $P_n(x) \;=\; x \;+\; \frac{x^2}{2} \;+\; \frac{x^3}{3} \;+\; \dots \;+\; \frac{x^n}{n}$, $x \;\in\; \left( 0, 1 \right)$. Then the integral $\int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{t^{50}}{1 \;-\; t} dt$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $t^{50} \;=\; \left( t^{50} \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; 1$ and use the geometric progression identity $\frac{1 \;-\; t^{50}}{1 \;-\; t} \;=\; 1 \;+\; t \;+\; t^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; t^{49}$. // 📝 Solution: We can rewrite the integral as $I \;=\; \int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{\left( t^{50} \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; 1}{1 \;-\; t} dt \;=\; -\int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{1 \;-\; t^{50}}{1 \;-\; t} dt \;+\; \int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{1}{1 \;-\; t} dt$. Using the geometric series sum $\frac{1 \;-\; t^{50}}{1 \;-\; t} \;=\; 1 \;+\; t \;+\; t^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; t^{49}$, we get $I \;=\; -\int_{0}^{\alpha} \left( 1 \;+\; t \;+\; t^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; t^{49} \right) dt \;+\; \left[ -\log_e\left( 1 \;-\; t \right) \right]_{0}^{\alpha} \;=\; -\left[ t \;+\; \frac{t^2}{2} \;+\; \frac{t^3}{3} \;+\; \dots \;+\; \frac{t^{50}}{50} \right]_{0}^{\alpha} \;-\; \log_e\left( 1 \;-\; \alpha \right) \;=\; -P_{50}(\alpha) \;-\; \beta \;=\; -\left( \beta \;+\; P_{50}(\alpha) \right)$.

questions.text: If $\left[ t \right]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le\; t$, then the value of $\frac{3\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)}{e} \int_{1}^{2} x^2 e^{\left[ x \right] \;+\; \left[ x^3 \right]} dx$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $x \;\in\; \left[ 1, 2 \right)$, $\left[ x \right] \;=\; 1$; substitute $x^3 \;=\; t$ so that $3x^2 \, dx \;=\; dt$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \;\in\; \left( 1, 2 \right)$, we have $\left[ x \right] \;=\; 1$. Let $J \;=\; \int_{1}^{2} x^2 e^{1 \;+\; \left[ x^3 \right]} dx$. Substitute $x^3 \;=\; t \;\implies\; 3x^2 \, dx \;=\; dt$. The limits change from $t \;=\; 1$ to $t \;=\; 8$: $J \;=\; \frac{e}{3} \int_{1}^{8} e^{\left[ t \right]} dt \;=\; \frac{e}{3} \left( \int_{1}^{2} e^1 \, dt \;+\; \int_{2}^{3} e^2 \, dt \;+\; \dots \;+\; \int_{7}^{8} e^7 \, dt \right) \;=\; \frac{e}{3} \left( e \;+\; e^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; e^7 \right) \;=\; \frac{e^2\left( e^7 \;-\; 1 \right)}{3\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)}$. Multiplying by $\frac{3\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)}{e}$, the required value is $\frac{3\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)}{e} \cdot \frac{e^2\left( e^7 \;-\; 1 \right)}{3\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)} \;=\; e\left( e^7 \;-\; 1 \right) \;=\; e^8 \;-\; e$.
questions.topic: Definite Integration of Greatest Integer Function

questions.text: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3}{n} \left\{ 4 \;+\; \left( 2 \;+\; \frac{1}{n} \right)^2 \;+\; \left( 2 \;+\; \frac{2}{n} \right)^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; \left( 3 \;-\; \frac{1}{n} \right)^2 \right\}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the sum as $\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \left( 2 \;+\; \frac{r}{n} \right)^2$ and convert it into a definite integral over $\left[ 0, 1 \right]$. // 📝 Solution: Notice that $4 \;=\; \left( 2 \;+\; \frac{0}{n} \right)^2$ and $3 \;-\; \frac{1}{n} \;=\; 2 \;+\; \frac{n \;-\; 1}{n}$. Thus, the given limit can be written as $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3}{n} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \left( 2 \;+\; \frac{r}{n} \right)^2$. Converting the Riemann sum into a definite integral by replacing $\frac{r}{n}$ with $x$ and $\frac{1}{n}$ with $dx$: $3 \int_{0}^{1} \left( 2 \;+\; x \right)^2 dx \;=\; 3 \left[ \frac{\left( 2 \;+\; x \right)^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{1} \;=\; 3^3 \;-\; 2^3 \;=\; 27 \;-\; 8 \;=\; 19$.
questions.topic: Definite Integral as the Limit of a Sum

questions.text: $\int_{\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}} \frac{48}{\sqrt{9 \;-\; 4x^2}} dx$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the standard integration formula $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 \;-\; x^2}} \;=\; \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{x}{a} \right) \;+\; C$. // 📝 Solution: Let $I \;=\; \int_{\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}} \frac{48}{\sqrt{3^2 \;-\; \left( 2x \right)^2}} dx$. Using $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 \;-\; \left( bx \right)^2}} \;=\; \frac{1}{b} \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{bx}{a} \right)$, we get $I \;=\; \frac{48}{2} \left[ \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{2x}{3} \right) \right]_{\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}} \;=\; 24 \left[ \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \right) \;-\; \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4} \right) \right] \;=\; 24 \left[ \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) \;-\; \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \right] \;=\; 24 \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \;-\; \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; 24 \cdot \frac{\pi}{12} \;=\; 2\pi$.
questions.topic: Evaluation of Definite Integrals by Standard Formulas

questions.text: Let $f(x) \;=\; x \;+\; \frac{a}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \sin x \;+\; \frac{b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \cos x$, $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ be a function which satisfies $f(x) \;=\; x \;+\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin\left( x \;+\; y \right) f(y) \, dy$. Then $\left( a \;+\; b \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand $\sin\left( x \;+\; y \right) \;=\; \sin x \cos y \;+\; \cos x \sin y$, compare coefficients of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, and add the resulting integrals using King's rule. // 📝 Solution: Expanding $\sin\left( x \;+\; y \right)$ in the given equation gives $f(x) \;=\; x \;+\; \left( \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos y \, f(y) \, dy \right) \sin x \;+\; \left( \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin y \, f(y) \, dy \right) \cos x$. Comparing coefficients with $f(x) \;=\; x \;+\; \frac{a}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \sin x \;+\; \frac{b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \cos x$, we get $\frac{a}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos y \, f(y) \, dy$ and $\frac{b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin y \, f(y) \, dy$. Adding both equations: $\frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left( \sin y \;+\; \cos y \right) f(y) \, dy \quad \text{...(1)}$. Applying King's rule $\left( y \to \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; y \right)$: $\frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left( \cos y \;+\; \sin y \right) f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; y \right) dy \quad \text{...(2)}$. Note that $f(y) \;+\; f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; y \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;+\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4}\left( \sin y \;+\; \cos y \right)$. Adding (1) and (2): $\frac{2\left( a \;+\; b \right)}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left( \sin y \;+\; \cos y \right)\left[ \frac{\pi}{2} \;+\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4}\left( \sin y \;+\; \cos y \right) \right] dy \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}(2) \;+\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4}\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \;+\; 1 \right) \;=\; \pi \;+\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4}\left( \frac{\pi \;+\; 2}{2} \right)$. Simplifying gives $\frac{a \;+\; b}{\pi^2 \;-\; 4}\left( \frac{2 \;-\; \pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \pi \;\implies\; a \;+\; b \;=\; -2\pi\left( \pi \;+\; 2 \right)$.

questions.text: The number of elements in the set $S \; = \; \left\{ x \; : \; x \; \in \; \left[ 0, \; 100 \right] \text{ and } \int_{0}^{x} t^2 \sin \left( x \; - \; t \right) dt \; = \; x^2 \right\}$ is ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the property $\int_{0}^{x} f\left( t \right) dt \; = \; \int_{0}^{x} f\left( x \; - \; t \right) dt$ and integrate by parts twice to evaluate the integral. // 📝 Solution: Let $I \; = \; \int_{0}^{x} t^2 \sin \left( x \; - \; t \right) dt$. Using the property $\int_{0}^{x} f\left( t \right) dt \; = \; \int_{0}^{x} f\left( x \; - \; t \right) dt$, we get $I \; = \; \int_{0}^{x} \left( x \; - \; t \right)^2 \sin t \, dt$. Integrating by parts twice: $I \; = \; \left[ -\left( x \; - \; t \right)^2 \cos t \right]_{0}^{x} \; - \; \int_{0}^{x} 2\left( x \; - \; t \right) \cos t \, dt \; = \; x^2 \; - \; 2 \left( \left[ \left( x \; - \; t \right) \sin t \right]_{0}^{x} \; + \; \int_{0}^{x} \sin t \, dt \right) \; = \; x^2 \; - \; 2 \left[ -\cos t \right]_{0}^{x} \; = \; x^2 \; + \; 2\cos x \; - \; 2$. Setting this equal to $x^2$ gives $x^2 \; + \; 2\cos x \; - \; 2 \; = \; x^2 \; \implies \; 2\cos x \; - \; 2 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; \cos x \; = \; 1 \; \implies \; x \; = \; 2n\pi$, where $n \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$. For $x \; \in \; \left[ 0, \; 100 \right]$, we have $0 \; \le \; 2n\pi \; \le \; 100 \; \implies \; 0 \; \le \; n \; \le \; \frac{50}{\pi} \; \approx \; 15.91$. Thus, $n \; \in \; \left\{ 0, \; 1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 15 \right\}$, which gives $16$ elements.

questions.text: The value of $12 \int_{0}^{3} \left\lvert x^2 \;-\; 3x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert dx$ is ______

Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36} f\left( \frac{tx}{36} \right) dt \; = \; 4\alpha f\left( x \right)$. If $y \; = \; f\left( x \right)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $\left( 2, \; 1 \right)$ and $\left( -4, \; \beta \right)$, then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $u \; = \; \frac{tx}{36}$ in the definite integral and differentiate with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz integral rule. // 📝 Solution: Substitute $u \; = \; \frac{tx}{36}$ so that $dt \; = \; \frac{36}{x} \, du$. The given equation becomes $\frac{36}{x} \int_{0}^{x} f\left( u \right) du \; = \; 4\alpha f\left( x \right) \; \implies \; 9 \int_{0}^{x} f\left( u \right) du \; = \; \alpha x f\left( x \right)$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives $9f\left( x \right) \; = \; \alpha \left( f\left( x \right) \; + \; x f'\left( x \right) \right) \; \implies \; \frac{f'\left( x \right)}{f\left( x \right)} \; = \; \frac{9 \; - \; \alpha}{\alpha x}$. Integrating gives $f\left( x \right) \; = \; K x^{\frac{9 \; - \; \alpha}{\alpha}}$. For $y \; = \; f\left( x \right)$ to be a standard parabola passing through $\left( 2, \; 1 \right)$ and $\left( -4, \; \beta \right)$, we must have $\frac{9 \; - \; \alpha}{\alpha} \; = \; 2 \; \implies \; \alpha \; = \; 3$, so $f\left( x \right) \; = \; K x^2$. Since it passes through $\left( 2, \; 1 \right)$, $1 \; = \; 4K \; \implies \; K \; = \; \frac{1}{4}$, giving $f\left( x \right) \; = \; \frac{x^2}{4}$. At $\left( -4, \; \beta \right)$, $\beta \; = \; \frac{\left( -4 \right)^2}{4} \; = \; 4$. Therefore, $\beta^{\alpha} \; = \; 4^3 \; = \; 64$.
questions.topic: Leibniz Integral Rule and Differential Equations

questions.text: The value of $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \left( \frac{1}{\left[ x \right] \; + \; 4} \right) dx$, where $\left[ \cdot \right]$ denotes the greatest integer function, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the limits of integration at the integer points inside $\left[ -\frac{\pi}{2}, \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right]$, namely $-1, \; 0,$ and $1$. // 📝 Solution: Let $I \; = \; \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1}{\left[ x \right] \; + \; 4} \, dx$. Since $-\frac{\pi}{2} \; \approx \; -1.57$ and $\frac{\pi}{2} \; \approx \; 1.57$, we split the integral at the integer points $x \; = \; -1, \; 0, \; 1$: $I \; = \; \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{-1} \frac{dx}{-2 \; + \; 4} \; + \; \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{dx}{-1 \; + \; 4} \; + \; \int_{0}^{1} \frac{dx}{0 \; + \; 4} \; + \; \int_{1}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{dx}{1 \; + \; 4} \; = \; \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{-1} \frac{dx}{2} \; + \; \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{dx}{3} \; + \; \int_{0}^{1} \frac{dx}{4} \; + \; \int_{1}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{dx}{5}$. Evaluating each definite integral gives $I \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \left( -1 \; + \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \; + \; \frac{1}{3} \left( 1 \right) \; + \; \frac{1}{4} \left( 1 \right) \; + \; \frac{1}{5} \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; \left( \frac{\pi}{4} \; + \; \frac{\pi}{10} \right) \; + \; \left( -\frac{1}{2} \; + \; \frac{1}{3} \; + \; \frac{1}{4} \; - \; \frac{1}{5} \right) \; = \; \frac{7\pi}{20} \; - \; \frac{7}{60} \; = \; \frac{7}{60} \left( 3\pi \; - \; 1 \right)$.
questions.topic: Definite Integral with Greatest Integer Function

questions.text: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy $f(x) \;+\; \int_{3}^{x} \frac{f(t)}{t} dt \;=\; \sqrt{x \;+\; 1}$, $x \;\ge\; 3$. Then $12 f(8)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate the equation with respect to $x$ to get a linear differential equation for $f(x)$, or notice that $\frac{d}{dx}\left( x f(x) \right) \;=\; x f'(x) \;+\; f(x)$. // 📝 Solution: Setting $x \;=\; 3$ in the given equation gives $f(3) \;+\; 0 \;=\; \sqrt{4} \;=\; 2$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$: $f'(x) \;+\; \frac{f(x)}{x} \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x \;+\; 1}} \;\implies\; x f'(x) \;+\; f(x) \;=\; \frac{x}{2\sqrt{x \;+\; 1}} \;\implies\; \frac{d}{dx}\left( x f(x) \right) \;=\; \frac{\left( x \;+\; 1 \right) \;-\; 1}{2\sqrt{x \;+\; 1}} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x \;+\; 1} \;-\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x \;+\; 1}}$. Integrating both sides: $x f(x) \;=\; \frac{\left( x \;+\; 1 \right)^{3/2}}{3} \;-\; \sqrt{x \;+\; 1} \;+\; C$. Putting $x \;=\; 3$ and $f(3) \;=\; 2$: $3(2) \;=\; \frac{8}{3} \;-\; 2 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 8 \;-\; \frac{8}{3} \;=\; \frac{16}{3}$. Now, putting $x \;=\; 8$: $8 f(8) \;=\; \frac{9^{3/2}}{3} \;-\; \sqrt{9} \;+\; \frac{16}{3} \;=\; 9 \;-\; 3 \;+\; \frac{16}{3} \;=\; \frac{34}{3} \;\implies\; f(8) \;=\; \frac{34}{24} \;=\; \frac{17}{12}$. Therefore, $12 f(8) \;=\; 17$.
questions.topic: Leibnitz Rule and Linear Differential Equations

questions.text: The value of $\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \left( \frac{\pi \; + \; 4x^{11}}{1 \; - \; \sin \left( \left\lvert x \right\rvert \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \right) dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the integrand into even and odd parts over the symmetric interval $\left[ -\frac{\pi}{6}, \; \frac{\pi}{6} \right]$. // 📝 Solution: Split the integral as $I \; = \; \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{\pi}{1 \; - \; \sin \left( \left\lvert x \right\rvert \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \, dx \; + \; \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{4x^{11}}{1 \; - \; \sin \left( \left\lvert x \right\rvert \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \, dx$. The second integrand is an odd function over a symmetric interval, so its integral is $0$. The first integrand is an even function, so $I \; = \; 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/6} \frac{1}{1 \; - \; \sin \left( x \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \, dx$. Substitute $u \; = \; x \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6}$: $I \; = \; 2\pi \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \frac{1}{1 \; - \; \sin u} \, du \; = \; 2\pi \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left( \sec^2 u \; + \; \sec u \tan u \right) du \; = \; 2\pi \left[ \tan u \; + \; \sec u \right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \; = \; 2\pi \left[ \left( \sqrt{3} \; + \; 2 \right) \; - \; \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \; + \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right) \right] \; = \; 2\pi \left( \sqrt{3} \; + \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3} \right) \; = \; 4\pi$.
questions.topic: Even and Odd Functions in Definite Integration

questions.text: The integral $16 \int_{1}^{2} \frac{dx}{x^3 \left( x^2 \;+\; 2 \right)^2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor $x^2$ out of $\left( x^2 \;+\; 2 \right)$ to write the denominator as $x^7 \left( 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{x^2} \right)^2$ and substitute $1 \;+\; \frac{2}{x^2} \;=\; t$. // 📝 Solution: Rewrite the integral as $I \;=\; 16 \int_{1}^{2} \frac{dx}{x^7 \left( 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{x^2} \right)^2} \;=\; 16 \int_{1}^{2} \frac{dx}{x^3 \cdot x^4 \left( 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{x^2} \right)^2}$. Let $1 \;+\; \frac{2}{x^2} \;=\; t \;\implies\; -\frac{4}{x^3} dx \;=\; dt$ and $\frac{1}{x^2} \;=\; \frac{t \;-\; 1}{2}$. When $x \;=\; 1$, $t \;=\; 3$; when $x \;=\; 2$, $t \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$. Thus, $I \;=\; -4 \int_{3}^{\frac{3}{2}} \left( \frac{t \;-\; 1}{2} \right)^2 \frac{dt}{t^2} \;=\; \int_{\frac{3}{2}}^{3} \left( 1 \;-\; \frac{2}{t} \;+\; \frac{1}{t^2} \right) dt \;=\; \left[ t \;-\; 2 \ln t \;-\; \frac{1}{t} \right]_{\frac{3}{2}}^{3} \;=\; \left( 3 \;-\; 2 \ln 3 \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \right) \;-\; \left( \frac{3}{2} \;-\; 2 \ln\left( \frac{3}{2} \right) \;-\; \frac{2}{3} \right) \;=\; \frac{8}{3} \;-\; \frac{5}{6} \;-\; 2 \ln 2 \;=\; \frac{11}{6} \;-\; \log_e 4$.

questions.text: The minimum value of the function $f(x) \;=\; \int_{0}^{2} e^{\left\lvert x \;-\; t \right\rvert} dt$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate $f(x)$ for $x \;\le\; 0$, $0 \;<\; x \;<\; 2$, and $x \;\ge\; 2$, then minimize $f(x)$ on $\left( 0, 2 \right)$ using the AM-GM inequality. // 📝 Solution: Case 1: For $x \;\le\; 0$, $\left\lvert x \;-\; t \right\rvert \;=\; t \;-\; x$ for $t \;\in\; \left[ 0, 2 \right]$, so $f(x) \;=\; \int_{0}^{2} e^{t \;-\; x} dt \;=\; e^{-x}\left( e^2 \;-\; 1 \right)$, which is strictly decreasing for $x \;\le\; 0$. Case 2: For $x \;\ge\; 2$, $\left\lvert x \;-\; t \right\rvert \;=\; x \;-\; t$, so $f(x) \;=\; \int_{0}^{2} e^{x \;-\; t} dt \;=\; e^{x \;-\; 2}\left( e^2 \;-\; 1 \right)$, which is strictly increasing for $x \;\ge\; 2$. Case 3: For $0 \;<\; x \;<\; 2$, $f(x) \;=\; \int_{0}^{x} e^{x \;-\; t} dt \;+\; \int_{x}^{2} e^{t \;-\; x} dt \;=\; \left( e^x \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; \left( e^{2 \;-\; x} \;-\; 1 \right) \;=\; e^x \;+\; e^{2 \;-\; x} \;-\; 2$. By the AM-GM inequality, $e^x \;+\; e^{2 \;-\; x} \;\ge\; 2\sqrt{e^x \cdot e^{2 \;-\; x}} \;=\; 2e$ (equality holds at $x \;=\; 1$). Thus, the minimum value of $f(x)$ is $2e \;-\; 2 \;=\; 2\left( e \;-\; 1 \right)$.
questions.topic: Definite Integral as a Function of Parameter

questions.text: If $\int_{\frac{1}{3}}^{3} \left\lvert \log_e x \right\rvert dx \;=\; \frac{m}{n} \log_e \left( \frac{n^2}{e} \right)$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime natural numbers, then $m^2 \;+\; n^2 \;-\; 5$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the integral at $x \;=\; 1$ where $\log_e x \;=\; 0$ and use $\int \ln x \, dx \;=\; x \ln x \;-\; x \;+\; C$. // 📝 Solution: Splitting the integral at $x \;=\; 1$: $I \;=\; \int_{\frac{1}{3}}^{1} \left( -\ln x \right) dx \;+\; \int_{1}^{3} \ln x \, dx \;=\; -\left[ x \ln x \;-\; x \right]_{\frac{1}{3}}^{1} \;+\; \left[ x \ln x \;-\; x \right]_{1}^{3}$. Evaluating at the limits gives $-\left[ -1 \;-\; \left( \frac{1}{3} \ln\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \right) \right] \;+\; \left[ \left( 3 \ln 3 \;-\; 3 \right) \;-\; (-1) \right] \;=\; \left( 1 \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \ln 3 \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \right) \;+\; \left( 3 \ln 3 \;-\; 2 \right) \;=\; \frac{8}{3} \ln 3 \;-\; \frac{4}{3} \;=\; \frac{4}{3}\left( 2 \ln 3 \;-\; 1 \right) \;=\; \frac{4}{3} \log_e\left( \frac{9}{e} \right) \;=\; \frac{4}{3} \log_e\left( \frac{3^2}{e} \right)$. Comparing with $\frac{m}{n} \log_e\left( \frac{n^2}{e} \right)$, we get $m \;=\; 4$ and $n \;=\; 3$. Therefore, $m^2 \;+\; n^2 \;-\; 5 \;=\; 16 \;+\; 9 \;-\; 5 \;=\; 20$.
questions.topic: Definite Integration of Modulus and Logarithmic Functions

questions.text: The value of $\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\left( 2 \;+\; 3 \sin x \right)}{\sin x \left( 1 \;+\; \cos x \right)} dx$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the integrand into $\frac{2}{\sin x\left( 1 \;+\; \cos x \right)} \;+\; \frac{3}{1 \;+\; \cos x}$ and use the half-angle substitution $t \;=\; \tan\left( \frac{x}{2} \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Substitute $t \;=\; \tan\left( \frac{x}{2} \right)$, so $dx \;=\; \frac{2 \, dt}{1 \;+\; t^2}$, $\sin x \;=\; \frac{2t}{1 \;+\; t^2}$, and $1 \;+\; \cos x \;=\; \frac{2}{1 \;+\; t^2}$. As $x$ goes from $\frac{\pi}{3}$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $t$ goes from $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ to $1$. The integral becomes $I \;=\; \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1} \frac{2 \;+\; \frac{6t}{1 \;+\; t^2}}{\left( \frac{2t}{1 \;+\; t^2} \right)\left( \frac{2}{1 \;+\; t^2} \right)} \cdot \frac{2 \, dt}{1 \;+\; t^2} \;=\; \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1} \frac{\left( 1 \;+\; t^2 \;+\; 3t \right) dt}{t} \;=\; \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1} \left( \frac{1}{t} \;+\; t \;+\; 3 \right) dt$. Evaluating the antiderivative: $\left[ \ln t \;+\; \frac{t^2}{2} \;+\; 3t \right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{1} \;=\; \left( 0 \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;+\; 3 \right) \;-\; \left( -\ln\sqrt{3} \;+\; \frac{1}{6} \;+\; \sqrt{3} \right) \;=\; \frac{7}{2} \;-\; \frac{1}{6} \;-\; \sqrt{3} \;+\; \log_e \sqrt{3} \;=\; \frac{10}{3} \;-\; \sqrt{3} \;+\; \log_e \sqrt{3}$.

questions.text: Let $\left[ x \right]$ denote the greatest integer $\le\; x$. Consider the function $f(x) \;=\; \max \left\{ x^2, 1 \;+\; \left[ x \right] \right\}$. Then the value of the integral $\int_{0}^{2} f(x) \, dx$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compare $x^2$ and $1 \;+\; \left[ x \right]$ on the sub-intervals $\left[ 0, 1 \right)$, $\left[ 1, \sqrt{2} \right)$, and $\left[ \sqrt{2}, 2 \right]$. // 📝 Solution: On $\left[ 0, 1 \right)$, $\left[ x \right] \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; \left[ x \right] \;=\; 1 \;>\; x^2$, so $f(x) \;=\; 1$. On $\left[ 1, 2 \right)$, $\left[ x \right] \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; \left[ x \right] \;=\; 2$. Comparing $x^2$ and $2$ on $\left[ 1, 2 \right)$: for $x \;\in\; \left[ 1, \sqrt{2} \right)$, $2 \;>\; x^2$, so $f(x) \;=\; 2$; for $x \;\in\; \left[ \sqrt{2}, 2 \right]$, $x^2 \;\ge\; 2$, so $f(x) \;=\; x^2$. Thus, $\int_{0}^{2} f(x) \, dx \;=\; \int_{0}^{1} 1 \, dx \;+\; \int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} 2 \, dx \;+\; \int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2} x^2 \, dx \;=\; 1 \;+\; 2\left( \sqrt{2} \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^{2} \;=\; 2\sqrt{2} \;-\; 1 \;+\; \frac{8 \;-\; 2\sqrt{2}}{3} \;=\; \frac{5 \;+\; 4\sqrt{2}}{3}$.
questions.topic: Definite Integration of Greatest Integer and Piecewise Functions

questions.text: $6 \int_{0}^{\pi} \left\lvert \sin 3x \; + \; \sin 2x \; + \; \sin x \right\rvert dx$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factorize the trigonometric expression using $\sin 3x \; + \; \sin x \; = \; 2\sin 2x \cos x$ to find the points where the integrand changes sign in $\left[ 0, \; \pi \right]$. // 📝 Solution: Using $\sin 3x \; + \; \sin x \; = \; 2\sin 2x \cos x$, we get $\sin 3x \; + \; \sin 2x \; + \; \sin x \; = \; \sin 2x \left( 2\cos x \; + \; 1 \right) \; = \; 2\sin x \cos x \left( 2\cos x \; + \; 1 \right)$. In $\left[ 0, \; \pi \right]$, the expression changes sign at $x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x \; = \; \frac{2\pi}{3}$; it is positive on $\left( 0, \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$, negative on $\left( \frac{\pi}{2}, \; \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)$, and positive on $\left( \frac{2\pi}{3}, \; \pi \right)$. Let $F\left( x \right) \; = \; -\frac{\cos 3x}{3} \; - \; \frac{\cos 2x}{2} \; - \; \cos x$. We have $F\left( 0 \right) \; = \; -\frac{11}{6}$, $F\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$, $F\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \; = \; \frac{5}{12}$, and $F\left( \pi \right) \; = \; \frac{5}{6}$. Thus, $\int_{0}^{\pi} \left\lvert \sin 3x \; + \; \sin 2x \; + \; \sin x \right\rvert dx \; = \; \left( F\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \; - \; F\left( 0 \right) \right) \; - \; \left( F\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \; - \; F\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \right) \; + \; \left( F\left( \pi \right) \; - \; F\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \right) \; = \; \frac{7}{3} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \; + \; \frac{5}{12} \; = \; \frac{17}{6}$. Multiplying by $6$ gives $6 \; \times \; \frac{17}{6} \; = \; 17$.

💡 Hint: Group the numerator into $n$ triplets of the form $\left( 3k \;-\; 2 \right) \;+\; \left( 3k \;-\; 1 \right) \;-\; 3k$ and divide numerator and denominator by $n^2$. // 📝 Solution: Grouping the numerator into $n$ triplets: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ \left( 3k \;-\; 2 \right) \;+\; \left( 3k \;-\; 1 \right) \;-\; 3k \right] \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left( 3k \;-\; 3 \right) \;=\; 0 \;+\; 3 \;+\; 6 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 3\left( n \;-\; 1 \right) \;=\; \frac{3n\left( n \;-\; 1 \right)}{2}$. Substituting this into the limit gives $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3n\left( n \;-\; 1 \right)}{2 \left( \sqrt{2n^4 \;+\; 4n \;+\; 3} \;-\; \sqrt{n^4 \;+\; 5n \;+\; 4} \right)}$. Dividing both the numerator and denominator by $n^2$, we obtain $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3\left( 1 \;-\; \frac{1}{n} \right)}{2 \left( \sqrt{2 \;+\; \frac{4}{n^3} \;+\; \frac{3}{n^4}} \;-\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; \frac{5}{n^3} \;+\; \frac{4}{n^4}} \right)} \;=\; \frac{3}{2\left( \sqrt{2} \;-\; 1 \right)} \;=\; \frac{3}{2}\left( \sqrt{2} \;+\; 1 \right)$.

questions.text: Let $f$ be a polynomial function such that $f\left( x^2 \; + \; 1 \right) \; = \; x^4 \; + \; 5x^2 \; + \; 2$, for all $x \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$. Then $\int_{0}^{3} f\left( x \right) dx$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $u \; = \; x^2 \; + \; 1$ to find the polynomial $f\left( x \right)$ and then integrate on $\left[ 0, \; 3 \right]$. // 📝 Solution: Let $u \; = \; x^2 \; + \; 1$, so $x^2 \; = \; u \; - \; 1$. Substituting into the given relation yields $f\left( u \right) \; = \; \left( u \; - \; 1 \right)^2 \; + \; 5\left( u \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; 2 \; = \; u^2 \; - \; 2u \; + \; 1 \; + \; 5u \; - \; 5 \; + \; 2 \; = \; u^2 \; + \; 3u \; - \; 2$. Since $f$ is a polynomial function, $f\left( x \right) \; = \; x^2 \; + \; 3x \; - \; 2$ for all $x \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$. Now, $\int_{0}^{3} f\left( x \right) dx \; = \; \int_{0}^{3} \left( x^2 \; + \; 3x \; - \; 2 \right) dx \; = \; \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \; + \; \frac{3x^2}{2} \; - \; 2x \right]_{0}^{3} \; = \; 9 \; + \; \frac{27}{2} \; - \; 6 \; = \; \frac{33}{2}$.

questions.text: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{48}{x^4} \int_{0}^{x} \frac{t^3}{t^6 \;+\; 1} dt$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply L'Hospital's rule along with the Newton-Leibnitz formula to differentiate the integral in the numerator. // 📝 Solution: The given limit is of the $\frac{0}{0}$ indeterminate form as $x \to 0$. Applying L'Hospital's rule and differentiating the numerator using the Newton-Leibnitz formula: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{48 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\left( \int_{0}^{x} \frac{t^3}{t^6 \;+\; 1} dt \right)}{\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^4 \right)} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{48 \cdot \frac{x^3}{x^6 \;+\; 1}}{4x^3} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{12}{x^6 \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{12}{0 \;+\; 1} \;=\; 12$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f \left( x \right) \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 2} \right)$, is $\left( -\infty, \; \alpha \right] \; \cup \; \left[ \beta, \; \gamma \right] \; \cup \; \left[ \delta, \; \infty \right)$, then $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma \; + \; \delta$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $\sin^{-1} \left( u \right)$ to be defined, we require $\left\lvert u \right\rvert \; \le \; 1$. // 📝 Solution: For $f \left( x \right)$ to be defined, we need $\left\lvert \frac{1}{x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 2} \right\rvert \; \le \; 1 \implies \left\lvert x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 2 \right\rvert \; \ge \; 1$. Case 1: $x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 2 \; \ge \; 1 \implies x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 3 \; \ge \; 0 \implies \left( x \; - \; 3 \right) \left( x \; + \; 1 \right) \; \ge \; 0 \implies x \; \le \; -1$ or $x \; \ge \; 3$. Case 2: $x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 2 \; \le \; -1 \implies x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 1 \; \le \; 0 \implies \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^2 \; \le \; 2 \implies 1 \; - \; \sqrt{2} \; \le \; x \; \le \; 1 \; + \; \sqrt{2}$. Combining both cases, the domain is $\left( -\infty, \; -1 \right] \; \cup \; \left[ 1 \; - \; \sqrt{2}, \; 1 \; + \; \sqrt{2} \right] \; \cup \; \left[ 3, \; \infty \right)$. Thus, $\alpha \; = \; -1, \; \beta \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sqrt{2}, \; \gamma \; = \; 1 \; + \; \sqrt{2}, \; \delta \; = \; 3$, and $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma \; + \; \delta \; = \; -1 \; + \; 1 \; - \; \sqrt{2} \; + \; 1 \; + \; \sqrt{2} \; + \; 3 \; = \; 4$.

questions.text: For $n \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$, if $\cot^{-1} 3 \; + \; \cot^{-1} 4 \; + \; \cot^{-1} 5 \; + \; \cot^{-1} n \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$, then $n$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert $\cot^{-1}$ into $\tan^{-1}$ using $\cot^{-1} x \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)$ for $x \; > \; 0$ and apply the addition formula for $\tan^{-1}$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting the equation in terms of $\tan^{-1}$, we get $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{3} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{4} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{5} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$. First, $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{3} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{4} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\frac{1}{3} \; + \; \frac{1}{4}}{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{12}} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{7}{11} \right)$. Next, $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{7}{11} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{5} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\frac{7}{11} \; + \; \frac{1}{5}}{1 \; - \; \frac{7}{55}} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{46}{48} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{23}{24} \right)$. Thus, $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4} \; - \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{23}{24} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( 1 \right) \; - \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{23}{24} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; \frac{23}{24}}{1 \; + \; \frac{23}{24}} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{47} \right) \implies n \; = \; 47$.

questions.text: If $\sin^{-1} \frac{\alpha}{17} \; + \; \cos^{-1} \frac{4}{5} \; - \; \tan^{-1} \frac{77}{36} \; = \; 0, \; 0 \; < \; \alpha \; < \; 13$, then $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin \alpha \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} \left( \cos \alpha \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert $\cos^{-1} \frac{4}{5}$ to $\tan^{-1} \frac{3}{4}$, find $\alpha$, and evaluate $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin \alpha \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} \left( \cos \alpha \right)$ using the principal value branches. // 📝 Solution: We have $\cos^{-1} \frac{4}{5} \; = \; \tan^{-1} \frac{3}{4}$. Thus, $\sin^{-1} \frac{\alpha}{17} \; = \; \tan^{-1} \frac{77}{36} \; - \; \tan^{-1} \frac{3}{4} \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\frac{77}{36} \; - \; \frac{3}{4}}{1 \; + \; \frac{77}{36} \cdot \frac{3}{4}} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{50}{144 \; + \; 231} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{50}{375} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{8}{15} \right) \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{8}{17} \right)$. Hence, $\alpha \; = \; 8$. Since $\frac{5\pi}{2} \; < \; 8 \; < \; 3\pi$, we have $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin 8 \right) \; = \; 3\pi \; - \; 8$ and $\cos^{-1} \left( \cos 8 \right) \; = \; 8 \; - \; 2\pi$. Adding both gives $\left( 3\pi \; - \; 8 \right) \; + \; \left( 8 \; - \; 2\pi \right) \; = \; \pi$.

questions.text: Let $S$ be the set of all solutions of the equation $\cos^{-1} \left( 2x \right) \; - \; 2 \cos^{-1} \left( \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \right) \; = \; \pi, \; x \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{1}{2}, \; \frac{1}{2} \right]$. Then $\sum_{x \in S} 2 \sin^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 1 \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $2 \cos^{-1} \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \right)$ and take cosine on both sides after rearranging. // 📝 Solution: Given $\cos^{-1} \left( 2x \right) \; - \; 2 \cos^{-1} \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \; = \; \pi$. Using $2 \cos^{-1} \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( 2 \left( 1 \; - \; x^2 \right) \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \right)$, we have $\cos^{-1} \left( 2x \right) \; - \; \cos^{-1} \left( 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \right) \; = \; \pi \implies -\cos^{-1} \left( 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \right) \; = \; \pi \; - \; \cos^{-1} \left( 2x \right)$. Taking cosine on both sides gives $\cos \left( -\cos^{-1} \left( 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \right) \right) \; = \; \cos \left( \pi \; - \; \cos^{-1} \left( 2x \right) \right) \implies 1 \; - \; 2x^2 \; = \; -2x \implies 2x^2 \; - \; 2x \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$. Solving this quadratic gives $x \; = \; \frac{1 \; \pm \; \sqrt{3}}{2}$. Since $x \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{1}{2}, \; \frac{1}{2} \right]$, $x \; = \; \frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{3}}{2}$ is rejected, leaving $x \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; \sqrt{3}}{2}$. For this value, $x^2 \; - \; 1 \; = \; \frac{2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}}{2} \; - \; 1 \; = \; -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Therefore, $2 \sin^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; 2 \sin^{-1} \left( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) \; = \; 2 \left( -\frac{\pi}{3} \right) \; = \; \frac{-2\pi}{3}$.

questions.text: Let $S \; = \; \left\{ x \; \in \; \mathbb{R} \; \mid \; 0 \; < \; x \; < \; 1 \text{ and } 2 \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x} \right) \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{1 \; + \; x^2} \right) \right\}$. If $n \left( S \right)$ denotes the number of elements in $S$ then :

options.text: $n \left( S \right) \; = \; 2$ and only one element in $S$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.
$n \left( S \right) \; = \; 1$ and the element in $S$ is more than $\frac{1}{2}$.
$n \left( S \right) \; = \; 1$ and the element in $S$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \; = \; \tan \theta$ for $\theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ to simplify both sides of the equation. // 📝 Solution: Given $0 \; < \; x \; < \; 1$, let $\tan^{-1} x \; = \; \theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ so that $x \; = \; \tan \theta$. Substituting into the given equation $2 \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x} \right) \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{1 \; + \; x^2} \right)$ gives $2 \tan^{-1} \left( \tan \left( \frac{\pi}{4} \; - \; \theta \right) \right) \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \cos 2\theta \right)$. Since $\frac{\pi}{4} \; - \; \theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ and $2\theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$, both angles lie within the principal value branches, yielding $2 \left( \frac{\pi}{4} \; - \; \theta \right) \; = \; 2\theta \implies 4\theta \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \theta \; = \; \frac{\pi}{8}$. Thus, $x \; = \; \tan \left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) \; = \; \sqrt{2} \; - \; 1 \; \approx \; 0.414 \; < \; \frac{1}{2}$. Hence, $n \left( S \right) \; = \; 1$ and the element in $S$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.text: Let the inverse trigonometric functions take principal values. The number of real solutions of the equation $2 \sin^{-1} x \; + \; 3 \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{2\pi}{5}$, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the complementary identity $\sin^{-1} x \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$ and check if the resulting value lies in the principal range $\left[ 0, \; \pi \right]$. // 📝 Solution: We know that $\sin^{-1} x \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$ for all $x \; \in \; \left[ -1, \; 1 \right]$. Rewriting the given equation as $2 \left( \sin^{-1} x \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{2\pi}{5}$, we get $2 \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{2\pi}{5} \implies \pi \; + \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{2\pi}{5} \implies \cos^{-1} x \; = \; -\frac{3\pi}{5}$. Since the principal value range of $\cos^{-1} x$ is $\left[ 0, \; \pi \right]$, $\cos^{-1} x \; = \; -\frac{3\pi}{5}$ is not possible. Hence, the number of real solutions is $0$.

questions.text: If $a \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \sin \left( 5 \right) \right)$ and $b \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \cos \left( 5 \right) \right)$, then $a^2 \; + \; b^2$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Locate $5$ radians in the interval $\left( \frac{3\pi}{2}, \; 2\pi \right)$ to express $a$ and $b$ within their respective principal value branches. // 📝 Solution: Since $\frac{3\pi}{2} \; < \; 5 \; < \; 2\pi$, for $a \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \sin 5 \right)$, we shift $5$ by $2\pi$ into $\left[ -\frac{\pi}{2}, \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right]$ to get $a \; = \; 5 \; - \; 2\pi$. Similarly, for $b \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \cos 5 \right)$, we reflect $5$ into $\left[ 0, \; \pi \right]$ using $\cos \left( 2\pi \; - \; 5 \right) \; = \; \cos 5$, giving $b \; = \; 2\pi \; - \; 5$. Therefore, $a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; = \; \left( 5 \; - \; 2\pi \right)^2 \; + \; \left( 2\pi \; - \; 5 \right)^2 \; = \; 2 \left( 4\pi^2 \; - \; 20\pi \; + \; 25 \right) \; = \; 8\pi^2 \; - \; 40\pi \; + \; 50$.
questions.topic: Composition of Trigonometric and Inverse Trigonometric Functions

questions.text: Let the maximum value of $\left( \sin^{-1} x \right)^2 \; + \; \left( \cos^{-1} x \right)^2$ for $x \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right]$ be $\frac{m}{n} \pi^2$, where $\gcd \left( m, \; n \right) \; = \; 1$. Then $m \; + \; n$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the function as a quadratic in $\alpha \; = \; \sin^{-1} x$ using $\cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \alpha$ and evaluate at the farthest endpoint from the vertex. // 📝 Solution: Let $\alpha \; = \; \sin^{-1} x$ and $\beta \; = \; \cos^{-1} x$. Using $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$, we have $f \left( x \right) \; = \; \alpha^2 \; + \; \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \alpha \right)^2 \; = \; 2\alpha^2 \; - \; \pi\alpha \; + \; \frac{\pi^2}{4} \; = \; 2 \left( \alpha \; - \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right)^2 \; + \; \frac{\pi^2}{8}$. For $x \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right]$, we have $\alpha \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{\pi}{3}, \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right]$. Since $f$ is an upward-opening parabola in $\alpha$ with vertex at $\alpha \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$, the maximum occurs at the endpoint farthest from $\frac{\pi}{4}$, which is $\alpha \; = \; -\frac{\pi}{3}$ (at $x \; = \; -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$). Substituting $\alpha \; = \; -\frac{\pi}{3}$ gives $2 \left( -\frac{\pi}{3} \; - \; \frac{\pi}{4} \right)^2 \; + \; \frac{\pi^2}{8} \; = \; 2 \left( \frac{49\pi^2}{144} \right) \; + \; \frac{\pi^2}{8} \; = \; \frac{49\pi^2 \; + \; 9\pi^2}{72} \; = \; \frac{58}{72} \pi^2 \; = \; \frac{29}{36} \pi^2$. Since $\gcd \left( 29, \; 36 \right) \; = \; 1$, we have $m \; = \; 29$ and $n \; = \; 36$, so $m \; + \; n \; = \; 65$.

questions.text: $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{3}}{3 \; + \; \sqrt{3}} \right) \; + \; \sec^{-1} \left( \sqrt{\frac{8 \; + \; 4\sqrt{3}}{6 \; + \; 3\sqrt{3}}} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor out common terms in the numerators and denominators inside both inverse trigonometric functions. // 📝 Solution: Simplifying the arguments, we have $\frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{3}}{3 \; + \; \sqrt{3}} \; = \; \frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3} \left( \sqrt{3} \; + \; 1 \right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{8 \; + \; 4\sqrt{3}}{6 \; + \; 3\sqrt{3}}} \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{4 \left( 2 \; + \; \sqrt{3} \right)}{3 \left( 2 \; + \; \sqrt{3} \right)}} \; = \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. Substituting these back, we get $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) \; + \; \sec^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{6} \; + \; \frac{\pi}{6} \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.text: If $k \; = \; \tan \left( \frac{\pi}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \right) \; + \; \tan \left( \frac{1}{2} \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \right)$, then the number of solutions of the equation $\sin^{-1} \left( kx \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; \sin^{-1} x \; - \; \cos^{-1} x$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)$ to simplify $k \; = \; \cot \theta \; + \; \tan \theta \; = \; \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $\theta \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)$, so $\sin 2\theta \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$. Since $\frac{\pi}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; 2\theta \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta$, we get $k \; = \; \tan \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta \right) \; + \; \tan \theta \; = \; \cot \theta \; + \; \tan \theta \; = \; \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta} \; = \; \frac{2}{\frac{2}{3}} \; = \; 3$. Now, the equation becomes $\sin^{-1} \left( 3x \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; \sin^{-1} x \; - \; \cos^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; 2\cos^{-1} x$. Taking sine on both sides gives $3x \; - \; 1 \; = \; \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; 2\cos^{-1} x \right) \; = \; \cos \left( 2\cos^{-1} x \right) \; = \; 2x^2 \; - \; 1 \implies 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; = \; 0 \implies x \; = \; 0$ or $x \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$. Since $x \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$ is outside $\left[ -1, \; 1 \right]$, it is rejected. Checking $x \; = \; 0$: LHS $= \; \sin^{-1} \left( -1 \right) \; = \; -\frac{\pi}{2}$ and RHS $= \; 0 \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; = \; -\frac{\pi}{2}$, which is valid. Thus, the number of solutions is $1$.

questions.text: The number of solutions of $\tan^{-1} 4x \; + \; \tan^{-1} 6x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{6}$, where $-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}} \; < \; x \; < \; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}$, is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since $24x^2 \; < \; 1$ on the given interval, apply $\tan^{-1} 4x \; + \; \tan^{-1} 6x \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{10x}{1 \; - \; 24x^2} \right)$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \; \in \; \left( -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}, \; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}} \right)$, we have $24x^2 \; < \; 1$. Thus, $\tan^{-1} \left( 4x \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( 6x \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{10x}{1 \; - \; 24x^2} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{6} \implies \frac{10x}{1 \; - \; 24x^2} \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies 24x^2 \; + \; 10\sqrt{3}x \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$. Solving the quadratic gives $x \; = \; \frac{-10\sqrt{3} \; \pm \; \sqrt{300 \; + \; 96}}{48} \; = \; \frac{-5\sqrt{3} \; \pm \; 3\sqrt{11}}{24}$. Since $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}} \; \approx \; 0.204$, $x_1 \; = \; \frac{-5\sqrt{3} \; + \; 3\sqrt{11}}{24} \; \approx \; 0.054$ lies in the range, while $x_2 \; = \; \frac{-5\sqrt{3} \; - \; 3\sqrt{11}}{24} \; \approx \; -0.776$ lies outside the range. Hence, the number of solutions is $1$.

questions.text: Let $a_1 \; = \; 1, \; a_2, \; a_3, \; a_4, \; \dots$ be consecutive natural numbers. Then $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1 \; + \; a_1 a_2} \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1 \; + \; a_2 a_3} \right) \; + \; \dots \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1 \; + \; a_{2021} a_{2022}} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the $k$-th numerator as $1 \; = \; a_{k+1} \; - \; a_k$ and use the telescoping identity $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{a_{k+1} \; - \; a_k}{1 \; + \; a_k a_{k+1}} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} a_{k+1} \; - \; \tan^{-1} a_k$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a_1 \; = \; 1, \; a_2 \; = \; 2, \; \dots, \; a_{2022} \; = \; 2022$ are consecutive natural numbers, we have $a_{k+1} \; - \; a_k \; = \; 1$. Rewriting the sum gives $\sum_{k=1}^{2021} \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{a_{k+1} \; - \; a_k}{1 \; + \; a_k a_{k+1}} \right) \; = \; \sum_{k=1}^{2021} \left( \tan^{-1} a_{k+1} \; - \; \tan^{-1} a_k \right)$. By telescoping cancellation, this equals $\tan^{-1} \left( a_{2022} \right) \; - \; \tan^{-1} \left( a_1 \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( 2022 \right) \; - \; \tan^{-1} \left( 1 \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( 2022 \right) \; - \; \frac{\pi}{4}$.
questions.topic: Telescoping Series in Inverse Trigonometric Functions

questions.text: Let $x \; = \; \frac{m}{n}$ ($m, \; n$ are co-prime natural numbers) be a solution of the equation $\cos \left( 2 \sin^{-1} x \right) \; = \; \frac{1}{9}$ and let $\alpha, \; \beta \; \left( \alpha \; > \; \beta \right)$ be the roots of the equation $mx^2 \; - \; nx \; - \; m \; + \; n \; = \; 0$. Then the point $\left( \alpha, \; \beta \right)$ lies on the line
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos \left( 2 \sin^{-1} x \right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; 2x^2$ to find $m$ and $n$, then solve the quadratic equation for $\alpha$ and $\beta$. // 📝 Solution: Let $\sin^{-1} x \; = \; \theta \implies \sin \theta \; = \; x$. Then $\cos \left( 2\theta \right) \; = \; \frac{1}{9} \implies 1 \; - \; 2\sin^2 \theta \; = \; \frac{1}{9} \implies 2x^2 \; = \; \frac{8}{9} \implies x^2 \; = \; \frac{4}{9} \implies x \; = \; \pm \frac{2}{3}$. Since $x \; = \; \frac{m}{n}$ where $m, \; n$ are co-prime natural numbers, $x \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$, so $m \; = \; 2$ and $n \; = \; 3$. Substituting into the quadratic equation gives $2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; - \; 2 \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0 \implies 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies \left( 2x \; - \; 1 \right) \left( x \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; 0$. Since $\alpha \; > \; \beta$, the roots are $\alpha \; = \; 1$ and $\beta \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. Checking the options for the point $\left( 1, \; \frac{1}{2} \right)$, we get $5 \left( 1 \right) \; + \; 8 \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \; = \; 5 \; + \; 4 \; = \; 9$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f \left( x \right) \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{2x \; - \; 5}{11 \; - \; 3x} \right) \; + \; \sin^{-1} \left( 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 1 \right)$ is the interval $\left[ \alpha, \; \beta \right]$, then $\alpha \; + \; 2\beta$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the intersection of the intervals where $\left\lvert \frac{2x \; - \; 5}{11 \; - \; 3x} \right\rvert \; \le \; 1$ and $\left\lvert 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 1 \right\rvert \; \le \; 1$. // 📝 Solution: For $\cos^{-1} \left( \frac{2x \; - \; 5}{11 \; - \; 3x} \right)$ to be defined, $-1 \; \le \; \frac{2x \; - \; 5}{11 \; - \; 3x} \; \le \; 1$, which yields $x \; \le \; \frac{16}{5}$ or $x \; > \; 6$. For $\sin^{-1} \left( 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 1 \right)$ to be defined, $-1 \; \le \; 2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 1 \; \le \; 1$. The left inequality $2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; + \; 2 \; \ge \; 0$ holds for all $x \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$ since its discriminant is negative ($9 \; - \; 16 \; < \; 0$). The right inequality $2x^2 \; - \; 3x \; \le \; 0 \implies x \left( 2x \; - \; 3 \right) \; \le \; 0 \implies 0 \; \le \; x \; \le \; \frac{3}{2}$. Taking the intersection of both conditions gives $\left[ 0, \; \frac{3}{2} \right]$. Thus, $\alpha \; = \; 0$ and $\beta \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$, so $\alpha \; + \; 2\beta \; = \; 0 \; + \; 3 \; = \; 3$.

questions.text: Considering only the principal values of inverse trigonometric functions, the number of positive real values of $x$ satisfying $\tan^{-1} \left( x \right) \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( 2x \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the formula $\tan^{-1} x \; + \; \tan^{-1} y \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{x \; + \; y}{1 \; - \; xy} \right)$ for $xy \; < \; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Given $\tan^{-1} x \; + \; \tan^{-1} 2x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$ for $x \; > \; 0$. Rewriting as $\tan^{-1} 2x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4} \; - \; \tan^{-1} x$ and taking tangent on both sides gives $2x \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x} \implies 2x \left( 1 \; + \; x \right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; x \implies 2x^2 \; + \; 3x \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$. Using the quadratic formula, $x \; = \; \frac{-3 \; \pm \; \sqrt{9 \; + \; 8}}{4} \; = \; \frac{-3 \; \pm \; \sqrt{17}}{4}$. Since $x \; > \; 0$, the only positive real solution is $x \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{17} \; - \; 3}{4}$. Thus, there is exactly $1$ positive real value of $x$.

questions.text: If the sum of all the solutions of $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right) \; + \; \cot^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3}, \; -1 \; < \; x \; < \; 1, \; x \; \ne \; 0$, is $\alpha \; - \; \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}$, then $\alpha$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split into two cases ($0 \; < \; x \; < \; 1$ and $-1 \; < \; x \; < \; 0$) to convert $\cot^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \right)$ into $\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Case I: Let $0 \; < \; x \; < \; 1$. Then $\frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \; > \; 0$, so $\cot^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \right) \; = \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right)$. The equation becomes $2 \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3} \implies 2 \left( 2 \tan^{-1} x \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3} \implies \tan^{-1} x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{12} \implies x \; = \; \tan \left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$. Case II: Let $-1 \; < \; x \; < \; 0$. Then $\frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \; < \; 0$, so $\cot^{-1} \left( \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{2x} \right) \; = \; \pi \; + \; \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right)$. The equation becomes $2 \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2x}{1 \; - \; x^2} \right) \; + \; \pi \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3} \implies 4 \tan^{-1} x \; = \; -\frac{2\pi}{3} \implies \tan^{-1} x \; = \; -\frac{\pi}{6} \implies x \; = \; -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. The sum of all solutions is $2 \; - \; \sqrt{3} \; - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}$. Comparing with $\alpha \; - \; \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}$, we get $\alpha \; = \; 2$.

questions.text: Considering the principal values of inverse trigonometric functions, the value of the expression $\tan \left( 2 \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \right) \; - \; 2 \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \right) \right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Let $\alpha \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \right)$ and $\gamma \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \right)$, compute $\tan 2\alpha$ and $\tan 2\gamma$, and use $\tan \left( 2\alpha \; - \; 2\gamma \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $\alpha \; = \; \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \right)$, then $\sin \alpha \; = \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}, \; \cos \alpha \; = \; \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}, \; \tan \alpha \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$. Thus, $\tan \left( 2\alpha \right) \; = \; \frac{2 \tan \alpha}{1 \; - \; \tan^2 \alpha} \; = \; \frac{2 \cdot \frac{2}{3}}{1 \; - \; \frac{4}{9}} \; = \; \frac{12}{5}$. Similarly, let $\gamma \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \right)$, then $\cos \gamma \; = \; \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}, \; \sin \gamma \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}, \; \tan \gamma \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Thus, $\tan \left( 2\gamma \right) \; = \; \frac{2 \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{9}} \; = \; \frac{3}{4}$. Therefore, $\tan \left( 2\alpha \; - \; 2\gamma \right) \; = \; \frac{\tan 2\alpha \; - \; \tan 2\gamma}{1 \; + \; \tan 2\alpha \tan 2\gamma} \; = \; \frac{\frac{12}{5} \; - \; \frac{3}{4}}{1 \; + \; \frac{12}{5} \cdot \frac{3}{4}} \; = \; \frac{\frac{33}{20}}{\frac{56}{20}} \; = \; \frac{33}{56}$.

questions.text: For $\alpha, \; \beta, \; \gamma \; \ne \; 0$. If $\sin^{-1} \alpha \; + \; \sin^{-1} \beta \; + \; \sin^{-1} \gamma \; = \; \pi$ and $\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma \right) \left( \alpha \; - \; \gamma \; + \; \beta \right) \; = \; 3\alpha\beta$, then $\gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Let $A \; = \; \sin^{-1} \alpha, \; B \; = \; \sin^{-1} \beta, \; C \; = \; \sin^{-1} \gamma$ so that $A \; + \; B \; + \; C \; = \; \pi$, and apply the cosine rule analogy. // 📝 Solution: Let $\sin^{-1} \alpha \; = \; A, \; \sin^{-1} \beta \; = \; B, \; \sin^{-1} \gamma \; = \; C$, so $A \; + \; B \; + \; C \; = \; \pi$. We are given $\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right)^2 \; - \; \gamma^2 \; = \; 3\alpha\beta \implies \alpha^2 \; + \; \beta^2 \; - \; \gamma^2 \; = \; \alpha\beta \implies \frac{\alpha^2 \; + \; \beta^2 \; - \; \gamma^2}{2\alpha\beta} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. Using the property that if $A \; + \; B \; + \; C \; = \; \pi$, then $\sin^2 A \; + \; \sin^2 B \; - \; \sin^2 C \; = \; 2 \sin A \sin B \cos C$, we have $\alpha^2 \; + \; \beta^2 \; - \; \gamma^2 \; = \; 2\alpha\beta \cos C$. Comparing the two relations gives $\cos C \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. Since $\sin C \; = \; \gamma$, we get $\gamma \; = \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; \cos^2 C} \; = \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{4}} \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.text: The integral $\int_{1/4}^{3/4} \cos \left( 2 \cot^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x}} \right) dx$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the identity $\cos \left( 2 \tan^{-1} u \right) \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; u^2}{1 \; + \; u^2}$ after converting $\cot^{-1}$ to $\tan^{-1}$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \; \in \; \left[ \frac{1}{4}, \; \frac{3}{4} \right]$, $\sqrt{\frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x}} \; > \; 0$, so $\cot^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1 \; - \; x}{1 \; + \; x}} \; = \; \tan^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1 \; + \; x}{1 \; - \; x}}$. Let $I \; = \; \int_{1/4}^{3/4} \cos \left( 2 \tan^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1 \; + \; x}{1 \; - \; x}} \right) dx$. Using $\cos \left( 2 \tan^{-1} u \right) \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; u^2}{1 \; + \; u^2}$, the integrand simplifies to $\frac{1 \; - \; \left( \frac{1 \; + \; x}{1 \; - \; x} \right)}{1 \; + \; \left( \frac{1 \; + \; x}{1 \; - \; x} \right)} \; = \; \frac{\left( 1 \; - \; x \right) \; - \; \left( 1 \; + \; x \right)}{\left( 1 \; - \; x \right) \; + \; \left( 1 \; + \; x \right)} \; = \; \frac{-2x}{2} \; = \; -x$. Therefore, $I \; = \; \int_{1/4}^{3/4} \left( -x \right) dx \; = \; -\left[ \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_{1/4}^{3/4} \; = \; -\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{9}{16} \; - \; \frac{1}{16} \right) \; = \; -\frac{1}{4}$.

questions.text: Given that the inverse trigonometric function assumes principal values only. Let $x, \; y$ be any two real numbers in $\left[ -1, \; 1 \right]$ such that $\cos^{-1} x \; - \; \sin^{-1} y \; = \; \alpha, \; -\frac{\pi}{2} \; \le \; \alpha \; \le \; \pi$. Then, the minimum value of $x^2 \; + \; y^2 \; + \; 2xy \sin \alpha$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sin^{-1} y \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \cos^{-1} y$ and apply the cosine of the sum of two inverse cosine functions. // 📝 Solution: Given $\cos^{-1} x \; - \; \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \cos^{-1} y \right) \; = \; \alpha \implies \cos^{-1} x \; + \; \cos^{-1} y \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; + \; \alpha$. Since $\alpha \; \in \; \left[ -\frac{\pi}{2}, \; \pi \right]$, we have $\frac{\pi}{2} \; + \; \alpha \; \in \; \left[ 0, \; \frac{3\pi}{2} \right]$. Taking cosine on both sides gives $xy \; - \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \sqrt{1 \; - \; y^2} \; = \; \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; + \; \alpha \right) \; = \; -\sin \alpha \implies xy \; + \; \sin \alpha \; = \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; x^2} \sqrt{1 \; - \; y^2}$. Squaring both sides, we get $\left( xy \; + \; \sin \alpha \right)^2 \; = \; \left( 1 \; - \; x^2 \right) \left( 1 \; - \; y^2 \right) \implies x^2 y^2 \; + \; 2xy \sin \alpha \; + \; \sin^2 \alpha \; = \; 1 \; - \; x^2 \; - \; y^2 \; + \; x^2 y^2 \implies x^2 \; + \; y^2 \; + \; 2xy \sin \alpha \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sin^2 \alpha \; = \; \cos^2 \alpha$. The minimum value of $\cos^2 \alpha$ on $\left[ -\frac{\pi}{2}, \; \pi \right]$ is $0$, which occurs at $\alpha \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: Let $\left( a, \; b \right) \; \subset \; \left( 0, \; 2\pi \right)$ be the largest interval for which $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \; - \; \cos^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \; > \; 0, \; \theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; 2\pi \right)$, holds. If $\alpha x^2 \; + \; \beta x \; + \; \sin^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 6x \; + \; 10 \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 6x \; + \; 10 \right) \; = \; 0$ and $\alpha \; - \; \beta \; = \; b \; - \; a$, then $\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \sin^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right)$ to find $\left( a, \; b \right)$, and note that $x^2 \; - \; 6x \; + \; 10 \; = \; \left( x \; - \; 3 \right)^2 \; + \; 1 \; \ge \; 1$ restricts the domain to $x \; = \; 3$. // 📝 Solution: The inequality $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \; - \; \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \sin^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \right) \; > \; 0$ simplifies to $\sin^{-1} \left( \sin \theta \right) \; > \; \frac{\pi}{4} \implies \sin \theta \; > \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. For $\theta \; \in \; \left( 0, \; 2\pi \right)$, this holds for $\theta \; \in \; \left( \frac{\pi}{4}, \; \frac{3\pi}{4} \right) \; = \; \left( a, \; b \right)$. Thus, $b \; - \; a \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; = \; \alpha \; - \; \beta \implies \beta \; = \; \alpha \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}$. Next, for $\sin^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 6x \; + \; 10 \right)$ and $\cos^{-1} \left( x^2 \; - \; 6x \; + \; 10 \right)$ to be defined, we need $\left( x \; - \; 3 \right)^2 \; + \; 1 \; \le \; 1 \implies x \; = \; 3$. Substituting $x \; = \; 3$ into the equation gives $9\alpha \; + \; 3\beta \; + \; \sin^{-1} \left( 1 \right) \; + \; \cos^{-1} \left( 1 \right) \; = \; 0 \implies 9\alpha \; + \; 3 \left( \alpha \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \; + \; \frac{\pi}{2} \; + \; 0 \; = \; 0 \implies 12\alpha \; - \; \pi \; = \; 0 \implies \alpha \; = \; \frac{\pi}{12}$.
questions.topic: Inequalities and Domain in Inverse Trigonometric Functions

questions.text: If $\tan 15^{\circ} \; + \; \dfrac{1}{\tan 75^{\circ}} \; + \; \dfrac{1}{\tan 105^{\circ}} \; + \; \tan 195^{\circ} \; = \; 2a$, then the value of $\left( a \; + \; \dfrac{1}{a} \right)$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\tan 15^{\circ} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$ and $\cot$ relations for allied angles // 📝 Solution: $\tan 15^{\circ} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$, $\dfrac{1}{\tan 75^{\circ}} \; = \; \cot 75^{\circ} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$, $\dfrac{1}{\tan 105^{\circ}} \; = \; \cot 105^{\circ} \; = \; \sqrt{3} \; - \; 2$, $\tan 195^{\circ} \; = \; \tan 15^{\circ} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$; So $2\left( 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3} \right) \; = \; 2a$ gives $a \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{3}$; Then $a \; + \; \dfrac{1}{a} \; = \; 4$

questions.text: For $\alpha, \beta \in \left( 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$, let $3\sin\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; = \; 2\sin\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right)$ and a real number $k$ be such that $\tan\alpha \; = \; k\tan\beta$. Then the value of $k$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand $\sin\left( \alpha \; \pm \; \beta \right)$ using $\sin A\cos B \; \pm \; \cos A\sin B$ // 📝 Solution: $3\left( \sin\alpha\cos\beta \; + \; \cos\alpha\sin\beta \right) \; = \; 2\left( \sin\alpha\cos\beta \; - \; \cos\alpha\sin\beta \right)$ gives $5\sin\beta\cos\alpha \; = \; -\sin\alpha\cos\beta$; Dividing by $\cos\alpha\cos\beta$ gives $\tan\beta \; = \; -\dfrac{1}{5}\tan\alpha$, so $\tan\alpha \; = \; -5\tan\beta$, hence $k \; = \; -5$

questions.text: If $\dfrac{\tan\left( A \; - \; B \right)}{\tan A} \; + \; \dfrac{\sin^{2}C}{\sin^{2}A} \; = \; 1$, $A, B, C \in \left( 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$, then

options.text: $\tan A, \tan C, \tan B$ are in A.P.
$\tan A, \tan B, \tan C$ are in G.P.
$\tan A, \tan C, \tan B$ are in G.P.
$\tan A, \tan B, \tan C$ are in A.P.

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rearrange to $\tan\left( A \; - \; B \right)\tan A \; = \; \sin^{2}A \; - \; \sin^{2}C$ and use $\sin^{2} \; = \; \dfrac{\tan^{2}}{1 \; + \; \tan^{2}}$ // 📝 Solution: $\dfrac{\tan\left( A \; - \; B \right)}{\tan A} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \dfrac{\sin^{2}C}{\sin^{2}A}$ gives $\tan\left( A \; - \; B \right)\tan A \; = \; \sin^{2}A \; - \; \sin^{2}C$; Simplifying with $\sin^{2}\theta \; = \; \dfrac{\tan^{2}\theta}{1 \; + \; \tan^{2}\theta}$ reduces to $\left( \tan C \right)^{2} \; = \; \tan A\cdot\tan B$, so $\tan A, \tan C, \tan B$ are in G.P.

questions.text: If $\dfrac{\cos^{2}48^{\circ} \; - \; \sin^{2}12^{\circ}}{\sin^{2}24^{\circ} \; - \; \sin^{2}6^{\circ}} \; = \; \dfrac{\alpha \; + \; \beta\sqrt{5}}{2}$, where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha \; + \; \beta$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos^{2}A \; - \; \sin^{2}B \; = \; \cos\left( A \; + \; B \right)\cos\left( A \; - \; B \right)$ and $\sin^{2}A \; - \; \sin^{2}B \; = \; \sin\left( A \; + \; B \right)\sin\left( A \; - \; B \right)$ // 📝 Solution: $\cos^{2}48^{\circ} \; - \; \sin^{2}12^{\circ} \; = \; \cos 60^{\circ}\cos 36^{\circ} \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 36^{\circ}$, $\sin^{2}24^{\circ} \; - \; \sin^{2}6^{\circ} \; = \; \sin 30^{\circ}\sin 18^{\circ} \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 18^{\circ}$; Ratio $\; = \; \dfrac{\cos 36^{\circ}}{\sin 18^{\circ}} \; = \; \dfrac{\left( 1 \; + \; \sqrt{5} \right)}{\left( \sqrt{5} \; - \; 1 \right)}$ $\; = \; \dfrac{3 \; + \; \sqrt{5}}{2}$, so $\alpha \; = \; 3$, $\beta \; = \; 1$, $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; = \; 4$

questions.text: The value of $\text{cosec }10^{\circ} \; - \; \sqrt{3}\sec 10^{\circ}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Combine over $\sin 10^{\circ}\cos 10^{\circ}$ and use $a\cos \; - \; b\sin$ as $R\cos$ form // 📝 Solution: $\text{cosec }10^{\circ} \; - \; \sqrt{3}\sec 10^{\circ} \; = \; \dfrac{\cos 10^{\circ} \; - \; \sqrt{3}\sin 10^{\circ}}{\sin 10^{\circ}\cos 10^{\circ}}$; Numerator $\; = \; 2\left( \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 10^{\circ} \; - \; \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin 10^{\circ} \right) \; = \; 2\cos 70^{\circ} \; = \; 2\sin 20^{\circ}$; Denominator $\; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 20^{\circ}$; Ratio $\; = \; 4$

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively be the maximum and the minimum values of the function $f\left( \theta \right) \; = \; 4\left( \sin^{4}\left( \dfrac{7\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta \right) \; + \; \sin^{4}\left( 11\pi \; + \; \theta \right) \right) \; - \; 2\left( \sin^{6}\left( \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta \right) \; + \; \sin^{6}\left( 9\pi \; - \; \theta \right) \right)$, $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\alpha \; + \; 2\beta$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Reduce allied angles to $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ then use $\sin^{4} \; + \; \cos^{4} \; = \; 1 \; - \; 2\sin^{2}\cos^{2}$ // 📝 Solution: $f\left( \theta \right) \; = \; 4\left( \cos^{4}\theta \; + \; \sin^{4}\theta \right) \; - \; 2\left( \cos^{6}\theta \; + \; \sin^{6}\theta \right)$ $\; = \; 4\left( 1 \; - \; 2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta \right) \; - \; 2\left( 1 \; - \; 3\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta \right)$ $\; = \; 2 \; - \; 2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$ $\; = \; 2 \; - \; \dfrac{\sin^{2}2\theta}{2}$; So $\alpha \; = \; 2$, $\beta \; = \; \dfrac{3}{2}$, hence $\alpha \; + \; 2\beta \; = \; 5$

questions.text: The least value of $\left( \cos^{2}\theta \; - \; 6\sin\theta\cos\theta \; + \; 3\sin^{2}\theta \; + \; 2 \right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert to $A \; + \; B\cos 2\theta \; + \; C\sin 2\theta$ using double-angle formulas // 📝 Solution: Expression $\; = \; \dfrac{1 \; + \; \cos 2\theta}{2} \; + \; \dfrac{3\left( 1 \; - \; \cos 2\theta \right)}{2} \; - \; 3\sin 2\theta \; + \; 2$ $\; = \; 4 \; - \; \cos 2\theta \; - \; 3\sin 2\theta$; Minimum of $\left( -\cos 2\theta \; - \; 3\sin 2\theta \right) \; = \; -\sqrt{1 \; + \; 9} \; = \; -\sqrt{10}$, so least value $\; = \; 4 \; - \; \sqrt{10}$
questions.topic: Range via a cos plus b sin Form

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute $\tan\left( A \; + \; B \right) \; = \; \dfrac{\tan A \; + \; \tan B}{1 \; - \; \tan A \tan B}$ // 📝 Solution: $\tan\left( A \; + \; B \right) \; = \; \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x\left( x^{2} \; + \; x \; + \; 1 \right)}} \; + \; \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2} \; + \; x \; + \; 1}}}{1 \; - \; \dfrac{1}{x^{2} \; + \; x \; + \; 1}}$ $\; = \; \dfrac{\left( 1 \; + \; x \right)\sqrt{x^{2} \; + \; x \; + \; 1}}{\left( x^{2} \; + \; x \right)\sqrt{x}}$ $\; = \; \dfrac{\sqrt{x^{2} \; + \; x \; + \; 1}}{x\sqrt{x}}$ $\; = \; \tan C$; Since $A, B, C \in \left( 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$ and $\tan\left( A \; + \; B \right) \; > \; 0$, $A \; + \; B \in \left( 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$, hence $A \; + \; B \; = \; C$

questions.text: Let $S \; = \; \left\{ \theta \in \left[ 0, 2\pi \right) \mid \tan\left( \pi\cos\theta \right) \; + \; \tan\left( \pi\sin\theta \right) \; = \; 0 \right\}$. Then $\sum_{\theta \in S}\sin^{2}\left( \theta \; + \; \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\tan A \; = \; -\tan B \; = \; \tan\left( -B \right)$ to get $\sin\theta \; + \; \cos\theta \; = \; n$ // 📝 Solution: $\tan\left( \pi\cos\theta \right) \; = \; \tan\left( -\pi\sin\theta \right)$ gives $\pi\cos\theta \; = \; n\pi \; - \; \pi\sin\theta$, so $\sin\theta \; + \; \cos\theta \; = \; n$ with $n \in \mathbb{Z}$; Since $-\sqrt{2} \; \le \; \sin\theta \; + \; \cos\theta \; \le \; \sqrt{2}$, $n \; = \; -1, 0, 1$; This gives $\theta \in \left\{ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \right\}$; Then $\sum \sin^{2}\left( \theta \; + \; \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \; = \; 4\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \; + \; 2\left( 0 \right) \; = \; 2$

questions.text: If $\sin x \; = \; -\dfrac{3}{5}$, where $\pi \; < \; x \; < \; \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, then $80\left( \tan^{2}x \; - \; \cos x \right)$ is equal to
