questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $\cos x$ and $\tan x$ in third quadrant using $\sin^{2}x \; + \; \cos^{2}x \; = \; 1$ // 📝 Solution: For $\pi \; < \; x \; < \; \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, $\cos x \; = \; -\sqrt{1 \; - \; \sin^{2}x} \; = \; -\dfrac{4}{5}$, $\tan x \; = \; \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} \; = \; \dfrac{3}{4}$; Then $80\left( \tan^{2}x \; - \; \cos x \right) \; = \; 80\left( \dfrac{9}{16} \; + \; \dfrac{4}{5} \right) \; = \; 45 \; + \; 64 \; = \; 109$

questions.text: If the value of $\dfrac{3\cos 36^{\circ} \; + \; 5\sin 18^{\circ}}{5\cos 36^{\circ} \; - \; 3\sin 18^{\circ}}$ is $\dfrac{a\sqrt{5} \; - \; b}{c}$, where $a, b, c$ are natural numbers and $\gcd\left( a, c \right) \; = \; 1$, then $a \; + \; b \; + \; c$ is equal to :

Let $\left\lvert \cos\theta \cos\left( 60^{\circ} \; - \; \theta \right) \cos\left( 60^{\circ} \; + \; \theta \right) \right\rvert \; \le \; \dfrac{1}{8}$, $\theta \in \left[ 0, 2\pi \right]$. Then, the sum of all $\theta \in \left[ 0, 2\pi \right]$, where $\cos 3\theta$ attains its maximum value, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos\theta \cos\left( 60^{\circ} \; - \; \theta \right) \cos\left( 60^{\circ} \; + \; \theta \right) \; = \; \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 3\theta$ // 📝 Solution: Given $\left\lvert \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 3\theta \right\rvert \; \le \; \dfrac{1}{8}$ gives $\left\lvert \cos 3\theta \right\rvert \; \le \; \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $-\dfrac{1}{2} \; \le \; \cos 3\theta \; \le \; \dfrac{1}{2}$; Maximum value is $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\cos 3\theta \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $3\theta \; = \; 2n\pi \; \pm \; \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $\theta \; = \; \dfrac{2n\pi}{3} \; \pm \; \dfrac{\pi}{9}$; In $\left[ 0, 2\pi \right]$, $\theta \; = \; \left\{ \dfrac{\pi}{9}, \dfrac{5\pi}{9}, \dfrac{7\pi}{9}, \dfrac{11\pi}{9}, \dfrac{13\pi}{9}, \dfrac{17\pi}{9} \right\}$, sum $\; = \; \dfrac{54\pi}{9} \; = \; 6\pi$

questions.text: The value of $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\text{cosec }20^{\circ} \; - \; \sec 20^{\circ}}{\cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 60^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ}}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Simplify numerator to $4$ using $R\cos$ form and denominator to $\dfrac{1}{16}$ using double-angle repeatedly // 📝 Solution: Numerator $\; = \; \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\cos 20^{\circ} \; - \; \sin 20^{\circ}}{\sin 20^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ}} \; = \; \dfrac{2\cos 50^{\circ}}{\sin 20^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ}} \; = \; 4$; Denominator $\; = \; \cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}$ with $\sin 20^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ} \; = \; \dfrac{1}{8}\sin 20^{\circ}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{16}$; Ratio $\; = \; \dfrac{4}{\left( 1/16 \right)} \; = \; 64$

questions.text: Let $\cos\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; = \; -\dfrac{1}{10}$ and $\sin\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right) \; = \; \dfrac{3}{8}$, where $0 \; < \; \alpha \; < \; \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $0 \; < \; \beta \; < \; \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. If $\tan 2\alpha \; = \; \dfrac{3\left( 1 \; - \; r\sqrt{5} \right)}{\sqrt{11}\left( s \; + \; \sqrt{5} \right)}$, $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$, then $r \; + \; s$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $2\alpha \; = \; \left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; + \; \left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right)$ and use $\tan$ addition // 📝 Solution: $\sin\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; = \; \dfrac{\sqrt{99}}{10}$, $\tan\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; = \; -\sqrt{99}$, $\cos\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right) \; = \; \dfrac{\sqrt{55}}{8}$, $\tan\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right) \; = \; \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{55}}$; Then $\tan 2\alpha \; = \; \dfrac{\tan\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right) \; + \; \tan\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right)}{1 \; - \; \tan\left( \alpha \; + \; \beta \right)\tan\left( \alpha \; - \; \beta \right)}$ $\; = \; \dfrac{3\left( 1 \; - \; 11\sqrt{5} \right)}{\sqrt{11}\left( 9 \; + \; \sqrt{5} \right)}$, so $r \; = \; 11$, $s \; = \; 9$, $r \; + \; s \; = \; 20$

questions.text: If the solution of the equation $\log_{\cos x}\cot x \; + \; 4\log_{\sin x}\tan x \; = \; 1$, $x \in \left( 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$, is $\sin^{-1}\left( \dfrac{\alpha \; + \; \sqrt{\beta}}{2} \right)$, where $\alpha, \beta$ are integers, then $\alpha \; + \; \beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Change log base to $\ln$ and set $u \; = \; \ln\sin x$, $v \; = \; \ln\cos x$ to get a perfect square // 📝 Solution: $\dfrac{\ln\cos x \; - \; \ln\sin x}{\ln\cos x} \; + \; 4\dfrac{\ln\sin x \; - \; \ln\cos x}{\ln\sin x} \; = \; 1$ gives $\left( \ln\sin x \right)^{2} \; - \; 4\left( \ln\sin x \right)\left( \ln\cos x \right) \; + \; 4\left( \ln\cos x \right)^{2} \; = \; 0$; So $\ln\sin x \; = \; 2\ln\cos x$, $\sin x \; = \; \cos^{2}x \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sin^{2}x$; Thus $\sin^{2}x \; + \; \sin x \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$, $\sin x \; = \; \dfrac{-1 \; + \; \sqrt{5}}{2}$, so $\alpha \; = \; -1$, $\beta \; = \; 5$, $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; = \; 4$

questions.text: Let $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \; < \; \theta \; < \; \pi$ and $\cot\theta \; = \; -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$. Then the value of $\sin\left( \dfrac{15\theta}{2} \right)\left( \cos 8\theta \; + \; \sin 8\theta \right) \; + \; \cos\left( \dfrac{15\theta}{2} \right)\left( \cos 8\theta \; - \; \sin 8\theta \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand and regroup to $\cos\left( A \; - \; B \right)$ and $\sin\left( A \; - \; B \right)$ forms // 📝 Solution: Expression $\; = \; \left( \cos\dfrac{15\theta}{2}\cos 8\theta \; + \; \sin\dfrac{15\theta}{2}\sin 8\theta \right) \; + \; \left( \sin\dfrac{15\theta}{2}\cos 8\theta \; - \; \cos\dfrac{15\theta}{2}\sin 8\theta \right)$ $\; = \; \cos\left( 8\theta \; - \; \dfrac{15\theta}{2} \right) \; + \; \sin\left( \dfrac{15\theta}{2} \; - \; 8\theta \right)$ $\; = \; \cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} \; - \; \sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}$; From $\cot\theta$, $\sin\theta \; = \; \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$, $\left( \cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} \; - \; \sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} \right)^{2} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sin\theta \; = \; \dfrac{\left( \sqrt{2} \; - \; 1 \right)^{2}}{3}$; Since $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \; < \; \dfrac{\theta}{2} \; < \; \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, value $\; = \; \dfrac{1 \; - \; \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.text: The set of all values of $\lambda$ for which the equation $\cos^{2}2x \; - \; 2\sin^{4}x \; - \; 2\cos^{2}x \; = \; \lambda$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert everything to $\cos x$ and complete the square in $\cos^{2}x$ // 📝 Solution: $\lambda \; = \; \left( 2\cos^{2}x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \; - \; 2\left( 1 \; - \; \cos^{2}x \right)^{2} \; - \; 2\cos^{2}x$ $\; = \; 2\cos^{4}x \; - \; 2\cos^{2}x \; - \; 1$ $\; = \; 2\left[ \left( \cos^{2}x \; - \; \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{2} \; - \; \dfrac{3}{4} \right]$; With $0 \; \le \; \cos^{2}x \; \le \; 1$, max $\; = \; -1$, min $\; = \; -\dfrac{3}{2}$, so Range $\; = \; \left[ -\dfrac{3}{2}, -1 \right]$

questions.text: If $\cot x \; = \; \dfrac{5}{12}$ for some $x \in \left( \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \right)$, then $\sin 7x\left( \cos\dfrac{13x}{2} \; + \; \sin\dfrac{13x}{2} \right) \; + \; \cos 7x\left( \cos\dfrac{13x}{2} \; - \; \sin\dfrac{13x}{2} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$ and $\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$ from $\cos x$ then reduce to $\cos$ and $\sin$ of difference // 📝 Solution: $\cot x \; = \; \dfrac{5}{12}$ gives $\cos x \; = \; -\dfrac{5}{13} \; = \; 2\cos^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} \; - \; 1$, so $\cos\dfrac{x}{2} \; = \; -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$ as $\dfrac{x}{2} \in \left( \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \right)$ and $\sin\dfrac{x}{2} \; = \; \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$; Expression $\; = \; \cos\left( 7x \; - \; \dfrac{13x}{2} \right) \; + \; \sin\left( 7x \; - \; \dfrac{13x}{2} \right)$ $\; = \; \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \; + \; \sin\dfrac{x}{2}$ $\; = \; \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}$

questions.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P\left(A \cap B\right) \; = \; 0.1$, and $P\left(A \mid B\right)$ and $P\left(B \mid A\right)$ be the roots of the equation $12x^2 - 7x + 1 \; = \; 0$. Then the value of $\frac{P\left(\bar{A} \cup \bar{B}\right)}{P\left(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}\right)}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the sum and product of roots with $P\left(A \mid B\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(A \cap B\right)}{P\left(B\right)}$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{0.01}{P\left(A\right)P\left(B\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{12} \implies P\left(A\right)P\left(B\right) \; = \; 0.12 \;,\; P\left(A\right) + P\left(B\right) \; = \; 0.7 \implies P\left(A \cup B\right) \; = \; 0.6 \implies \frac{1 - 0.1}{1 - 0.6} \; = \; \frac{9}{4}$

questions.text: All five-letter words formed using all the letters $A,B,C,D,E$ (each once) are arranged as in an English dictionary with serial numbers. Let the word at serial number $n$ be $W_n$ and $P(W_n)$ be its probability, with $P(W_n)=2P(W_{n-1})$ for $n>1$. If $P(CDBEA)=\dfrac{2^{\alpha}}{2^{\beta}-1}$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The probabilities form a geometric progression summing to $1$; find the dictionary rank of CDBEA. // 📝 Solution: $P(W_n)=2^{n-1}P(W_1)$, $P(W_1)=\dfrac{1}{2^{120}-1}$; CDBEA is $W_{64}$ $\implies P=\dfrac{2^{63}}{2^{120}-1} \implies \alpha+\beta=63+120=183$

questions.text: Three identical bags each contain $10$ balls. Bag I has $3$ red, $2$ blue and $5$ green balls; Bag II has $4$ red, $3$ blue and $3$ green balls; Bag III has $5$ red, $1$ blue and $4$ green balls. A bag is chosen at random and a ball is taken out. If the ball is red, the probability that it is from Bag I is $p$; if the ball is green, the probability that it is from Bag III is $q$. Then $\frac1p+\frac1q$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Bayes' theorem with equal priors. // 📝 Solution: $p=\dfrac{3}{3+4+5}=\dfrac14$; $q=\dfrac{4}{5+3+4}=\dfrac13 \implies \dfrac1p+\dfrac1q=4+3=7$

questions.text: The probability of forming a $12$-person committee from $4$ engineers, $2$ doctors and $10$ professors containing at least $3$ engineers and at least $1$ doctor is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count favourable cases by engineer-doctor split over the total $\binom{16}{12}$. // 📝 Solution: $\binom{16}{12}=1820$; favourable $=\binom43\binom21\binom{10}{8}+\binom43\binom22\binom{10}{7}+\binom44\binom21\binom{10}{7}+\binom44\binom22\binom{10}{6}=360+480+240+210=1290 \implies P=\dfrac{1290}{1820}=\dfrac{129}{182}$

questions.text: The coefficients $a, \; b, \; c$ in the quadratic equation $ax^{2} \; + \; bx \; + \; c \; = \; 0$ are chosen from the set $\left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6, \; 7, \; 8\right\}$. The probability of this equation having repeated roots is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A quadratic equation $ax^{2} \; + \; bx \; + \; c \; = \; 0$ has repeated roots if and only if its discriminant $D \; = \; b^{2} \; - \; 4ac \; = \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Total number of ways to choose $a, \; b, \; c \; \in \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6, \; 7, \; 8\right\}$ is $8 \; \times \; 8 \; \times \; 8 \; = \; 512$. For repeated roots, $b^{2} \; = \; 4ac \implies ac \; = \; \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2}$, which requires $b$ to be even. Checking even values of $b$: for $b \; = \; 2$, $ac \; = \; 1 \implies \left(1, \; 2, \; 1\right)$; for $b \; = \; 4$, $ac \; = \; 4 \implies \left(1, \; 4, \; 4\right), \; \left(2, \; 4, \; 2\right), \; \left(4, \; 4, \; 1\right)$; for $b \; = \; 6$, $ac \; = \; 9 \implies \left(3, \; 6, \; 3\right)$; for $b \; = \; 8$, $ac \; = \; 16 \implies \left(2, \; 8, \; 8\right), \; \left(4, \; 8, \; 4\right), \; \left(8, \; 8, \; 2\right)$. This gives a total of $8$ favourable triplets $\left(a, \; b, \; c\right)$. Hence, the required probability is $\frac{8}{8 \; \times \; 8 \; \times \; 8} \; = \; \frac{1}{64}$.

questions.text: A bag contains $6$ balls. Two balls are drawn from it at random and both are found to be black. The probability that the bag contains at least $5$ black balls is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' Theorem assuming that the number of black balls in the bag can be $2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5,$ or $6$ with equal prior probability. // 📝 Solution: Since $2$ black balls are drawn, the bag can contain $2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5,$ or $6$ black balls, each with equal prior probability $\frac{1}{5}$. By Bayes' Theorem, the probability that the bag contains at least $5$ black balls ($5$ or $6$ black balls) is $P \; = \; \frac{{}^{5}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{6}C_{2}}{{}^{2}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{3}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{4}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{5}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{6}C_{2}} \; = \; \frac{10 \; + \; 15}{1 \; + \; 3 \; + \; 6 \; + \; 10 \; + \; 15} \; = \; \frac{25}{35} \; = \; \frac{5}{7}$.

questions.text: Fifteen football players of a club-team are given $15$ T-shirts with their names written on the backside. If the players pick up the T-shirts randomly, then the probability that at least $3$ players pick the correct T-shirt is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the derangement formula $D_{n} \; \approx \; \frac{n!}{e}$ to find the complementary probability that $0, \; 1,$ or $2$ players pick the correct T-shirt. // 📝 Solution: Total ways to distribute $15$ T-shirts is $15!$. The probability that at least $3$ players pick the correct T-shirt is $1 \; - \; \frac{D_{15} \; + \; {}^{15}C_{1} D_{14} \; + \; {}^{15}C_{2} D_{13}}{15!}$. Approximating $D_{n} \; \approx \; \frac{n!}{e}$, we get $1 \; - \; \frac{\frac{15!}{e} \; + \; 15 \; \cdot \; \frac{14!}{e} \; + \; \frac{15 \; \times \; 14}{2} \; \cdot \; \frac{13!}{e}}{15!} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \left(\frac{1}{e} \; + \; \frac{1}{e} \; + \; \frac{1}{2e}\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{5}{2e} \; \approx \; 0.08$ (as per the official answer key, option C is marked correct).

questions.text: Let the sum of two positive integers be $24$. If the probability, that their product is not less than $\frac{3}{4}$ times their greatest possible product, is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $n \; - \; m$ equals
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For two positive integers $x, \; y$ with $x \; + \; y \; = \; 24$, the maximum product is $12 \; \times \; 12 \; = \; 144$, so find the pairs satisfying $xy \; \ge \; \frac{3}{4} \; \times \; 144$. // 📝 Solution: Let the two positive integers be $x$ and $y$ such that $x \; + \; y \; = \; 24$, where $x, \; y \; \in \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 23\right\}$. There are $23$ ordered pairs $\left(x, \; y\right)$. By AM-GM inequality, the greatest possible product is $\left(\frac{24}{2}\right)^{2} \; = \; 144$. We need $xy \; \ge \; \frac{3}{4} \; \times \; 144 \; = \; 108$. Substituting $y \; = \; 24 \; - \; x$, we get $x\left(24 \; - \; x\right) \; \ge \; 108 \implies x^{2} \; - \; 24x \; + \; 108 \; \le \; 0 \implies \left(x \; - \; 6\right)\left(x \; - \; 18\right) \; \le \; 0 \implies x \; \in \; \left\{6, \; 7, \; \dots, \; 18\right\}$. This gives $18 \; - \; 6 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 13$ favourable values of $x$. Thus, the probability is $\frac{m}{n} \; = \; \frac{13}{23}$, and $n \; - \; m \; = \; 23 \; - \; 13 \; = \; 10$.

questions.text: Let Ajay will not appear in JEE exam with probability $p \; = \; \frac{2}{7}$, while both Ajay and Vijay will appear in the exam with probability $q \; = \; \frac{1}{5}$. Then the probability, that Ajay will appear in the exam and Vijay will not appear is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $P\left(A \cap \bar{V}\right) \; = \; P\left(A\right) \; - \; P\left(A \cap V\right)$, where $P\left(A\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; P\left(\bar{A}\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $A$ and $V$ be the events that Ajay and Vijay appear in the exam, respectively. Given $P\left(\bar{A}\right) \; = \; p \; = \; \frac{2}{7}$, so $P\left(A\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{2}{7} \; = \; \frac{5}{7}$. Also given $P\left(A \cap V\right) \; = \; q \; = \; \frac{1}{5}$. Therefore, the probability that Ajay appears and Vijay does not appear is $P\left(A \cap \bar{V}\right) \; = \; P\left(A\right) \; - \; P\left(A \cap V\right) \; = \; \frac{5}{7} \; - \; \frac{1}{5} \; = \; \frac{25 \; - \; 7}{35} \; = \; \frac{18}{35}$.
questions.topic: Addition and Multiplication Theorems of Probability

questions.text: Three distinct numbers are selected randomly from the set $\{1,2,3,\dots,40\}$. If the probability that the selected numbers are in an increasing G.P. (if $r\in\mathbb{N}$) is $\frac{m}{n}$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then $m+n$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count increasing G.P. triples with integer ratio $r$, then divide by $\binom{40}{3}$. // 📝 Solution: $\binom{40}{3}=9880$; $r=2,3,4,5,6$ give $10+4+2+1+1=18$ triples $\implies P=\dfrac{18}{9880}=\dfrac{9}{4940} \implies m+n=4949$

questions.text: From a lot containing $10$ defective and $90$ non-defective bulbs, $8$ bulbs are selected one by one with replacement. Then the probability of getting at least $7$ defective bulbs is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Binomial Distribution with $n \; = \; 8$, $p \; = \; \frac{10}{100} \; = \; \frac{1}{10}$, and $q \; = \; \frac{9}{10}$ to compute $P\left(X \; = \; 7\right) \; + \; P\left(X \; = \; 8\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Since bulbs are selected with replacement, the number of defective bulbs $X$ follows a binomial distribution with $n \; = \; 8$, $p \; = \; \frac{10}{100} \; = \; \frac{1}{10}$, and $q \; = \; \frac{9}{10}$. Then $P\left(X \; \ge \; 7\right) \; = \; P\left(X \; = \; 7\right) \; + \; P\left(X \; = \; 8\right) \; = \; {}^{8}C_{7} \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{7} \left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{1} \; + \; {}^{8}C_{8} \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{8} \; = \; \frac{72}{10^{8}} \; + \; \frac{1}{10^{8}} \; = \; \frac{73}{10^{8}}$.

questions.text: Let $M$ be the maximum value of the product of two positive integers when their sum is $66$. Let the sample space $S \; = \; \left\{x \; \in \; \mathbb{Z} \; : \; x\left(66 \; - \; x\right) \; \ge \; \frac{5}{9}M\right\}$ and the event $A \; = \; \left\{x \; \in \; S \; : \; x \text{ is a multiple of } 3\right\}$. Then $P\left(A\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $M \; = \; 33 \; \times \; 33$, solve the quadratic inequality $x\left(66 \; - \; x\right) \; \ge \; \frac{5}{9}M$ to determine the integers in $S$, and count the multiples of $3$. // 📝 Solution: When the sum of two positive integers is $66$, the maximum value of their product is $M \; = \; 33 \; \times \; 33$. The condition for $S$ is $x\left(66 \; - \; x\right) \; \ge \; \frac{5}{9} \; \times \; 33 \; \times \; 33 \; = \; 605 \implies x^{2} \; - \; 66x \; + \; 605 \; \le \; 0 \implies \left(x \; - \; 11\right)\left(x \; - \; 55\right) \; \le \; 0 \implies 11 \; \le \; x \; \le \; 55$. Since $x \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$, $S$ contains $55 \; - \; 11 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 45$ integers. The multiples of $3$ in $S$ are $A \; = \; \left\{12, \; 15, \; 18, \; \dots, \; 54\right\}$, which has $15$ elements. Therefore, $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{15}{45} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: Two balls are selected at random one by one without replacement from a bag containing 4 white and 6 black balls. If the probability that the first selected ball is black, given that the second selected ball is also black, is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $\gcd\left(m, n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $m + n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use conditional probability $P\left(A \mid B\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(A \cap B\right)}{P\left(B\right)}$. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(B_1 \mid B_2\right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9}}{\frac{4}{10} \cdot \frac{6}{9} + \frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9}} \; = \; \frac{30}{54} \; = \; \frac{5}{9} \implies m + n \; = \; 14$

questions.text: Let $A \; = \; \left[a_{ij}\right]$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix such that $a_{ij} \in \left\{0, 1\right\}$ for all $i$ and $j$. Let the random event $E$ denote that $A$ is an invertible matrix. Then the probability $P\left(E\right)$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count the total matrices and the singular ones among them. // 📝 Solution: $\text{Total} \; = \; 2^4 \; = \; 16 \;,\; \text{singular} \; = \; 10 \implies \text{invertible} \; = \; 6 \implies P\left(E\right) \; = \; \frac{6}{16} \; = \; \frac{3}{8}$

questions.text: Let $S$ be a set of $5$ elements and $P\left(S\right)$ denote the power set of $S$. Let $E$ be an event of choosing an ordered pair $\left(A, \; B\right)$ from the set $P\left(S\right) \; \times \; P\left(S\right)$ such that $A \cap B \; = \; \emptyset$. If the probability of the event $E$ is $\frac{3^{p}}{2^{q}}$, where $p, \; q \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$, then $p \; + \; q$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For each of the $5$ elements in $S$, there are $3$ valid choices for $A \cap B \; = \; \emptyset$ (in $A$ only, in $B$ only, or in neither) out of $4$ total choices. // 📝 Solution: Since $S$ has $5$ elements, the power set $P\left(S\right)$ has $2^{5} \; = \; 32$ subsets, so the total number of ordered pairs $\left(A, \; B\right) \; \in \; P\left(S\right) \; \times \; P\left(S\right)$ is $32^{2} \; = \; 2^{10} \; = \; 1024$. For $A \cap B \; = \; \emptyset$, each of the $5$ elements of $S$ has $3$ independent possibilities: belong to $A$ only, belong to $B$ only, or belong to neither $A$ nor $B$. Thus, the number of favourable ordered pairs is $3^{5} \; = \; 243$. Therefore, $P\left(E\right) \; = \; \frac{3^{5}}{2^{10}} \; = \; \frac{3^{p}}{2^{q}}$, which gives $p \; = \; 5$ and $q \; = \; 10$, so $p \; + \; q \; = \; 15$.

questions.text: A box contains $10$ pens of which $3$ are defective. A sample of $2$ pens is drawn at random and let $X$ denote the number of defective pens. Then the variance of $X$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the distribution of $X$ and compute $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-(E(X))^2$. // 📝 Solution: $P(0)=\frac{7}{15},\ P(1)=\frac{7}{15},\ P(2)=\frac{1}{15} \implies E(X)=\frac35,\ E(X^2)=\frac{11}{15} \implies \operatorname{Var}=\frac{11}{15}-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{28}{75}$

questions.text: There are three bags $X, \; Y$ and $Z$. Bag $X$ contains $5$ one-rupee coins and $4$ five-rupee coins; Bag $Y$ contains $4$ one-rupee coins and $5$ five-rupee coins and Bag $Z$ contains $3$ one-rupee coins and $6$ five-rupee coins. A bag is selected at random and a coin drawn from it at random is found to be a one-rupee coin. Then the probability, that it came from bag $Y$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' Theorem with equal prior probabilities $P\left(X\right) \; = \; P\left(Y\right) \; = \; P\left(Z\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $E$ be the event of drawing a one-rupee coin. Each bag contains $9$ coins in total. The probabilities of drawing a one-rupee coin from bags $X, \; Y, \; Z$ are $P\left(E \mid X\right) \; = \; \frac{5}{9}$, $P\left(E \mid Y\right) \; = \; \frac{4}{9}$, and $P\left(E \mid Z\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{9}$. By Bayes' Theorem, $P\left(Y \mid E\right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{3} \; \cdot \; \frac{4}{9}}{\frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{5}{9} \; + \; \frac{4}{9} \; + \; \frac{3}{9}\right)} \; = \; \frac{4}{5 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 3} \; = \; \frac{4}{12} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: The coefficients $a, \; b, \; c$ in the quadratic equation $ax^{2} \; + \; bx \; + \; c \; = \; 0$ are from the set $\left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6\right\}$. If the probability of this equation having one real root bigger than the other is $p$, then $216 p$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For one real root to be strictly greater than the other, the equation must have two distinct real roots, so $b^{2} \; - \; 4ac \; > \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Total outcomes for $a, \; b, \; c \; \in \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6\right\}$ are $6^{3} \; = \; 216$. We need $b^{2} \; > \; 4ac \implies ac \; < \; \frac{b^{2}}{4}$. Counting favourable pairs $\left(a, \; c\right)$ for each $b$: for $b \; = \; 1, \; 2$, $ac \; < \; 1$ (no cases); for $b \; = \; 3$, $ac \; \le \; 2$ gives $\left(1, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 1\right)$ ($3$ cases); for $b \; = \; 4$, $ac \; \le \; 3$ gives $\left(1, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 3\right), \; \left(3, \; 1\right)$ ($5$ cases); for $b \; = \; 5$, $ac \; \le \; 6$ gives $\left(1, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 3\right), \; \left(3, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 4\right), \; \left(4, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 5\right), \; \left(5, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 6\right), \; \left(6, \; 1\right), \; \left(2, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 3\right), \; \left(3, \; 2\right)$ ($14$ cases); for $b \; = \; 6$, $ac \; \le \; 8$ gives the same $14$ cases plus $\left(2, \; 4\right), \; \left(4, \; 2\right)$ ($16$ cases). Total favourable outcomes $= \; 3 \; + \; 5 \; + \; 14 \; + \; 16 \; = \; 38$. Thus, $p \; = \; \frac{38}{216}$, which gives $216 p \; = \; 38$.

questions.text: An integer is chosen at random from the integers $1, \; 2, \; 3, \; \dots, \; 50$. The probability that the chosen integer is a multiple of atleast one of $4, \; 6$ and $7$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the inclusion-exclusion principle: $P\left(A \cup B \cup C\right) \; = \; P\left(A\right) \; + \; P\left(B\right) \; + \; P\left(C\right) \; - \; P\left(A \cap B\right) \; - \; P\left(B \cap C\right) \; - \; P\left(A \cap C\right) \; + \; P\left(A \cap B \cap C\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $A, \; B, \; C$ be the events that the chosen integer from $\left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 50\right\}$ is a multiple of $4, \; 6, \; 7$ respectively. Then $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{12}{50}$, $P\left(B\right) \; = \; \frac{8}{50}$, and $P\left(C\right) \; = \; \frac{7}{50}$. For intersections, $\operatorname{LCM}\left(4, \; 6\right) \; = \; 12 \implies P\left(A \cap B\right) \; = \; \frac{4}{50}$; $\operatorname{LCM}\left(6, \; 7\right) \; = \; 42 \implies P\left(B \cap C\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{50}$; $\operatorname{LCM}\left(4, \; 7\right) \; = \; 28 \implies P\left(A \cap C\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{50}$; and $\operatorname{LCM}\left(4, \; 6, \; 7\right) \; = \; 84 \implies P\left(A \cap B \cap C\right) \; = \; 0$. By inclusion-exclusion, $P\left(A \cup B \cup C\right) \; = \; \frac{12 \; + \; 8 \; + \; 7 \; - \; 4 \; - \; 1 \; - \; 1 \; + \; 0}{50} \; = \; \frac{21}{50}$.

questions.text: Two numbers $k_1$ and $k_2$ are randomly chosen from the set of natural numbers. Then the probability that the value of $i^{k_1} + i^{k_2}$, $i \; = \; \sqrt{-1}$, is non-zero equals:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Powers of $i$ repeat with period 4, so only the residues of $k_1, k_2$ modulo 4 matter. // 📝 Solution: $i^{k_1} + i^{k_2} \; = \; 0 \iff \left(k_1, k_2\right) \text{ residues } \left(0, 2\right), \left(2, 0\right), \left(1, 3\right), \left(3, 1\right) \implies P\left(\text{zero}\right) \; = \; \frac{4}{16} \; = \; \frac{1}{4} \implies P\left(\text{non-zero}\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{4}$
questions.topic: Probability with Powers of Complex Numbers

questions.text: Bag $B_1$ contains 6 white and 4 blue balls, Bag $B_2$ contains 4 white and 6 blue balls, and Bag $B_3$ contains 5 white and 5 blue balls. One of the bags is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. If the ball is white, then the probability that the ball is drawn from Bag $B_2$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Bayes' theorem with equal prior probabilities for the bags. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(B_2 \mid W\right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{10}}{\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{6}{10} + \frac{4}{10} + \frac{5}{10}\right)} \; = \; \frac{4}{15}$

questions.text: A bag contains $10$ balls out of which $k$ are red and $\left(10 \; - \; k\right)$ are black, where $0 \; \le \; k \; \le \; 10$. If three balls are drawn at random without replacement and all of them are found to be black, then the probability that the bag contains $1$ red and $9$ black balls is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' Theorem with uniform prior $P\left(k\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{11}$ and combinatorial identity $\sum_{k=0}^{7} {}^{10-k}C_{3} \; = \; {}^{11}C_{4}$. // 📝 Solution: Each value of $k \; \in \; \left\{0, \; 1, \; \dots, \; 10\right\}$ is equally likely with $P\left(k\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{11}$. The probability of drawing $3$ black balls given $k$ red balls is $P\left(\text{all } 3 \text{ black} \mid k\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{10-k}C_{3}}{{}^{10}C_{3}}$. For $k \; = \; 1$, this is $\frac{{}^{9}C_{3}}{{}^{10}C_{3}} \; = \; \frac{84}{120}$. By Bayes' Theorem, $P\left(k \; = \; 1 \mid \text{all } 3 \text{ black}\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{9}C_{3}}{\sum_{k=0}^{7} {}^{10-k}C_{3}} \; = \; \frac{84}{120 \; + \; 84 \; + \; 56 \; + \; 35 \; + \; 20 \; + \; 10 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 1} \; = \; \frac{84}{330} \; = \; \frac{14}{55}$.

questions.text: From a lot of $12$ items containing $3$ defectives, a sample of $5$ items is drawn at random. Let the random variable $X$ denote the number of defective items in the sample. Let items in the sample be drawn one by one without replacement. If variance of $X$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $n \; - \; m$ is equal to ______
A fair die is thrown until $2$ appears. Then the probability, that $2$ appears in even number of throws, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Sum the infinite geometric series of probabilities where $2$ appears for the first time on the $2^{\text{nd}}, \; 4^{\text{th}}, \; 6^{\text{th}}, \; \dots$ throw. // 📝 Solution: Let $p \; = \; \frac{1}{6}$ be the probability of getting $2$ in a single throw, and $q \; = \; \frac{5}{6}$ be the probability of not getting $2$. The probability that $2$ appears in an even number of throws ($2^{\text{nd}}, \; 4^{\text{th}}, \; 6^{\text{th}}, \; \dots$) is $P \; = \; q p \; + \; q^{3} p \; + \; q^{5} p \; + \; \dots \; = \; \frac{5}{6} \; \times \; \frac{1}{6} \; + \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3} \; \times \; \frac{1}{6} \; + \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{5} \; \times \; \frac{1}{6} \; + \; \dots \; = \; \frac{\frac{5}{36}}{1 \; - \; \frac{25}{36}} \; = \; \frac{5}{11}$.

questions.text: Three balls are drawn at random from a bag containing $5$ blue and $4$ yellow balls. Let the random variables $X$ and $Y$ respectively denote the number of blue and yellow balls. If $\bar{X}$ and $\bar{Y}$ are the means of $X$ and $Y$ respectively, then $7\bar{X} \; + \; 4\bar{Y}$ is equal to ______
Two distinct numbers $a$ and $b$ are selected at random from $1, \; 2, \; 3, \; \dots, \; 50$. The probability, that their product $ab$ is divisible by $3$, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The product $ab$ is divisible by $3$ unless neither $a$ nor $b$ is a multiple of $3$; use complementary probability. // 📝 Solution: Total ways to select $2$ distinct numbers from $50$ is ${}^{50}C_{2} \; = \; 1225$. Among $\left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 50\right\}$, the multiples of $3$ are $3, \; 6, \; \dots, \; 48$, which gives $16$ numbers, leaving $50 \; - \; 16 \; = \; 34$ numbers that are not divisible by $3$. The probability that neither $a$ nor $b$ is divisible by $3$ is $\frac{{}^{34}C_{2}}{{}^{50}C_{2}} \; = \; \frac{561}{1225}$. Hence, the probability that $ab$ is divisible by $3$ is $1 \; - \; \frac{561}{1225} \; = \; \frac{664}{1225}$.

questions.text: If an unbiased dice is rolled thrice, then the probability of getting a greater number in the $i^{\text{th}}$ roll than the number obtained in the $\left(i \; - \; 1\right)^{\text{th}}$ roll, $i \; = \; 2, \; 3$, is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Any selection of $3$ distinct numbers from $\left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6\right\}$ can be arranged in strictly increasing order in exactly $1$ way. // 📝 Solution: Total outcomes when an unbiased die is rolled thrice $= \; 6^{3} \; = \; 216$. We require $x_{1} \; < \; x_{2} \; < \; x_{3}$, where $x_{1}, \; x_{2}, \; x_{3}$ are the outcomes of the $1^{\text{st}}, \; 2^{\text{nd}}, \; 3^{\text{rd}}$ rolls respectively. The number of ways to choose $3$ distinct numbers from $6$ is ${}^{6}C_{3} \; = \; 20$, and each selection corresponds to a unique strictly increasing sequence. Hence, the required probability is $\frac{{}^{6}C_{3}}{6^{3}} \; = \; \frac{20}{216} \; = \; \frac{5}{54}$.

questions.text: Let a random variable $X$ take values $0,1,2,3$ with $P(X=0)=P(X=1)=p$, $P(X=2)=P(X=3)$ and $E(X^2)=2E(X)$. Then the value of $8p-1$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Let $P(X=2)=P(X=3)=q$ with $2p+2q=1$ and use the given expectation relation. // 📝 Solution: $E(X)=p+5q,\ E(X^2)=p+13q \implies p+13q=2p+10q \implies p=3q \implies q=\frac18,\ p=\frac38 \implies 8p-1=2$

questions.text: Two dice are thrown independently. Let $A$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is less than the number appeared on the $2^{\text{nd}}$ die, $B$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is even and that on the second die is odd, and $C$ be the event that the number appeared on the $1^{\text{st}}$ die is odd and that on the $2^{\text{nd}}$ is even. Then

options.text: the number of favourable cases of the event $\left(A \cup B\right) \cap C$ is $6$
The number of favourable cases of the events $A, \; B$ and $C$ are $15, \; 6$ and $6$ respectively

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the distributive law $\left(A \cup B\right) \cap C \; = \; \left(A \cap C\right) \cup \left(B \cap C\right)$ and note that $B$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive. // 📝 Solution: Let $\left(x, \; y\right)$ denote the outcomes on the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ dice. Event $A \; = \; \left\{\left(x, \; y\right) \; : \; x \; < \; y\right\}$ has $5 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 3 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 15$ outcomes. Event $B \; = \; \left\{\left(x, \; y\right) \; : \; x \text{ is even}, \; y \text{ is odd}\right\}$ has $3 \; \times \; 3 \; = \; 9$ outcomes, and Event $C \; = \; \left\{\left(x, \; y\right) \; : \; x \text{ is odd}, \; y \text{ is even}\right\}$ also has $3 \; \times \; 3 \; = \; 9$ outcomes. Clearly, $B \cap C \; = \; \phi$. Thus, $\left(A \cup B\right) \cap C \; = \; \left(A \cap C\right) \cup \left(B \cap C\right) \; = \; A \cap C$. Favourable cases for $A \cap C$ ($x$ odd, $y$ even, $x \; < \; y$) are $\left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(1, \; 4\right), \; \left(1, \; 6\right), \; \left(3, \; 4\right), \; \left(3, \; 6\right), \; \left(5, \; 6\right)$, which gives $3 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 6$ cases.

questions.text: If an unbiased die, marked with $-2, \; -1, \; 0, \; 1, \; 2, \; 3$ on its faces, is thrown five times, then the probability that the product of the outcomes is positive, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For the product of $5$ outcomes to be positive, $0$ must not appear and the number of negative outcomes must be $0, \; 2,$ or $4$. // 📝 Solution: On a single throw of the die, the probability of getting a positive number ($1, \; 2, \; 3$) is $p \; = \; \frac{3}{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$, and the probability of getting a negative number ($-2, \; -1$) is $q \; = \; \frac{2}{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. For the product of $5$ throws to be positive, either all $5$ outcomes are positive, or $2$ are negative and $3$ are positive, or $4$ are negative and $1$ is positive. Thus, the required probability is ${}^{5}C_{5} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{5} \; + \; {}^{5}C_{2} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} \; + \; {}^{5}C_{4} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{4} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1} \; = \; \frac{1}{32} \; + \; \frac{10}{72} \; + \; \frac{5}{162} \; = \; \frac{81 \; + \; 360 \; + \; 80}{2592} \; = \; \frac{521}{2592}$.

questions.text: An urn contains $6$ white and $9$ black balls. Two successive draws of $4$ balls are made without replacement. The probability, that the first draw gives all white balls and the second draw gives all black balls, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the multiplication theorem of probability: $P\left(A \cap B\right) \; = \; P\left(A\right) \; \cdot \; P\left(B \mid A\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Total balls initially $= \; 6 \; + \; 9 \; = \; 15$. Let $A$ be the event of drawing $4$ white balls in the first draw, and $B$ be the event of drawing $4$ black balls in the second draw. Then $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{6}C_{4}}{{}^{15}C_{4}} \; = \; \frac{15}{1365} \; = \; \frac{1}{91}$. After removing $4$ white balls, $11$ balls remain ($2$ white and $9$ black), so $P\left(B \mid A\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{9}C_{4}}{{}^{11}C_{4}} \; = \; \frac{126}{330} \; = \; \frac{21}{55}$. Thus, the required probability is $\frac{{}^{6}C_{4}}{{}^{15}C_{4}} \; \times \; \frac{{}^{9}C_{4}}{{}^{11}C_{4}} \; = \; \frac{1}{91} \; \times \; \frac{21}{55} \; = \; \frac{3}{715}$.

questions.text: In a binomial distribution $B\left(n, \; p\right)$, the sum and product of the mean & variance are $5$ and $6$ respectively, then find $6\left(n \; + \; p \; - \; q\right)$ is equal to :-
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\text{Mean} \; = \; np$ and $\text{Variance} \; = \; npq$ with $np \; > \; npq$ to find $n, \; p,$ and $q$. // 📝 Solution: Given $np \; + \; npq \; = \; 5$ and $np \; \cdot \; npq \; = \; 6$. Since $0 \; < \; q \; < \; 1$, we have $np \; > \; npq$, which immediately gives $np \; = \; 3$ and $npq \; = \; 2$. Dividing the two equations gives $q \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$, so $p \; = \; 1 \; - \; q \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Substituting $p \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$ into $np \; = \; 3$ gives $n \; = \; 9$. Therefore, $6\left(n \; + \; p \; - \; q\right) \; = \; 6\left(9 \; + \; \frac{1}{3} \; - \; \frac{2}{3}\right) \; = \; 54 \; - \; 2 \; = \; 52$.

questions.text: Bag 1 contains 4 white and 5 black balls, and Bag 2 contains $n$ white and 3 black balls. One ball is drawn from Bag 1 and transferred to Bag 2. A ball is then drawn from Bag 2. If the probability that the ball drawn is white is $\frac{29}{45}$, then $n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the total probability theorem over the colour of the transferred ball. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{n + 1}{n + 4} + \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{n}{n + 4} \; = \; \frac{9n + 4}{9n + 36} \; = \; \frac{29}{45} \implies 45n + 20 \; = \; 29n + 116 \implies n \; = \; 6$

questions.text: Two integers $x$ and $y$ are chosen with replacement from the set $\left\{0, \; 1, \; 2, \; 3, \; \dots, \; 10\right\}$. Then the probability that $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; > \; 5$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count the pairs $\left(x, \; y\right)$ with $y \; - \; x \; > \; 5$ and multiply by $2$ due to symmetry. // 📝 Solution: Since $x$ and $y$ are chosen with replacement from $11$ integers $\left\{0, \; 1, \; \dots, \; 10\right\}$, total outcomes $= \; 11 \; \times \; 11 \; = \; 121$. For $y \; - \; x \; > \; 5$: if $x \; = \; 0$, $y \; \in \; \left\{6, \; 7, \; 8, \; 9, \; 10\right\}$ ($5$ ways); if $x \; = \; 1$, $y \; \in \; \left\{7, \; 8, \; 9, \; 10\right\}$ ($4$ ways); if $x \; = \; 2$, $y \; \in \; \left\{8, \; 9, \; 10\right\}$ ($3$ ways); if $x \; = \; 3$, $y \; \in \; \left\{9, \; 10\right\}$ ($2$ ways); if $x \; = \; 4$, $y \; = \; 10$ ($1$ way). By symmetry for $x \; - \; y \; > \; 5$, total favourable outcomes $= \; 2 \; \times \; \left(5 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 3 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 1\right) \; = \; 30$. Hence, the required probability is $\frac{30}{121}$.

questions.text: Let $A \; = \; \left[a_{ij}\right]$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix with $a_{ij} \in \left\{0, 1\right\}$. Let the random variable $X$ denote the possible values of the determinant of $A$. Then the variance of $X$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the probability distribution of $\det A$ over the 16 matrices and use $\operatorname{Var}\left(X\right) \; = \; E\left(X^2\right) - \left[E\left(X\right)\right]^2$. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(X = 0\right) \; = \; \frac{10}{16} \;,\; P\left(X = 1\right) \; = \; P\left(X = -1\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{16} \implies E\left(X\right) \; = \; 0 \;,\; E\left(X^2\right) \; = \; \frac{6}{16} \implies \operatorname{Var}\left(X\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{8}$
questions.topic: Variance of a Discrete Random Variable (Determinant)

questions.text: A coin is tossed three times. Let $X$ denote the number of times a tail follows a head. If $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ denote the mean and variance of $X$, then the value of $64\left(\mu + \sigma^2\right)$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: List the outcomes of three tosses and count the occurrences of the pattern HT. // 📝 Solution: $X \; = \; 1 \text{ for HHT, HTH, HTT, THT} \implies P\left(X = 1\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \implies \mu \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \;,\; \sigma^2 \; = \; \frac{1}{4} \implies 64 \cdot \frac{3}{4} \; = \; 48$

questions.text: Let $N$ be the sum of the numbers appeared when two fair dice are rolled and let the probability that $N \; - \; 2, \; \sqrt{3N}, \; N \; + \; 2$ are in geometric progression be $\frac{k}{48}$. Then the value of $k$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the G.P. condition $\left(\sqrt{3N}\right)^{2} \; = \; \left(N \; - \; 2\right)\left(N \; + \; 2\right)$ to find $N$, and then find the probability of getting that sum with two dice. // 📝 Solution: Total outcomes when two fair dice are rolled is $n\left(S\right) \; = \; 36$. Since $N \; - \; 2, \; \sqrt{3N}, \; N \; + \; 2$ are in G.P., we have $3N \; = \; \left(N \; - \; 2\right)\left(N \; + \; 2\right) \; = \; N^{2} \; - \; 4 \implies N^{2} \; - \; 3N \; - \; 4 \; = \; 0 \implies \left(N \; - \; 4\right)\left(N \; + \; 1\right) \; = \; 0$. Since the sum $N \; \ge \; 2$, $N \; = \; -1$ is rejected and $N \; = \; 4$. The outcomes giving a sum of $4$ are $\left\{\left(1, \; 3\right), \; \left(3, \; 1\right), \; \left(2, \; 2\right)\right\}$, so $n\left(A\right) \; = \; 3$. Thus, the probability is $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{36} \; = \; \frac{1}{12} \; = \; \frac{4}{48} \; = \; \frac{k}{48} \implies k \; = \; 4$.

questions.text: If $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.7$, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(A\cap\overline{B})=0.5$, where $\overline{B}$ denotes the complement of $B$, then $P\big(B\mid(A\cup\overline{B})\big)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Note $B\cap(A\cup\overline{B})=A\cap B$ and use inclusion-exclusion. // 📝 Solution: $P(A\cap B)=0.7-0.5=0.2$; $P(A\cup\overline{B})=0.7+0.6-0.5=0.8 \implies P=\dfrac{0.2}{0.8}=\dfrac14$

questions.text: A company has two plants $A$ and $B$ to manufacture motorcycles. $60\%$ motorcycles are manufactured at plant $A$ and the remaining are manufactured at plant $B$. $80\%$ of the motorcycles manufactured at plant $A$ are rated of the standard quality, while $90\%$ of the motorcycles manufactured at plant $B$ are rated of the standard quality. A motorcycle picked up randomly from the total production is found to be of the standard quality. If $p$ is the probability that it was manufactured at plant $B$, then $126p$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Bayes' Theorem to find the posterior probability $P\left(B \mid S\right)$ where $S$ is the event of picking a standard quality motorcycle. // 📝 Solution: Let $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ be the events that the motorcycle is manufactured at plant $B$ and plant $A$ respectively, and $S$ be the event that it is of standard quality. Given $P\left(E_{1}\right) \; = \; \frac{40}{100}$, $P\left(E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{60}{100}$, $P\left(S \mid E_{1}\right) \; = \; \frac{90}{100}$, and $P\left(S \mid E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{80}{100}$. By Bayes' Theorem, $p \; = \; P\left(E_{1} \mid S\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(S \mid E_{1}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(S \mid E_{1}\right) \; + \; P\left(E_{2}\right) \; P\left(S \mid E_{2}\right)} \; = \; \frac{40 \; \times \; 90}{40 \; \times \; 90 \; + \; 60 \; \times \; 80} \; = \; \frac{3600}{3600 \; + \; 4800} \; = \; \frac{3600}{8400} \; = \; \frac{3}{7}$. Therefore, $126p \; = \; 126 \; \times \; \frac{3}{7} \; = \; 54$.

questions.text: A bag contains six balls of different colours. Two balls are drawn in succession with replacement. The probability that both the balls are of the same colour is $p$. Next four balls are drawn in succession with replacement and the probability that exactly three balls are of the same colour is $q$. If $p \; : \; q \; = \; m \; : \; n$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime, then $m \; + \; n$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Calculate $p \; = \; \frac{6}{6^{2}}$ and $q \; = \; \frac{{}^{6}C_{1} \; \times \; {}^{5}C_{1} \; \times \; 4}{6^{4}}$ using multinomial/binomial selection with replacement. // 📝 Solution: When $2$ balls are drawn with replacement from $6$ different coloured balls, the probability that both have the same colour is $p \; = \; \frac{{}^{6}C_{1}}{6 \; \times \; 6} \; = \; \frac{1}{6}$. When $4$ balls are drawn with replacement, the probability that exactly $3$ balls are of the same colour and $1$ is of a different colour is $q \; = \; \frac{{}^{6}C_{1} \; \times \; {}^{5}C_{1} \; \times \; {}^{4}C_{3}}{6 \; \times \; 6 \; \times \; 6 \; \times \; 6} \; = \; \frac{6 \; \times \; 5 \; \times \; 4}{6^{4}} \; = \; \frac{5}{54}$. Therefore, $p \; : \; q \; = \; \frac{1}{6} \; : \; \frac{5}{54} \; = \; 9 \; : \; 5 \; = \; m \; : \; n$, which gives $m \; + \; n \; = \; 9 \; + \; 5 \; = \; 14$.

questions.text: $25\%$ of the population are smokers. A smoker has $27$ times more chances to develop lung cancer than a non-smoker. A person is diagnosed with lung cancer and the probability that this person is a smoker is $\frac{k}{10}$. Then the value of $k$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' Theorem with $P\left(E_{1}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{4}$, $P\left(E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{4}$, and $P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right) \; = \; 27 P\left(E \mid E_{2}\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $E_{1}$ be the event that a person is a smoker, $E_{2}$ be the event that a person is a non-smoker, and $E$ be the event that the person is diagnosed with lung cancer. Given $P\left(E_{1}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{4}$, $P\left(E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{4}$, and $\frac{P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right)}{P\left(E \mid E_{2}\right)} \; = \; 27$. By Bayes' Theorem, $P\left(E_{1} \mid E\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right) \; + \; P\left(E_{2}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{2}\right)} \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{4} \; \times \; 27}{\frac{1}{4} \; \times \; 27 \; + \; \frac{3}{4} \; \times \; 1} \; = \; \frac{27}{30} \; = \; \frac{9}{10} \; = \; \frac{k}{10} \implies k \; = \; 9$.

questions.text: One die has two faces marked 1, two faces marked 2, one face marked 3 and one face marked 4. Another die has one face marked 1, two faces marked 2, two faces marked 3 and one face marked 4. The probability of getting the sum of numbers to be 4 or 5, when both the dice are thrown together, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count favourable weighted outcomes out of the 36 equally likely face pairs. // 📝 Solution: $\text{Sum } 4: \; 4 + 4 + 1 \; = \; 9 \;,\; \text{Sum } 5: \; 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 \; = \; 9 \implies P \; = \; \frac{18}{36} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$

questions.text: If three letters can be posted to any one of the $5$ different addresses, then the probability that the three letters are posted to exactly two addresses is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Select $2$ addresses out of $5$ in ${}^{5}C_{2}$ ways and distribute the $3$ letters such that neither of the $2$ addresses is empty. // 📝 Solution: Each of the $3$ letters can be posted to any of the $5$ addresses, so the total number of ways is $5^{3} \; = \; 125$. The number of ways to choose $2$ addresses out of $5$ is ${}^{5}C_{2} \; = \; 10$. For a chosen pair of addresses, the number of ways to post the $3$ letters so that both addresses receive at least one letter is $2^{3} \; - \; 2 \; = \; 6$. Thus, the number of favourable ways is ${}^{5}C_{2} \left(2^{3} \; - \; 2\right) \; = \; 10 \; \times \; 6 \; = \; 60$. The required probability is $\frac{60}{125} \; = \; \frac{12}{25}$.

questions.text: Let $N$ denote the number that turns up when a fair die is rolled. If the probability that the system of equations $x \; + \; y \; + \; z \; = \; 1$, $2x \; + \; Ny \; + \; 2z \; = \; 2$, $3x \; + \; 3y \; + \; Nz \; = \; 3$ has unique solution is $\frac{k}{6}$, then the sum of value of $k$ and all possible values of $N$ is

A and B alternately throw a pair of dice. A wins if he throws a sum of 5 before B throws a sum of 8, and B wins if he throws a sum of 8 before A throws a sum of 5. The probability, that A wins if A makes the first throw, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the infinite geometric series for alternate trials. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{4}{36} \;,\; P\left(B\right) \; = \; \frac{5}{36} \implies P\left(\text{A wins}\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(A\right)}{1 - P\left(\bar{A}\right)P\left(\bar{B}\right)} \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{9}}{1 - \frac{8}{9} \cdot \frac{31}{36}} \; = \; \frac{9}{19}$

questions.text: The probability distribution of a random variable $X$ is given below : $X$ takes values $4k, \; \frac{30}{7}k, \; \frac{32}{7}k, \; \frac{34}{7}k, \; \frac{36}{7}k, \; \frac{38}{7}k, \; \frac{40}{7}k, \; 6k$ with probabilities $P\left(X\right) \; = \; \frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{1}{15}, \; \frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{1}{5}, \; \frac{1}{15}, \; \frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{1}{5}, \; \frac{1}{15}$ respectively. If $E\left(X\right) \; = \; \frac{263}{15}$, then $P\left(X \; < \; 20\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $E\left(X\right) \; = \; \sum X_{i} P\left(X_{i}\right) \; = \; \frac{263}{15}$ to solve for $k$, then sum the probabilities for which $X \; < \; 20$. // 📝 Solution: Expressing all values of $X$ with denominator $7$, $X$ takes values $\frac{28k}{7}, \; \frac{30k}{7}, \; \frac{32k}{7}, \; \frac{34k}{7}, \; \frac{36k}{7}, \; \frac{38k}{7}, \; \frac{40k}{7}, \; \frac{42k}{7}$ with probabilities $\frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{1}{15}, \; \frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{3}{15}, \; \frac{1}{15}, \; \frac{2}{15}, \; \frac{3}{15}, \; \frac{1}{15}$. Then $E\left(X\right) \; = \; \frac{k}{7 \; \times \; 15} \left(56 \; + \; 30 \; + \; 64 \; + \; 102 \; + \; 36 \; + \; 76 \; + \; 120 \; + \; 42\right) \; = \; \frac{526k}{7 \; \times \; 15} \; = \; \frac{263}{15} \implies k \; = \; \frac{7}{2}$. Substituting $k \; = \; \frac{7}{2}$, the values of $X$ become $14, \; 15, \; 16, \; 17, \; 18, \; 19, \; 20, \; 21$. Thus, $P\left(X \; < \; 20\right) \; = \; P\left(14\right) \; + \; P\left(15\right) \; + \; P\left(16\right) \; + \; P\left(17\right) \; + \; P\left(18\right) \; + \; P\left(19\right) \; = \; \frac{2}{15} \; + \; \frac{1}{15} \; + \; \frac{2}{15} \; + \; \frac{1}{5} \; + \; \frac{1}{15} \; + \; \frac{2}{15} \; = \; \frac{11}{15}$.

questions.text: A board has 16 squares as shown in the figure. [FIGURE] Out of these 16 squares, two squares are chosen at random. The probability that they have no side in common is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Subtract the number of side-sharing pairs from the total number of pairs. // 📝 Solution: $\text{Total} \; = \; {}^{16}C_2 \; = \; 120 \;,\; \text{adjacent pairs} \; = \; 3 \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 4 \; = \; 24 \implies \text{favourable} \; = \; 96 \implies P \; = \; \frac{96}{120} \; = \; \frac{4}{5}$

questions.text: Let $a, \; b$ and $c$ denote the outcome of three independent rolls of a fair tetrahedral die, whose four faces are marked $1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4$. If the probability that $ax^{2} \; + \; bx \; + \; c \; = \; 0$ has all real roots is $\frac{m}{n}$, $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $m \; + \; n$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $ax^{2} \; + \; bx \; + \; c \; = \; 0$ to have all real roots, the discriminant must satisfy $b^{2} \; - \; 4ac \; \ge \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Total outcomes for $\left(a, \; b, \; c\right) \; \in \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4\right\}^{3}$ are $4^{3} \; = \; 64$. For real roots, $b^{2} \; \ge \; 4ac \implies ac \; \le \; \frac{b^{2}}{4}$. Checking for each value of $b$: for $b \; = \; 1$, $ac \; \le \; \frac{1}{4}$ (no cases); for $b \; = \; 2$, $ac \; \le \; 1 \implies \left(a, \; c\right) \; = \; \left(1, \; 1\right)$ ($1$ case); for $b \; = \; 3$, $ac \; \le \; \frac{9}{4} \implies \left(a, \; c\right) \; \in \; \left\{\left(1, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 1\right)\right\}$ ($3$ cases); for $b \; = \; 4$, $ac \; \le \; 4 \implies \left(a, \; c\right) \; \in \; \left\{\left(1, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 2\right), \; \left(2, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 3\right), \; \left(3, \; 1\right), \; \left(1, \; 4\right), \; \left(4, \; 1\right), \; \left(2, \; 2\right)\right\}$ ($8$ cases). Total favourable outcomes $= \; 0 \; + \; 1 \; + \; 3 \; + \; 8 \; = \; 12$. Thus, the probability is $\frac{m}{n} \; = \; \frac{12}{64} \; = \; \frac{3}{16}$, and $m \; + \; n \; = \; 3 \; + \; 16 \; = \; 19$.

questions.text: Let $S$ be the set of all words that can be formed by arranging all the letters of the word GARDEN. From the set $S$, one word is selected at random. The probability that the selected word will NOT have vowels in the alphabetical order is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The two vowels A and E are equally likely to appear in either relative order. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(\text{vowels in alphabetical order}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \implies P\left(\text{not in order}\right) \; = \; 1 - \frac{1}{2} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$

questions.text: From the first $100$ natural numbers, two numbers first $a$ and then $b$ are selected randomly without replacement. If the probability that $a \; - \; b \; \ge \; 10$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $m \; + \; n$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For each $b \; \in \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 90\right\}$, count the valid choices of $a \; \in \; \left\{b \; + \; 10, \; \dots, \; 100\right\}$ and divide by total ordered pairs $100 \; \times \; 99$. // 📝 Solution: Total ordered selections of $\left(a, \; b\right)$ without replacement from $\left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 100\right\}$ is $100 \; \times \; 99 \; = \; 9900$. For $a \; - \; b \; \ge \; 10 \implies a \; \ge \; b \; + \; 10$, as $b$ ranges from $1$ to $90$, $a$ can take values from $b \; + \; 10$ to $100$, giving $91 \; - \; b$ choices for each $b$. Thus, the number of favourable outcomes is $\sum_{b=1}^{90} \left(91 \; - \; b\right) \; = \; \sum_{k=1}^{90} k \; = \; \frac{90 \; \times \; 91}{2} \; = \; 4095$. Therefore, the probability is $\frac{4095}{9900} \; = \; \frac{91}{220} \; = \; \frac{m}{n}$. Since $\gcd\left(91, \; 220\right) \; = \; 1$, we have $m \; = \; 91$ and $n \; = \; 220$, so $m \; + \; n \; = \; 311$.

questions.text: Let the mean and the standard deviation of the probability distribution where $X$ takes values $\alpha, \; 1, \; 0, \; -3$ with probabilities $P\left(X\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3}, \; K, \; \frac{1}{6}, \; \frac{1}{4}$ respectively, be $\mu$ and $\sigma$, respectively. If $\sigma \; - \; \mu \; = \; 2$, then $\sigma \; + \; \mu$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sum P\left(X\right) \; = \; 1$ to find $K$, and then apply $\mu \; = \; E\left(X\right)$ and $\sigma^{2} \; = \; E\left(X^{2}\right) \; - \; \mu^{2}$. // 📝 Solution: Since the sum of probabilities is $1$, we have $\frac{1}{3} \; + \; K \; + \; \frac{1}{6} \; + \; \frac{1}{4} \; = \; 1 \implies K \; = \; \frac{1}{4}$. Now, the mean is $\mu \; = \; \alpha \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \; + \; 1 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \; + \; 0 \left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \; - \; 3 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \; = \; \frac{\alpha}{3} \; - \; \frac{1}{2}$. Also, $E\left(X^{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{\alpha^{2}}{3} \; + \; \frac{1}{4} \; + \; 0 \; + \; \frac{9}{4} \; = \; \frac{\alpha^{2}}{3} \; + \; \frac{5}{2}$. Given $\sigma \; - \; \mu \; = \; 2 \implies \sigma \; = \; \mu \; + \; 2 \implies \sigma^{2} \; = \; \left(\mu \; + \; 2\right)^{2} \; = \; \mu^{2} \; + \; 4\mu \; + \; 4$. Using $\sigma^{2} \; + \; \mu^{2} \; = \; E\left(X^{2}\right)$, we get $2\mu^{2} \; + \; 4\mu \; + \; 4 \; = \; \frac{\alpha^{2}}{3} \; + \; \frac{5}{2}$. Substituting $\mu \; = \; \frac{\alpha}{3} \; - \; \frac{1}{2}$, we obtain $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{9} \; - \; \frac{2\alpha}{3} \; = \; 0 \implies \alpha \; = \; 0$ or $\alpha \; = \; 6$. Since $X \; = \; 0$ is already a distinct value in the distribution, $\alpha \; = \; 6$. Thus, $\mu \; = \; \frac{6}{3} \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$, and $\sigma \; + \; \mu \; = \; 2\mu \; + \; 2 \; = \; 3 \; + \; 2 \; = \; 5$.

questions.text: Three urns $A, \; B$ and $C$ contain $7$ red, $5$ black; $5$ red, $7$ black and $6$ red, $6$ black balls, respectively. One of the urn is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. If the ball drawn is black, then the probability that it is drawn from urn $A$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' Theorem: $P\left(A \mid E\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(A\right) \; P\left(E \mid A\right)}{P\left(A\right) \; P\left(E \mid A\right) \; + \; P\left(B\right) \; P\left(E \mid B\right) \; + \; P\left(C\right) \; P\left(E \mid C\right)}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $E$ be the event of drawing a black ball, and $A, \; B, \; C$ be the events of selecting urn $A, \; B, \; C$ respectively. Since an urn is chosen at random, $P\left(A\right) \; = \; P\left(B\right) \; = \; P\left(C\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. The conditional probabilities of drawing a black ball are $P\left(E \mid A\right) \; = \; \frac{5}{12}$, $P\left(E \mid B\right) \; = \; \frac{7}{12}$, and $P\left(E \mid C\right) \; = \; \frac{6}{12}$. By Bayes' Theorem, $P\left(A \mid E\right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{3} \; \cdot \; \frac{5}{12}}{\frac{1}{3} \; \cdot \; \left[\frac{5}{12} \; + \; \frac{7}{12} \; + \; \frac{6}{12}\right]} \; = \; \frac{5}{5 \; + \; 7 \; + \; 6} \; = \; \frac{5}{18}$.

questions.text: If a random variable $x$ has the probability distribution where $x$ takes values $0, \; 1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5, \; 6, \; 7$ with probabilities $P\left(x\right) \; = \; 0, \; 2k, \; k, \; 3k, \; 2k^{2}, \; 2k, \; k^{2} \; + \; k, \; 7k^{2}$ respectively, then $P\left(3 \; < \; x \; \le \; 6\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sum P\left(x\right) \; = \; 1$ with $k \; > \; 0$ to find $k$, then compute $P\left(4\right) \; + \; P\left(5\right) \; + \; P\left(6\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Since the sum of all probabilities is $1$, we have $0 \; + \; 2k \; + \; k \; + \; 3k \; + \; 2k^{2} \; + \; 2k \; + \; \left(k^{2} \; + \; k\right) \; + \; 7k^{2} \; = \; 1 \implies 10k^{2} \; + \; 9k \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies \left(10k \; - \; 1\right)\left(k \; + \; 1\right) \; = \; 0$. Since probabilities must be non-negative, we reject $k \; = \; -1$ and get $k \; = \; \frac{1}{10} \; = \; 0.1$. Now, $P\left(3 \; < \; x \; \le \; 6\right) \; = \; P\left(4\right) \; + \; P\left(5\right) \; + \; P\left(6\right) \; = \; 2k^{2} \; + \; 2k \; + \; k^{2} \; + \; k \; = \; 3k^{2} \; + \; 3k \; = \; 3\left(0.01\right) \; + \; 3\left(0.1\right) \; = \; 0.33$.

questions.text: Two marbles are drawn in succession from a box containing $10$ red, $30$ white, $20$ blue and $15$ orange marbles, with replacement being made after each drawing. Then the probability, that first drawn marble is red and second drawn marble is white, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since drawings are made with replacement, the two events are independent, so multiply their individual probabilities. // 📝 Solution: Total number of marbles in the box $= \; 10 \; + \; 30 \; + \; 20 \; + \; 15 \; = \; 75$. The probability of drawing a red marble in the first draw is $\frac{10}{75}$, and since it is replaced, the probability of drawing a white marble in the second draw is $\frac{30}{75}$. Therefore, the required probability is $\frac{10}{75} \; \times \; \frac{30}{75} \; = \; \frac{2}{15} \; \times \; \frac{2}{5} \; = \; \frac{4}{75}$.

questions.text: Let $S \; = \; \left\{w_{1}, \; w_{2}, \; \dots\right\}$ be the sample space associated to a random experiment. Let $P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(w_{n-1}\right)}{2}, \; n \; \ge \; 2$. Let $A \; = \; \left\{2k \; + \; 3\ell \; ; \; k, \; \ell \; \in \; \mathbb{N}\right\}$ and $B \; = \; \left\{w_{n} \; : \; n \; \in \; A\right\}$. Then $P\left(B\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2^{n}}$ using $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; 1$, identify the positive integers not in $A$, and use complementary probability. // 📝 Solution: Let $P\left(w_{1}\right) \; = \; \lambda$; then $P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; \frac{\lambda}{2^{n-1}}$. Since $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; 1 \implies \frac{\lambda}{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{2}} \; = \; 1 \implies \lambda \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$, so $P\left(w_{n}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2^{n}}$. For $k, \; \ell \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \; = \; \left\{2k \; + \; 3\ell \; : \; k, \; \ell \; \in \; \mathbb{N}\right\} \; = \; \left\{5, \; 7, \; 8, \; 9, \; 10, \; 11, \; \dots\right\} \; = \; \mathbb{N} \; - \; \left\{1, \; 2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 6\right\}$. Therefore, $P\left(B\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; \left[P\left(w_{1}\right) \; + \; P\left(w_{2}\right) \; + \; P\left(w_{3}\right) \; + \; P\left(w_{4}\right) \; + \; P\left(w_{6}\right)\right] \; = \; 1 \; - \; \left[\frac{1}{2} \; + \; \frac{1}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{8} \; + \; \frac{1}{16} \; + \; \frac{1}{64}\right] \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{32 \; + \; 16 \; + \; 8 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 1}{64} \; = \; \frac{3}{64}$.

questions.text: Bag $A$ contains $9$ white and $8$ black balls, while bag $B$ contains $6$ white and $4$ black balls. One ball is randomly picked up from the bag $B$ and mixed up with the balls in the bag $A$. Then a ball is randomly drawn from the bag $A$. If the probability, that the ball drawn is white, is $\frac{p}{q}$, $\gcd\left(p, \; q\right) \; = \; 1$, then $p \; + \; q$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the Law of Total Probability considering the two cases: transferring a white ball or transferring a black ball from bag $B$ to bag $A$. // 📝 Solution: Bag $A$ initially has $9$ white and $8$ black balls ($17$ total), and bag $B$ has $6$ white and $4$ black balls ($10$ total). Case 1: A white ball is transferred from $B$ to $A$ with probability $\frac{6}{10}$, making bag $A$ have $10$ white and $8$ black balls; then the probability of drawing a white ball from $A$ is $\frac{10}{18} \; = \; \frac{5}{9}$. Case 2: A black ball is transferred from $B$ to $A$ with probability $\frac{4}{10}$, making bag $A$ have $9$ white and $9$ black balls; then the probability of drawing a white ball from $A$ is $\frac{9}{18} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. By Total Probability, $P\left(\text{white from } A\right) \; = \; \frac{6}{10} \; \cdot \; \frac{5}{9} \; + \; \frac{4}{10} \; \cdot \; \frac{1}{2} \; = \; \frac{1}{3} \; + \; \frac{1}{5} \; = \; \frac{8}{15} \; = \; \frac{p}{q}$. Since $\gcd\left(8, \; 15\right) \; = \; 1$, $p \; + \; q \; = \; 8 \; + \; 15 \; = \; 23$.

questions.text: If the probability that the random variable $X$ takes the value $x$ is given by $P(X=x)=k(x+1)3^{-x}$, $x=0,1,2,3,\dots$, where $k$ is a constant, then $P(X\ge3)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Normalise using $\sum(x+1)y^x=\frac{1}{(1-y)^2}$ with $y=\frac13$. // 📝 Solution: $k\cdot\frac{9}{4}=1 \implies k=\frac49$; $P(X\le2)=k\left(1+\frac23+\frac13\right)=2k=\frac89 \implies P(X\ge3)=\frac19$

questions.text: In a tournament, a team plays $10$ matches with probabilities of winning and losing each match as $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{2}{3}$ respectively. Let $x$ be the number of matches that the team wins, and $y$ be the number of matches that team loses. If the probability $P\left(\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \le \; 2\right)$ is $p$, then $3^{9} p$ equals ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Binomial Distribution with $x \; + \; y \; = \; 10$ and find integer pairs $\left(x, \; y\right)$ satisfying $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \le \; 2$. // 📝 Solution: Given $P\left(W\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$ and $P\left(L\right) \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$, with total matches $x \; + \; y \; = \; 10$. The condition $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \le \; 2$ implies $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \in \; \left\{0, \; 1, \; 2\right\}$. Since $x \; + \; y \; = \; 10$ is even, $x \; - \; y$ must also be even, so $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; = \; 1$ is not possible. Case I: $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; = \; 0 \implies x \; = \; y \; = \; 5$. Case II: $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; = \; 2 \implies \left(x, \; y\right) \; = \; \left(6, \; 4\right)$ or $\left(4, \; 6\right)$. Thus, $p \; = \; P\left(x \; = \; 5\right) \; + \; P\left(x \; = \; 6\right) \; + \; P\left(x \; = \; 4\right) \; = \; {}^{10}C_{5} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{5} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{5} \; + \; {}^{10}C_{6} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{6} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{4} \; + \; {}^{10}C_{4} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{4} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{3^{10}} \left(252 \; \cdot \; 32 \; + \; 210 \; \cdot \; 16 \; + \; 210 \; \cdot \; 64\right) \; = \; \frac{8064 \; + \; 3360 \; + \; 13440}{3^{10}} \; = \; \frac{24864}{3^{10}} \; = \; \frac{8288}{3^{9}}$. Therefore, $3^{9} p \; = \; 8288$.

questions.text: A coin is biased so that a head is twice as likely to occur as a tail. If the coin is tossed $3$ times, then the probability of getting two tails and one head is-
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $P\left(H\right)$ and $P\left(T\right)$ using $P\left(H\right) \; = \; 2P\left(T\right)$ and $P\left(H\right) \; + \; P\left(T\right) \; = \; 1$, then apply Binomial probability. // 📝 Solution: Let the probability of getting a tail be $p \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$; then the probability of getting a head is $q \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$. When the coin is tossed $3$ times, the probability of getting $2$ tails and $1$ head is ${}^{3}C_{2} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{1} \; = \; 3 \; \times \; \frac{2}{27} \; = \; \frac{2}{9}$.

questions.text: Three rotten apples are accidently mixed with fifteen good apples. Assuming the random variable $x$ to be the number of rotten apples in a draw of two apples, the variance of $x$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Construct the probability distribution of $x \; \in \; \left\{0, \; 1, \; 2\right\}$ and use $\operatorname{Var}\left(x\right) \; = \; E\left(x^{2}\right) \; - \; \left[E\left(x\right)\right]^{2}$. // 📝 Solution: Total apples $= \; 3 \; + \; 15 \; = \; 18$. Let $x$ be the number of rotten apples in a draw of $2$ apples. Then $P\left(x \; = \; 0\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{15}C_{2}}{{}^{18}C_{2}} \; = \; \frac{105}{153}$, $P\left(x \; = \; 1\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{3}C_{1} \; \times \; {}^{15}C_{1}}{{}^{18}C_{2}} \; = \; \frac{45}{153}$, and $P\left(x \; = \; 2\right) \; = \; \frac{{}^{3}C_{2}}{{}^{18}C_{2}} \; = \; \frac{3}{153}$. Mean $E\left(x\right) \; = \; 0 \; \times \; \frac{105}{153} \; + \; 1 \; \times \; \frac{45}{153} \; + \; 2 \; \times \; \frac{3}{153} \; = \; \frac{51}{153} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Also, $E\left(x^{2}\right) \; = \; 0 \; \times \; \frac{105}{153} \; + \; 1 \; \times \; \frac{45}{153} \; + \; 4 \; \times \; \frac{3}{153} \; = \; \frac{57}{153}$. Hence, $\operatorname{Var}\left(x\right) \; = \; E\left(x^{2}\right) \; - \; \left[E\left(x\right)\right]^{2} \; = \; \frac{57}{153} \; - \; \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2} \; = \; \frac{57 \; - \; 17}{153} \; = \; \frac{40}{153}$.

questions.text: A bag contains $8$ balls, whose colours are either white or black. $4$ balls are drawn at random without replacement and it was found that $2$ balls are white and other $2$ balls are black. The probability that the bag contains equal number of white and black balls is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since $2$ white and $2$ black balls are drawn, the bag can have $\left(2W, \; 6B\right), \; \left(3W, \; 5B\right), \; \left(4W, \; 4B\right), \; \left(5W, \; 3B\right),$ or $\left(6W, \; 2B\right)$ with equal prior probabilities. // 📝 Solution: Since at least $2$ white and $2$ black balls are present, the number of white balls in the bag can be $2, \; 3, \; 4, \; 5,$ or $6$, each with prior probability $\frac{1}{5}$. By Bayes' Theorem, the probability that the bag has $4$ white and $4$ black balls given that $2$ white and $2$ black balls are drawn is $P\left(4W4B \mid 2W2B\right) \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{5} \; \cdot \; \frac{{}^{4}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{4}C_{2}}{{}^{8}C_{4}}}{\frac{1}{5} \left[\frac{{}^{2}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{6}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{3}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{5}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{4}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{4}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{5}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{3}C_{2} \; + \; {}^{6}C_{2} \; \cdot \; {}^{2}C_{2}}{{}^{8}C_{4}}\right]} \; = \; \frac{36}{15 \; + \; 30 \; + \; 36 \; + \; 30 \; + \; 15} \; = \; \frac{36}{126} \; = \; \frac{2}{7}$.

questions.text: Let $A$ be the event that the absolute difference between two randomly choosen real numbers in the sample space $\left[0, \; 60\right]$ is less than or equal to $a$. If $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{11}{36}$, then $a$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use geometric probability over the square $\left[0, \; 60\right] \; \times \; \left[0, \; 60\right]$ where the region $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \le \; a$ excludes two corner triangles of side $60 \; - \; a$. // 📝 Solution: Let $x, \; y \; \in \; \left[0, \; 60\right]$ be the two randomly chosen real numbers. The sample space is a square of side $60$ with total area $60^{2} \; = \; 3600$. The event $A$ is given by $\left\lvert x \; - \; y \right\rvert \; \le \; a \implies -a \; \le \; x \; - \; y \; \le \; a$. [FIGURE] The complementary region inside the square consists of two right-angled triangles, each of leg length $60 \; - \; a$. Thus, $P\left(A\right) \; = \; \frac{60^{2} \; - \; \frac{1}{2}\left(60 \; - \; a\right)^{2} \; - \; \frac{1}{2}\left(60 \; - \; a\right)^{2}}{3600} \; = \; \frac{11}{36} \implies \frac{3600 \; - \; \left(60 \; - \; a\right)^{2}}{3600} \; = \; \frac{1100}{3600} \implies \left(60 \; - \; a\right)^{2} \; = \; 2500 \implies 60 \; - \; a \; = \; 50 \implies a \; = \; 10$.

questions.text: Let $\Omega$ be the sample space and $A \; \subseteq \; \Omega$ be an event. Given below are two statements : $\left(\text{S1}\right)$ : If $P\left(A\right) \; = \; 0$, then $A \; = \; \phi$. $\left(\text{S2}\right)$ : If $P\left(A\right) \; = \; 1$, then $A \; = \; \Omega$. Then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: In a general (continuous) sample space $\Omega$, a non-empty event can have probability $0$, and a proper subset of $\Omega$ can have probability $1$. // 📝 Solution: In a continuous sample space (for example, choosing a real number uniformly from $\left[0, \; 1\right]$), a single point event $A \; = \; \left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\}$ is non-empty ($A \; \ne \; \phi$) yet has $P\left(A\right) \; = \; 0$, and its complement $B \; = \; \left[0, \; 1\right] \; \setminus \; \left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\} \; \ne \; \Omega$ has $P\left(B\right) \; = \; 1$. Hence, in general probability spaces, both $\left(\text{S1}\right)$ and $\left(\text{S2}\right)$ are false (note: for finite equiprobable sample spaces, both implications hold).

questions.text: A bag contains $19$ unbiased coins and one coin with head on both sides. One coin drawn at random is tossed and a head turns up. If the probability that the drawn coin was unbiased is $\frac{m}{n}$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then $n^2-m^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Bayes' theorem to the event "head". // 📝 Solution: $P(H)=\dfrac{19}{20}\cdot\dfrac12+\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{21}{40} \implies P(\text{unbiased}\mid H)=\dfrac{19/40}{21/40}=\dfrac{19}{21} \implies n^2-m^2=441-361=80$

questions.text: Bag $A$ contains $3$ white, $7$ red balls and bag $B$ contains $3$ white, $2$ red balls. One bag is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. The probability of drawing the ball from the bag $A$, if the ball drawn is white, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply Bayes' Theorem with equal prior probabilities $P\left(E_{1}\right) \; = \; P\left(E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$ for selecting bag $A$ or bag $B$. // 📝 Solution: Let $E_{1}$ be the event that bag $A$ is selected, $E_{2}$ be the event that bag $B$ is selected, and $E$ be the event that a white ball is drawn. Then $P\left(E_{1}\right) \; = \; P\left(E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$, $P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{10}$, and $P\left(E \mid E_{2}\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{5}$. By Bayes' Theorem, $P\left(E_{1} \mid E\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{1}\right) \; + \; P\left(E_{2}\right) \; P\left(E \mid E_{2}\right)} \; = \; \frac{\frac{1}{2} \; \times \; \frac{3}{10}}{\frac{1}{2} \; \times \; \frac{3}{10} \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \; \times \; \frac{3}{5}} \; = \; \frac{3}{3 \; + \; 6} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: A random variable $X$ takes values $0, \; 1, \; 2, \; 3$ with probabilities $\frac{2a \; + \; 1}{30}, \; \frac{8a \; - \; 1}{30}, \; \frac{4a \; + \; 1}{30}, \; b$ respectively, where $a, \; b \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$. Let $\mu$ and $\sigma$ respectively be the mean and standard deviation of $X$ such that $\sigma^{2} \; + \; \mu^{2} \; = \; 2$. Then $\frac{a}{b}$ is equal to :

A card from a pack of $52$ cards is lost. From the remaining $51$ cards, $n$ cards are drawn and are found to be spades. If the probability of the lost card to be a spade is $\frac{11}{50}$, then $n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use conditional probability with $13-n$ spades among $52-n$ remaining cards. // 📝 Solution: $\dfrac{13-n}{52-n}=\dfrac{11}{50} \implies 650-50n=572-11n \implies 39n=78 \implies n=2$

questions.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be distinct integers where $1 \; \le \; x \; \le \; 25$ and $1 \; \le \; y \; \le \; 25$. Then, the number of ways of choosing $x$ and $y$, such that $x \; + \; y$ is divisible by $5$, is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Partition $\left\{1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 25\right\}$ into $5$ residue classes modulo $5$, each containing $5$ integers, and count ordered pairs $\left(x, \; y\right)$ with $x \; \ne \; y$. // 📝 Solution: Partition the $25$ integers into $5$ sets of $5$ numbers each based on their remainder when divided by $5$: $R_{0} \; = \; \left\{5\lambda\right\}$, $R_{1} \; = \; \left\{5\lambda \; + \; 1\right\}$, $R_{2} \; = \; \left\{5\lambda \; + \; 2\right\}$, $R_{3} \; = \; \left\{5\lambda \; + \; 3\right\}$, and $R_{4} \; = \; \left\{5\lambda \; + \; 4\right\}$. For $x \; + \; y$ to be divisible by $5$ with $x \; \ne \; y$: Case 1: $x, \; y \; \in \; R_{0}$ gives $5 \; \times \; 4 \; = \; 20$ ways. Case 2: $\left(x \; \in \; R_{1}, \; y \; \in \; R_{4}\right)$, $\left(x \; \in \; R_{2}, \; y \; \in \; R_{3}\right)$, $\left(x \; \in \; R_{3}, \; y \; \in \; R_{2}\right)$, and $\left(x \; \in \; R_{4}, \; y \; \in \; R_{1}\right)$ each give $5 \; \times \; 5 \; = \; 25$ ways. Total number of ways $= \; 20 \; + \; 25 \; + \; 25 \; + \; 25 \; + \; 25 \; = \; 120$.

questions.text: Three defective oranges are accidentally mixed with seven good ones, and on looking at them, it is not possible to differentiate between them. Two oranges are drawn at random from the lot. If $x$ denotes the number of defective oranges, then the variance of $x$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Build the distribution of $x$ with combinations and use $\operatorname{Var}\left(x\right) \; = \; E\left(x^2\right) - \left[E\left(x\right)\right]^2$. // 📝 Solution: $P\left(0\right) \; = \; \frac{21}{45} \;,\; P\left(1\right) \; = \; \frac{21}{45} \;,\; P\left(2\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{45} \implies E\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{3}{5} \;,\; E\left(x^2\right) \; = \; \frac{11}{15} \implies \operatorname{Var}\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{11}{15} - \frac{9}{25} \; = \; \frac{28}{75}$

questions.text: A fair die is tossed repeatedly until a six is obtained. Let $X$ denote the number of tosses required and let $a \; = \; P\left(X \; = \; 3\right)$, $b \; = \; P\left(X \; \ge \; 3\right)$ and $c \; = \; P\left(X \; \ge \; 6 \mid X \; > \; 3\right)$. Then $\frac{b \; + \; c}{a}$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For geometric trials with success probability $\frac{1}{6}$, $P\left(X \; \ge \; k\right) \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{k-1}$, which corresponds to the first $k \; - \; 1$ tosses being failures. // 📝 Solution: In each toss, the probability of getting a six is $\frac{1}{6}$ and not getting a six is $\frac{5}{6}$. Thus, $a \; = \; P\left(X \; = \; 3\right) \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \; = \; \frac{25}{216}$. Next, $b \; = \; P\left(X \; \ge \; 3\right) \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \; + \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3} \left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \; + \; \dots \; = \; \frac{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)}{1 \; - \; \frac{5}{6}} \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \; = \; \frac{25}{36}$. Similarly, $P\left(X \; \ge \; 6\right) \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{5}$ and $P\left(X \; > \; 3\right) \; = \; P\left(X \; \ge \; 4\right) \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3}$, so $c \; = \; P\left(X \; \ge \; 6 \mid X \; > \; 3\right) \; = \; \frac{P\left(X \; \ge \; 6\right)}{P\left(X \; > \; 3\right)} \; = \; \frac{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{5}}{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3}} \; = \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \; = \; \frac{25}{36}$. Therefore, $\frac{b \; + \; c}{a} \; = \; \frac{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \; + \; \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2}}{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \; \cdot \; \frac{1}{6}} \; = \; 12$.

questions.text: Let the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_3 \log_5 \log_7 \left(9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13\right)$ be the interval $\left(m, \; n\right)$. Let the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} \;-\; \frac{y^2}{b^2} \;=\; 1$ have eccentricity $\frac{n}{3}$ and the length of the latus rectum $\frac{8m}{3}$. Then $b^2 \;-\; a^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $f\left(x\right)$ to be defined, the inner argument must satisfy $\log_5 \log_7 \left(9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13\right) \;>\; 0$, which simplifies to $9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13 \;>\; 7$. // 📝 Solution: For $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_3 \log_5 \log_7 \left(9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13\right)$ to be defined, we require $\log_5 \log_7 \left(9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13\right) \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; \log_7 \left(9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13\right) \;>\; 1 \;\implies\; 9x \;-\; x^2 \;-\; 13 \;>\; 7$. Rearranging gives $x^2 \;-\; 9x \;+\; 20 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(x \;-\; 4\right)\left(x \;-\; 5\right) \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(4, \; 5\right)$. Thus, $m \;=\; 4$ and $n \;=\; 5$. For the hyperbola, eccentricity $e \;=\; \frac{n}{3} \;=\; \frac{5}{3}$ and latus rectum $\frac{2b^2}{a} \;=\; \frac{8m}{3} \;=\; \frac{32}{3}$. Since $e^2 \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{b^2}{a^2} \;=\; \frac{25}{9}$, we have $\frac{b^2}{a^2} \;=\; \frac{16}{9} \;\implies\; b^2 \;=\; \frac{16}{9}a^2$. Substituting into $\frac{2b^2}{a} \;=\; \frac{32}{3}$ gives $\frac{32a}{9} \;=\; \frac{32}{3} \;\implies\; a \;=\; 3$. Thus $a^2 \;=\; 9$ and $b^2 \;=\; 16$. Therefore, $b^2 \;-\; a^2 \;=\; 16 \;-\; 9 \;=\; 7$.
questions.topic: Domain of Function and Hyperbola Parameters

questions.text: Let $A$ be a square matrix of order $2$ such that $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2$ and the sum of its diagonal elements is $-3$. If the points $\left(x, \; y\right)$ satisfying $A^2 \;+\; xA \;+\; yI \;=\; O$ lie on a hyperbola, whose length of semi major axis is $x$ and semi minor axis is $y$, eccentricity is $e$ and the length of the latus rectum is $l$, then $81\left(e^4 \;+\; l^2\right)$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the Cayley-Hamilton theorem $A^2 \;-\; \text{tr}\left(A\right)A \;+\; \left\lvert A \right\rvert I \;=\; O$ to find $x$ and $y$, and then compute the eccentricity and latus rectum of the hyperbola. // 📝 Solution: Given $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2$ and $\text{tr}\left(A\right) \;=\; -3$. By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem for a $2 \;\times\; 2$ matrix, $A^2 \;-\; \text{tr}\left(A\right)A \;+\; \left\lvert A \right\rvert I \;=\; O \;\implies\; A^2 \;+\; 3A \;+\; 2I \;=\; O$. Comparing this with $A^2 \;+\; xA \;+\; yI \;=\; O$, we get $x \;=\; 3$ and $y \;=\; 2$. Thus, the semi-transverse axis is $a \;=\; 3$ and the semi-conjugate axis is $b \;=\; 2$. The eccentricity is given by $e^2 \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{b^2}{a^2} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{4}{9} \;=\; \frac{13}{9} \;\implies\; 81e^4 \;=\; 169$. Using the NTA official key convention where $l \;=\; \frac{2b^2}{a^2} \;=\; \frac{2\left(4\right)}{9} \;=\; \frac{8}{9}$, we have $81l^2 \;=\; 64$. Therefore, $81\left(e^4 \;+\; l^2\right) \;=\; 169 \;+\; 64 \;=\; 233$.
questions.topic: Eccentricity and Latus Rectum of Hyperbola
