questions.solution: 💡 Hint: negative roots need $D\ge0$, negative sum and positive product // 📝 Solution: $D=(p-8)(p+4)\ge0$, $p+2<0$, $2p+9>0\implies p\in\left(-\tfrac92,-4\right]\implies\alpha=-\tfrac92,\ \beta=-4\implies\beta-2\alpha=5$

questions.text: The number of real roots of the equation $x\left\lvert x-2\right\rvert+3\left\lvert x-3\right\rvert+1=0$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: split the real line at $x=2$ and $x=3$ and solve each branch // 📝 Solution: $x<2$: $x^{2}+x-10=0\implies x=\tfrac{-1-\sqrt{41}}{2}$ only; $2\le x<3$: $x^{2}-5x+10=0$ has no real root; $x\ge3$: $x^{2}+x-8=0\implies\tfrac{-1+\sqrt{33}}{2}<3$ rejected; one root

questions.text: The number of solutions of the equation $\left(\frac{9}{x}-\frac{9}{\sqrt{x}}+2\right)\left(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{7}{\sqrt{x}}+3\right)=0$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ with $x>0$ so that $\frac{1}{x}=\alpha^{2}$. // 📝 Solution: $(9\alpha^{2}-9\alpha+2)(2\alpha^{2}-7\alpha+3)=0$ $\implies \alpha=\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},3$ $\implies x=9,\frac{9}{4},4,\frac{1}{9}$ $\implies 4$ solutions
questions.topic: Equations reducible to quadratic by substitution

questions.text: If the set of all $a\in\mathbb{R}-\{1\}$, for which the roots of $(1-a)x^{2}+2(a-3)x+9=0$ are positive is $(-\infty,-\alpha]\cup[\beta,\gamma)$, then $2\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: both roots positive needs $D\ge0$, positive sum and positive product // 📝 Solution: $D\ge0\implies a\le-3$ or $a\ge0$; $\dfrac{9}{1-a}>0\implies a<1$; so $a\in(-\infty,-3]\cup[0,1)$ gives $\alpha=3,\ \beta=0,\ \gamma=1\implies 2\alpha+\beta+\gamma=7$

questions.text: Let $f : \left( 0, \pi \right) \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function given by $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \left( \frac{8}{7} \right)^{\frac{\tan 8x}{\tan 7x}}, & 0 \;<\; x \;<\; \frac{\pi}{2} \\ a \;-\; 8, & x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \left( 1 \;+\; \left\lvert \cot x \right\rvert \right)^{\frac{b}{a}\left\lvert \tan x \right\rvert}, & \frac{\pi}{2} \;<\; x \;<\; \pi \end{cases}$, where $a, b \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, then $a^2 \;+\; b^2$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the left-hand limit and right-hand limit at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$ by substituting $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; h$ and $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;+\; h$ as $h \to 0^+$. // 📝 Solution: For continuity at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, we must have $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^-} f(x) \;=\; f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+} f(x)$. First, evaluate the left-hand limit by letting $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;-\; h$ as $h \to 0^+$: $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\tan\left( 4\pi \;-\; 8h \right)}{\tan\left( \frac{7\pi}{2} \;-\; 7h \right)} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{-\tan 8h}{\cot 7h} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} \left( -\tan 8h \cdot \tan 7h \right) \;=\; 0$. Thus, $\text{LHL} \;=\; \left( \frac{8}{7} \right)^0 \;=\; 1$. Equating $\text{LHL} \;=\; f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$, we get $a \;-\; 8 \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 9$. Next, evaluate the right-hand limit: $\text{RHL} \;=\; \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+} \left( 1 \;+\; \left\lvert \cot x \right\rvert \right)^{\frac{b}{a} \left\lvert \tan x \right\rvert}$. Since $\left\lvert \cot x \right\rvert \to 0$ as $x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+$, this is a $1^\infty$ form, which evaluates to $e^{\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+} \left\lvert \cot x \right\rvert \cdot \frac{b}{a} \left\lvert \tan x \right\rvert} \;=\; e^{\frac{b}{a}}$. Equating $\text{RHL} \;=\; \text{LHL}$, we have $e^{\frac{b}{a}} \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \frac{b}{a} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; b \;=\; 0$. Therefore, $a^2 \;+\; b^2 \;=\; 9^2 \;+\; 0^2 \;=\; 81$.

questions.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real constants such that the function $f$ defined by $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} x^2 \;+\; 3x \;+\; a, & x \;\le\; 1 \\ bx \;+\; 2, & x \;>\; 1 \end{cases}$ be differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$. Then, the value of $\int_{-2}^{2} f(x) \, dx$ equals
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $a$ and $b$ using continuity and differentiability at $x \;=\; 1$, then split the definite integral at $x \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x \;=\; 1$, we equate the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at $x \;=\; 1$: $f'(1^-) \;=\; f'(1^+) \;\implies\; \left. \left( 2x \;+\; 3 \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; b \;\implies\; b \;=\; 5$. Also, since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 1$, we have $f(1) \;=\; f(1^+) \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; 3 \;+\; a \;=\; b \;+\; 2 \;\implies\; 4 \;+\; a \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 3$. Now, split the integral at $x \;=\; 1$: $\int_{-2}^{2} f(x) \, dx \;=\; \int_{-2}^{1} \left( x^2 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 3 \right) dx \;+\; \int_{1}^{2} \left( 5x \;+\; 2 \right) dx \;=\; \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \;+\; \frac{3x^2}{2} \;+\; 3x \right]_{-2}^{1} \;+\; \left[ \frac{5x^2}{2} \;+\; 2x \right]_{1}^{2}$. Evaluating the limits gives $\left( \frac{1}{3} \;+\; \frac{3}{2} \;+\; 3 \right) \;-\; \left( -\frac{8}{3} \;+\; 6 \;-\; 6 \right) \;+\; \left( 10 \;+\; 4 \right) \;-\; \left( \frac{5}{2} \;+\; 2 \right) \;=\; 3 \;+\; \frac{3}{2} \;+\; 3 \;+\; 14 \;-\; \frac{5}{2} \;-\; 2 \;=\; 17$.
questions.topic: Continuity and Differentiability of Piecewise Functions

questions.text: If the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \left( 1 \;+\; \left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert \right)^{\frac{\lambda}{\left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert}}, & 0 \;<\; x \;<\; \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \mu, & x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \\ e^{\frac{\cot 6x}{\cot 4x}}, & \frac{\pi}{2} \;<\; x \;<\; \pi \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, then $9\lambda \;+\; 6 \log_e \mu \;+\; \mu^6 \;-\; e^{6\lambda}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate the left-hand limit ($1^\infty$ form) and right-hand limit at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\mu$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, we have $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^-} f(x) \;=\; f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+} f(x)$. Evaluating the left-hand limit: $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^-} \left( 1 \;+\; \left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert \right)^{\frac{\lambda}{\left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert}} \;=\; e^{\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^-} \left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert \cdot \frac{\lambda}{\left\lvert \cos x \right\rvert}} \;=\; e^\lambda$. Evaluating the right-hand limit by putting $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;+\; h$ as $h \to 0^+$: $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}^+} e^{\frac{\cot 6x}{\cot 4x}} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} e^{\frac{\cot\left( 3\pi \;+\; 6h \right)}{\cot\left( 2\pi \;+\; 4h \right)}} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} e^{\frac{\cot 6h}{\cot 4h}} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} e^{\frac{\tan 4h}{\tan 6h}} \;=\; e^{\frac{4}{6}} \;=\; e^{\frac{2}{3}}$. Equating the limits to $f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \mu$, we get $e^\lambda \;=\; \mu \;=\; e^{\frac{2}{3}}$, which gives $\lambda \;=\; \frac{2}{3}$ and $\mu \;=\; e^{\frac{2}{3}}$. Substituting these values into the required expression: $9\lambda \;+\; 6 \log_e \mu \;+\; \mu^6 \;-\; e^{6\lambda} \;=\; 9\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;+\; 6\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;+\; e^4 \;-\; e^4 \;=\; 6 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 0 \;=\; 10$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{ 0 \right\} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function satisfying $f\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) \;=\; \frac{f(x)}{f(y)}$ for all $x, y, f(y) \;\neq\; 0$. If $f'(1) \;=\; 2024$, then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate the given functional equation partially with respect to $x$ and then substitute $y \;=\; x$. // 📝 Solution: Given the functional relation $f\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) \;=\; \frac{f(x)}{f(y)}$ for all $x, y \;\neq\; 0$. Differentiating both sides partially with respect to $x$ (treating $y$ as a constant), we get $f'\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{y} \;=\; \frac{f'(x)}{f(y)}$. Now, substituting $y \;=\; x$ into this relation yields $f'(1) \cdot \frac{1}{x} \;=\; \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$. Since $f'(1) \;=\; 2024$, we have $\frac{2024}{x} \;=\; \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \;\implies\; x f'(x) \;-\; 2024 f(x) \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: If the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\left\lvert x \right\rvert}, & \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;\ge\; 2 \\ ax^2 \;+\; 2b, & \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;<\; 2 \end{cases}$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, then $48\left( a \;+\; b \right)$ is equal to _____
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the conditions of continuity and differentiability at $x \;=\; 2$ to find $a$ and $b$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is an even function and differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, it is continuous and differentiable at $x \;=\; 2$. For $x \;\ge\; 2$, $f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{x}$. By continuity at $x \;=\; 2$: $f(2^-) \;=\; f(2^+) \;\implies\; 4a \;+\; 2b \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. By differentiability at $x \;=\; 2$: $f'(2^-) \;=\; f'(2^+) \;\implies\; \left. \left( 2ax \right) \right\rvert_{x=2} \;=\; \left. \left( -\frac{1}{x^2} \right) \right\rvert_{x=2} \;\implies\; 4a \;=\; -\frac{1}{4} \;\implies\; a \;=\; -\frac{1}{16}$. Substituting $4a \;=\; -\frac{1}{4}$ into $4a \;+\; 2b \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$ gives $-\frac{1}{4} \;+\; 2b \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; 2b \;=\; \frac{3}{4} \;\implies\; b \;=\; \frac{3}{8}$. Therefore, $48\left( a \;+\; b \right) \;=\; 48\left( -\frac{1}{16} \;+\; \frac{3}{8} \right) \;=\; 48\left( \frac{5}{16} \right) \;=\; 15$.
questions.topic: Continuity and Differentiability of Piecewise Functions

questions.text: Let $\left[ t \right]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Let $f : \left[ 0, \infty \right) \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x) \;=\; \left[ \frac{x}{2} \;+\; 3 \right] \;-\; \left[ \sqrt{x} \right]$. Let $S$ be the set of all points in the interval $\left[ 0, 8 \right]$ at which $f$ is not continuous. Then $\sum_{a \in S} a$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the points in $\left[ 0, 8 \right]$ where $\frac{x}{2} \;+\; 3$ or $\sqrt{x}$ becomes an integer, and check where the jumps do not cancel out. // 📝 Solution: In the interval $\left[ 0, 8 \right]$, let $g(x) \;=\; \left[ \frac{x}{2} \;+\; 3 \right] \;=\; \left[ \frac{x}{2} \right] \;+\; 3$ and $h(x) \;=\; \left[ \sqrt{x} \right]$. The function $g(x)$ is discontinuous when $\frac{x}{2} \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$ in $\left( 0, 8 \right]$, which gives $x \;\in\; \left\{ 2, 4, 6, 8 \right\}$. The function $h(x)$ is discontinuous when $\sqrt{x} \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$ in $\left( 0, 8 \right]$, which gives $x \;\in\; \left\{ 1, 4 \right\}$. At $x \;=\; 1, 2, 6, 8$, only one of $g(x)$ or $h(x)$ is discontinuous, so $f(x) \;=\; g(x) \;-\; h(x)$ is definitely discontinuous at $x \;=\; 1, 2, 6, 8$. Now check the common point $x \;=\; 4$: $\lim_{x \to 4^-} f(x) \;=\; 4 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 3$, $f(4) \;=\; 5 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 3$, and $\lim_{x \to 4^+} f(x) \;=\; 5 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 3$. Since the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value all equal $3$, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 4$. Thus, $S \;=\; \left\{ 1, 2, 6, 8 \right\}$, and $\sum_{a \in S} a \;=\; 1 \;+\; 2 \;+\; 6 \;+\; 8 \;=\; 17$.

questions.text: If $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{a\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; x^2 \;-\; 2\left( \sin \left\lvert x \right\rvert \right)\left( \cos \left\lvert x \right\rvert \right)}{x}, & x \;\neq\; 0 \\ b, & x \;=\; 0 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then $a \;+\; b$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the identity $2 \sin\left\lvert x \right\rvert \cos\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \sin\left( 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \right)$ and equate the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and $f(0)$. // 📝 Solution: Using $2 \sin\left\lvert x \right\rvert \cos\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \sin\left( 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \right)$, for $x \;>\; 0$ we have $f(x) \;=\; \frac{ax \;+\; x^2 \;-\; \sin 2x}{x} \;=\; a \;+\; x \;-\; \frac{\sin 2x}{x}$. Taking the right-hand limit: $\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) \;=\; a \;+\; 0 \;-\; 2 \;=\; a \;-\; 2$. For $x \;<\; 0$, we have $\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; -x$, so $f(x) \;=\; \frac{-ax \;+\; x^2 \;+\; \sin 2x}{x} \;=\; -a \;+\; x \;+\; \frac{\sin 2x}{x}$. Taking the left-hand limit: $\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) \;=\; -a \;+\; 0 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 2 \;-\; a$. Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we must have $a \;-\; 2 \;=\; 2 \;-\; a \;=\; b$. From $a \;-\; 2 \;=\; 2 \;-\; a$, we get $2a \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 2$, and consequently $b \;=\; 2 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0$. Therefore, $a \;+\; b \;=\; 2 \;+\; 0 \;=\; 2$.
questions.topic: Continuity of Piecewise and Modulus Functions

questions.text: Let $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} x^2 \sin\left( \frac{1}{x} \right), & x \;\neq\; 0 \\ 0, & x \;=\; 0 \end{cases}$; Then at $x \;=\; 0$

options.text: $f$ is continuous but $f'$ is not continuous

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check continuity and differentiability of $f$ at $x \;=\; 0$ using first principles, then examine $\lim_{x \to 0} f'(x)$. // 📝 Solution: First, check continuity at $x \;=\; 0$: $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) \;=\; 0 \;=\; f(0)$ (since $\left\lvert \sin\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) \right\rvert \;\le\; 1$). Thus, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$. Next, check differentiability at $x \;=\; 0$: $f'(0) \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(h) \;-\; f(0)}{h} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h^2 \sin\left( \frac{1}{h} \right) \;-\; 0}{h} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0} h \sin\left( \frac{1}{h} \right) \;=\; 0$. Thus, $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x \;=\; 0$ with $f'(0) \;=\; 0$. For $x \;\neq\; 0$, differentiating $f(x)$ using the product rule gives $f'(x) \;=\; 2x \sin\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) \;-\; \cos\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)$. As $x \to 0$, $2x \sin\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) \to 0$, but $\cos\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ and does not approach a unique limit. Hence, $\lim_{x \to 0} f'(x)$ does not exist, so $f'$ is not continuous at $x \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: For $a, b \;>\; 0$, let $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{\tan\left( (a \;+\; 1)x \right) \;+\; b \tan x}{x}, & x \;<\; 0 \\ 3, & x \;=\; 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{ax \;+\; b^2 x^2} \;-\; \sqrt{ax}}{b\sqrt{ax}\sqrt{x}}, & x \;>\; 0 \end{cases}$ be a continuous function at $x \;=\; 0$. Then $\frac{b}{a}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the right-hand limit $\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x)$ by rationalizing the numerator and equate it to $f(0) \;=\; 3$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we have $\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) \;=\; f(0) \;=\; 3$. Rationalizing the numerator for $x \;>\; 0$ (with denominator $b\sqrt{a}x^{3/2}$): $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\left( ax \;+\; b^2 x^2 \right) \;-\; ax}{b\sqrt{a}x^{3/2} \left( \sqrt{ax \;+\; b^2 x^2} \;+\; \sqrt{ax} \right)} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{b^2 x^2}{b\sqrt{a}x^2 \left( \sqrt{a \;+\; b^2 x} \;+\; \sqrt{a} \right)} \;=\; \frac{b^2}{b\sqrt{a}\left( 2\sqrt{a} \right)} \;=\; \frac{b}{2a}$. Equating this limit to $f(0) \;=\; 3$, we get $\frac{b}{2a} \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \frac{b}{a} \;=\; 6$.

questions.text: Let $f : \left[ -1, 2 \right] \to \mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(x) \;=\; 2x^2 \;+\; x \;+\; \left[ x^2 \right] \;-\; \left[ x \right]$, where $\left[ t \right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. The number of points, where $f$ is not continuous, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Identify the points in $\left[ -1, 2 \right]$ where $x$ or $x^2$ is an integer, and check the continuity of $f(x)$ at each of these doubtful points. // 📝 Solution: We can write $f(x) \;=\; \left( 2x^2 \;+\; x \right) \;+\; \left[ x^2 \right] \;-\; \left[ x \right]$. Since $2x^2 \;+\; x$ is a polynomial, it is continuous everywhere. The doubtful points of discontinuity in $\left[ -1, 2 \right]$ are where $x \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$ or $x^2 \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$, which gives $x \;\in\; \left\{ -1, 0, 1, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, 2 \right\}$. At $x \;=\; \sqrt{2}$ and $x \;=\; \sqrt{3}$, $\left[ x \right]$ is continuous while $\left[ x^2 \right]$ is discontinuous, so $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x \;=\; \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}$. Now check the integer points: At $x \;=\; -1$: $f(-1) \;=\; 2 \;-\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;-\; (-1) \;=\; 3$, while $\lim_{x \to -1^+} f(x) \;=\; 2 \;-\; 1 \;+\; 0 \;-\; (-1) \;=\; 2 \;\neq\; f(-1)$ (discontinuous). At $x \;=\; 0$: $f(0) \;=\; 0$, while $\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) \;=\; 0 \;+\; 0 \;+\; 0 \;-\; (-1) \;=\; 1 \;\neq\; f(0)$ (discontinuous). At $x \;=\; 1$: $\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 0 \;-\; 0 \;=\; 3$, $f(1) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 3$, and $\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 3$ (continuous). At $x \;=\; 2$: $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) \;=\; 10 \;+\; 3 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 12$, and $f(2) \;=\; 10 \;+\; 4 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 12$ (continuous). Thus, $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $4$ points: $\left\{ -1, 0, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \right\}$.

questions.text: Let $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{ax^2 \;+\; 2ax \;+\; 3}{4x^2 \;+\; 4x \;-\; 3}, & x \;\neq\; -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \\ b, & x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \end{cases}$ be continuous at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$. If $f \circ f(x) \;=\; \frac{7}{5}$, then $x$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$, the numerator must vanish at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$ since the denominator is zero there. // 📝 Solution: Note that the denominator factorizes as $4x^2 \;+\; 4x \;-\; 3 \;=\; \left( 2x \;+\; 3 \right)\left( 2x \;-\; 1 \right)$, which vanishes at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$. For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$, $\lim_{x \to -\frac{3}{2}} f(x)$ must exist finitely, so the numerator must also be zero at $x \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$: $a\left( \frac{9}{4} \right) \;+\; 2a\left( -\frac{3}{2} \right) \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -\frac{3a}{4} \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 4$. Substituting $a \;=\; 4$, we get $f(x) \;=\; \frac{4x^2 \;+\; 8x \;+\; 3}{\left( 2x \;+\; 3 \right)\left( 2x \;-\; 1 \right)} \;=\; \frac{\left( 2x \;+\; 1 \right)\left( 2x \;+\; 3 \right)}{\left( 2x \;+\; 3 \right)\left( 2x \;-\; 1 \right)} \;=\; \frac{2x \;+\; 1}{2x \;-\; 1}$ for $x \;\neq\; -\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}$. Now, $f \circ f(x) \;=\; f\left( \frac{2x \;+\; 1}{2x \;-\; 1} \right) \;=\; \frac{2\left( \frac{2x \;+\; 1}{2x \;-\; 1} \right) \;+\; 1}{2\left( \frac{2x \;+\; 1}{2x \;-\; 1} \right) \;-\; 1} \;=\; \frac{6x \;+\; 1}{2x \;+\; 3}$. Equating this to $\frac{7}{5}$: $\frac{6x \;+\; 1}{2x \;+\; 3} \;=\; \frac{7}{5} \;\implies\; 30x \;+\; 5 \;=\; 14x \;+\; 21 \;\implies\; 16x \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 1$.
questions.topic: Continuity of Rational and Composite Functions

questions.text: If the function $f(x) \;=\; \frac{e^x \left( e^{\tan x \;-\; x} \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; \log_e \left( \sec x \;+\; \tan x \right) \;-\; x}{\tan x \;-\; x}$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then the value of $f(0)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the fraction into two parts and apply standard exponential limits and L'Hospital's rule as $x \to 0$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we have $f(0) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \left[ e^x \left( \frac{e^{\tan x \;-\; x} \;-\; 1}{\tan x \;-\; x} \right) \;+\; \frac{\log_e \left( \sec x \;+\; \tan x \right) \;-\; x}{\tan x \;-\; x} \right]$. As $x \to 0$, $\tan x \;-\; x \to 0$, so the first term evaluates to $e^0 \cdot 1 \;=\; 1$. For the second term, applying L'Hospital's rule gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{d}{dx}\left[ \log_e\left( \sec x \;+\; \tan x \right) \;-\; x \right]}{\frac{d}{dx}\left[ \tan x \;-\; x \right]} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sec x \;-\; 1}{\sec^2 x \;-\; 1} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sec x \;-\; 1}{\left( \sec x \;-\; 1 \right)\left( \sec x \;+\; 1 \right)} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{\sec x \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{1}{1 \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $f(0) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$.

questions.text: Let $\left[ \cdot \right]$ denote the greatest integer function, and let $f(x) \;=\; \min\left\{ \sqrt{2}x, x^2 \right\}$. Let $S \;=\; \left\{ x \;\in\; \left( -2, 2 \right) : \text{the function } g(x) \;=\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert \left[ x^2 \right] \text{ is discontinuous at } x \right\}$. Then $\sum_{x \in S} f(x)$ equals
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find all points in $\left( -2, 2 \right)$ where $x^2$ is a positive integer, as $\left[ x^2 \right]$ is discontinuous at those points and $\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;\neq\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \;\in\; \left( -2, 2 \right)$, we have $x^2 \;\in\; \left[ 0, 4 \right)$. In the neighbourhood of $x \;=\; 0$, i.e., $x \;\in\; \left( -1, 1 \right)$, we have $\left[ x^2 \right] \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; g(x) \;=\; 0$, so $g(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$. The function $g(x) \;=\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert \left[ x^2 \right]$ is discontinuous where $x^2 \;\in\; \left\{ 1, 2, 3 \right\}$, which gives $S \;=\; \left\{ -1, 1, -\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}, -\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} \right\}$. Now evaluate $f(x) \;=\; \min\left\{ \sqrt{2}x, x^2 \right\}$ at each point in $S$: $f(-1) \;=\; \min\left\{ -\sqrt{2}, 1 \right\} \;=\; -\sqrt{2}$; $f(1) \;=\; \min\left\{ \sqrt{2}, 1 \right\} \;=\; 1$; $f(-\sqrt{2}) \;=\; \min\left\{ -2, 2 \right\} \;=\; -2$; $f(\sqrt{2}) \;=\; \min\left\{ 2, 2 \right\} \;=\; 2$; $f(-\sqrt{3}) \;=\; \min\left\{ -\sqrt{6}, 3 \right\} \;=\; -\sqrt{6}$; and $f(\sqrt{3}) \;=\; \min\left\{ \sqrt{6}, 3 \right\} \;=\; \sqrt{6}$. Summing these values: $\sum_{x \in S} f(x) \;=\; -\sqrt{2} \;+\; 1 \;-\; 2 \;+\; 2 \;-\; \sqrt{6} \;+\; \sqrt{6} \;=\; 1 \;-\; \sqrt{2}$.

questions.text: Let $g(x)$ be a linear function and $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} g(x), & x \;\le\; 0 \\ \left( \frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \right)^{\frac{1}{x}}, & x \;>\; 0 \end{cases}$, is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$. If $f'(1) \;=\; f(-1)$, then the value of $g(3)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use continuity at $x \;=\; 0$ to find the constant term of $g(x) \;=\; ax \;+\; b$, and differentiate $f(x)$ for $x \;>\; 0$ to find $f'(1)$. // 📝 Solution: Let the linear function be $g(x) \;=\; ax \;+\; b$. Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we have $f(0) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) \;\implies\; b \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \left( \frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \right)^{\frac{1}{x}}$. As $x \to 0^+$, the base $\frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \to \frac{1}{2}$ and the exponent $\frac{1}{x} \to \infty$, so $\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^\infty \;=\; 0$. Thus, $b \;=\; 0$ and $g(x) \;=\; ax$. For $x \;>\; 0$, let $y \;=\; \left( \frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \right)^{\frac{1}{x}}$. Taking natural logarithms: $\ln y \;=\; \frac{1}{x} \ln\left( \frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \right)$. Differentiating with respect to $x$: $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \;=\; -\frac{1}{x^2} \ln\left( \frac{1 \;+\; x}{2 \;+\; x} \right) \;+\; \frac{1}{x} \left( \frac{1}{1 \;+\; x} \;-\; \frac{1}{2 \;+\; x} \right)$. At $x \;=\; 1$, $f(1) \;=\; \frac{2}{3}$, so $f'(1) \;=\; \frac{2}{3} \left[ -\ln\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;+\; \left( \frac{1}{2} \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \right) \right] \;=\; \frac{1}{9} \;-\; \frac{2}{3} \ln\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)$. Given $f'(1) \;=\; f(-1) \;=\; g(-1) \;=\; -a$, we get $a \;=\; \frac{2}{3} \ln\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;-\; \frac{1}{9}$. Therefore, $g(3) \;=\; 3a \;=\; 2 \ln\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;-\; \frac{1}{3} \;=\; \ln\left( \frac{4}{9} \right) \;-\; \ln\left( e^{1/3} \right) \;=\; \log_e \left( \frac{4}{9e^{1/3}} \right)$.

questions.text: Consider the function $f : \left( 0, \infty \right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) \;=\; e^{-\left\lvert \log_e x \right\rvert}$. If $m$ and $n$ be respectively the number of points at which $f$ is not continuous and $f$ is not differentiable, then $m \;+\; n$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite $f(x)$ as a piecewise function by splitting at $x \;=\; 1$ where $\log_e x \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \;\in\; \left( 0, \infty \right)$, we have $\left\lvert \log_e x \right\rvert \;=\; \begin{cases} -\log_e x, & 0 \;<\; x \;<\; 1 \\ \log_e x, & x \;\ge\; 1 \end{cases}$. Substituting this into $f(x) \;=\; e^{-\left\lvert \log_e x \right\rvert}$ gives $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} e^{\log_e x}, & 0 \;<\; x \;<\; 1 \\ e^{-\log_e x}, & x \;\ge\; 1 \end{cases} \;=\; \begin{cases} x, & 0 \;<\; x \;<\; 1 \\ \frac{1}{x}, & x \;\ge\; 1 \end{cases}$. Clearly, $f(x)$ is continuous for all $x \;\in\; \left( 0, \infty \right)$ since $\lim_{x \to 1^-} x \;=\; 1 \;=\; \lim_{x \to 1^+} \frac{1}{x}$, so $m \;=\; 0$. Checking differentiability at $x \;=\; 1$: $f'(1^-) \;=\; 1$ and $f'(1^+) \;=\; \left. \left( -\frac{1}{x^2} \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; -1$. Since $f'(1^-) \;\neq\; f'(1^+)$, $f(x)$ is not differentiable only at $x \;=\; 1$, so $n \;=\; 1$. Thus, $m \;+\; n \;=\; 0 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 1$.
questions.topic: Differentiability of Modulus and Logarithmic Functions

questions.text: Let $f(x) \;=\; \left\lvert 2x^2 \;+\; 5\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 3 \right\rvert$, $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $m$ and $n$ denote the number of points where $f$ is not continuous and not differentiable respectively, then $m \;+\; n$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factorize the quadratic expression in terms of $\left\lvert x \right\rvert$ and identify the points where the graph has sharp corners. // 📝 Solution: The given function is $f(x) \;=\; \left\lvert 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert^2 \;+\; 5\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert \left( 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1 \right)\left( \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 3 \right) \right\rvert$. Since $f(x)$ is a composition of continuous polynomial and modulus functions, it is continuous for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, which means $m \;=\; 0$. Since $\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 3 \;>\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, we can write $f(x) \;=\; \left( \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 3 \right)\left\lvert 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$. The function has sharp corners (points of non-differentiability) at $x \;=\; 0$ (where $\left\lvert x \right\rvert$ is not differentiable and the factor does not vanish) and where $2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; x \;=\; \pm \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $3$ points: $x \;\in\; \left\{ -\frac{1}{2}, 0, \frac{1}{2} \right\}$, so $n \;=\; 3$. Therefore, $m \;+\; n \;=\; 0 \;+\; 3 \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{a \;-\; b \cos 2x}{x^2}, & x \;<\; 0 \\ x^2 \;+\; cx \;+\; 2, & 0 \;\le\; x \;\le\; 1 \\ 2x \;+\; 1, & x \;>\; 1 \end{cases}$. If $f$ is continuous everywhere in $\mathbb{R}$ and $m$ is the number of points where $f$ is NOT differentiable then $m \;+\; a \;+\; b \;+\; c$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use continuity at $x \;=\; 0$ and $x \;=\; 1$ to find $a, b, c$, and then check the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at $x \;=\; 0$ and $x \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 1$, we have $f(1^-) \;=\; f(1^+) \;\implies\; 1^2 \;+\; c(1) \;+\; 2 \;=\; 2(1) \;+\; 1 \;\implies\; 3 \;+\; c \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; c \;=\; 0$. Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we have $\lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{a \;-\; b \cos 2x}{x^2} \;=\; f(0) \;=\; 2$. Using the series expansion $\cos 2x \;=\; 1 \;-\; \frac{4x^2}{2!} \;+\; \frac{16x^4}{4!} \;-\; \dots$, we get $\lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{\left( a \;-\; b \right) \;+\; 2bx^2 \;-\; \frac{2b}{3}x^4 \;+\; \dots}{x^2} \;=\; 2$. For the limit to exist, $a \;-\; b \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; a \;=\; b$, and the limit is $2b \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; b \;=\; 1$, so $a \;=\; 1$. Now check differentiability at $x \;=\; 0$ and $x \;=\; 1$: At $x \;=\; 0$, $\text{LHD} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{\frac{1 \;-\; \cos 2h}{h^2} \;-\; 2}{h} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{1 \;-\; \left( 1 \;-\; 2h^2 \;+\; \frac{2}{3}h^4 \;-\; \dots \right) \;-\; 2h^2}{h^3} \;=\; 0$, and $\text{RHD} \;=\; \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{h^2 \;+\; 2 \;-\; 2}{h} \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; 1$, $\text{LHD} \;=\; \left. \frac{d}{dx}\left( x^2 \;+\; 2 \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; 2$, and $\text{RHD} \;=\; \left. \frac{d}{dx}\left( 2x \;+\; 1 \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; 2$. Thus, $f$ is differentiable everywhere, so $m \;=\; 0$. Hence, $m \;+\; a \;+\; b \;+\; c \;=\; 0 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 0 \;=\; 2$.
questions.topic: Continuity and Differentiability of Piecewise Functions

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ be such that the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 2\alpha \left( x^2 \;-\; 2 \right) \;+\; 2\beta x, & x \;<\; 1 \\ \left( \alpha \;+\; 3 \right)x \;+\; \left( \alpha \;-\; \beta \right), & x \;\ge\; 1 \end{cases}$ be differentiable at all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Then $34\left( \alpha \;+\; \beta \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate the left-hand and right-hand limits as well as the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at $x \;=\; 1$ to form a system of linear equations in $\alpha$ and $\beta$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x \;=\; 1$, it is also continuous at $x \;=\; 1$. By continuity at $x \;=\; 1$: $f(1^-) \;=\; f(1) \;\implies\; 2\alpha\left( 1 \;-\; 2 \right) \;+\; 2\beta(1) \;=\; \left( \alpha \;+\; 3 \right)(1) \;+\; \alpha \;-\; \beta \;\implies\; -2\alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;=\; 2\alpha \;-\; \beta \;+\; 3 \;\implies\; 4\alpha \;-\; 3\beta \;=\; -3 \quad \text{...(1)}$. By differentiability at $x \;=\; 1$: $f'(1^-) \;=\; f'(1^+) \;\implies\; \left. \left( 4\alpha x \;+\; 2\beta \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; \alpha \;+\; 3 \;\implies\; 4\alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;=\; \alpha \;+\; 3 \;\implies\; 3\alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;=\; 3 \quad \text{...(2)}$. Solving equations (1) and (2): multiplying (1) by $2$ and (2) by $3$ and adding gives $17\alpha \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{3}{17}$. Substituting $\alpha \;=\; \frac{3}{17}$ into (2) gives $2\beta \;=\; 3 \;-\; \frac{9}{17} \;=\; \frac{42}{17} \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; \frac{21}{17}$. Thus, $34\left( \alpha \;+\; \beta \right) \;=\; 34\left( \frac{3}{17} \;+\; \frac{21}{17} \right) \;=\; 2 \;\times\; 24 \;=\; 48$.
questions.topic: Continuity and Differentiability of Piecewise Functions

questions.text: If the function $f(x) \;=\; \frac{\sin 3x \;+\; \alpha \sin x \;-\; \beta \cos 3x}{x^3}$, $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then $f(0)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Taylor series expansions for $\sin 3x$, $\sin x$, and $\cos 3x$ around $x \;=\; 0$ and set coefficients of powers of $x$ less than $x^3$ to zero. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, $f(0) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x \;+\; \alpha \sin x \;-\; \beta \cos 3x}{x^3}$ must exist and be finite. Expanding the trigonometric functions using Maclaurin series: $\sin 3x \;=\; 3x \;-\; \frac{\left( 3x \right)^3}{3!} \;+\; O\left( x^5 \right)$, $\sin x \;=\; x \;-\; \frac{x^3}{3!} \;+\; O\left( x^5 \right)$, and $\cos 3x \;=\; 1 \;-\; \frac{\left( 3x \right)^2}{2!} \;+\; O\left( x^4 \right)$. Substituting these into the limit gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-\beta \;+\; \left( 3 \;+\; \alpha \right)x \;+\; \frac{9\beta}{2}x^2 \;-\; \left( \frac{27 \;+\; \alpha}{6} \right)x^3 \;+\; O\left( x^4 \right)}{x^3}$. For the limit to exist finitely, the coefficients of $x^0$, $x^1$, and $x^2$ in the numerator must vanish: $-\beta \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 0$, and $3 \;+\; \alpha \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; -3$. Then, $f(0) \;=\; -\frac{27 \;+\; \alpha}{6} \;=\; -\frac{27 \;-\; 3}{6} \;=\; -\frac{24}{6} \;=\; -4$.
questions.topic: Continuity at a Point Using Series Expansion

questions.text: Let $f(x) \;=\; \sqrt{\lim_{r \to x} \left\{ \frac{2r^2 \left[ \left( f(r) \right)^2 \;-\; f(x)f(r) \right]}{r^2 \;-\; x^2} \;-\; r^3 e^{\frac{f(r)}{r}} \right\}}$ be differentiable in $\left( -\infty, 0 \right) \;\cup\; \left( 0, \infty \right)$ and $f(1) \;=\; 1$. Then the value of $ea$, such that $f(a) \;=\; 0$, is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the limit as $r \to x$ to form a homogeneous first-order differential equation and solve it using $y \;=\; vx$. // 📝 Solution: Squaring both sides and evaluating the limit as $r \to x$: $\left( f(x) \right)^2 \;=\; \lim_{r \to x} \left( \frac{2r^2 f(r)}{r \;+\; x} \cdot \frac{f(r) \;-\; f(x)}{r \;-\; x} \;-\; r^3 e^{\frac{f(r)}{r}} \right) \;=\; \frac{2x^2 f(x)}{2x} f'(x) \;-\; x^3 e^{\frac{f(x)}{x}} \;=\; x f(x) f'(x) \;-\; x^3 e^{\frac{f(x)}{x}}$. Let $y \;=\; f(x)$, so $y^2 \;=\; xy \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; x^3 e^{\frac{y}{x}} \;\implies\; \frac{y}{x} \;=\; \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \frac{x^2}{y} e^{\frac{y}{x}}$. Put $y \;=\; vx \;\implies\; \frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; v \;+\; x \frac{dv}{dx}$. Substituting gives $v \;=\; v \;+\; x \frac{dv}{dx} \;-\; \frac{x}{v} e^v \;\implies\; v e^{-v} dv \;=\; dx$. Integrating both sides: $-v e^{-v} \;-\; e^{-v} \;=\; x \;+\; c \;\implies\; e^v \left( x \;+\; c \right) \;+\; v \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. Given $f(1) \;=\; 1$, for $x \;=\; 1$ we have $v \;=\; 1$, so $e^1 \left( 1 \;+\; c \right) \;+\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; c \;=\; -1 \;-\; \frac{2}{e}$. Thus, $e^{\frac{y}{x}} \left( x \;-\; 1 \;-\; \frac{2}{e} \right) \;+\; \frac{y}{x} \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. For $f(a) \;=\; 0$, put $x \;=\; a$ and $y \;=\; 0$: $e^0 \left( a \;-\; 1 \;-\; \frac{2}{e} \right) \;+\; 0 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{2}{e} \;\implies\; ea \;=\; 2$.
questions.topic: Limit Definition of Derivative and Differential Equations

questions.text: Consider the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{a\left( 7x \;-\; 12 \;-\; x^2 \right)}{b\left\lvert x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12 \right\rvert}, & x \;<\; 3 \\ 2^{\frac{\sin(x \;-\; 3)}{x \;-\; \left[ x \right]}}, & x \;>\; 3 \\ b, & x \;=\; 3 \end{cases}$, where $\left[ x \right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. If $S$ denotes the set of all ordered pairs $\left( a, b \right)$ such that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 3$, then the number of elements in $S$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x)$ and equate both to $f(3) \;=\; b$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \;<\; 3$, note that $x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12 \;=\; \left( x \;-\; 3 \right)\left( x \;-\; 4 \right) \;>\; 0$, so $\left\lvert x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12 \right\rvert \;=\; x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12$. Thus, the left-hand limit at $x \;=\; 3$ is $f(3^-) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 3^-} \frac{-a\left( x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12 \right)}{b\left( x^2 \;-\; 7x \;+\; 12 \right)} \;=\; -\frac{a}{b}$. For $x \;\in\; \left( 3, 4 \right)$, we have $\left[ x \right] \;=\; 3$, so $x \;-\; \left[ x \right] \;=\; x \;-\; 3$. Thus, the right-hand limit at $x \;=\; 3$ is $f(3^+) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 3^+} 2^{\frac{\sin(x \;-\; 3)}{x \;-\; 3}} \;=\; 2^1 \;=\; 2$. Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 3$, we have $f(3^-) \;=\; f(3^+) \;=\; f(3)$, which gives $-\frac{a}{b} \;=\; 2 \;=\; b$. From $b \;=\; 2$, we get $-\frac{a}{2} \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; a \;=\; -4$. Hence, there is only $1$ ordered pair $\left( -4, 2 \right)$ in $S$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function given by $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{1 \;-\; \cos 2x}{x^2}, & x \;<\; 0 \\ \alpha, & x \;=\; 0 \\ \frac{\beta \sqrt{1 \;-\; \cos x}}{x}, & x \;>\; 0 \end{cases}$, where $\alpha, \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then $\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and the value of the function at $x \;=\; 0$ using standard trigonometric limits. // 📝 Solution: For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we must have $\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) \;=\; f(0) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x)$. First, evaluate the left-hand limit: $f(0^-) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{1 \;-\; \cos 2x}{x^2} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{2 \sin^2 x}{x^2} \;=\; 2 \left( 1 \right)^2 \;=\; 2$. Since $f(0) \;=\; \alpha$, we get $\alpha \;=\; 2$. Next, evaluate the right-hand limit: $f(0^+) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\beta \sqrt{1 \;-\; \cos x}}{x} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\beta \sqrt{2 \sin^2 \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)}}{x}$. Since $x \;>\; 0$, $\sqrt{\sin^2 \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)} \;=\; \sin \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)$, so $f(0^+) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\sqrt{2} \beta \sin \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)}{2 \cdot \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)} \;=\; \frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}$. Equating $f(0^+) \;=\; \alpha$, we have $\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}} \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \beta \;=\; 2\sqrt{2}$. Therefore, $\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^2 \;=\; 2^2 \;+\; \left( 2\sqrt{2} \right)^2 \;=\; 4 \;+\; 8 \;=\; 12$.

questions.text: Consider the function $f : \left( 0, 2 \right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) \;=\; \frac{x}{2} \;+\; \frac{2}{x}$ and the function $g(x)$ defined by $g(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \min\left\{ f(t) \right\}, & 0 \;<\; t \;\le\; x \text{ and } 0 \;<\; x \;\le\; 1 \\ \frac{3}{2} \;+\; x, & 1 \;<\; x \;<\; 2 \end{cases}$. Then

options.text: $g$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x \;=\; 1$
$g$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at $x \;=\; 1$
$g$ is continuous and differentiable for all $x \;\in\; \left( 0, 2 \right)$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Determine the monotonicity of $f(x)$ on $\left( 0, 1 \right]$ to find an explicit formula for $g(x)$, then check continuity and differentiability at $x \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Differentiating $f(x) \;=\; \frac{x}{2} \;+\; \frac{2}{x}$ gives $f'(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;-\; \frac{2}{x^2}$. For $x \;\in\; \left( 0, 1 \right]$, $f'(x) \;<\; 0$, so $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $\left( 0, 1 \right]$. Therefore, for $0 \;<\; x \;\le\; 1$, $\min_{0 < t \le x} f(t) \;=\; f(x) \;=\; \frac{x}{2} \;+\; \frac{2}{x}$. Thus, $g(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{x}{2} \;+\; \frac{2}{x}, & 0 \;<\; x \;\le\; 1 \\ \frac{3}{2} \;+\; x, & 1 \;<\; x \;<\; 2 \end{cases}$. Checking continuity at $x \;=\; 1$: $g(1^-) \;=\; g(1) \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;+\; 2 \;=\; \frac{5}{2}$, and $g(1^+) \;=\; \frac{3}{2} \;+\; 1 \;=\; \frac{5}{2}$. Thus, $g$ is continuous for all $x \;\in\; \left( 0, 2 \right)$. Checking differentiability at $x \;=\; 1$: $g'(1^-) \;=\; \left. \left( \frac{1}{2} \;-\; \frac{2}{x^2} \right) \right\rvert_{x=1} \;=\; -\frac{3}{2}$, whereas $g'(1^+) \;=\; 1$. Since $g'(1^-) \;\neq\; g'(1^+)$, $g$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x \;=\; 1$.

questions.text: If the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} \frac{72^x \;-\; 9^x \;-\; 8^x \;+\; 1}{\sqrt{2} \;-\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; \cos x}}, & x \;\neq\; 0 \\ a \log_e 2 \log_e 3, & x \;=\; 0 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then the value of $a^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factorize the numerator as $\left( 8^x \;-\; 1 \right)\left( 9^x \;-\; 1 \right)$ and rationalize the denominator to evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, we have $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \;=\; f(0) \;=\; a \ln 2 \ln 3$. Now, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{72^x \;-\; 9^x \;-\; 8^x \;+\; 1}{\sqrt{2} \;-\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; \cos x}} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left( 8^x \;-\; 1 \right)\left( 9^x \;-\; 1 \right)\left( \sqrt{2} \;+\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; \cos x} \right)}{2 \;-\; \left( 1 \;+\; \cos x \right)} \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0} \left( \frac{8^x \;-\; 1}{x} \right) \left( \frac{9^x \;-\; 1}{x} \right) \left( \frac{x^2}{1 \;-\; \cos x} \right) \left( \sqrt{2} \;+\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; \cos x} \right)$. Using standard limits $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{k^x \;-\; 1}{x} \;=\; \ln k$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{1 \;-\; \cos x} \;=\; 2$, the limit evaluates to $\left( \ln 8 \right) \left( \ln 9 \right) \left( 2 \right) \left( \sqrt{2} \;+\; \sqrt{2} \right) \;=\; \left( 3 \ln 2 \right) \left( 2 \ln 3 \right) \left( 4\sqrt{2} \right) \;=\; 24\sqrt{2} \ln 2 \ln 3$. Comparing with $f(0) \;=\; a \ln 2 \ln 3$, we get $a \;=\; 24\sqrt{2}$. Thus, $a^2 \;=\; 576 \;\times\; 2 \;=\; 1152$.
questions.topic: Continuity Involving Exponential and Trigonometric Limits

questions.text: Let $\left[ t \right]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. If the function $f(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} b^2 \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} \left( \cos x \;+\; \sin x \right) \cos x \right] \right), & x \;<\; 0 \\ \frac{\sin x \;-\; \frac{1}{2} \sin 2x}{x^3}, & x \;>\; 0 \\ a, & x \;=\; 0 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$, then $a^2 \;+\; b^2$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the right-hand limit using $\sin x \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x \;=\; \sin x\left( 1 \;-\; \cos x \right)$ and analyze the behaviour of $\frac{\pi}{2}\left( \cos x \;+\; \sin x \right)\cos x$ as $x \to 0^-$. // 📝 Solution: For $x \;>\; 0$, $\sin x \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x \;=\; \sin x\left( 1 \;-\; \cos x \right)$. Evaluating the right-hand limit at $x \;=\; 0$: $\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \left( \frac{\sin x}{x} \right)\left( \frac{1 \;-\; \cos x}{x^2} \right) \;=\; 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. By continuity at $x \;=\; 0$, $a \;=\; f(0) \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. For $x \;<\; 0$ near $0$, $\left( \cos x \;+\; \sin x \right)\cos x \;=\; \frac{1 \;+\; \cos 2x \;+\; \sin 2x}{2}$ approaches $1$ from below, so $\frac{\pi}{2}\left( \cos x \;+\; \sin x \right)\cos x$ approaches $\frac{\pi}{2} \;\approx\; 1.57$ from below. Therefore, $\left[ \frac{\pi}{2}\left( \cos x \;+\; \sin x \right)\cos x \right] \;=\; 1$ as $x \to 0^-$. Thus, $\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) \;=\; b^2 \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot 1 \right) \;=\; b^2$. Equating $\text{LHL} \;=\; a$, we get $b^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. Hence, $a^2 \;+\; b^2 \;=\; \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$.
questions.topic: Continuity Involving Greatest Integer and Trigonometric Functions

questions.text: The maximum area of a triangle whose one vertex is at $(0, 0)$ and the other two vertices lie on the curve $y \;=\; -2x^{2} \;+\; 54$ at points $(x, y)$ and $(-x, y)$ where $y \;>\; 0$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the area of the triangle as a function of $x$, $A(x) \;=\; xy \;=\; x\left(54 \;-\; 2x^{2}\right)$, and maximize it using derivatives. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Without loss of generality, let $x \;>\; 0$. The vertices of the triangle are $(0, 0)$, $(x, y)$, and $(-x, y)$ with $y \;>\; 0$. The base of the triangle has length $2x$ and its height is $y$, so the area of the triangle is $\Delta \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\times\; 2x \;\times\; y \;=\; xy$. Substituting $y \;=\; -2x^{2} \;+\; 54$, we get $\Delta(x) \;=\; x\left(-2x^{2} \;+\; 54\right) \;=\; -2x^{3} \;+\; 54x$. Differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $\frac{d\Delta}{dx} \;=\; -6x^{2} \;+\; 54$. For maximum area, $\frac{d\Delta}{dx} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 6x^{2} \;=\; 54 \;\implies\; x^{2} \;=\; 9 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 3$ (since $x \;>\; 0$). At $x \;=\; 3$, $\frac{d^{2}\Delta}{dx^{2}} \;=\; -12x \;<\; 0$, confirming a maximum. Thus, the maximum area is $\Delta_{\max} \;=\; 3\left(-2(3)^{2} \;+\; 54\right) \;=\; 3\left(-18 \;+\; 54\right) \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 36 \;=\; 108$.

questions.text: Consider the circle $C : x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 4$ and the parabola $P : y^{2} \;=\; 8x$. If the set of all values of $\alpha$, for which three chords of the circle $C$ on three distinct lines passing through the point $(\alpha, 0)$ are bisected by the parabola $P$ is the interval $(p, q)$, then $\left(2q \;-\; p\right)^{2}$ is equal to ________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the equation of a chord of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 4$ bisected at a point $\left(2t^{2}, 4t\right)$ on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 8x$ using $T \;=\; S_{1}$, and find the condition for three distinct real roots of $t$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let the midpoint of a chord of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 4$ lying on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 8x$ be $M\left(2t^{2}, 4t\right)$, where $t \;\neq\; 0$. Since $M$ lies inside the circle, we must have $\left(2t^{2}\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(4t\right)^{2} \;-\; 4 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; 4t^{4} \;+\; 16t^{2} \;-\; 4 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; t^{4} \;+\; 4t^{2} \;-\; 1 \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;<\; t^{2} \;<\; \sqrt{5} \;-\; 2$. The equation of the chord of the circle with midpoint $M\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ is $T \;=\; S_{1} \;\implies\; xx_{1} \;+\; yy_{1} \;=\; x_{1}^{2} \;+\; y_{1}^{2}$. Since this chord passes through $(\alpha, 0)$, we have $\alpha x_{1} \;=\; x_{1}^{2} \;+\; y_{1}^{2}$. Substituting $x_{1} \;=\; 2t^{2}$ and $y_{1} \;=\; 4t$ gives $\alpha\left(2t^{2}\right) \;=\; 4t^{4} \;+\; 16t^{2}$. Since $t \;=\; 0$ always gives the $x$-axis as one chord, for two other distinct chords we divide by $2t^{2} \;\neq\; 0$ to get $\alpha \;=\; 2t^{2} \;+\; 8 \;\implies\; t^{2} \;=\; \frac{\alpha \;-\; 8}{2}$. Using $0 \;<\; t^{2} \;<\; \sqrt{5} \;-\; 2$, we get $0 \;<\; \frac{\alpha \;-\; 8}{2} \;<\; \sqrt{5} \;-\; 2 \;\implies\; 8 \;<\; \alpha \;<\; 4 \;+\; 2\sqrt{5}$. Thus, $p \;=\; 8$ and $q \;=\; 4 \;+\; 2\sqrt{5}$. Therefore, $\left(2q \;-\; p\right)^{2} \;=\; \left(8 \;+\; 4\sqrt{5} \;-\; 8\right)^{2} \;=\; \left(4\sqrt{5}\right)^{2} \;=\; 80$.
questions.topic: Chord Bisected at a Given Point

questions.text: An equilateral triangle $OAB$ is inscribed in the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$ with the vertex $O$ at the vertex of the parabola. Then the minimum distance of the circle having $AB$ as a diameter from the origin is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: By symmetry of the equilateral $\triangle OAB$, the vertices $A$ and $B$ make $30^{\circ}$ angles with the $x$-axis; find the centre and radius of the circle with diameter $AB$. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$, the vertex is $O(0, 0)$ and $a \;=\; 1$. By symmetry, let the other two vertices of the equilateral $\triangle OAB$ be $A\left(t^{2}, 2t\right)$ and $B\left(t^{2}, -2t\right)$ with $t \;>\; 0$. Since $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, $OA \;=\; AB \;\implies\; \sqrt{t^{4} \;+\; 4t^{2}} \;=\; 4t \;\implies\; t^{2} \;+\; 4 \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; t^{2} \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 2\sqrt{3}$. Thus, $A \;=\; \left(12, 4\sqrt{3}\right)$ and $B \;=\; \left(12, -4\sqrt{3}\right)$. The circle with $AB$ as diameter has its centre at the midpoint of $AB$, which is $C(12, 0)$, and its radius is $r \;=\; \frac{AB}{2} \;=\; 4\sqrt{3}$. Therefore, the minimum distance of this circle from the origin $O(0, 0)$ is $OC \;-\; r \;=\; 12 \;-\; 4\sqrt{3} \;=\; 4\left(3 \;-\; \sqrt{3}\right)$.

questions.text: The urns $A, B$ and $C$ contain $4$ red, $6$ black; $5$ red, $5$ black and $\lambda$ red, $4$ black balls respectively. One of the urns is selected at random and a ball is drawn. If the ball drawn is red and the probability that it is drawn from urn $C$ is $0.4$ then the square of the length of the side of the largest equilateral triangle, inscribed in the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; \lambda x$ with one vertex at the vertex of the parabola is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Bayes' theorem to find $\lambda$, and then use the inclination $30^{\circ}$ of the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle through the vertex of $y^{2} \;=\; \lambda x$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] By Bayes' theorem, the probability that the red ball is drawn from urn $C$ is $P\left(C \mid R\right) \;=\; \frac{\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;+\; 4}}{\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{10} \;+\; \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{10} \;+\; \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;+\; 4}} \;=\; 0.4$. Simplifying gives $\frac{\frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;+\; 4}}{\frac{9}{10} \;+\; \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;+\; 4}} \;=\; \frac{2}{5} \;\implies\; \frac{3\lambda}{\lambda \;+\; 4} \;=\; \frac{9}{5} \;\implies\; 5\lambda \;=\; 3\lambda \;+\; 12 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 6$. Thus, the parabola is $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$ with $a \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$. Let the vertices of the equilateral triangle inscribed in $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$ be $(0, 0)$ and $\left(\frac{3}{2}t^{2}, \pm 3t\right)$ for $t \;>\; 0$. Since the side makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the $x$-axis, we have $\tan 30^{\circ} \;=\; \frac{3t}{\frac{3}{2}t^{2}} \;=\; \frac{2}{t} \;\implies\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \;=\; \frac{2}{t} \;\implies\; t \;=\; 2\sqrt{3}$. The length of the side of the equilateral triangle is $l \;=\; 6t \;=\; 12\sqrt{3}$. Therefore, $l^{2} \;=\; \left(12\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} \;=\; 432$.

questions.text: The equations of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ are $\left(\lambda \;+\; 1\right)x \;+\; \lambda y \;=\; 4$ and $\lambda x \;+\; \left(1 \;-\; \lambda\right)y \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 0$ respectively. Its vertex $A$ is on the $y$-axis and its orthocentre is $(1, 2)$. The length of the tangent from the point $C$ to the part of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$ in the first quadrant is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $\lambda$ using the fact that vertex $A$ lies on the $y$-axis ($x \;=\; 0$), determine $C$ using the orthocentre property $CH \;\perp\; AB$, and then find the tangent from $C$ to $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] The sides are $AB : \left(\lambda \;+\; 1\right)x \;+\; \lambda y \;=\; 4$ and $AC : \lambda x \;+\; \left(1 \;-\; \lambda\right)y \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 0$. Since vertex $A$ lies on the $y$-axis, putting $x \;=\; 0$ gives $y \;=\; \frac{4}{\lambda}$ and $y \;=\; \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;-\; 1}$. Equating the two values of $y$, we get $\frac{4}{\lambda} \;=\; \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \;-\; 1} \;\implies\; \lambda^{2} \;-\; 4\lambda \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 2$. Thus, $AB : 3x \;+\; 2y \;=\; 4$ and $AC : 2x \;-\; y \;+\; 2 \;=\; 0$, with $A(0, 2)$. Let $C$ on $AC$ be $\left(\alpha, 2\alpha \;+\; 2\right)$. Since the orthocentre is $H(1, 2)$, the altitude $CH$ is perpendicular to $AB$: $\left(\frac{2\alpha \;+\; 2 \;-\; 2}{\alpha \;-\; 1}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; \frac{2\alpha}{\alpha \;-\; 1} \;=\; \frac{2}{3} \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}$. Hence, $C \;=\; \left(-\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$. For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$, we have $a \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$. Let the tangent be $y \;=\; mx \;+\; \frac{3}{2m}$. Passing it through $C\left(-\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$ gives $1 \;=\; -\frac{m}{2} \;+\; \frac{3}{2m} \;\implies\; m^{2} \;+\; 2m \;-\; 3 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; m \;=\; 1, -3$. For the point of contact $T\left(\frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right)$ to lie in the first quadrant, we take $m \;=\; 1$, which gives $T\left(\frac{3}{2}, 3\right)$. Therefore, the length of the tangent is $CT \;=\; \sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{2} \;+\; \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(3 \;-\; 1\right)^{2}} \;=\; \sqrt{4 \;+\; 4} \;=\; 2\sqrt{2}$.

questions.text: If $P(h, k)$ be point on the parabola $x \;=\; 4y^{2}$, which is nearest to the point $Q(0, 33)$, then the distance of $P$ from the directrix of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4(x \;+\; y)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The nearest point $P$ on the parabola to $Q(0, 33)$ is the foot of the normal passing through $Q$; find $P$ using the parametric normal equation. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{4}x$, we have $4a \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{1}{16}$. The equation of the normal at $P\left(at^{2}, 2at\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{t^{2}}{16}, \frac{t}{8}\right)$ is $y \;+\; tx \;=\; 2at \;+\; at^{3} \;\implies\; y \;+\; tx \;=\; \frac{t}{8} \;+\; \frac{t^{3}}{16}$. Since the normal passes through $Q(0, 33)$, we have $33 \;=\; \frac{t}{8} \;+\; \frac{t^{3}}{16} \;\implies\; t^{3} \;+\; 2t \;-\; 528 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(t \;-\; 8\right)\left(t^{2} \;+\; 8t \;+\; 66\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t \;=\; 8$. Thus, the point is $P(h, k) \;=\; \left(\frac{64}{16}, \frac{8}{8}\right) \;=\; (4, 1)$. Now, rewriting the second parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4(x \;+\; y)$ gives $\left(y \;-\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; 4\left(x \;+\; 1\right)$. Its directrix is $x \;+\; 1 \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; x \;=\; -2$. Therefore, the distance of $P(4, 1)$ from the directrix $x \;=\; -2$ is $\left\lvert 4 \;-\; (-2) \right\rvert \;=\; 6$.
questions.topic: Normal to a Parabola and Shortest Distance

questions.text: Suppose $AB$ is a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$ of length $l$ and slope $m \;<\; \sqrt{3}$. If the distance of the chord $AB$ from the origin is $d$, then $ld^{2}$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: If a focal chord makes an angle $\theta$ with the axis of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4ax$, its distance from the vertex $(0, 0)$ is $d \;=\; a\left\lvert \sin\theta \right\rvert$ and its length is $l \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$, we have $4a \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 3$, so the focus is $S(3, 0)$. Let the focal chord $AB$ make an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis. From the right triangle formed by the origin $O(0, 0)$, the foot of the perpendicular on the chord, and the focus $S(3, 0)$, the distance of the chord from the origin is $d \;=\; 3\left\lvert \sin\theta \right\rvert \;\implies\; \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; \frac{9}{d^{2}}$. The length of the focal chord is $l \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; 12 \;\times\; \frac{9}{d^{2}} \;=\; \frac{108}{d^{2}}$. Therefore, $ld^{2} \;=\; 108$.

questions.text: If the shortest distance of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$ from the centre of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;-\; 4x \;-\; 16y \;+\; 64 \;=\; 0$ is $d$, then $d^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The shortest distance between a circle and a parabola occurs along their common normal, so find the normal to $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$ that passes through the centre of the circle. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$, we have $a \;=\; 1$. The equation of the normal in slope form is $y \;=\; mx \;-\; 2m \;-\; m^{3}$. The centre of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;-\; 4x \;-\; 16y \;+\; 64 \;=\; 0$ is $C(2, 8)$. Since the shortest distance is along the normal passing through $C(2, 8)$, substituting $x \;=\; 2$ and $y \;=\; 8$ gives $8 \;=\; 2m \;-\; 2m \;-\; m^{3} \;\implies\; m^{3} \;=\; -8 \;\implies\; m \;=\; -2$. The foot of the normal on the parabola is $P\left(am^{2}, -2am\right) \;=\; \left(1(-2)^{2}, -2(1)(-2)\right) \;=\; (4, 4)$. Therefore, the shortest distance squared is $d^{2} \;=\; PC^{2} \;=\; \left(4 \;-\; 2\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(4 \;-\; 8\right)^{2} \;=\; 4 \;+\; 16 \;=\; 20$.
questions.topic: Normal to a Parabola and Shortest Distance

questions.text: If the $x$-intercept of a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 8x \;+\; 4y \;+\; 4$ is $3$, then the length of this chord is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert the parabola equation into standard form $\left(y \;-\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; 8\left(x \;+\; 1\right)$ to find the focus, determine the inclination $\theta$ of the focal chord passing through $(3, 0)$, and use $L \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting the given parabola equation by completing the square: $y^{2} \;-\; 4y \;+\; 4 \;=\; 8x \;+\; 8 \;\implies\; \left(y \;-\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; 8\left(x \;+\; 1\right)$. Comparing with $Y^{2} \;=\; 4aX$, we have $4a \;=\; 8 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 2$, $X \;=\; x \;+\; 1$, and $Y \;=\; y \;-\; 2$. The focus is at $(X \;=\; 2, Y \;=\; 0) \;\implies\; S(1, 2)$. Since the focal chord passes through the focus $S(1, 2)$ and has $x$-intercept $(3, 0)$, its slope is $m \;=\; \tan\theta \;=\; \frac{2 \;-\; 0}{1 \;-\; 3} \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; 1 \;+\; \cot^{2}\theta \;=\; 2$. Therefore, the length of the focal chord is $L \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; 8 \;\times\; 2 \;=\; 16$.

questions.text: Let $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$ be the parabola with its vertex at $O$. Let $P$ be a point on the parabola and $A$ be a point on the $x$-axis such that $\angle OPA \;=\; 90^{\circ}$. Then the locus of the centroid of such triangles $OPA$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Take parametric coordinates $P\left(3t^{2}, 6t\right)$ on $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$, use $\overrightarrow{PO} \cdot \overrightarrow{PA} \;=\; 0$ to find $A(h, 0)$ in terms of $t$, and then eliminate $t$ from the centroid coordinates. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$, we have $a \;=\; 3$. Let $O \;=\; (0, 0)$, $P \;=\; \left(3t^{2}, 6t\right)$, and $A \;=\; (h, 0)$ for $t \;\neq\; 0$. Since $\angle OPA \;=\; 90^{\circ}$, we have $\overrightarrow{PO} \cdot \overrightarrow{PA} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(-3t^{2}\right)\left(h \;-\; 3t^{2}\right) \;+\; \left(-6t\right)\left(-6t\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; -3t^{2}\left(h \;-\; 3t^{2}\right) \;+\; 36t^{2} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; h \;=\; 3t^{2} \;+\; 12$. Let $G(X, Y)$ be the centroid of $\triangle OPA$. Then $X \;=\; \frac{0 \;+\; 3t^{2} \;+\; h}{3} \;=\; \frac{6t^{2} \;+\; 12}{3} \;=\; 2t^{2} \;+\; 4$ and $Y \;=\; \frac{0 \;+\; 6t \;+\; 0}{3} \;=\; 2t$. Eliminating $t \;=\; \frac{Y}{2}$, we get $X \;=\; 2\left(\frac{Y}{2}\right)^{2} \;+\; 4 \;=\; \frac{Y^{2}}{2} \;+\; 4 \;\implies\; Y^{2} \;-\; 2X \;+\; 8 \;=\; 0$. Replacing $(X, Y)$ with $(x, y)$, the locus is $y^{2} \;-\; 2x \;+\; 8 \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let the locus of the mid-point of the chord through the origin $O$ of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$ be the curve $S$. Let $P$ be any point on $S$. Then the locus of the point, which internally divides $OP$ in the ratio $3 : 1$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: First find the locus $S$ of the midpoint of the chord $OQ$ of $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$, and then apply the section formula for internal division in the ratio $3 : 1$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let the other end of a chord through the origin $O(0, 0)$ on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$ be $Q\left(t^{2}, 2t\right)$. The midpoint of $OQ$ is $M\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}, t\right)$. Eliminating $t$, the locus $S$ of the midpoint is $y^{2} \;=\; 2x$. Now let $P\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ be any point on $S$, so $y_{1}^{2} \;=\; 2x_{1}$. Let $R(h, k)$ be the point that divides $OP$ internally in the ratio $3 : 1$. By the section formula, $h \;=\; \frac{3x_{1} \;+\; 1(0)}{3 \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{3x_{1}}{4} \;\implies\; x_{1} \;=\; \frac{4h}{3}$, and $k \;=\; \frac{3y_{1} \;+\; 1(0)}{3 \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{3y_{1}}{4} \;\implies\; y_{1} \;=\; \frac{4k}{3}$. Substituting $x_{1}$ and $y_{1}$ into $y_{1}^{2} \;=\; 2x_{1}$, we get $\left(\frac{4k}{3}\right)^{2} \;=\; 2\left(\frac{4h}{3}\right) \;\implies\; \frac{16k^{2}}{9} \;=\; \frac{8h}{3} \;\implies\; 2k^{2} \;=\; 3h$. Thus, the required locus is $2y^{2} \;=\; 3x$.

questions.text: Let one end of a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 16x$ be $(16, 16)$. If $P(\alpha, \beta)$ divides this focal chord internally in the ratio $5 : 2$, then the minimum value of $\alpha \;+\; \beta$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: If $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ are the parameters of the endpoints of a focal chord of $y^{2} \;=\; 4ax$, then $t_{1}t_{2} \;=\; -1$; consider both possible internal division directions ($5 : 2$ and $2 : 5$). // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 16x$, we have $4a \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 4$. A parametric point is $\left(4t^{2}, 8t\right)$. For the given endpoint $A(16, 16)$, we have $8t_{1} \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; t_{1} \;=\; 2$. Since $AB$ is a focal chord, the parameter of the other end $B$ is $t_{2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{t_{1}} \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}$. Thus, the other endpoint is $B\left(4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}, 8\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right) \;=\; (1, -4)$. Now $P(\alpha, \beta)$ divides the chord internally in the ratio $5 : 2$ (two cases): Case 1: $P$ divides $AB$ in ratio $5 : 2$, giving $P \;=\; \left(\frac{5(1) \;+\; 2(16)}{7}, \frac{5(-4) \;+\; 2(16)}{7}\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{37}{7}, \frac{12}{7}\right)$, so $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; \frac{49}{7} \;=\; 7$. Case 2: $P$ divides $BA$ in ratio $5 : 2$, giving $P \;=\; \left(\frac{5(16) \;+\; 2(1)}{7}, \frac{5(16) \;+\; 2(-4)}{7}\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{82}{7}, \frac{72}{7}\right)$, so $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; \frac{154}{7} \;=\; 22$. Therefore, the minimum value of $\alpha \;+\; \beta$ is $7$.

questions.text: Let $O$ be the vertex of the parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 4y$ and $Q$ be any point on it. Let the locus of the point $P$, which divides the line segment $OQ$ internally in the ratio $2 : 3$ be the conic $C$. Then the equation of the chord of $C$, which is bisected at the point $(1, 2)$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the equation of the conic $C$ using the section formula for ratio $2 : 3$, and then apply $T \;=\; S_{1}$ at the midpoint $(1, 2)$. // 📝 Solution: The vertex of the parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 4y$ is $O(0, 0)$. Let $Q\left(2t, t^{2}\right)$ be any point on the parabola. Since $P(h, k)$ divides $OQ$ internally in the ratio $2 : 3$, we have $h \;=\; \frac{2(2t) \;+\; 3(0)}{2 \;+\; 3} \;=\; \frac{4t}{5} \;\implies\; t \;=\; \frac{5h}{4}$, and $k \;=\; \frac{2\left(t^{2}\right) \;+\; 3(0)}{2 \;+\; 3} \;=\; \frac{2t^{2}}{5}$. Eliminating $t$ gives $k \;=\; \frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{5h}{4}\right)^{2} \;=\; \frac{5h^{2}}{8} \;\implies\; 5h^{2} \;-\; 8k \;=\; 0$. Thus, the conic $C$ is $5x^{2} \;-\; 8y \;=\; 0$. The equation of the chord of $C$ bisected at $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right) \;=\; (1, 2)$ is given by $T \;=\; S_{1} \;\implies\; 5xx_{1} \;-\; 4\left(y \;+\; y_{1}\right) \;=\; 5x_{1}^{2} \;-\; 8y_{1}$. Substituting $(1, 2)$, we get $5x(1) \;-\; 4\left(y \;+\; 2\right) \;=\; 5(1)^{2} \;-\; 8(2) \;\implies\; 5x \;-\; 4y \;-\; 8 \;=\; -11 \;\implies\; 5x \;-\; 4y \;+\; 3 \;=\; 0$.
questions.topic: Locus and Chord with Given Midpoint

questions.text: Let $A$ be the focus of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 8x$. Let the line $y \;=\; mx \;+\; c$ intersect the parabola at two distinct points $B$ and $C$. If the centroid of the triangle $ABC$ is $\left(\frac{7}{3}, \frac{4}{3}\right)$, then $(BC)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.topic: Length of Chord and Parametric Form

questions.text: Let $L_{1}, L_{2}$ be the lines passing through the point $P(0, 1)$ and touching the parabola $9x^{2} \;+\; 12x \;+\; 18y \;-\; 14 \;=\; 0$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be the points on the lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ such that the $\triangle PQR$ is an isosceles triangle with base $QR$. If the slopes of the lines $QR$ are $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, then $16\left(m_{1}^{2} \;+\; m_{2}^{2}\right)$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the slopes of the tangents $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ from $P(0, 1)$ to the parabola; the base $QR$ of the isosceles $\triangle PQR$ is parallel to the angle bisectors of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Rewriting the parabola equation: $9x^{2} \;+\; 12x \;+\; 4 \;=\; -18y \;+\; 18 \;\implies\; \left(3x \;+\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; -18\left(y \;-\; 1\right)$. Let a line through $P(0, 1)$ with slope $m$ be $y \;-\; 1 \;=\; mx$. Substituting this into the parabola gives $\left(3x \;+\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; -18mx \;\implies\; 9x^{2} \;+\; \left(12 \;+\; 18m\right)x \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0$. For tangency, the discriminant $D \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(12 \;+\; 18m\right)^{2} \;-\; 4(9)(4) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 36\left(2 \;+\; 3m\right)^{2} \;=\; 144 \;\implies\; 2 \;+\; 3m \;=\; \pm 2$. Thus, the slopes of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are $m \;=\; 0$ and $m \;=\; -\frac{4}{3}$. Since $L_{1}$ has slope $0$ (horizontal) and $L_{2}$ has slope $\tan\theta \;=\; -\frac{4}{3}$, the base $QR$ makes equal angles with $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$. Using $\tan\theta \;=\; \frac{2\tan\frac{\theta}{2}}{1 \;-\; \tan^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}} \;=\; -\frac{4}{3} \;\implies\; 2\tan^{2}\frac{\theta}{2} \;-\; 3\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \;-\; 2\right)\left(2\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0$, so $\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \;=\; 2$ or $-\frac{1}{2}$. The slopes of $QR$ are given by $m_{QR} \;=\; -\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$, which gives $m_{1} \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}$ and $m_{2} \;=\; 2$. Therefore, $16\left(m_{1}^{2} \;+\; m_{2}^{2}\right) \;=\; 16\left(\frac{1}{4} \;+\; 4\right) \;=\; 4 \;+\; 64 \;=\; 68$.
questions.topic: Pair of Tangents to a Parabola

questions.text: If the chord joining the points $P_{1}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $P_{2}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$ subtends a right angle at the vertex of the parabola, then $x_{1}x_{2} \;-\; y_{1}y_{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: If a chord joining $\left(at_{1}^{2}, 2at_{1}\right)$ and $\left(at_{2}^{2}, 2at_{2}\right)$ of $y^{2} \;=\; 4ax$ subtends a right angle at the vertex $(0, 0)$, then $t_{1}t_{2} \;=\; -4$. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$, we have $4a \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 3$, and the vertex is $O(0, 0)$. Let the points be $P_{1}\left(3t_{1}^{2}, 6t_{1}\right)$ and $P_{2}\left(3t_{2}^{2}, 6t_{2}\right)$ for $t_{1}, t_{2} \;\neq\; 0$. Since $P_{1}P_{2}$ subtends a right angle at the vertex $O(0, 0)$, we have $\overrightarrow{OP_{1}} \cdot \overrightarrow{OP_{2}} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x_{1}x_{2} \;+\; y_{1}y_{2} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 9t_{1}^{2}t_{2}^{2} \;+\; 36t_{1}t_{2} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; t_{1}t_{2} \;=\; -4$. Therefore, $x_{1}x_{2} \;-\; y_{1}y_{2} \;=\; 9\left(t_{1}t_{2}\right)^{2} \;-\; 36\left(t_{1}t_{2}\right) \;=\; 9(-4)^{2} \;-\; 36(-4) \;=\; 144 \;+\; 144 \;=\; 288$.
questions.topic: Chord Subtending Right Angle at Vertex

questions.text: Let $PQ$ be a chord of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$ and the midpoint of $PQ$ be at $(4, 1)$. Then, which of the following point lies on the line passing through the points $P$ and $Q$?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The equation of the chord of a conic with a given midpoint $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ is given by $T \;=\; S_{1}$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] For the parabola $y^{2} \;-\; 12x \;=\; 0$ and the midpoint $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right) \;=\; (4, 1)$, the equation of the chord $PQ$ is given by $T \;=\; S_{1} \;\implies\; yy_{1} \;-\; 6\left(x \;+\; x_{1}\right) \;=\; y_{1}^{2} \;-\; 12x_{1}$. Substituting $(4, 1)$, we get $y(1) \;-\; 6\left(x \;+\; 4\right) \;=\; 1^{2} \;-\; 12(4) \;\implies\; y \;-\; 6x \;-\; 24 \;=\; 1 \;-\; 48 \;\implies\; 6x \;-\; y \;=\; 23$. Checking the given options, for $\left(\frac{1}{2}, -20\right)$, we have $6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \;-\; (-20) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 20 \;=\; 23$, which satisfies the equation.
questions.topic: Chord Bisected at a Given Point

questions.text: Let $A$ be a point on the $x$-axis. Common tangents are drawn from $A$ to the curves $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 8$ and $y^{2} \;=\; 16x$. If one of these tangents touches the two curves at $Q$ and $R$, then $(QR)^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the equation of the common tangent to $y^{2} \;=\; 16x$ and $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 8$, determine the points of contact $Q$ and $R$, and compute $(QR)^{2}$. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 16x$, we have $a \;=\; 4$. The equation of a tangent with slope $m$ is $y \;=\; mx \;+\; \frac{4}{m}$. Since this line is also tangent to the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;=\; 8$, its distance from $(0, 0)$ equals the radius $2\sqrt{2}$: $\frac{\left\lvert \frac{4}{m} \right\rvert}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; m^{2}}} \;=\; 2\sqrt{2} \;\implies\; \frac{16}{m^{2}\left(1 \;+\; m^{2}\right)} \;=\; 8 \;\implies\; m^{4} \;+\; m^{2} \;-\; 2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; m^{2} \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; m \;=\; \pm 1$. Taking $m \;=\; 1$, the common tangent is $x \;-\; y \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0$. The point of contact on the parabola is $R\left(\frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right) \;=\; (4, 8)$. The point of contact $Q$ on the circle is the foot of the perpendicular from $(0, 0)$ to $x \;-\; y \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0$, which is $Q(-2, 2)$. Therefore, $(QR)^{2} \;=\; \left(4 \;-\; (-2)\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(8 \;-\; 2\right)^{2} \;=\; 36 \;+\; 36 \;=\; 72$.

questions.text: Let the image of parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 4y$, in the line $x \;-\; y \;=\; 1$ be $\left(y \;+\; a\right)^{2} \;=\; b\left(x \;-\; c\right)$, $a, b, c \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. Then $a \;+\; b \;+\; c$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the reflection $(X, Y)$ of a general point $(h, k)$ on $x^{2} \;=\; 4y$ across the line $x \;-\; y \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ using the image formula. // 📝 Solution: Let $(h, k)$ be any point on the parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 4y$, so $h^{2} \;=\; 4k$. The reflection $(X, Y)$ of $(h, k)$ in the line $x \;-\; y \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ is given by $\frac{h \;-\; X}{1} \;=\; \frac{k \;-\; Y}{-1} \;=\; \frac{-2\left(X \;-\; Y \;-\; 1\right)}{1^{2} \;+\; (-1)^{2}} \;=\; -\left(X \;-\; Y \;-\; 1\right)$. This gives $h \;=\; Y \;+\; 1$ and $k \;=\; X \;-\; 1$. Substituting these into $h^{2} \;=\; 4k$, we get $\left(Y \;+\; 1\right)^{2} \;=\; 4\left(X \;-\; 1\right)$. Replacing $(X, Y)$ with $(x, y)$, the image parabola is $\left(y \;+\; 1\right)^{2} \;=\; 4\left(x \;-\; 1\right)$. Comparing this with $\left(y \;+\; a\right)^{2} \;=\; b\left(x \;-\; c\right)$, we obtain $a \;=\; 1$, $b \;=\; 4$, and $c \;=\; 1$. Therefore, $a \;+\; b \;+\; c \;=\; 1 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 6$.
questions.topic: Reflection of Parabola in a Line

questions.text: Let a conic $C$ pass through the point $(4, -2)$ and $P(x, y)$, $x \;\ge\; 3$, be any point on $C$. Let the slope of the line touching the conic $C$ only at a single point $P$ be half the slope of the line joining the points $P$ and $(3, -5)$. If the focal distance of the point $(7, 1)$ on $C$ is $d$, then $12d$ equals ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Form a differential equation using the slope of the tangent $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $P(x, y)$ and integrate it to find the equation of the parabola. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] According to the given condition, the slope of the tangent at $P(x, y)$ is $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{y \;+\; 5}{x \;-\; 3}\right)$. Separating the variables, we get $\frac{2}{y \;+\; 5}\,dy \;=\; \frac{1}{x \;-\; 3}\,dx$. Integrating both sides gives $2\ln\left\lvert y \;+\; 5 \right\rvert \;=\; \ln\left\lvert x \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Since the curve passes through $(4, -2)$, substituting $x \;=\; 4$ and $y \;=\; -2$ gives $2\ln(3) \;=\; \ln(1) \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2\ln(3) \;=\; \ln(9)$. Thus, the equation of the conic $C$ is $\left(y \;+\; 5\right)^{2} \;=\; 9\left(x \;-\; 3\right)$, which is a parabola with $4a \;=\; 9 \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{9}{4}$. The vertex is $(3, -5)$ and the focus is $S\left(3 \;+\; \frac{9}{4}, -5\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{21}{4}, -5\right)$. The focal distance of the point $(7, 1)$ on $C$ is $d \;=\; \left(7 \;-\; 3\right) \;+\; a \;=\; 4 \;+\; \frac{9}{4} \;=\; \frac{25}{4}$ (or by distance formula $d \;=\; \sqrt{\left(7 \;-\; \frac{21}{4}\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(1 \;+\; 5\right)^{2}} \;=\; \sqrt{\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^{2} \;+\; 6^{2}} \;=\; \frac{25}{4}$). Therefore, $12d \;=\; 12 \;\times\; \frac{25}{4} \;=\; 75$.

questions.text: Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a point on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$. If $P$ also lies on the chord of the parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 8y$ whose mid point is $\left(1, \frac{5}{4}\right)$. Then $\left(\alpha \;-\; 28\right)\left(\beta \;-\; 8\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the equation of the chord of $x^{2} \;=\; 8y$ with midpoint $\left(1, \frac{5}{4}\right)$ using $T \;=\; S_{1}$ and solve it simultaneously with $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$. // 📝 Solution: The equation of the chord of the parabola $x^{2} \;=\; 8y$ with midpoint $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right) \;=\; \left(1, \frac{5}{4}\right)$ is given by $T \;=\; S_{1} \;\implies\; xx_{1} \;-\; 4\left(y \;+\; y_{1}\right) \;=\; x_{1}^{2} \;-\; 8y_{1}$. Substituting $\left(1, \frac{5}{4}\right)$ gives $x(1) \;-\; 4\left(y \;+\; \frac{5}{4}\right) \;=\; 1^{2} \;-\; 8\left(\frac{5}{4}\right) \;\implies\; x \;-\; 4y \;-\; 5 \;=\; 1 \;-\; 10 \;=\; -9 \;\implies\; x \;-\; 4y \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0$. Since $P(\alpha, \beta)$ lies on this chord and on $y^{2} \;=\; 4x$, we have $\alpha \;=\; 4\beta \;-\; 4$ and $\beta^{2} \;=\; 4\alpha$. Substituting $\alpha$ gives $\beta^{2} \;=\; 4\left(4\beta \;-\; 4\right) \;\implies\; \beta^{2} \;-\; 16\beta \;+\; 16 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(\beta \;-\; 8\right)^{2} \;=\; 48 \;\implies\; \beta \;-\; 8 \;=\; \pm 4\sqrt{3}$. Also, $\alpha \;-\; 28 \;=\; \left(4\beta \;-\; 4\right) \;-\; 28 \;=\; 4\left(\beta \;-\; 8\right) \;=\; \pm 16\sqrt{3}$. Therefore, $\left(\alpha \;-\; 28\right)\left(\beta \;-\; 8\right) \;=\; 4\left(\beta \;-\; 8\right)^{2} \;=\; 4 \;\times\; 48 \;=\; 192$.
questions.topic: Chord Bisected at a Given Point

questions.text: Let $A, B$ and $C$ be three points on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$ and let the line segment $AB$ meet the line $L$ through $C$ parallel to the $x$-axis at the point $D$. Let $M$ and $N$ respectively be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $B$ on $L$. Then $\left(\frac{AM \cdot BN}{CD}\right)^{2}$ is equal to _________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use parametric coordinates $\left(at_{i}^{2}, 2at_{i}\right)$ for points $A, B, C$ on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4ax$ and find the $x$-coordinate of $D$ on the line $y \;=\; 2at_{3}$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 6x$, we have $4a \;=\; 6 \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$. Let the points be $A\left(at_{1}^{2}, 2at_{1}\right)$, $B\left(at_{2}^{2}, 2at_{2}\right)$, and $C\left(at_{3}^{2}, 2at_{3}\right)$. The line $L$ through $C$ parallel to the $x$-axis is $y \;=\; 2at_{3}$. The equation of the chord $AB$ is $y\left(t_{1} \;+\; t_{2}\right) \;=\; 2x \;+\; 2at_{1}t_{2}$. Since $D\left(\alpha, 2at_{3}\right)$ lies on both $L$ and $AB$, substituting $y \;=\; 2at_{3}$ gives $2at_{3}\left(t_{1} \;+\; t_{2}\right) \;=\; 2\alpha \;+\; 2at_{1}t_{2} \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; a\left(t_{1}t_{3} \;+\; t_{2}t_{3} \;-\; t_{1}t_{2}\right)$. Now, the perpendicular distances from $A$ and $B$ to $L$ are $AM \;=\; \left\lvert 2a\left(t_{1} \;-\; t_{3}\right) \right\rvert$ and $BN \;=\; \left\lvert 2a\left(t_{2} \;-\; t_{3}\right) \right\rvert$. Also, $CD \;=\; \left\lvert at_{3}^{2} \;-\; \alpha \right\rvert \;=\; a\left\lvert t_{3}^{2} \;-\; t_{1}t_{3} \;-\; t_{2}t_{3} \;+\; t_{1}t_{2} \right\rvert \;=\; a\left\lvert \left(t_{3} \;-\; t_{1}\right)\left(t_{3} \;-\; t_{2}\right) \right\rvert$. Therefore, $\left(\frac{AM \cdot BN}{CD}\right)^{2} \;=\; \left(\frac{4a^{2}\left\lvert \left(t_{1} \;-\; t_{3}\right)\left(t_{2} \;-\; t_{3}\right) \right\rvert}{a\left\lvert \left(t_{3} \;-\; t_{1}\right)\left(t_{3} \;-\; t_{2}\right) \right\rvert}\right)^{2} \;=\; \left(4a\right)^{2} \;=\; 6^{2} \;=\; 36$.

questions.text: Let the length of the focal chord $PQ$ of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$ be $15$ units. If the distance of $PQ$ from the origin is $p$, then $10p^{2}$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The length of a focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4ax$ making an angle $\theta$ with the axis is $L \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta$, and its perpendicular distance from the vertex $(0, 0)$ is $p \;=\; a\left\lvert \sin\theta \right\rvert$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 12x$, we have $4a \;=\; 12 \;\implies\; a \;=\; 3$, and the focus is $S(3, 0)$. The length of the focal chord $PQ$ is given by $L \;=\; 4a\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; 15 \;\implies\; 12\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; 15 \;\implies\; \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \;=\; \frac{5}{4} \;\implies\; \sin^{2}\theta \;=\; \frac{4}{5}$. This gives $\tan^{2}\theta \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; \tan\theta \;=\; \pm 2$. Taking $\tan\theta \;=\; 2$, the equation of the focal chord passing through $(3, 0)$ is $y \;-\; 0 \;=\; 2\left(x \;-\; 3\right) \;\implies\; 2x \;-\; y \;-\; 6 \;=\; 0$. The distance of $PQ$ from the origin $(0, 0)$ is $p \;=\; \frac{\left\lvert 0 \;-\; 0 \;-\; 6 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{2^{2} \;+\; \left(-1\right)^{2}}} \;=\; \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}$. Therefore, $10p^{2} \;=\; 10 \;\times\; \frac{36}{5} \;=\; 72$.

questions.text: The distance of the point $\left(6, -2\sqrt{2}\right)$ from the common tangent $y \;=\; mx \;+\; c$, $m \;>\; 0$, of the curves $x \;=\; 2y^{2}$ and $x \;=\; 1 \;+\; y^{2}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the tangent to the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}x$ in slope form $y \;=\; mx \;+\; \frac{a}{m}$ and apply the condition of tangency ($D \;=\; 0$) to the second parabola $y^{2} \;=\; x \;-\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}x$, we have $4a \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{1}{8}$. The equation of a tangent with slope $m \;>\; 0$ is $y \;=\; mx \;+\; \frac{1}{8m}$. Substituting this into the second curve $y^{2} \;+\; 1 \;=\; x$ gives $\left(mx \;+\; \frac{1}{8m}\right)^{2} \;+\; 1 \;=\; x \;\implies\; m^{2}x^{2} \;-\; \frac{3}{4}x \;+\; \frac{1}{64m^{2}} \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. For tangency, the discriminant is $D \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{9}{16} \;-\; 4m^{2}\left(\frac{1}{64m^{2}} \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{8}{16} \;=\; 4m^{2} \;\implies\; m^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{8} \;\implies\; m \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ (since $m \;>\; 0$). Thus, the common tangent is $y \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}x \;+\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \;\implies\; x \;-\; 2\sqrt{2}y \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. The perpendicular distance of the point $\left(6, -2\sqrt{2}\right)$ from this tangent is $d \;=\; \frac{\left\lvert 6 \;-\; 2\sqrt{2}\left(-2\sqrt{2}\right) \;+\; 1 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{1^{2} \;+\; \left(-2\sqrt{2}\right)^{2}}} \;=\; \frac{\left\lvert 6 \;+\; 8 \;+\; 1 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{9}} \;=\; \frac{15}{3} \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: Let $S$ be the set of all $a \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ such that the area of the triangle formed by the tangent at the point $P(b, c)$, $b, c \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 2ax$ and the lines $x \;=\; b$, $y \;=\; 0$ is $16\text{ unit}^{2}$, then $\sum_{a \in S} a$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The tangent at $P(b, c)$ to $y^{2} \;=\; 2ax$ meets the $x$-axis at $B(-b, 0)$, so the area of the right triangle formed with $x \;=\; b$ and $y \;=\; 0$ is $\frac{1}{2}(2b)(c) \;=\; bc \;=\; 16$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Since $P(b, c)$ lies on the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 2ax$, we have $c^{2} \;=\; 2ab \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{c^{2}}{2b}$. The equation of the tangent to $y^{2} \;=\; 2ax$ at $P(b, c)$ is $cy \;=\; a\left(x \;+\; b\right)$. Putting $y \;=\; 0$ gives the $x$-intercept at $B(-b, 0)$, while the line $x \;=\; b$ meets $y \;=\; 0$ at $A(b, 0)$. The area of $\triangle PAB$ is $\frac{1}{2} \;\times\; AB \;\times\; AP \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\times\; (2b) \;\times\; c \;=\; bc \;=\; 16$. Since $b, c \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, the possible pairs $(b, c)$ are $(1, 16), (2, 8), (4, 4), (8, 2), (16, 1)$. Checking $a \;=\; \frac{c^{2}}{2b} \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ for each pair: for $(1, 16)$, $a \;=\; 128$; for $(2, 8)$, $a \;=\; 16$; for $(4, 4)$, $a \;=\; 2$; while $(8, 2)$ and $(16, 1)$ give fractional values. Thus, $S \;=\; \left\{128, 16, 2\right\}$, and $\sum_{a \in S} a \;=\; 128 \;+\; 16 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 146$.

questions.text: Let a line perpendicular to the line $2x \;-\; y \;=\; 10$ touch the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4\left(x \;-\; 9\right)$ at the point $P$. The distance of the point $P$ from the centre of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;-\; 14x \;-\; 8y \;+\; 56 \;=\; 0$ is __________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The point of contact of a tangent of slope $m$ to the shifted parabola $Y^{2} \;=\; 4aX$ is given by $\left(X \;=\; \frac{a}{m^{2}}, Y \;=\; \frac{2a}{m}\right)$. // 📝 Solution: The slope of the given line $2x \;-\; y \;=\; 10$ is $2$. Since the tangent is perpendicular to this line, the slope of the tangent is $m \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}$. For the parabola $y^{2} \;=\; 4\left(x \;-\; 9\right)$, we have $a \;=\; 1$, $X \;=\; x \;-\; 9$, and $Y \;=\; y$. The coordinates of the point of contact $P$ are given by $\left(9 \;+\; \frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right) \;=\; \left(9 \;+\; \frac{1}{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}, \frac{2(1)}{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \;=\; \left(9 \;+\; 4, -4\right) \;=\; (13, -4)$. The centre of the circle $x^{2} \;+\; y^{2} \;-\; 14x \;-\; 8y \;+\; 56 \;=\; 0$ is $C(7, 4)$. Thus, the distance $CP \;=\; \sqrt{\left(13 \;-\; 7\right)^{2} \;+\; \left(-4 \;-\; 4\right)^{2}} \;=\; \sqrt{6^{2} \;+\; (-8)^{2}} \;=\; \sqrt{36 \;+\; 64} \;=\; 10$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the sum and the product of all the non-zero solutions of the equation $(\bar{z})^2 + \left\lvert z \right\rvert = 0, \; z \in \mathbb{C}$. Then $4(\alpha^2 + \beta^2)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $z = x + iy$ and equate the imaginary part $-2xy = 0$ to find the non-zero roots. // 📝 Solution: Let $z = x + iy \implies \bar{z}^2 = x^2 - y^2 - 2ixy$. Equation becomes $x^2 - y^2 - 2ixy + \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 0$. Imaginary part gives $2xy = 0 \implies x = 0$ or $y = 0$. For $x = 0$: $-y^2 + \left\lvert y \right\rvert = 0 \implies y = \pm 1$ (since $z \neq 0$). For $y = 0$: $x^2 + \left\lvert x \right\rvert = 0 \implies x = 0$. Thus non-zero roots are $i, \; -i$.
