questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Take general points on the two lines and force $\vec{PQ}$ to be proportional to the given direction ratios. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let $P\;=\;\left(t,\;t\;-\;2,\;t\right)$ and $Q\;=\;\left(2s\;-\;2,\;s,\;s\right)$. Then $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(2s\;-\;2\;-\;t,\;s\;-\;t\;+\;2,\;s\;-\;t\right)\;\parallel\;\left(2,\;1,\;2\right)$. From the last two components, $2\left(s\;-\;t\;+\;2\right)\;=\;s\;-\;t\;\implies\;s\;-\;t\;=\;-4$. Then $\frac{2s\;-\;2\;-\;t}{2}\;=\;-2\;\implies\;2s\;-\;t\;=\;-2$. Solving, $t\;=\;6$ and $s\;=\;2$, so $P\;=\;\left(6,\;4,\;6\right)$ and $Q\;=\;\left(2,\;2,\;2\right)$. Take $A\;=\;\left(1,\;2,\;12\right)$ and $\vec{QA}\;=\;\left(-1,\;0,\;10\right)$. Then $\vec{QA}\;\times\;\left(2,\;1,\;2\right)\;=\;\left(-10,\;22,\;-1\right)$ with squared magnitude $585$. So $l^2\;=\;\frac{585}{9}\;=\;65$. Correct option: A.
questions.topic: Line meeting two given lines; perpendicular distance from a point to a line

questions.text: Let $Q$ and $R$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from the point $P\left(a,\;a,\;a\right)$ on the lines $x\;=\;y,\;z\;=\;1$ and $x\;=\;-y,\;z\;=\;-1$ respectively. If $\angle QPR$ is a right angle, then $12a^2$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Take a general point on each line, use a zero dot product with the direction for each foot, then impose $\vec{PQ}\;\cdot\;\vec{PR}\;=\;0$. // 📝 Solution: The first line has direction $\left(1,\;1,\;0\right)$, so let $Q\;=\;\left(r,\;r,\;1\right)$. Then $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(r\;-\;a,\;r\;-\;a,\;1\;-\;a\right)$ and $\vec{PQ}\;\cdot\;\left(1,\;1,\;0\right)\;=\;2\left(r\;-\;a\right)\;=\;0\;\implies\;r\;=\;a$, so $Q\;=\;\left(a,\;a,\;1\right)$. The second line has direction $\left(1,\;-1,\;0\right)$, so let $R\;=\;\left(k,\;-k,\;-1\right)$. Then $\vec{PR}\;=\;\left(k\;-\;a,\;-k\;-\;a,\;-1\;-\;a\right)$ and $\vec{PR}\;\cdot\;\left(1,\;-1,\;0\right)\;=\;2k\;=\;0\;\implies\;k\;=\;0$, so $R\;=\;\left(0,\;0,\;-1\right)$. Now $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(0,\;0,\;1\;-\;a\right)$ and $\vec{PR}\;=\;\left(-a,\;-a,\;-1\;-\;a\right)$. The condition $\vec{PQ}\;\cdot\;\vec{PR}\;=\;0$ gives $\left(1\;-\;a\right)\left(-1\;-\;a\right)\;=\;a^2\;-\;1\;=\;0\;\implies\;a^2\;=\;1$. Hence $12a^2\;=\;12$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Foot of the perpendicular on a line; perpendicular vectors

questions.text: If $Q\left(a,\;b,\;c\right)$ is the image of the point $P\left(3,\;2,\;1\right)$ in the line $\frac{x\;-\;1}{1}\;=\;\frac{y}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;1}{1}$, then the distance of $Q$ from the line $\frac{x\;-\;9}{3}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;9}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;5}{-2}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: First find the foot of the perpendicular from $P$, double it and subtract $P$ to get the image, then use the point-to-line distance formula. // 📝 Solution: Let the foot be $F\;=\;\left(1\;+\;t,\;2t,\;1\;+\;t\right)$. Then $\vec{PF}\;=\;\left(t\;-\;2,\;2t\;-\;2,\;t\right)$ and $\vec{PF}\;\cdot\;\left(1,\;2,\;1\right)\;=\;6t\;-\;6\;=\;0\;\implies\;t\;=\;1$, so $F\;=\;\left(2,\;2,\;2\right)$. The image is $Q\;=\;2F\;-\;P\;=\;\left(1,\;2,\;3\right)$. Take $R\;=\;\left(9,\;9,\;5\right)$ on the second line with direction $\vec{d}\;=\;\left(3,\;2,\;-2\right)$, so $\left\lvert\vec{d}\right\rvert^2\;=\;17$. Then $\vec{QR}\;=\;\left(8,\;7,\;2\right)$ and $\vec{QR}\;\times\;\vec{d}\;=\;\left(-18,\;22,\;-5\right)$ with squared magnitude $324\;+\;484\;+\;25\;=\;833$. The distance is $\sqrt{\frac{833}{17}}\;=\;\sqrt{49}\;=\;7$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line; distance of a point from a line

questions.text: Let $P\left(43,\;\alpha,\;\beta\right)$ with $\beta\;<\;0$ be a point. The distance of $P$ from the line $\vec{r}\;=\;4\hat{i}\;-\;\hat{k}\;+\;\mu\left(2\hat{i}\;+\;3\hat{k}\right)$, measured along a line with direction ratios $3,\;-1,\;0$, is $13\sqrt{10}$. Then $\alpha^2\;+\;\beta^2$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Move from $P$ along the given direction, use the condition that the path meets the given line, and relate the distance travelled to the parameter. // 📝 Solution: The given line passes through $\left(4,\;0,\;-1\right)$ with direction $\left(2,\;0,\;3\right)$. A point on the path from $P$ is $\left(43\;+\;3s,\;\alpha\;-\;s,\;\beta\right)$. It lies on the given line only if its $y$-coordinate is $0$, so $s\;=\;\alpha$ and the meeting point is $\left(43\;+\;3\alpha,\;0,\;\beta\right)$. The distance travelled is $\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert\sqrt{9\;+\;1}\;=\;13\sqrt{10}\;\implies\;\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert\;=\;13$. The meeting point satisfies $\frac{39\;+\;3\alpha}{2}\;=\;\frac{\beta\;+\;1}{3}$. For $\alpha\;=\;13$ this gives $\beta\;=\;116\;>\;0$, which is rejected. For $\alpha\;=\;-13$ it gives $\beta\;+\;1\;=\;0$, so $\beta\;=\;-1$, which is valid. Hence $\alpha^2\;+\;\beta^2\;=\;169\;+\;1\;=\;170$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Distance of a point from a line along a given direction

questions.text: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x \; + \; 2}{2} \; = \; \frac{y \; + \; 3}{3} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 5}{4}$ and $\frac{x \; - \; 3}{1} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 2}{-3} \; = \; \frac{z \; + \; 4}{2}$ is $\frac{38}{3\sqrt{5}} k$, and $\int_0^k \left[ x^2 \right] dx \; = \; \alpha \; - \; \sqrt{\alpha}$, where $\left[ x \right]$ denotes the greatest integer function, then $6\alpha^3$ is equal to ________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $k$ from the skew-lines distance formula, then split the integral of the greatest integer function at the points where $x^2$ crosses an integer. // 📝 Solution: Here $\vec{a_1} \; = \; \left( -2, -3, 5 \right)$, $\vec{b_1} \; = \; \left( 2, 3, 4 \right)$, $\vec{a_2} \; = \; \left( 3, 2, -4 \right)$, $\vec{b_2} \; = \; \left( 1, -3, 2 \right)$. Then $\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} \; = \; \left( 18, 0, -9 \right)$ with magnitude $9\sqrt{5}$, and $\vec{a_2} \; - \; \vec{a_1} \; = \; \left( 5, 5, -9 \right)$. The dot product is $90 \; + \; 81 \; = \; 171$, so $d \; = \; \frac{171}{9\sqrt{5}} \; = \; \frac{19}{\sqrt{5}}$. Equating, $\frac{38}{3\sqrt{5}} k \; = \; \frac{19}{\sqrt{5}} \; \implies \; k \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$. Now $\int_0^{3/2} \left[ x^2 \right] dx \; = \; \int_0^1 0 \, dx \; + \; \int_1^{\sqrt{2}} 1 \, dx \; + \; \int_{\sqrt{2}}^{3/2} 2 \, dx \; = \; \left( \sqrt{2} \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; 2 \left( \frac{3}{2} \; - \; \sqrt{2} \right) \; = \; 2 \; - \; \sqrt{2}$. Hence $\alpha \; = \; 2$ and $6\alpha^3 \; = \; 6 \cdot 8 \; = \; 48$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Shortest distance between skew lines combined with greatest integer integral

questions.text: The shortest distance between the line $L_1:\;\frac{x\;-\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;1}{-3}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;4}{2}$ and the line $L_2$, which passes through the points $A\left(-4,\;4,\;3\right)$ and $B\left(-1,\;6,\;3\right)$ and is perpendicular to the line $\frac{x\;-\;3}{-2}\;=\;\frac{y}{3}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;1}{1}$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the direction of $L_2$ from the two given points, then use the scalar triple product formula for skew lines. // 📝 Solution: The direction of $AB$ is $\left(3,\;2,\;0\right)$, and $\left(3,\;2,\;0\right)\;\cdot\;\left(-2,\;3,\;1\right)\;=\;-6\;+\;6\;+\;0\;=\;0$, so $L_2:\;\frac{x\;+\;4}{3}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;4}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;3}{0}$. Here $\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(1,\;-1,\;-4\right)$, $\vec{a_2}\;=\;\left(-4,\;4,\;3\right)$, so $\vec{a_2}\;-\;\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(-5,\;5,\;7\right)$. Then $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(2,\;-3,\;2\right)\;\times\;\left(3,\;2,\;0\right)\;=\;\left(-4,\;6,\;13\right)$ with magnitude $\sqrt{16\;+\;36\;+\;169}\;=\;\sqrt{221}$. The dot product is $20\;+\;30\;+\;91\;=\;141$. So $SD\;=\;\frac{141}{\sqrt{221}}$. Correct option: C.

questions.text: Let the equation of the plane $P$ containing the line $x \; + \; 10 \; = \; \frac{8 - y}{2} \; = \; z$ be $ax \; + \; by \; + \; 3z \; = \; 2\left( a + b \right)$ and the distance of the plane $P$ from the point $\left( 1,\; 27,\; 7 \right)$ be $c$. Then $a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The plane contains a point of the line and its normal is perpendicular to the line direction. // 📝 Solution: The line is $\frac{x + 10}{1} \; = \; \frac{y - 8}{-2} \; = \; \frac{z}{1}$, through $\left( -10,\; 8,\; 0 \right)$ with direction $\left( 1,\; -2,\; 1 \right)$. The point lies on the plane: $-10a \; + \; 8b \; = \; 2a \; + \; 2b \; \implies \; b \; = \; 2a$. Normal perpendicular to the direction: $a \; - \; 2b \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; a \; - \; 4a \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; a \; = \; 1,\; b \; = \; 2$. Plane: $x \; + \; 2y \; + \; 3z \; = \; 6$. $c \; = \; \frac{\left\lvert 1 \; + \; 54 \; + \; 21 \; - \; 6 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{14}} \; = \; \frac{70}{\sqrt{14}} \; = \; 5\sqrt{14}$, so $c^2 \; = \; 350$. $a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2 \; = \; 1 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 350 \; = \; 355$.
questions.topic: Plane containing a line; distance of a point from a plane

questions.text: Let the point, on the line passing through the points $P \left( 1, -2, 3 \right)$ and $Q \left( 5, -4, 7 \right)$, farther from the origin and at a distance of $9$ units from the point $P$, be $\left( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \right)$. Then $\alpha^2 \; + \; \beta^2 \; + \; \gamma^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write a general point on line $PQ$ using its direction ratios and impose the distance condition from $P$. // 📝 Solution: The direction ratios of $PQ$ are $\left( 4, -2, 4 \right)$, so a general point is $\left( 4t \; + \; 1, \; -2t \; - \; 2, \; 4t \; + \; 3 \right)$. Its squared distance from $P$ is $16t^2 \; + \; 4t^2 \; + \; 16t^2 \; = \; 36t^2 \; = \; 81 \; \implies \; t \; = \; \pm \frac{3}{2}$. For $t \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$ the point is $\left( 7, -5, 9 \right)$, with squared distance from the origin $49 \; + \; 25 \; + \; 81 \; = \; 155$. For $t \; = \; -\frac{3}{2}$ the point is $\left( -5, 1, -6 \right)$, with squared distance $25 \; + \; 1 \; + \; 36 \; = \; 62$. The farther point is $\left( 7, -5, 9 \right)$, so $\alpha^2 \; + \; \beta^2 \; + \; \gamma^2 \; = \; 155$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Point on a line at a given distance from a point

questions.text: If the direction cosines $l,\;m,\;n$ of a line satisfy $4l\;+\;m\;-\;n\;=\;0$ and $2mn\;+\;10nl\;+\;3lm\;=\;0$, then the cosine of the acute angle between the two such lines is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Eliminate $n$ using the linear relation to get a homogeneous quadratic in $l$ and $m$, then factor it. // 📝 Solution: From $n\;=\;4l\;+\;m$, the second equation becomes $2m\left(4l\;+\;m\right)\;+\;10l\left(4l\;+\;m\right)\;+\;3lm\;=\;0\;\implies\;40l^2\;+\;21lm\;+\;2m^2\;=\;0\;\implies\;\left(8l\;+\;m\right)\left(5l\;+\;2m\right)\;=\;0$. Case 1: $m\;=\;-8l$ and $n\;=\;-4l$, giving direction ratios $\left(1,\;-8,\;-4\right)$. Case 2: $m\;=\;-\frac{5l}{2}$ and $n\;=\;\frac{3l}{2}$, giving direction ratios $\left(2,\;-5,\;3\right)$. Then $\cos\theta\;=\;\frac{\left\lvert2\;+\;40\;-\;12\right\rvert}{\sqrt{81}\;\sqrt{38}}\;=\;\frac{30}{9\sqrt{38}}\;=\;\frac{10}{3\sqrt{38}}$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Direction cosines; angle between two lines

questions.text: Let $O$ be the origin and $M$, $N$ be the points on the lines $\frac{x\;-\;5}{4}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;4}{1}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;5}{3}$ and $\frac{x\;+\;8}{12}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;2}{5}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;11}{9}$ respectively such that $MN$ is the shortest distance between them. Then $\vec{OM}\;\cdot\;\vec{ON}$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The shortest-distance segment $MN$ is parallel to $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}$; use this to fix both parameters. // 📝 Solution: Let $M\;=\;\left(4\lambda\;+\;5,\;\lambda\;+\;4,\;3\lambda\;+\;5\right)$ and $N\;=\;\left(12\mu\;-\;8,\;5\mu\;-\;2,\;9\mu\;-\;11\right)$. $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(4,\;1,\;3\right)\;\times\;\left(12,\;5,\;9\right)\;=\;\left(-6,\;0,\;8\right)\;\parallel\;\left(-3,\;0,\;4\right)$. So $\vec{MN}\;=\;\left(12\mu\;-\;4\lambda\;-\;13,\;5\mu\;-\;\lambda\;-\;6,\;9\mu\;-\;3\lambda\;-\;16\right)$ must have zero $y$-component, giving $5\mu\;-\;\lambda\;=\;6$. Also $\frac{12\mu\;-\;4\lambda\;-\;13}{-3}\;=\;\frac{9\mu\;-\;3\lambda\;-\;16}{4}\;\implies\;3\mu\;-\;\lambda\;=\;4$. Solving, $\mu\;=\;1$ and $\lambda\;=\;-1$. So $M\;=\;\left(1,\;3,\;2\right)$ and $N\;=\;\left(4,\;3,\;-2\right)$. Then $\vec{OM}\;\cdot\;\vec{ON}\;=\;4\;+\;9\;-\;4\;=\;9$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Shortest distance between skew lines; feet of the common perpendicular

questions.text: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x \; - \; \lambda}{2} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 4}{3} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 3}{4}$ and $\frac{x \; - \; 2}{4} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 4}{6} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 7}{8}$ is $\frac{13}{\sqrt{29}}$, then a value of $\lambda$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The lines are parallel, so use $d \; = \; \frac{\left\lvert \vec{b} \times \left( \vec{a_2} \; - \; \vec{a_1} \right) \right\rvert}{\left\lvert \vec{b} \right\rvert}$. // 📝 Solution: Both lines have direction $\vec{b} \; = \; \left( 2, 3, 4 \right)$ with $\left\lvert \vec{b} \right\rvert \; = \; \sqrt{29}$. With $\vec{a_1} \; = \; \left( \lambda, 4, 3 \right)$ and $\vec{a_2} \; = \; \left( 2, 4, 7 \right)$ we get $\vec{a_2} \; - \; \vec{a_1} \; = \; \left( 2 \; - \; \lambda, 0, 4 \right)$. Then $\vec{b} \times \left( \vec{a_2} \; - \; \vec{a_1} \right) \; = \; \left( 12, \; -4\lambda, \; 3\lambda \; - \; 6 \right)$. Setting $\frac{\left\lvert \vec{b} \times \left( \vec{a_2} \; - \; \vec{a_1} \right) \right\rvert}{\sqrt{29}} \; = \; \frac{13}{\sqrt{29}}$ gives $144 \; + \; 16\lambda^2 \; + \; \left( 3\lambda \; - \; 6 \right)^2 \; = \; 169$, i.e. $25\lambda^2 \; - \; 36\lambda \; + \; 11 \; = \; 0$, so $\left( 25\lambda \; - \; 11 \right) \left( \lambda \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; 0$. Thus $\lambda \; = \; 1$ or $\lambda \; = \; \frac{11}{25}$; only $\lambda \; = \; 1$ appears among the options. Correct option: D.

questions.text: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x\;-\;\lambda}{-2}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;2}{1}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;1}{1}$ and $\frac{x\;-\;\sqrt{3}}{1}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;1}{-2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;2}{1}$ is $1$. Then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $SD\;=\;\frac{\left\lvert\left(\vec{a_2}\;-\;\vec{a_1}\right)\;\cdot\;\left(\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\right)\right\rvert}{\left\lvert\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\right\rvert}$ for two skew lines. // 📝 Solution: Here $\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(\lambda,\;2,\;1\right)$, $\vec{a_2}\;=\;\left(\sqrt{3},\;1,\;2\right)$, $\vec{b_1}\;=\;\left(-2,\;1,\;1\right)$, $\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(1,\;-2,\;1\right)$. Then $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(3,\;3,\;3\right)$ with magnitude $3\sqrt{3}$, and $\vec{a_2}\;-\;\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(\sqrt{3}\;-\;\lambda,\;-1,\;1\right)$. The dot product is $3\left(\sqrt{3}\;-\;\lambda\right)\;-\;3\;+\;3\;=\;3\left(\sqrt{3}\;-\;\lambda\right)$. So $1\;=\;\frac{3\left\lvert\sqrt{3}\;-\;\lambda\right\rvert}{3\sqrt{3}}\;\implies\;\left\lvert\sqrt{3}\;-\;\lambda\right\rvert\;=\;\sqrt{3}\;\implies\;\lambda\;=\;0\;\text{ or }\;2\sqrt{3}$. The sum is $2\sqrt{3}$. Correct option: B.

questions.text: If the image of the point $P\left(1,\;2,\;a\right)$ in the line $\frac{x\;-\;6}{3}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;7}{2}\;=\;\frac{7\;-\;z}{2}$ is $Q\left(5,\;b,\;c\right)$, then $a^2\;+\;b^2\;+\;c^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The segment $PQ$ is perpendicular to the line and its midpoint lies on the line. // 📝 Solution: The line passes through $\left(6,\;7,\;7\right)$ with direction $\left(3,\;2,\;-2\right)$. Since $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(4,\;b\;-\;2,\;c\;-\;a\right)$ is perpendicular to it, $12\;+\;2\left(b\;-\;2\right)\;-\;2\left(c\;-\;a\right)\;=\;0\;\implies\;a\;+\;b\;-\;c\;=\;-4$. The midpoint is $\left(3,\;\frac{b\;+\;2}{2},\;\frac{a\;+\;c}{2}\right)$, and on the line $\frac{3\;-\;6}{3}\;=\;-1$ is the parameter $t$. So $\frac{b\;+\;2}{2}\;=\;7\;+\;2t\;=\;5\;\implies\;b\;=\;8$ and $\frac{a\;+\;c}{2}\;=\;7\;-\;2t\;=\;9\;\implies\;a\;+\;c\;=\;18$. From $a\;-\;c\;=\;-12$ we get $a\;=\;3$ and $c\;=\;15$. Hence $a^2\;+\;b^2\;+\;c^2\;=\;9\;+\;64\;+\;225\;=\;298$. Correct option: A.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line

questions.text: Consider the line $L$ passing through the points $\left( 1, 2, 3 \right)$ and $\left( 2, 3, 5 \right)$. The distance of the point $\left( \frac{11}{3}, \frac{11}{3}, \frac{19}{3} \right)$ from the line $L$ along the line $\frac{3x \; - \; 11}{2} \; = \; \frac{3y \; - \; 11}{1} \; = \; \frac{3z \; - \; 19}{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find where the second line meets $L$; the distance along a line is the parameter difference times the length of its direction vector. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Line $L$ is $\frac{x \; - \; 1}{1} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 2}{1} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 3}{2}$, so $B \; = \; \left( 1 \; + \; \lambda, \; 2 \; + \; \lambda, \; 3 \; + \; 2\lambda \right)$. The other line is $\frac{x \; - \; \frac{11}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; \frac{11}{3}}{\frac{1}{3}} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; \frac{19}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}}$ through $A \; = \; \left( \frac{11}{3}, \frac{11}{3}, \frac{19}{3} \right)$ with direction $\left( 2, 1, 2 \right)$, so $B \; = \; \left( \frac{11}{3} \; + \; 2s, \; \frac{11}{3} \; + \; s, \; \frac{19}{3} \; + \; 2s \right)$. Equating $x$ and $y$: $1 \; + \; \lambda \; = \; \frac{11}{3} \; + \; 2s$ and $2 \; + \; \lambda \; = \; \frac{11}{3} \; + \; s$. Subtracting gives $1 \; = \; -s$, so $s \; = \; -1$ and $\lambda \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$ (the $z$-coordinates agree: $\frac{13}{3}$). Thus $B \; = \; \left( \frac{5}{3}, \frac{8}{3}, \frac{13}{3} \right)$ and $AB \; = \; \left\lvert s \right\rvert \sqrt{4 \; + \; 1 \; + \; 4} \; = \; 3$. Correct option: D.
questions.topic: Distance between a point and a line measured along a given line

questions.text: Let the equation of the plane passing through the line $x \; - \; 2y \; - \; z \; - \; 5 \; = \; 0 \; = \; x \; + \; y \; + \; 3z \; - \; 5$ and parallel to the line $x \; + \; y \; + \; 2z \; - \; 7 \; = \; 0 \; = \; 2x \; + \; 3y \; + \; z \; - \; 2$ be $ax \; + \; by \; + \; cz \; = \; 65$. Then the distance of the point $\left( a,\; b,\; c \right)$ from the plane $2x \; + \; 2y \; - \; z \; + \; 16 \; = \; 0$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the family $P_1 \; + \; b P_2 \; = \; 0$ and make its normal perpendicular to the direction of the given parallel line. // 📝 Solution: Plane: $\left( x \; - \; 2y \; - \; z \; - \; 5 \right) \; + \; b\left( x \; + \; y \; + \; 3z \; - \; 5 \right) \; = \; 0$ with normal $\left( 1 \; + \; b,\; -2 \; + \; b,\; -1 \; + \; 3b \right)$. Direction of the parallel line: $\left( 1,\; 1,\; 2 \right) \times \left( 2,\; 3,\; 1 \right) \; = \; \left( -5,\; 3,\; 1 \right)$. Perpendicular: $-5\left( 1 \; + \; b \right) \; + \; 3\left( -2 \; + \; b \right) \; + \; \left( -1 \; + \; 3b \right) \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; b \; = \; 12$. Plane: $13x \; + \; 10y \; + \; 35z \; = \; 65$, so $\left( a,\; b,\; c \right) \; = \; \left( 13,\; 10,\; 35 \right)$. Distance from $2x \; + \; 2y \; - \; z \; + \; 16 \; = \; 0$: $\frac{\left\lvert 26 \; + \; 20 \; - \; 35 \; + \; 16 \right\rvert}{3} \; = \; \frac{27}{3} \; = \; 9$.
questions.topic: Plane through a line and parallel to another line

questions.text: The distance of the point $\left( -1,\; 9,\; -16 \right)$ from the plane $2x \; + \; 3y \; - \; z \; = \; 5$ measured parallel to the line $\frac{x + 4}{3} \; = \; \frac{2 - y}{4} \; = \; \frac{z - 3}{12}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write a general point on the line through the given point with the given direction, impose the plane equation, then find the length from the parameter. // 📝 Solution: The line through $\left( -1,\; 9,\; -16 \right)$ with direction ratios $\left( 3,\; -4,\; 12 \right)$ has general point $\left( 3\lambda \; - \; 1,\; -4\lambda \; + \; 9,\; 12\lambda \; - \; 16 \right)$. Put it in the plane: $2\left( 3\lambda \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; 3\left( -4\lambda \; + \; 9 \right) \; - \; \left( 12\lambda \; - \; 16 \right) \; = \; 5 \; \implies \; -18\lambda \; + \; 41 \; = \; 5 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; 2$. The point is $\left( 5,\; 1,\; 8 \right)$. Distance $\; = \; \sqrt{36 \; + \; 64 \; + \; 576} \; = \; \sqrt{676} \; = \; 26$.
questions.topic: Distance of a point from a plane measured along a line

questions.text: Consider a line $L$ passing through the points $P \left( 1, 2, 1 \right)$ and $Q \left( 2, 1, -1 \right)$. If the mirror image of the point $A \left( 2, 2, 2 \right)$ in the line $L$ is $\left( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \right)$, then $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; 6\gamma$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $L$; the image is twice the foot minus $A$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] The direction ratios of $L$ are $\left( 1, -1, -2 \right)$, so a point on $L$ is $\left( 1 \; + \; t, \; 2 \; - \; t, \; 1 \; - \; 2t \right)$. The vector from $A$ is $\left( t \; - \; 1, \; -t, \; -1 \; - \; 2t \right)$; perpendicularity to $\left( 1, -1, -2 \right)$ gives $t \; - \; 1 \; + \; t \; + \; 2 \; + \; 4t \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; 6t \; + \; 1 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; t \; = \; -\frac{1}{6}$. The foot is $C \; = \; \left( \frac{5}{6}, \frac{13}{6}, \frac{4}{3} \right)$. The image is $2C \; - \; A \; = \; \left( \frac{5}{3} \; - \; 2, \; \frac{13}{3} \; - \; 2, \; \frac{8}{3} \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; \left( -\frac{1}{3}, \frac{7}{3}, \frac{2}{3} \right)$. Therefore $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; 6\gamma \; = \; -\frac{1}{3} \; + \; \frac{7}{3} \; + \; 4 \; = \; 6$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line

questions.text: The foot of perpendicular of the point $\left( 2,\; 0,\; 5 \right)$ on the line $\frac{x + 1}{2} \; = \; \frac{y - 1}{5} \; = \; \frac{z + 1}{-1}$ is $\left( \alpha,\; \beta,\; \gamma \right)$. Then which of the following is NOT correct?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the foot using $\overrightarrow{AP} \cdot \overrightarrow{b} \; = \; 0$ and then test each option. // 📝 Solution: Let the foot be $P\left( 2\lambda \; - \; 1,\; 5\lambda \; + \; 1,\; -\lambda \; - \; 1 \right)$ and $A \; = \; \left( 2,\; 0,\; 5 \right)$. $\overrightarrow{PA} \; = \; \left( 3 \; - \; 2\lambda,\; -5\lambda \; - \; 1,\; 6 \; + \; \lambda \right)$ and $\overrightarrow{b} \; = \; \left( 2,\; 5,\; -1 \right)$. $2\left( 3 \; - \; 2\lambda \right) \; - \; 5\left( 5\lambda \; + \; 1 \right) \; - \; \left( 6 \; + \; \lambda \right) \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; -30\lambda \; - \; 5 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; -\frac{1}{6}$. So $\alpha \; = \; -\frac{4}{3}$, $\beta \; = \; \frac{1}{6}$, $\gamma \; = \; -\frac{5}{6}$. Then $\frac{\alpha \beta}{\gamma} \; = \; \frac{4}{15}$, $\frac{\alpha}{\beta} \; = \; -8$, $\frac{\gamma}{\alpha} \; = \; \frac{5}{8}$ are all correct, but $\frac{\beta}{\gamma} \; = \; -\frac{1}{5} \; \ne \; -5$. So option C is NOT correct.
questions.topic: Foot of perpendicular from a point on a line

questions.text: Let $A\left(2,\;-3,\;3\right)$, $B\left(2,\;2,\;3\right)$ and $C\left(-1,\;1,\;3\right)$ be the vertices of a triangle. If $l$ is the length of the angle bisector $AD$ of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on $BC$, then $2l^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check whether two sides at $A$ are equal; then the bisector hits the base at a special point. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $AB\;=\;\sqrt{0\;+\;25\;+\;0}\;=\;5$ and $AC\;=\;\sqrt{9\;+\;16\;+\;0}\;=\;5$. The triangle is isosceles with $AB\;=\;AC$, so the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at its midpoint $D\;=\;\left(\frac{1}{2},\;\frac{3}{2},\;3\right)$. Then $l^2\;=\;AD^2\;=\;\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2\;+\;\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)^2\;+\;0\;=\;\frac{90}{4}\;=\;\frac{45}{2}$. Hence $2l^2\;=\;45$. Correct option: D.
questions.topic: Angle bisector in a triangle; distance between points in 3D

questions.text: Let $P \left( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \right)$ be the image of the point $Q \left( 1, 6, 4 \right)$ in the line $\frac{x}{1} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 1}{2} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 2}{3}$. Then $2\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the foot $A$ of the perpendicular from $Q$, then $P \; = \; 2A \; - \; Q$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let $A \; = \; \left( t, \; 2t \; + \; 1, \; 3t \; + \; 2 \right)$. Then $\vec{QA} \; = \; \left( t \; - \; 1, \; 2t \; - \; 5, \; 3t \; - \; 2 \right)$ and $\vec{QA} \cdot \left( 1, 2, 3 \right) \; = \; \left( t \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; 2 \left( 2t \; - \; 5 \right) \; + \; 3 \left( 3t \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; 14t \; - \; 17 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; t \; = \; \frac{17}{14}$. So $A \; = \; \left( \frac{17}{14}, \frac{48}{14}, \frac{79}{14} \right)$ and $P \; = \; 2A \; - \; Q \; = \; \left( \frac{20}{14}, \frac{12}{14}, \frac{102}{14} \right)$. Then $2\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma \; = \; \frac{40 \; + \; 12 \; + \; 102}{14} \; = \; \frac{154}{14} \; = \; 11$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line

questions.text: Let $O$ be the origin and let $A\;=\;2\hat{i}\;+\;2\hat{j}\;+\;\hat{k}$ and $B\;=\;2\hat{i}\;+\;4\hat{j}\;+\;4\hat{k}$. If the internal bisector of $\angle AOB$ meets the line $AB$ at $C$, then the length of $OC$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The internal angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $OA\;=\;\sqrt{4\;+\;4\;+\;1}\;=\;3$ and $OB\;=\;\sqrt{4\;+\;16\;+\;16}\;=\;6$. So $AC\;:\;CB\;=\;OA\;:\;OB\;=\;1\;:\;2$. Then $C\;=\;\frac{2A\;+\;B}{3}\;=\;\left(\frac{4\;+\;2}{3},\;\frac{4\;+\;4}{3},\;\frac{2\;+\;4}{3}\right)\;=\;\left(2,\;\frac{8}{3},\;2\right)$. Hence $OC^2\;=\;4\;+\;\frac{64}{9}\;+\;4\;=\;\frac{136}{9}$ and $OC\;=\;\frac{2\sqrt{34}}{3}$. Correct option: B.

questions.text: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x \; - \; \lambda}{3} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; 2}{-1} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 1}{1}$ and $\frac{x \; + \; 2}{-3} \; = \; \frac{y \; + \; 5}{2} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 4}{4}$ is $\frac{44}{\sqrt{30}}$, then the largest possible value of $\left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert$ is equal to _________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute the scalar triple product as a linear expression in $\lambda$ and equate its absolute value over $\left\lvert \vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} \right\rvert$ to the given distance. // 📝 Solution: Here $\vec{a_1} \; = \; \left( \lambda, 2, 1 \right)$, $\vec{b_1} \; = \; \left( 3, -1, 1 \right)$, $\vec{a_2} \; = \; \left( -2, -5, 4 \right)$, $\vec{b_2} \; = \; \left( -3, 2, 4 \right)$. Then $\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} \; = \; \left( -6, -15, 3 \right)$ with magnitude $\sqrt{36 \; + \; 225 \; + \; 9} \; = \; 3\sqrt{30}$. Also $\vec{a_1} \; - \; \vec{a_2} \; = \; \left( \lambda \; + \; 2, 7, -3 \right)$, and the dot product is $-6 \left( \lambda \; + \; 2 \right) \; - \; 105 \; - \; 9 \; = \; -6\lambda \; - \; 126$. So $\frac{\left\lvert 6\lambda \; + \; 126 \right\rvert}{3\sqrt{30}} \; = \; \frac{44}{\sqrt{30}} \; \implies \; \left\lvert 6\lambda \; + \; 126 \right\rvert \; = \; 132$. Hence $\lambda \; = \; 1$ or $\lambda \; = \; -43$, and the largest $\left\lvert \lambda \right\rvert$ is $43$. Correct option: D.
questions.topic: Shortest distance between skew lines with a parameter

questions.text: If the line $\frac{2 \; - \; x}{3} \; = \; \frac{3y \; - \; 2}{4\lambda \; + \; 1} \; = \; 4 \; - \; z$ makes a right angle with the line $\frac{x \; + \; 3}{3\mu} \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; 2y}{6} \; = \; \frac{5 \; - \; z}{7}$, then $4\lambda \; + \; 9\mu$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite both lines in standard symmetric form with unit coefficients on $x, y, z$, then set the dot product of direction ratios to zero. // 📝 Solution: The first line is $\frac{x \; - \; 2}{-3} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; \frac{2}{3}}{\frac{4\lambda + 1}{3}} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 4}{-1}$, with direction ratios $\left( -3, \frac{4\lambda \; + \; 1}{3}, -1 \right)$. The second line is $\frac{x \; + \; 3}{3\mu} \; = \; \frac{y \; - \; \frac{1}{2}}{-3} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 5}{-7}$, with direction ratios $\left( 3\mu, -3, -7 \right)$. Perpendicularity gives $\left( -3 \right) \left( 3\mu \right) \; + \; \frac{4\lambda \; + \; 1}{3} \cdot \left( -3 \right) \; + \; \left( -1 \right) \left( -7 \right) \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; -9\mu \; - \; 4\lambda \; - \; 1 \; + \; 7 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; 4\lambda \; + \; 9\mu \; = \; 6$. Correct option: D.

questions.text: Let $\left( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \right)$ be the image of the point $\left( 8, 5, 7 \right)$ in the line $\frac{x \; - \; 1}{2} \; = \; \frac{y \; + \; 1}{3} \; = \; \frac{z \; - \; 2}{5}$. Then $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of the point and its image. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let $A \; = \; \left( 8, 5, 7 \right)$ and let the foot be $M \; = \; \left( 2\lambda \; + \; 1, \; 3\lambda \; - \; 1, \; 5\lambda \; + \; 2 \right)$. Then $\vec{AM} \; = \; \left( 2\lambda \; - \; 7, \; 3\lambda \; - \; 6, \; 5\lambda \; - \; 5 \right)$ and $\vec{AM} \cdot \left( 2, 3, 5 \right) \; = \; 0$ gives $2 \left( 2\lambda \; - \; 7 \right) \; + \; 3 \left( 3\lambda \; - \; 6 \right) \; + \; 5 \left( 5\lambda \; - \; 5 \right) \; = \; 38\lambda \; - \; 57 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$. So $M \; = \; \left( 4, \frac{7}{2}, \frac{19}{2} \right)$ and the image is $2M \; - \; A \; = \; \left( 0, 2, 12 \right)$. Hence $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; + \; \gamma \; = \; 0 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 12 \; = \; 14$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line

questions.text: If $\left(\alpha,\;\beta,\;\gamma\right)$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the point $\left(1,\;2,\;3\right)$ on the line $\frac{x\;+\;3}{5}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;4}{3}$, then $19\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The vector from the given point to the foot is perpendicular to the direction vector of the line. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let the foot be $P\;=\;\left(5k\;-\;3,\;2k\;+\;1,\;3k\;-\;4\right)$. Then $\vec{AP}\;=\;\left(5k\;-\;4,\;2k\;-\;1,\;3k\;-\;7\right)$, and $\vec{AP}\;\cdot\;\left(5,\;2,\;3\right)\;=\;25k\;-\;20\;+\;4k\;-\;2\;+\;9k\;-\;21\;=\;38k\;-\;43\;=\;0\;\implies\;k\;=\;\frac{43}{38}$. So $\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\;=\;10k\;-\;6$ and $19\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)\;=\;190k\;-\;114\;=\;215\;-\;114\;=\;101$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line

questions.text: The distances of the point $\left(1,\;2,\;a\right)$ from the line $\frac{x\;-\;1}{1}\;=\;\frac{y}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;1}{1}$ along the lines $L_1:\;\frac{x\;-\;1}{3}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;2}{4}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;a}{b}$ and $L_2:\;\frac{x\;-\;1}{1}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;2}{4}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;a}{c}$ are equal. Then $a\;+\;b\;+\;c$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find where each of $L_1$ and $L_2$ meets the given line, then equate the two distances from $\left(1,\;2,\;a\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $P\;=\;\left(1,\;2,\;a\right)$. A point of $L_1$ is $\left(1\;+\;3\lambda,\;2\;+\;4\lambda,\;a\;+\;b\lambda\right)$. On the given line, $3\lambda\;=\;\frac{2\;+\;4\lambda}{2}\;\implies\;\lambda\;=\;1$ and $z\;-\;1\;=\;3$, so $a\;+\;b\;=\;4$ and $A\;=\;\left(4,\;6,\;4\right)$. A point of $L_2$ is $\left(1\;+\;\mu,\;2\;+\;4\mu,\;a\;+\;c\mu\right)$. On the given line, $\mu\;=\;\frac{2\;+\;4\mu}{2}\;\implies\;\mu\;=\;-1$ and $z\;-\;1\;=\;-1$, so $a\;=\;c$ and $B\;=\;\left(0,\;-2,\;0\right)$. Now $PA\;=\;PB$ gives $9\;+\;16\;+\;\left(4\;-\;a\right)^2\;=\;1\;+\;16\;+\;a^2\;\implies\;24\;=\;8a\;\implies\;a\;=\;3$. Then $b\;=\;1$ and $c\;=\;3$, so $a\;+\;b\;+\;c\;=\;7$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Distance of a point from a line along a given direction

questions.text: Consider the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ given by $L_1 : \frac{x - 1}{2} \; = \; \frac{y - 3}{1} \; = \; \frac{z - 2}{2}$ and $L_2 : \frac{x - 2}{1} \; = \; \frac{y - 2}{2} \; = \; \frac{z - 3}{3}$. A line $L_3$ having direction ratios $1,\; -1,\; -2$ intersects $L_1$ and $L_2$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Then the length of line segment $PQ$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Take general points $P$ on $L_1$ and $Q$ on $L_2$ and make $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ proportional to $\left( 1,\; -1,\; -2 \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $P \; = \; \left( 2\lambda \; + \; 1,\; \lambda \; + \; 3,\; 2\lambda \; + \; 2 \right)$ and $Q \; = \; \left( \mu \; + \; 2,\; 2\mu \; + \; 2,\; 3\mu \; + \; 3 \right)$. Then $\overrightarrow{PQ} \; = \; \left( \mu \; - \; 2\lambda \; + \; 1,\; 2\mu \; - \; \lambda \; - \; 1,\; 3\mu \; - \; 2\lambda \; + \; 1 \right) \; = \; k\left( 1,\; -1,\; -2 \right)$. Adding the first two components gives $3\mu \; - \; 3\lambda \; = \; 0$, so $\mu \; = \; \lambda$. The third component gives $\lambda \; + \; 1 \; = \; -2k$ and the first gives $1 \; - \; \lambda \; = \; k$, so $\lambda \; + \; 1 \; = \; 2\lambda \; - \; 2 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; \mu \; = \; 3$. $P \; = \; \left( 7,\; 6,\; 8 \right)$, $Q \; = \; \left( 5,\; 8,\; 12 \right)$. $PQ \; = \; \sqrt{4 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 16} \; = \; 2\sqrt{6}$.
questions.topic: Line intersecting two skew lines; length of segment

questions.text: Let $L_1:\;\vec{r}\;=\;\left(\hat{i}\;-\;\hat{j}\;+\;2\hat{k}\right)\;+\;\lambda\left(\hat{i}\;-\;\hat{j}\;+\;2\hat{k}\right)$, $\lambda\;\in\;R$, $L_2:\;\vec{r}\;=\;\left(\hat{j}\;-\;\hat{k}\right)\;+\;\mu\left(3\hat{i}\;+\;\hat{j}\;+\;p\hat{k}\right)$, $\mu\;\in\;R$ and $L_3:\;\vec{r}\;=\;\delta\left(l\hat{i}\;+\;m\hat{j}\;+\;n\hat{k}\right)$, $\delta\;\in\;R$ be three lines such that $L_1$ is perpendicular to $L_2$ and $L_3$ is perpendicular to both $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then which one of the following points lies on $L_3$?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Perpendicular lines have zero dot product of directions; a line perpendicular to two lines is along their cross product. // 📝 Solution: $L_1\;\perp\;L_2\;\implies\;3\;-\;1\;+\;2p\;=\;0\;\implies\;p\;=\;-1$. The direction of $L_3$ is $\left(1,\;-1,\;2\right)\;\times\;\left(3,\;1,\;-1\right)\;=\;\left(-1,\;7,\;4\right)$. $L_3$ passes through the origin, so its points are $\delta\left(-1,\;7,\;4\right)$. For $\delta\;=\;1$ we get $\left(-1,\;7,\;4\right)$. Correct option: A.
questions.topic: Perpendicular lines; cross product of direction vectors

questions.text: Let the plane containing the line of intersection of the planes $P_1 : x \; + \; \left( \lambda + 4 \right) y \; + \; z \; = \; 1$ and $P_2 : 2x \; + \; y \; + \; z \; = \; 2$ pass through the points $\left( 0,\; 1,\; 0 \right)$ and $\left( 1,\; 0,\; 1 \right)$. Then the distance of the point $\left( 2\lambda,\; \lambda,\; -\lambda \right)$ from the plane $P_2$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Family of planes through the intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$ is $P_1 \; + \; k P_2 \; = \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: The plane is $\left( x \; + \; \left( \lambda + 4 \right) y \; + \; z \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; k\left( 2x \; + \; y \; + \; z \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; 0$. Through $\left( 1,\; 0,\; 1 \right)$: $1 \; + \; k \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; k \; = \; -1$. Through $\left( 0,\; 1,\; 0 \right)$: $\left( \lambda \; + \; 4 \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; k\left( 1 \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; \lambda \; + \; 3 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; -4$. The point is $\left( -8,\; -4,\; 4 \right)$. Distance from $P_2$: $\frac{\left\lvert -16 \; - \; 4 \; + \; 4 \; - \; 2 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{6}} \; = \; \frac{18}{\sqrt{6}} \; = \; 3\sqrt{6}$.
questions.topic: Family of planes through line of intersection of two planes

questions.text: Let $\left(\alpha,\;\beta,\;\gamma\right)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from the point $\left(5,\;4,\;2\right)$ on the line $\vec{r}\;=\;\left(-\hat{i}\;+\;3\hat{j}\;+\;\hat{k}\right)\;+\;\lambda\left(2\hat{i}\;+\;3\hat{j}\;-\;\hat{k}\right)$. Then the length of the projection of the vector $\alpha\hat{i}\;+\;\beta\hat{j}\;+\;\gamma\hat{k}$ on the vector $6\hat{i}\;+\;2\hat{j}\;+\;3\hat{k}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the foot using the zero dot product with the direction, then use $\frac{\left\lvert\vec{u}\;\cdot\;\vec{v}\right\rvert}{\left\lvert\vec{v}\right\rvert}$ for the projection length. // 📝 Solution: Let the foot be $Q\;=\;\left(-1\;+\;2\lambda,\;3\;+\;3\lambda,\;1\;-\;\lambda\right)$. Then $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(2\lambda\;-\;6,\;3\lambda\;-\;1,\;-\lambda\;-\;1\right)$ and $\vec{PQ}\;\cdot\;\left(2,\;3,\;-1\right)\;=\;14\lambda\;-\;14\;=\;0\;\implies\;\lambda\;=\;1$. So the foot is $\left(1,\;6,\;0\right)$. The projection length is $\frac{\left\lvert6\;+\;12\;+\;0\right\rvert}{\sqrt{36\;+\;4\;+\;9}}\;=\;\frac{18}{7}$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Foot of the perpendicular; projection of a vector

questions.text: Let $L$ be the line $\frac{x\;+\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;1}{3}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;3}{6}$. Let $S$ be the set of all points $\left(a,\;b,\;c\right)$ on $L$ whose distance from the line $\frac{x\;+\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;1}{3}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;9}{0}$ along the line $L$ is $7$. Then $\sum_{\left(a,\;b,\;c\right)\;\in\;S}\left(a\;+\;b\;+\;c\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find where $L$ meets the second line, then move $7$ units along $L$ in both directions from that point. // 📝 Solution: A point of $L$ is $\left(2K\;-\;1,\;3K\;-\;1,\;6K\;-\;3\right)$. The second line lies in the plane $z\;=\;9$, so $6K\;-\;3\;=\;9\;\implies\;K\;=\;2$, giving the meeting point $M\;=\;\left(3,\;5,\;9\right)$, which indeed satisfies $\frac{3\;+\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{5\;+\;1}{3}\;=\;2$. For a point $P$ of $L$, $PM\;=\;\left\lvert K\;-\;2\right\rvert\sqrt{4\;+\;9\;+\;36}\;=\;7\left\lvert K\;-\;2\right\rvert\;=\;7\;\implies\;K\;=\;1\;\text{ or }\;3$. The points are $\left(1,\;2,\;3\right)$ and $\left(5,\;8,\;15\right)$. The sum of all coordinates is $6\;+\;28\;=\;34$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Points on a line at a given distance; intersection of lines

questions.text: Let $A\left(2\hat{i}\;+\;2\hat{j}\;+\;\hat{k}\right)$, $B\left(\hat{i}\;+\;2\hat{j}\;+\;2\hat{k}\right)$ and $C\left(2\hat{i}\;+\;\hat{j}\;+\;2\hat{k}\right)$ be the vertices of a triangle. If $l_1$, $l_2$ and $l_3$ are the lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the orthocentre of the triangle on the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ respectively, then $l_1^2\;+\;l_2^2\;+\;l_3^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute the three side lengths first; a special triangle makes the orthocentre coincide with the centroid. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $AB\;=\;BC\;=\;CA\;=\;\sqrt{2}$, so the triangle is equilateral and the orthocentre equals the centroid $G\;=\;\left(\frac{5}{3},\;\frac{5}{3},\;\frac{5}{3}\right)$. The midpoint of $AB$ is $D\;=\;\left(\frac{3}{2},\;2,\;\frac{3}{2}\right)$ and $GD$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Then $l_1^2\;=\;GD^2\;=\;\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2\;+\;\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\;+\;\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2\;=\;\frac{1}{36}\;+\;\frac{4}{36}\;+\;\frac{1}{36}\;=\;\frac{1}{6}$. By symmetry $l_1\;=\;l_2\;=\;l_3$, so $l_1^2\;+\;l_2^2\;+\;l_3^2\;=\;\frac{3}{6}\;=\;\frac{1}{2}$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Orthocentre of an equilateral triangle; distance of a point from a line

questions.text: Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points on the line $\frac{x\;+\;3}{8}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;4}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;1}{2}$ which are at a distance of $6$ units from the point $R\left(1,\;2,\;3\right)$. If the centroid of the triangle $PQR$ is $\left(\alpha,\;\beta,\;\gamma\right)$, then $\alpha^2\;+\;\beta^2\;+\;\gamma^2$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write a general point of the line in parameter form and use the distance formula with $R$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let $P\;=\;\left(8\lambda\;-\;3,\;2\lambda\;+\;4,\;2\lambda\;-\;1\right)$. Then $PR^2\;=\;\left(8\lambda\;-\;4\right)^2\;+\;\left(2\lambda\;+\;2\right)^2\;+\;\left(2\lambda\;-\;4\right)^2\;=\;72\lambda^2\;-\;72\lambda\;+\;36\;=\;36\;\implies\;\lambda\left(\lambda\;-\;1\right)\;=\;0$. So the two points are $\left(-3,\;4,\;-1\right)$ and $\left(5,\;6,\;1\right)$. The centroid is $\left(\frac{-3\;+\;5\;+\;1}{3},\;\frac{4\;+\;6\;+\;2}{3},\;\frac{-1\;+\;1\;+\;3}{3}\right)\;=\;\left(1,\;4,\;1\right)$. Therefore $\alpha^2\;+\;\beta^2\;+\;\gamma^2\;=\;1\;+\;16\;+\;1\;=\;18$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Points on a line at a given distance; centroid of a triangle

questions.text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with $R\left(-1,\;4,\;2\right)$. Suppose $M\left(2,\;1,\;2\right)$ is the mid point of $PQ$. The distance of the centroid of $\triangle PQR$ from the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x\;-\;2}{0}\;=\;\frac{y}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;3}{-1}$ and $\frac{x\;-\;1}{1}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;3}{-3}\;=\;\frac{z\;+\;1}{1}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The centroid lies on the median $RM$ and divides it in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex. // 📝 Solution: The centroid is $G\;=\;\frac{R\;+\;2M}{3}\;=\;\left(\frac{-1\;+\;4}{3},\;\frac{4\;+\;2}{3},\;\frac{2\;+\;4}{3}\right)\;=\;\left(1,\;2,\;2\right)$. A point on the first line is $\left(2,\;2s,\;-s\;-\;3\right)$ and on the second is $\left(t\;+\;1,\;-3t\;-\;3,\;t\;-\;1\right)$. From $x$: $t\;=\;1$. From $y$: $2s\;=\;-6\;\implies\;s\;=\;-3$. Check $z$: $0\;=\;0$. So the intersection point is $A\left(2,\;-6,\;0\right)$. Then $AG^2\;=\;1\;+\;64\;+\;4\;=\;69$ and $AG\;=\;\sqrt{69}$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Centroid of a triangle; intersection of lines

questions.text: Let the line of shortest distance between the lines $L_1:\;\vec{r}\;=\;\left(\hat{i}\;+\;2\hat{j}\;+\;3\hat{k}\right)\;+\;\lambda\left(\hat{i}\;-\;\hat{j}\;+\;\hat{k}\right)$ and $L_2:\;\vec{r}\;=\;\left(4\hat{i}\;+\;5\hat{j}\;+\;6\hat{k}\right)\;+\;\mu\left(\hat{i}\;+\;\hat{j}\;-\;\hat{k}\right)$ intersect $L_1$ and $L_2$ at $P$ and $Q$ respectively. If $\left(\alpha,\;\beta,\;\gamma\right)$ is the midpoint of the line segment $PQ$, then $2\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The common perpendicular $PQ$ is perpendicular to both direction vectors, so take general points on both lines and impose two dot-product conditions. // 📝 Solution: Take $P\;=\;\left(1\;+\;\lambda,\;2\;-\;\lambda,\;3\;+\;\lambda\right)$ and $Q\;=\;\left(4\;+\;\mu,\;5\;+\;\mu,\;6\;-\;\mu\right)$, so $\vec{PQ}\;=\;\left(3\;+\;\mu\;-\;\lambda,\;3\;+\;\mu\;+\;\lambda,\;3\;-\;\mu\;-\;\lambda\right)$. Perpendicular to $\left(1,\;-1,\;1\right)$: $3\;-\;\mu\;-\;3\lambda\;=\;0$. Perpendicular to $\left(1,\;1,\;-1\right)$: $3\;+\;3\mu\;+\;\lambda\;=\;0$. Solving gives $\lambda\;=\;\frac{3}{2}$ and $\mu\;=\;-\frac{3}{2}$. Hence $P\;=\;\left(\frac{5}{2},\;\frac{1}{2},\;\frac{9}{2}\right)$ and $Q\;=\;\left(\frac{5}{2},\;\frac{7}{2},\;\frac{15}{2}\right)$. The midpoint is $\left(\frac{5}{2},\;2,\;6\right)$, so $2\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)\;=\;5\;+\;4\;+\;12\;=\;21$. Correct option: B.
questions.topic: Line of shortest distance between skew lines (vector form)

questions.text: The distance of the point $P\left( 4,\; 6,\; -2 \right)$ from the line passing through the point $\left( -3,\; 2,\; 3 \right)$ and parallel to a line with direction ratios $3,\; 3,\; -1$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Foot of the perpendicular $M$ on the line satisfies $\overrightarrow{PM} \cdot \overrightarrow{d} \; = \; 0$; the required distance is $PM$. // 📝 Solution: Line: $\frac{x + 3}{3} \; = \; \frac{y - 2}{3} \; = \; \frac{z - 3}{-1} \; = \; \lambda$, so $M \; = \; \left( 3\lambda \; - \; 3,\; 3\lambda \; + \; 2,\; 3 \; - \; \lambda \right)$. $\overrightarrow{PM} \; = \; \left( 3\lambda \; - \; 7,\; 3\lambda \; - \; 4,\; 5 \; - \; \lambda \right)$. Perpendicularity: $3\left( 3\lambda \; - \; 7 \right) \; + \; 3\left( 3\lambda \; - \; 4 \right) \; - \; \left( 5 \; - \; \lambda \right) \; = \; 0 \; \implies \; 19\lambda \; = \; 38 \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; 2$. $M \; = \; \left( 3,\; 8,\; 1 \right)$. $PM \; = \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; 4 \; + \; 9} \; = \; \sqrt{14}$.
questions.topic: Distance of a point from a line

questions.text: Let $d_1$ be the shortest distance between the lines $x\;+\;1\;=\;2y\;=\;-12z$ and $x\;=\;y\;+\;2\;=\;6z\;-\;6$, and $d_2$ be the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x\;-\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;8}{-7}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;4}{5}$ and $\frac{x\;-\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{y\;-\;2}{1}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;6}{-3}$. Then the value of $\frac{32\sqrt{3}\,d_1}{d_2}$ is ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert each line to symmetric form first, then apply the skew-line distance formula twice. // 📝 Solution: First pair: $L_1:\;\frac{x\;+\;1}{12}\;=\;\frac{y}{6}\;=\;\frac{z}{-1}$ and $L_2:\;\frac{x}{6}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;2}{6}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;1}{1}$. Then $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(12,\;-18,\;36\right)$ with magnitude $42$, and $\vec{a_2}\;-\;\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(1,\;-2,\;1\right)$ gives dot product $12\;+\;36\;+\;36\;=\;84$. So $d_1\;=\;\frac{84}{42}\;=\;2$. Second pair: $\vec{b_1}\;\times\;\vec{b_2}\;=\;\left(2,\;-7,\;5\right)\;\times\;\left(2,\;1,\;-3\right)\;=\;\left(16,\;16,\;16\right)$ with magnitude $16\sqrt{3}$, and $\vec{a_2}\;-\;\vec{a_1}\;=\;\left(0,\;10,\;2\right)$ gives dot product $192$. So $d_2\;=\;\frac{192}{16\sqrt{3}}\;=\;4\sqrt{3}$. Therefore $\frac{32\sqrt{3}\;\cdot\;2}{4\sqrt{3}}\;=\;16$. Correct option: B.

questions.text: If the mirror image of the point $P\left(3,\;4,\;9\right)$ in the line $\frac{x\;-\;1}{3}\;=\;\frac{y\;+\;1}{2}\;=\;\frac{z\;-\;2}{1}$ is $\left(\alpha,\;\beta,\;\gamma\right)$, then $14\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line is the midpoint of $P$ and its image. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Let the foot be $N\;=\;\left(3\lambda\;+\;1,\;2\lambda\;-\;1,\;\lambda\;+\;2\right)$. Then $\vec{PN}\;=\;\left(3\lambda\;-\;2,\;2\lambda\;-\;5,\;\lambda\;-\;7\right)$ is perpendicular to $\left(3,\;2,\;1\right)$: $9\lambda\;-\;6\;+\;4\lambda\;-\;10\;+\;\lambda\;-\;7\;=\;0\;\implies\;\lambda\;=\;\frac{23}{14}$. So $N\;=\;\left(\frac{83}{14},\;\frac{32}{14},\;\frac{51}{14}\right)$. The image is $2N\;-\;P\;=\;\left(\frac{62}{7},\;\frac{4}{7},\;-\frac{12}{7}\right)$. Hence $14\left(\alpha\;+\;\beta\;+\;\gamma\right)\;=\;14\;\cdot\;\frac{54}{7}\;=\;108$. Correct option: C.
questions.topic: Image of a point in a line

questions.text: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x + \sqrt{6}}{2} \; = \; \frac{y - \sqrt{6}}{3} \; = \; \frac{z - \sqrt{6}}{4}$ and $\frac{x - \lambda}{3} \; = \; \frac{y - 2\sqrt{6}}{4} \; = \; \frac{z + 2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ is $6$, then the square of the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate $\frac{\left\lvert \left( \overrightarrow{a_2} \; - \; \overrightarrow{a_1} \right) \cdot \left( \overrightarrow{b_1} \times \overrightarrow{b_2} \right) \right\rvert}{\left\lvert \overrightarrow{b_1} \times \overrightarrow{b_2} \right\rvert}$ to $6$ and solve the modulus equation for $\lambda$. // 📝 Solution: $\overrightarrow{b_1} \times \overrightarrow{b_2} \; = \; \left( 2,\; 3,\; 4 \right) \times \left( 3,\; 4,\; 5 \right) \; = \; \left( -1,\; 2,\; -1 \right)$ with magnitude $\sqrt{6}$. $\overrightarrow{a_2} \; - \; \overrightarrow{a_1} \; = \; \left( \lambda \; + \; \sqrt{6},\; \sqrt{6},\; -3\sqrt{6} \right)$. Dot product $\; = \; -\left( \lambda \; + \; \sqrt{6} \right) \; + \; 2\sqrt{6} \; + \; 3\sqrt{6} \; = \; 4\sqrt{6} \; - \; \lambda$. So $\frac{\left\lvert 4\sqrt{6} \; - \; \lambda \right\rvert}{\sqrt{6}} \; = \; 6 \; \implies \; \left\lvert 4\sqrt{6} \; - \; \lambda \right\rvert \; = \; 6\sqrt{6} \; \implies \; \lambda \; = \; -2\sqrt{6}$ or $\lambda \; = \; 10\sqrt{6}$. Sum $\; = \; 8\sqrt{6}$, and its square is $384$.
questions.topic: Shortest distance between skew lines with a parameter

questions.text: Let $a, \; b, \; c \; > \; 1, \; a^3, \; b^3$ and $c^3$ be in A.P., and $\log_a b, \; \log_c a$ and $\log_b c$ be in G.P. If the sum of first $20$ terms of an A.P., whose first term is $\frac{a \; + \; 4b \; + \; c}{3}$ and the common difference is $\frac{a \; - \; 8b \; + \; c}{10}$ is $-444$, then $abc$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the G.P. condition on the logarithms to show $a \; = \; c$, which together with the A.P. condition on $a^3, \; b^3, \; c^3$ implies $a \; = \; b \; = \; c$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\log_a b, \; \log_c a, \; \log_b c$ are in G.P., $\left(\log_c a\right)^2 \; = \; \left(\log_a b\right)\left(\log_b c\right) \; = \; \log_a c \; = \; \frac{1}{\log_c a} \implies \left(\log_c a\right)^3 \; = \; 1 \implies \log_c a \; = \; 1 \implies a \; = \; c$. Since $a^3, \; b^3, \; c^3$ are in A.P., $2b^3 \; = \; a^3 \; + \; c^3 \; = \; 2a^3 \implies b \; = \; a$. Thus, $a \; = \; b \; = \; c$. For the given A.P., the first term is $T_1 \; = \; \frac{6a}{3} \; = \; 2a$ and the common difference is $d \; = \; \frac{-6a}{10} \; = \; -\frac{3a}{5}$. Given $S_{20} \; = \; -444 \implies 10\left[4a \; + \; 19\left(-\frac{3a}{5}\right)\right] \; = \; -444 \implies 2\left(20a \; - \; 57a\right) \; = \; -444 \implies -74a \; = \; -444 \implies a \; = \; 6$. Therefore, $abc \; = \; a^3 \; = \; 6^3 \; = \; 216$.

questions.text: A software company sets up $m$ number of computer systems to finish an assignment in $17$ days. If $4$ computer systems crashed on the start of the second day, $4$ more computer systems crashed on the start of the third day and so on, then it took $8$ more days to finish the assignment. The value of $m$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Equate the total computer-days required ($17m$) to the sum of active computers over $17 \; + \; 8 \; = \; 25$ days. // 📝 Solution: Total work in computer-days is $17m$. Since it took $8$ more days, the assignment was completed in $17 \; + \; 8 \; = \; 25$ days. The number of active computers on days $1, \; 2, \; 3, \; \dots, \; 25$ forms an A.P.: $m, \; m \; - \; 4, \; m \; - \; 8, \; \dots$ up to $25$ terms. Equating the total work: $17m \; = \; \frac{25}{2}\left[2m \; + \; \left(25 \; - \; 1\right)\left(-4\right)\right] \implies 17m \; = \; 25\left(m \; - \; 48\right) \implies 8m \; = \; 25 \times 48 \implies m \; = \; 25 \times 6 \; = \; 150$.

questions.text: Let $\Big(\ldots\Big)$ denote the given series: if $7=5+\frac{1}{7}(5+\alpha)+\frac{1}{7^{2}}(5+2\alpha)+\frac{1}{7^{3}}(5+3\alpha)+\cdots\,\infty$, then the value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the series into a geometric part and an arithmetico-geometric part. // 📝 Solution: $7=5+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{5+n\alpha}{7^{n}}=5+\frac{5}{6}+\frac{7\alpha}{36}$ $\implies \frac{7\alpha}{36}=\frac{7}{6}\implies \alpha=6$

questions.text: If $1 \; + \; \frac{\sqrt{3} \; - \; \sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{3}} \; + \; \frac{5 \; - \; 2\sqrt{6}}{18} \; + \; \frac{9\sqrt{3} \; - \; 11\sqrt{2}}{36\sqrt{3}} \; + \; \frac{49 \; - \; 20\sqrt{6}}{180} \; + \; \dots$ upto $\infty \; = \; 2 \; + \; \left( \sqrt{\frac{b}{a}} \; + \; 1 \right) \log_e \left( \frac{a}{b} \right)$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers with $\gcd\left(a, \; b\right) \; = \; 1$, then $11a \; + \; 18b$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $t \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{3} \; - \; \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}$ to rewrite the series as $1 \; + \; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n\left(n \; + \; 1\right)}$ and use the Taylor series of $-\log_e\left(1 \; - \; t\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Notice that for $x \; = \; \sqrt{3} \; - \; \sqrt{2}$, we have $x^2 \; = \; 5 \; - \; 2\sqrt{6}$, $x^3 \; = \; 9\sqrt{3} \; - \; 11\sqrt{2}$, and $x^4 \; = \; 49 \; - \; 20\sqrt{6}$. Let $t \; = \; \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$. The given series becomes $S \; = \; 1 \; + \; \frac{t}{1 \cdot 2} \; + \; \frac{t^2}{2 \cdot 3} \; + \; \frac{t^3}{3 \cdot 4} \; + \; \frac{t^4}{4 \cdot 5} \; + \; \dots \; = \; 1 \; + \; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} t^n \left(\frac{1}{n} \; - \; \frac{1}{n \; + \; 1}\right) \; = \; 1 \; + \; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n} \; - \; \frac{1}{t}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{t^{n+1}}{n \; + \; 1}$. Using $-\log_e\left(1 \; - \; t\right) \; = \; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n}$, we get $S \; = \; 1 \; - \; \log_e\left(1 \; - \; t\right) \; - \; \frac{1}{t}\left[-\log_e\left(1 \; - \; t\right) \; - \; t\right] \; = \; 2 \; + \; \left(\frac{1}{t} \; - \; 1\right)\log_e\left(1 \; - \; t\right)$. Since $1 \; - \; t \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$, we have $\frac{1}{t} \; - \; 1 \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; t}{t} \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3} \; - \; \sqrt{2}} \; = \; \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{3} \; + \; \sqrt{2}\right) \; = \; \sqrt{6} \; + \; 2$. Thus, $S \; = \; 2 \; + \; \left(\sqrt{6} \; + \; 2\right)\log_e\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right) \; = \; 2 \; + \; \left(\frac{\sqrt{6} \; + \; 2}{2}\right)\log_e\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \; = \; 2 \; + \; \left(\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \; + \; 1\right)\log_e\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)$. Comparing with the given form, we get $a \; = \; 2$ and $b \; = \; 3$. Therefore, $11a \; + \; 18b \; = \; 11\left(2\right) \; + \; 18\left(3\right) \; = \; 22 \; + \; 54 \; = \; 76$.

💡 Hint: Use the identity $1 \; + \; r^2 \; + \; r^4 \; = \; \left(r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1\right)\left(r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1\right)$ to split the $r^{\text{th}}$ term into a telescoping difference. // 📝 Solution: The $r^{\text{th}}$ term of the series is $T_r \; = \; \frac{r}{1 \; + \; r^2 \; + \; r^4} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\left(r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1\right) \; - \; \left(r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1\right)}{\left(r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1\right)\left(r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1\right)}\right] \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1} \; - \; \frac{1}{r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1}\right)$. Summing from $r \; = \; 1$ to $10$, the series telescopes: $S_{10} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1^2 \; - \; 1 \; + \; 1} \; - \; \frac{1}{10^2 \; + \; 10 \; + \; 1}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \; - \; \frac{1}{111}\right) \; = \; \frac{55}{111}$.

questions.text: Consider an A. P. of positive integers, whose sum of the first three terms is $54$ and the sum of the first twenty terms lies between $1600$ and $1800$. Then its $11^{\text{th}}$ term is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $S_3=54$ to relate $a$ and $d$, then bound $S_{20}$ to find $d$. // 📝 Solution: $S_3=54 \implies a+d=18$ $\implies S_{20}=10(36+17d)\in(1600,1800) \implies 7<d<8$ $\implies d=8,\; a=10$ $\implies T_{11}=10+10\cdot8=90$

questions.text: Let $2^{\text{nd}}, \; 8^{\text{th}}$ and $44^{\text{th}}$ terms of a non-constant A.P. be respectively the $1^{\text{st}}, \; 2^{\text{nd}}$ and $3^{\text{rd}}$ terms of G.P. If the first term of A.P. is $1$ then the sum of first $20$ terms is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the G.P. condition $T_8^2 \; = \; T_2 \cdot T_{44}$ with $a \; = \; 1$ to find the non-zero common difference $d$. // 📝 Solution: Given the first term of the A.P. is $a \; = \; 1$ and let the common difference be $d \; \neq \; 0$. The $2^{\text{nd}}, \; 8^{\text{th}},$ and $44^{\text{th}}$ terms of the A.P. are $1 \; + \; d, \; 1 \; + \; 7d,$ and $1 \; + \; 43d$. Since these three terms are in G.P., we have $\left(1 \; + \; 7d\right)^2 \; = \; \left(1 \; + \; d\right)\left(1 \; + \; 43d\right) \implies 1 \; + \; 14d \; + \; 49d^2 \; = \; 1 \; + \; 44d \; + \; 43d^2 \implies 6d^2 \; - \; 30d \; = \; 0 \implies d \; = \; 5$ (since $d \; \neq \; 0$). The sum of the first $20$ terms of the A.P. is $S_{20} \; = \; \frac{20}{2}\left[2\left(1\right) \; + \; \left(20 \; - \; 1\right)5\right] \; = \; 10\left(2 \; + \; 95\right) \; = \; 970$.

questions.text: Let the first three terms $2, \; p$ and $q$, with $q \; \neq \; 2$, of a G.P. be respectively the $7^{\text{th}}, \; 8^{\text{th}}$ and $13^{\text{th}}$ terms of an A.P. If the $5^{\text{th}}$ term of the G.P. is the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of the A.P., then $n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the condition $p^2 \; = \; 2q$ for the G.P. and express $2, \; p, \; q$ in terms of the first term $a$ and common difference $d$ of the A.P. // 📝 Solution: Since $2, \; p, \; q$ are in G.P., we have $p^2 \; = \; 2q$. Let the first term and common difference of the A.P. be $a$ and $d$ respectively. Then $T_7 \; = \; a \; + \; 6d \; = \; 2 \implies (1)$, $T_8 \; = \; a \; + \; 7d \; = \; p \implies (2)$, and $T_{13} \; = \; a \; + \; 12d \; = \; q \implies (3)$. Subtracting $(1)$ from $(2)$ gives $d \; = \; p \; - \; 2$, and subtracting $(2)$ from $(3)$ gives $5d \; = \; q \; - \; p$. Thus, $q \; - \; p \; = \; 5\left(p \; - \; 2\right) \implies q \; = \; 6p \; - \; 10$. Substituting in $p^2 \; = \; 2q$, we get $p^2 \; = \; 2\left(6p \; - \; 10\right) \implies p^2 \; - \; 12p \; + \; 20 \; = \; 0 \implies p \; = \; 10$ or $p \; = \; 2$. Since $q \; \neq \; 2$, we take $p \; = \; 10$, which gives $q \; = \; 50$, $d \; = \; 8$, and $a \; = \; 2 \; - \; 48 \; = \; -46$. The common ratio of the G.P. is $r \; = \; \frac{10}{2} \; = \; 5$, so the $5^{\text{th}}$ term of the G.P. is $2 \cdot 5^4 \; = \; 1250$. Equating this to the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of the A.P., we get $-46 \; + \; \left(n \; - \; 1\right)8 \; = \; 1250 \implies 8\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; 1296 \implies n \; - \; 1 \; = \; 162 \implies n \; = \; 163$.

questions.text: The $20^{\text{th}}$ term from the end of the progression $20, \; 19\frac{1}{4}, \; 18\frac{1}{2}, \; 17\frac{3}{4}, \; \dots, \; -129\frac{1}{4}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The $n^{\text{th}}$ term from the end of an A.P. with last term $l$ and common difference $d$ is $l \; - \; \left(n \; - \; 1\right)d$. // 📝 Solution: In the given A.P., the first term is $a \; = \; 20$, the common difference is $d \; = \; 19\frac{1}{4} \; - \; 20 \; = \; -\frac{3}{4}$, and the last term is $l \; = \; -129\frac{1}{4}$. The $20^{\text{th}}$ term from the end is given by $l \; - \; \left(20 \; - \; 1\right)d \; = \; -129\frac{1}{4} \; - \; 19\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) \; = \; -\frac{517}{4} \; + \; \frac{57}{4} \; = \; -\frac{460}{4} \; = \; -115$.

questions.text: The number of terms of an A.P. is even; the sum of all the odd terms is $24$, the sum of all the even terms is $30$ and the last term exceeds the first by $\dfrac{21}{2}$. Then the number of terms which are integers in the A.P. is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: the even-minus-odd sum gives $nd$, and last minus first gives $(n-1)d$ // 📝 Solution: $\tfrac n2 d=6\implies nd=12$; $(n-1)d=\tfrac{21}{2}\implies d=\tfrac32,\ n=8$; terms $\tfrac32,3,\ldots,\tfrac{21}{2}$ with integers $3,6,9,12$, so $4$
questions.topic: AP with odd and even terms

questions.text: For $x \; \ge \; 0$, the least value of $K$, for which $4^{1+x} \; + \; 4^{1-x}, \; \frac{K}{2}, \; 16^x \; + \; 16^{-x}$ are three consecutive terms of an A.P., is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the A.P. condition $2\left(\frac{K}{2}\right) \; = \; \left(4^{1+x} \; + \; 4^{1-x}\right) \; + \; \left(16^x \; + \; 16^{-x}\right)$ and apply the AM-GM inequality. // 📝 Solution: Since the three terms are in A.P., we have $2\left(\frac{K}{2}\right) \; = \; 4\left(4^x \; + \; 4^{-x}\right) \; + \; \left(16^x \; + \; 16^{-x}\right)$. By the AM-GM inequality, for any positive real number $t$, $t \; + \; \frac{1}{t} \; \ge \; 2$, with equality holding when $t \; = \; 1$. For $x \; = \; 0$, both $4^x \; = \; 1$ and $16^x \; = \; 1$ simultaneously achieve their minimum values: $4^x \; + \; 4^{-x} \; \ge \; 2$ and $16^x \; + \; 16^{-x} \; \ge \; 2$. Therefore, $K \; \ge \; 4\left(2\right) \; + \; 2 \; = \; 10$. Hence, the least value of $K$ is $10$.

💡 Hint: Pair consecutive terms in $A_k$ using $a_{2r-1}^2 \; - \; a_{2r}^2 \; = \; -d\left(a_{2r-1} \; + \; a_{2r}\right)$ where $d$ is the common difference. // 📝 Solution: Let $a_1 \; = \; a$ and the common difference be $d$. Then $A_k \; = \; \left(a_1^2 \; - \; a_2^2\right) \; + \; \left(a_3^2 \; - \; a_4^2\right) \; + \; \dots \; + \; \left(a_{2k-1}^2 \; - \; a_{2k}^2\right) \; = \; -d\left(a_1 \; + \; a_2 \; + \; a_3 \; + \; \dots \; + \; a_{2k}\right) \; = \; -kd\left[2a \; + \; \left(2k \; - \; 1\right)d\right]$. Given $A_3 \; = \; -153 \implies -3d\left(2a \; + \; 5d\right) \; = \; -153 \implies d\left(2a \; + \; 5d\right) \; = \; 51 \implies (1)$. Also $A_5 \; = \; -435 \implies -5d\left(2a \; + \; 9d\right) \; = \; -435 \implies d\left(2a \; + \; 9d\right) \; = \; 87 \implies (2)$. Subtracting $(1)$ from $(2)$ gives $4d^2 \; = \; 36 \implies d^2 \; = \; 9 \implies d \; = \; 3$ (since terms are positive and $A_k \; < \; 0$). From $(1)$, $3\left(2a \; + \; 15\right) \; = \; 51 \implies 2a \; + \; 15 \; = \; 17 \implies a \; = \; 1$ (which also satisfies $a_1^2 \; + \; a_2^2 \; + \; a_3^2 \; = \; 1^2 \; + \; 4^2 \; + \; 7^2 \; = \; 66$). Now, $a_{17} \; = \; a \; + \; 16d \; = \; 1 \; + \; 48 \; = \; 49$, and $A_7 \; = \; -7\left(3\right)\left[2\left(1\right) \; + \; 13\left(3\right)\right] \; = \; -21 \times 41 \; = \; -861$. Therefore, $a_{17} \; - \; A_7 \; = \; 49 \; - \; \left(-861\right) \; = \; 910$.

questions.text: Let $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},\ldots$ be a G.P. of increasing positive numbers. If $a_{3}a_{5}=729$ and $a_{2}+a_{4}=\dfrac{111}{4}$, then $24(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3})$ is equal to
Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ be a G.P. of increasing positive terms. If $a_1a_5=28$ and $a_2+a_4=29$, then $a_6$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: In a G.P., $a_1a_5=a_3^{2}$, so first find $a_3$ and the common ratio. // 📝 Solution: $a_3^{2}=28 \implies a_3=\sqrt{28}$ $\implies a_3\left(r+\frac{1}{r}\right)=29 \implies r=\sqrt{28}$ $\implies a_6=a_3r^{3}=(\sqrt{28})^{4}=784$

questions.text: Let $a_{n}$ be the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of an A.P. If $S_{n}=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=700$, $a_{6}=7$ and $S_{7}=7$, then $a_{n}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: from $a_6$ and $S_7$ find $a$ and $d$, then solve $S_n=700$ // 📝 Solution: $a+5d=7,\ a+3d=1\implies d=3,\ a=-8$; $\tfrac n2(3n-19)=700\implies n=25$; $a_{25}=-8+72=64$
questions.topic: nth term and sum of AP

questions.text: Let $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}$ be in a geometric progression. If $2,7,9,5$ are subtracted respectively from $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}$, then the resulting numbers are in an arithmetic progression. Then the value of $\dfrac{1}{24}(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4})$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: write $x_i=ar^{i-1}$ and impose the AP condition on the shifted terms // 📝 Solution: $2(ar-7)=(a-2)+(ar^{2}-9)$ and $2(ar^{2}-9)=(ar-7)+(ar^{3}-5)\implies r=2,\ a=-3$; $x_1x_2x_3x_4=a^{4}r^{6}=5184\implies\dfrac{5184}{24}=216$

💡 Hint: Use $a_n \; = \; a_1 \; + \; \left(n \; - \; 1\right)d \; = \; \frac{1}{4}a_1$ and $\frac{n}{2}\left(a_1 \; + \; a_n\right) \; = \; \frac{525}{2}$ to find $a_1$ and $n$. // 📝 Solution: Here $d \; = \; -\frac{3}{4}$. Given $a_n \; = \; a_1 \; - \; \frac{3}{4}\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{4}a_1 \implies \frac{3}{4}a_1 \; = \; \frac{3}{4}\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \implies a_1 \; = \; n \; - \; 1$. Also, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \; = \; \frac{n}{2}\left(a_1 \; + \; \frac{1}{4}a_1\right) \; = \; \frac{525}{2} \implies \frac{5}{4}n\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; 525 \implies n\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; 420 \implies n \; = \; 21$ and $a_1 \; = \; 20$. Therefore, $\sum_{i=1}^{17} a_i \; = \; \frac{17}{2}\left[2\left(20\right) \; + \; 16\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)\right] \; = \; \frac{17}{2}\left(40 \; - \; 12\right) \; = \; 17 \times 14 \; = \; 238$.

questions.text: In an increasing geometric progression of positive terms, the sum of the second and sixth terms is $\frac{70}{3}$ and the product of the third and fifth terms is $49$. Then the sum of the $4^{\text{th}}, \; 6^{\text{th}}$ and $8^{\text{th}}$ terms is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $T_3 \cdot T_5 \; = \; T_4^2 \; = \; 49$ to find $T_4 \; = \; ar^3$, then express $T_2 \; + \; T_6$ in terms of $T_4$ and $r^2$. // 📝 Solution: Let the first term be $a$ and common ratio be $r \; > \; 1$. Given $T_3 \cdot T_5 \; = \; \left(ar^2\right)\left(ar^4\right) \; = \; \left(ar^3\right)^2 \; = \; 49 \implies ar^3 \; = \; 7$ (since terms are positive). Also, $T_2 \; + \; T_6 \; = \; ar \; + \; ar^5 \; = \; \frac{70}{3}$. Writing this in terms of $ar^3$: $ar^3\left(\frac{1}{r^2} \; + \; r^2\right) \; = \; \frac{70}{3} \implies 7\left(\frac{1}{r^2} \; + \; r^2\right) \; = \; \frac{70}{3} \implies r^2 \; + \; \frac{1}{r^2} \; = \; \frac{10}{3} \implies 3r^4 \; - \; 10r^2 \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0 \implies \left(3r^2 \; - \; 1\right)\left(r^2 \; - \; 3\right) \; = \; 0$. Since the G.P. is increasing, $r^2 \; = \; 3$. Now, $T_4 \; + \; T_6 \; + \; T_8 \; = \; ar^3 \; + \; ar^5 \; + \; ar^7 \; = \; ar^3\left(1 \; + \; r^2 \; + \; r^4\right) \; = \; 7\left(1 \; + \; 3 \; + \; 9\right) \; = \; 7 \times 13 \; = \; 91$.

questions.text: Let $S_n$ denote the sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression. If $S_{10} \; = \; 390$ and the ratio of the tenth and the fifth terms is $15 \; : \; 7$, then $S_{15} \; - \; S_5$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the given conditions to set up two linear equations in the first term $a$ and common difference $d$. // 📝 Solution: Let the first term be $a$ and common difference be $d$. Given $S_{10} \; = \; 390 \implies \frac{10}{2}\left(2a \; + \; 9d\right) \; = \; 390 \implies 2a \; + \; 9d \; = \; 78 \implies (1)$. Also, $\frac{T_{10}}{T_5} \; = \; \frac{a \; + \; 9d}{a \; + \; 4d} \; = \; \frac{15}{7} \implies 7a \; + \; 63d \; = \; 15a \; + \; 60d \implies 8a \; = \; 3d \implies d \; = \; \frac{8}{3}a \implies (2)$. Substituting $(2)$ into $(1)$: $2a \; + \; 9\left(\frac{8}{3}a\right) \; = \; 78 \implies 26a \; = \; 78 \implies a \; = \; 3$, and $d \; = \; 8$. Now, $S_{15} \; - \; S_5 \; = \; \frac{15}{2}\left[2\left(3\right) \; + \; 14\left(8\right)\right] \; - \; \frac{5}{2}\left[2\left(3\right) \; + \; 4\left(8\right)\right] \; = \; \frac{15 \times 118 \; - \; 5 \times 38}{2} \; = \; 15 \times 59 \; - \; 5 \times 19 \; = \; 885 \; - \; 95 \; = \; 790$.

💡 Hint: Factor the denominator $4n^2 \; - \; 16n \; + \; 15 \; = \; \left(2n \; - \; 5\right)\left(2n \; - \; 3\right)$ and split $a_n$ into partial fractions. // 📝 Solution: We can factor the denominator as $4n^2 \; - \; 16n \; + \; 15 \; = \; \left(2n \; - \; 5\right)\left(2n \; - \; 3\right)$. Thus, $a_n \; = \; \frac{-2}{\left(2n \; - \; 5\right)\left(2n \; - \; 3\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{2n \; - \; 3} \; - \; \frac{1}{2n \; - \; 5}$. Summing from $n \; = \; 1$ to $25$, the series telescopes: $\sum_{n=1}^{25} a_n \; = \; \left(-\frac{1}{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{3}\right) \; + \; \left(-\frac{1}{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{1}\right)$? Let us write terms explicitly: for $n \; = \; 1$, $\frac{1}{-1} \; - \; \frac{1}{-3}$; for $n \; = \; 2$, $\frac{1}{1} \; - \; \frac{1}{-1}$; $\dots$; for $n \; = \; 25$, $\frac{1}{47} \; - \; \frac{1}{45}$. Canceling adjacent terms gives $\sum_{n=1}^{25} a_n \; = \; \frac{1}{47} \; - \; \frac{1}{-3} \; = \; \frac{1}{47} \; + \; \frac{1}{3} \; = \; \frac{50}{141}$.

questions.text: If $\sum_{r=1}^{25} \left( \frac{r}{r^4 \; + \; r^2 \; + \; 1} \right) \; = \; \frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers such that $\gcd\left(p, \; q\right) \; = \; 1$, then $p \; + \; q$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the factorization $r^4 \; + \; r^2 \; + \; 1 \; = \; \left(r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1\right)\left(r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1\right)$ to split the general term into a telescoping difference. // 📝 Solution: We can write the $r^{\text{th}}$ term as $T_r \; = \; \frac{r}{\left(r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1\right)\left(r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r^2 \; - \; r \; + \; 1} \; - \; \frac{1}{r^2 \; + \; r \; + \; 1}\right)$. Summing from $r \; = \; 1$ to $25$, the series telescopes: $\sum_{r=1}^{25} T_r \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1^2 \; - \; 1 \; + \; 1} \; - \; \frac{1}{25^2 \; + \; 25 \; + \; 1}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \; - \; \frac{1}{651}\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{650}{651} \; = \; \frac{325}{651}$. Since $\gcd\left(325, \; 651\right) \; = \; 1$, we have $p \; = \; 325$ and $q \; = \; 651$. Thus, $p \; + \; q \; = \; 325 \; + \; 651 \; = \; 976$.

questions.text: Suppose $a, \; b, \; c$ are in A.P. and $a^2, \; 2b^2, \; c^2$ are in G.P. If $a \; < \; b \; < \; c$ and $a \; + \; b \; + \; c \; = \; 1$, then $9\left(a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $3b \; = \; 1$ from the A.P. sum and write $a \; = \; b \; - \; d, \; c \; = \; b \; + \; d$, then apply the G.P. condition $\left(2b^2\right)^2 \; = \; a^2 c^2$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a, \; b, \; c$ are in A.P. and $a \; + \; b \; + \; c \; = \; 1$, we have $3b \; = \; 1 \implies b \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Let the common difference be $d \; > \; 0$, so $a \; = \; \frac{1}{3} \; - \; d$ and $c \; = \; \frac{1}{3} \; + \; d$. Since $a^2, \; 2b^2, \; c^2$ are in G.P., we have $\left(2b^2\right)^2 \; = \; a^2 c^2 \implies ac \; = \; \pm 2b^2$. Thus, $\frac{1}{9} \; - \; d^2 \; = \; \pm \frac{2}{9}$. Since $d^2 \; > \; 0$, we must have $\frac{1}{9} \; - \; d^2 \; = \; -\frac{2}{9} \implies d^2 \; = \; \frac{3}{9} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Now, $9\left(a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2\right) \; = \; 9\left[\left(b \; - \; d\right)^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; \left(b \; + \; d\right)^2\right] \; = \; 9\left(3b^2 \; + \; 2d^2\right) \; = \; 9\left(\frac{3}{9} \; + \; \frac{6}{9}\right) \; = \; 9$.

questions.text: Let $S_n=\frac12+\frac16+\frac1{12}+\frac1{20}+\ldots$ upto $n$ terms. If the sum of the first six terms of an A.P. with first term $-p$ and common difference $p$ is $\sqrt{2026\,S_{2025}}$, then the absolute difference between $20^{th}$ and $15^{th}$ terms of the A.P. is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Telescope $S_n$ using $\frac{1}{n\left(n+1\right)}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}$, then use the A.P. sum formula. // 📝 Solution: $S_{2025}\;=\;\frac{2025}{2026}\;\implies\;\sqrt{2026\,S_{2025}}\;=\;45\;,\;\frac62\left[-2p+5p\right]\;=\;45\;\implies\;p\;=\;5\;\implies\;T_{20}-T_{15}\;=\;5p\;=\;25$

questions.text: Let $a_1, \; a_2, \; a_3, \; \dots$ be a GP of increasing positive numbers. If the product of fourth and sixth terms is $9$ and the sum of fifth and seventh terms is $24$, then $a_1 a_9 \; + \; a_2 a_4 a_9 \; + \; a_5 \; + \; a_7$ is equal to:
Let $\left\langle a_n\right\rangle$ be a sequence such that $a_0=0,\;a_1=\frac12$ and $2a_{n+2}=5a_{n+1}-3a_n,\;n=0,1,2,3,\ldots$ Then $\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_k$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the characteristic equation of the linear recurrence and use the G.P. sum. // 📝 Solution: $2x^2-5x+3=0\;\implies\;x=1,\;\frac32\;\implies\;a_n\;=\;\left(\frac32\right)^n-1\;\implies\;\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_k\;=\;-100+3\left[\left(\frac32\right)^{100}-1\right]\;=\;3a_{100}-100$

questions.text: The positive integer $n$, for which the solutions of the equation $x\left(x \; + \; 2\right) \; + \; \left(x \; + \; 2\right)\left(x \; + \; 4\right) \; + \; \dots \; + \; \left(x \; + \; 2n \; - \; 2\right)\left(x \; + \; 2n\right) \; = \; \frac{8n}{3}$ are two consecutive even integers, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the $k^{\text{th}}$ term as $\left(x \; + \; 2k \; - \; 1\right)^2 \; - \; 1$, sum over $k \; = \; 1$ to $n$ to form a quadratic in $x$, and set the difference of its roots to $2$. // 📝 Solution: The given equation is $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \left(x \; + \; 2k \; - \; 2\right)\left(x \; + \; 2k\right) \; = \; \frac{8n}{3} \implies \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[x^2 \; + \; 2\left(2k \; - \; 1\right)x \; + \; 4k\left(k \; - \; 1\right)\right] \; = \; \frac{8n}{3}$. Using $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \left(2k \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; n^2$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n} 4k\left(k \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; \frac{4n\left(n^2 \; - \; 1\right)}{3}$, we get $nx^2 \; + \; 2n^2x \; + \; \frac{4n\left(n^2 \; - \; 1\right)}{3} \; = \; \frac{8n}{3}$. Dividing by $n \; > \; 0$ gives $x^2 \; + \; 2nx \; + \; \frac{4\left(n^2 \; - \; 3\right)}{3} \; = \; 0$. Since the roots $\alpha, \; \beta$ are two consecutive even integers, $\left\lvert \alpha \; - \; \beta \right\rvert \; = \; 2 \implies \left(\alpha \; + \; \beta\right)^2 \; - \; 4\alpha\beta \; = \; 4$. Thus, $\left(2n\right)^2 \; - \; \frac{16\left(n^2 \; - \; 3\right)}{3} \; = \; 4 \implies n^2 \; - \; \frac{4\left(n^2 \; - \; 3\right)}{3} \; = \; 1 \implies 3n^2 \; - \; 4n^2 \; + \; 12 \; = \; 3 \implies n^2 \; = \; 9 \implies n \; = \; 3$.

questions.text: $1+3+5^{2}+7+9^{2}+\cdots$ upto $40$ terms is equal to

If $8 \; = \; 3 \; + \; \frac{1}{4}\left(3 \; + \; p\right) \; + \; \frac{1}{4^2}\left(3 \; + \; 2p\right) \; + \; \frac{1}{4^3}\left(3 \; + \; 3p\right) \; + \; \dots \; \infty$, then the value of $p$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the infinite Arithmetico-Geometric Progression (A.G.P.) sum formula $S_{\infty} \; = \; \frac{a}{1 \; - \; r} \; + \; \frac{dr}{\left(1 \; - \; r\right)^2}$. // 📝 Solution: The given series is an infinite A.G.P. with first term $a \; = \; 3$, common difference $d \; = \; p$, and common ratio $r \; = \; \frac{1}{4}$. Using the sum to infinity formula $S_{\infty} \; = \; \frac{a}{1 \; - \; r} \; + \; \frac{dr}{\left(1 \; - \; r\right)^2}$, we have $8 \; = \; \frac{3}{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{4}} \; + \; \frac{p \cdot \frac{1}{4}}{\left(1 \; - \; \frac{1}{4}\right)^2} \implies 8 \; = \; \frac{3}{\frac{3}{4}} \; + \; \frac{\frac{p}{4}}{\frac{9}{16}} \implies 8 \; = \; 4 \; + \; \frac{4p}{9} \implies \frac{4p}{9} \; = \; 4 \implies p \; = \; 9$.

questions.text: If $\log_e a, \; \log_e b, \; \log_e c$ are in an A.P. and $\log_e a \; - \; \log_e 2b, \; \log_e 2b \; - \; \log_e 3c, \; \log_e 3c \; - \; \log_e a$ are also in an A.P., then $a \; : \; b \; : \; c$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use properties of logarithms to convert the A.P. conditions into multiplicative relations between $a, \; b,$ and $c$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\log_e a, \; \log_e b, \; \log_e c$ are in A.P., we have $2\log_e b \; = \; \log_e a \; + \; \log_e c \implies b^2 \; = \; ac \implies (1)$. Also, $\log_e\left(\frac{a}{2b}\right), \; \log_e\left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right), \; \log_e\left(\frac{3c}{a}\right)$ are in A.P., which implies $\left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right)^2 \; = \; \left(\frac{a}{2b}\right)\left(\frac{3c}{a}\right) \; = \; \frac{3c}{2b} \implies \left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right)^3 \; = \; \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^0$? Wait: $\frac{4b^2}{9c^2} \; = \; \frac{3c}{2b}?$ No! $\left(\frac{a}{2b}\right)\left(\frac{3c}{a}\right) \; = \; \frac{3c}{2b}$, so $\left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right)^2 \; = \; \frac{3c}{2b} \implies \left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right)^3 \; = \; 1 \implies \frac{2b}{3c} \; = \; 1 \implies \frac{b}{c} \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$. Substituting $c \; = \; \frac{2}{3}b$ into $(1)$ gives $b^2 \; = \; a\left(\frac{2}{3}b\right) \implies \frac{a}{b} \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$. Thus, $a \; : \; b \; : \; c \; = \; \frac{3}{2}b \; : \; b \; : \; \frac{2}{3}b \; = \; 9 \; : \; 6 \; : \; 4$.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is a tautology?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the implication equivalence $A \; \to \; B \; \equiv \; \sim A \; \lor \; B$ to simplify each compound statement. // 📝 Solution: Consider option (B): $\left(p \; \land \; q\right) \; \to \; \left(\sim p \; \to \; q\right)$. Since $\sim p \; \to \; q \; \equiv \; \sim\left(\sim p\right) \; \lor \; q \; \equiv \; p \; \lor \; q$, the statement becomes $\sim\left(p \; \land \; q\right) \; \lor \; \left(p \; \lor \; q\right) \; \equiv \; \left(\sim p \; \lor \; \sim q\right) \; \lor \; \left(p \; \lor \; q\right) \; \equiv \; \left(\sim p \; \lor \; p\right) \; \lor \; \left(\sim q \; \lor \; q\right) \; \equiv \; T \; \lor \; T \; \equiv \; T$. Hence, it is a tautology.

questions.text: If the sum of the first $10$ terms of the series $\dfrac{4.1}{1+4.1^{4}}+\dfrac{4.2}{1+4.2^{4}}+\dfrac{4.3}{1+4.3^{4}}+\cdots$ is $\dfrac{m}{n}$, where $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then $m+n$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: factor $1+4r^{4}=(2r^{2}+2r+1)(2r^{2}-2r+1)$ and telescope // 📝 Solution: $T_r=\dfrac{1}{2r^{2}-2r+1}-\dfrac{1}{2r^{2}+2r+1}\implies S_{10}=1-\dfrac{1}{221}=\dfrac{220}{221}\implies m+n=441$

questions.text: Let $a_1, \; \frac{a_2}{2}, \; \frac{a_3}{2^2}, \; \dots, \; \frac{a_{10}}{2^9}$ be a G.P. of common ratio $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. If $a_1 \; + \; a_2 \; + \; \dots \; + \; a_{10} \; = \; 62$, then $a_1$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the $k^{\text{th}}$ term of the given G.P. as $\frac{a_k}{2^{k-1}} \; = \; a_1 \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{k-1}$ to show that $a_k$ is a G.P. with common ratio $\sqrt{2}$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a_1, \; \frac{a_2}{2}, \; \frac{a_3}{2^2}, \; \dots, \; \frac{a_{10}}{2^9}$ is a G.P. with common ratio $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, we have $\frac{a_k}{2^{k-1}} \; = \; a_1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{k-1} \implies a_k \; = \; a_1\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{k-1}$. Thus, $a_1, \; a_2, \; \dots, \; a_{10}$ is a G.P. with first term $a_1$ and common ratio $r \; = \; \sqrt{2}$. Given $a_1 \; + \; a_2 \; + \; \dots \; + \; a_{10} \; = \; 62 \implies \frac{a_1\left[\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{10} \; - \; 1\right]}{\sqrt{2} \; - \; 1} \; = \; 62 \implies \frac{a_1\left(32 \; - \; 1\right)}{\sqrt{2} \; - \; 1} \; = \; 62 \implies 31a_1 \; = \; 62\left(\sqrt{2} \; - \; 1\right) \implies a_1 \; = \; 2\left(\sqrt{2} \; - \; 1\right)$.

questions.text: The value of $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{k^{3}+6k^{2}+11k+5}{(k+3)!}\right)$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $k^{3}+6k^{2}+11k+6=(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)$ and split the fraction. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{k^{3}+6k^{2}+11k+5}{(k+3)!}=\frac{1}{k!}-\frac{1}{(k+3)!}$ $\implies \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{1}{k!}=e-1,\; \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{1}{(k+3)!}=e-\frac{8}{3}$ $\implies \text{limit}=(e-1)-\left(e-\frac{8}{3}\right)=\frac{5}{3}$

questions.text: If in a G.P. of $64$ terms, the sum of all the terms is $7$ times the sum of the odd terms of the G.P., then the common ratio of the G.P. is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the sum of all $64$ terms into odd-indexed terms and even-indexed terms, or use the G.P. sum formula with ratios $r$ and $r^2$. // 📝 Solution: Let the G.P. be $a, \; ar, \; ar^2, \; \dots, \; ar^{63}$. The sum of all $64$ terms is $S \; = \; a\left(1 \; + \; r \; + \; r^2 \; + \; \dots \; + \; r^{63}\right) \; = \; \frac{a\left(r^{64} \; - \; 1\right)}{r \; - \; 1}$. The odd-indexed terms ($T_1, \; T_3, \; \dots, \; T_{63}$) form a G.P. of $32$ terms with first term $a$ and common ratio $r^2$, whose sum is $S_{\text{odd}} \; = \; \frac{a\left[\left(r^2\right)^{32} \; - \; 1\right]}{r^2 \; - \; 1} \; = \; \frac{a\left(r^{64} \; - \; 1\right)}{\left(r \; - \; 1\right)\left(r \; + \; 1\right)}$. Given $S \; = \; 7S_{\text{odd}} \implies 1 \; = \; \frac{7}{r \; + \; 1} \implies r \; + \; 1 \; = \; 7 \implies r \; = \; 6$.

questions.text: If three successive terms of a G.P. with common ratio $r \; \left(r \; > \; 1\right)$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle and $\left[r\right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$, then $3\left[r\right] \; + \; \left[-r\right]$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the triangle inequality $a \; + \; ar \; > \; ar^2$ for the largest side $ar^2$ (since $r \; > \; 1$). // 📝 Solution: Let the three sides of the triangle be $a, \; ar, \; ar^2$ with $a \; > \; 0$ and $r \; > \; 1$. Since $r \; > \; 1$, the largest side is $ar^2$. By the triangle inequality, the sum of the two smaller sides must exceed the largest side: $a \; + \; ar \; > \; ar^2 \implies r^2 \; - \; r \; - \; 1 \; < \; 0$. The roots of $r^2 \; - \; r \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$ are $\frac{1 \; \pm \; \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Since $r \; > \; 1$, we get $r \; \in \; \left(1, \; \frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$. Since $\frac{1 \; + \; \sqrt{5}}{2} \; \approx \; 1.618$, we have $1 \; < \; r \; < \; 1.618$. Therefore, $\left[r\right] \; = \; 1$ and $\left[-r\right] \; = \; -2$. Thus, $3\left[r\right] \; + \; \left[-r\right] \; = \; 3\left(1\right) \; + \; \left(-2\right) \; = \; 1$.

questions.text: Let the positive integers be written in the form: [FIGURE] Row 1: $1$; Row 2: $2, \; 3$; Row 3: $4, \; 5, \; 6$; Row 4: $7, \; 8, \; 9, \; 10$; and so on. If the $k^{\text{th}}$ row contains exactly $k$ numbers for every natural number $k$, then the row in which the number $5310$ will be, is:
