questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \alpha & \beta \\ 0 & \beta & \alpha \end{bmatrix}$ and $\left\lvert 2A \right\rvert^3 \;=\; 2^{21}$ where $\alpha, \;\beta \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$. Then a value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\left\lvert 2A \right\rvert \;=\; 2^3 \left\lvert A \right\rvert$ for a $3 \;\times\; 3$ matrix and factorize $\alpha^2 \;-\; \beta^2 \;=\; \left(\alpha \;-\; \beta\right)\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right)$ over integers. // 📝 Solution: Expanding $\left\lvert A \right\rvert$ along the first row gives $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; \alpha^2 \;-\; \beta^2$. Since $A$ is of order $3$, $\left\lvert 2A \right\rvert \;=\; 2^3 \left\lvert A \right\rvert$. Given $\left\lvert 2A \right\rvert^3 \;=\; 2^{21} \;\implies\; \left(2^3 \left\lvert A \right\rvert\right)^3 \;=\; 2^{21} \;\implies\; 2^9 \left\lvert A \right\rvert^3 \;=\; 2^{21} \;\implies\; \left\lvert A \right\rvert^3 \;=\; 2^{12} \;\implies\; \left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 2^4 \;=\; 16$. Thus, $\alpha^2 \;-\; \beta^2 \;=\; 16 \;\implies\; \left(\alpha \;-\; \beta\right)\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta\right) \;=\; 16$. Since $\alpha, \;\beta \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$, $\alpha \;-\; \beta$ and $\alpha \;+\; \beta$ must have the same parity (both even). Using the even factor pairs $\left(2, \;8\right)$ and $\left(4, \;4\right)$, we get $\alpha \;=\; \frac{2 \;+\; 8}{2} \;=\; 5$ or $\alpha \;=\; \frac{4 \;+\; 4}{2} \;=\; 4$. From the given options, $\alpha \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \;\infty\right)$ and $A \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. If $\det\left(\text{adj}\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right) \;\cdot\; \text{adj}\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right)\right) \;=\; 2^8$, then $\left(\det\left(A\right)\right)^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the properties $\text{adj}\left(XY\right) \;=\; \text{adj}\left(Y\right)\text{adj}\left(X\right)$, $\det\left(\text{adj}\left(M\right)\right) \;=\; \left(\det\left(M\right)\right)^{n-1}$, and $\det\left(M^T\right) \;=\; \det\left(M\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Given $\det\left(\text{adj}\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right) \;\cdot\; \text{adj}\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right)\right) \;=\; 2^8$. Since $A$ is of order $3$, $\left(\det\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right)\right)^2 \;\cdot\; \left(\det\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right)\right)^2 \;=\; 2^8$. Notice that $\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right)^T \;=\; A^T \;-\; 2A \;=\; -\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right)$, so $\det\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right) \;=\; \det\left(-\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right)\right) \;=\; -\det\left(2A \;-\; A^T\right)$. Thus, $\left(\det\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right)\right)^4 \;=\; 2^8 \;\implies\; \left\lvert A \;-\; 2A^T \right\rvert \;=\; \pm 4$. Now, $A \;-\; 2A^T \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \;-\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 2 \\ 2\alpha & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & \alpha \\ -3 & 0 & -1 \\ -2\alpha & -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$. Expanding along the second column gives $\det\left(A \;-\; 2A^T\right) \;=\; 1 \;\cdot\; \left(1 \;+\; 3\alpha\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; 3\alpha$. Since $\alpha \;\in\; \left(0, \;\infty\right)$, $1 \;+\; 3\alpha \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 1$. Substituting $\alpha \;=\; 1$ in $A$, we get $\det\left(A\right) \;=\; 1\left(0 \;-\; 1\right) \;-\; 2\left(2 \;-\; 0\right) \;+\; 1\left(1 \;-\; 0\right) \;=\; -4$. Therefore, $\left(\det\left(A\right)\right)^2 \;=\; \left(-4\right)^2 \;=\; 16$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sec x \, dy \;+\; \left\{ 2(1 \;-\; x) \tan x \;+\; x(2 \;-\; x) \right\} dx \;=\; 0$ such that $y(0) \;=\; 2$. Then $y(2)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $\sec x \, dx$ and integrate $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; 2(x \;-\; 1) \sin x \;+\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 2x \right) \cos x$ by recognizing the product rule. // 📝 Solution: Multiplying by $\cos x$ and rearranging gives $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; 2(x \;-\; 1) \sin x \;+\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 2x \right) \cos x \;=\; \frac{d}{dx}\left[ \left( x^2 \;-\; 2x \right) \sin x \right]$. Integrating both sides gives $y(x) \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 2x \right) \sin x \;+\; C$. Given $y(0) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2$. Thus $y(x) \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 2x \right) \sin x \;+\; 2$. At $x \;=\; 2$, $y(2) \;=\; 0 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 2$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; f(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $y(x \;+\; 1) dx \;-\; x^2 dy \;=\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; e$. Then $\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables as $\frac{x \;+\; 1}{x^2} \, dx \;=\; \frac{dy}{y}$ and integrate. // 📝 Solution: Separating variables and integrating gives $\int \left( \frac{1}{x} \;+\; \frac{1}{x^2} \right) dx \;=\; \int \frac{dy}{y} \;\implies\; \ln x \;-\; \frac{1}{x} \;=\; \ln y \;+\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; e \;\implies\; 0 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; -2$. Thus $f(x) \;=\; x e^{2 - \frac{1}{x}}$. Taking the right-hand limit at $0$, $\lim_{x \to 0^+} x e^{2 - \frac{1}{x}} \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sec^2 x \, dx \;+\; \left( e^{2y} \tan^2 x \;+\; \tan x \right) dy \;=\; 0$, $0 \;<\; x \;<\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; 0$. If $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; \alpha$, then $e^{8\alpha}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $\frac{1}{\tan x} \;=\; u$ to convert this Bernoulli equation in $\tan x$ into a linear differential equation in $u(y)$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $\tan^2 x \, dy$ gives $\frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x} \frac{dx}{dy} \;+\; \frac{1}{\tan x} \;=\; -e^{2y}$. Let $\frac{1}{\tan x} \;=\; u \;\implies\; -\frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x} \frac{dx}{dy} \;=\; \frac{du}{dy}$, so $\frac{du}{dy} \;-\; u \;=\; e^{2y}$. With $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-y}$, we get $u e^{-y} \;=\; \int e^y \, dy \;=\; e^y \;+\; C \;\implies\; \frac{e^{-y}}{\tan x} \;=\; e^y \;+\; C$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}, y \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6}, y \;=\; \alpha \;\implies\; \sqrt{3} e^{-\alpha} \;=\; e^\alpha \;\implies\; e^{2\alpha} \;=\; \sqrt{3} \;\implies\; e^{8\alpha} \;=\; 9$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x \log_e x \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; y \;=\; x^2 \log_e x$, $(x \;>\; 1)$. If $y(2) \;=\; 2$, then $y(e)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $x \log_e x$ to form a linear differential equation with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \log_e x$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $x \log_e x$ gives $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{x \ln x} \;=\; x$, with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \ln x$. Multiplying and integrating by parts gives $y \ln x \;=\; \int x \ln x \, dx \;=\; \frac{x^2}{2} \ln x \;-\; \frac{x^2}{4} \;+\; C$. Given $y(2) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; 2 \ln 2 \;=\; 2 \ln 2 \;-\; 1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 1$. At $x \;=\; e$, $y(e) \cdot 1 \;=\; \frac{e^2}{2} \;-\; \frac{e^2}{4} \;+\; 1 \;=\; \frac{4 \;+\; e^2}{4}$.

questions.text: If the solution curve $y \;=\; f(x)$ of the differential equation $\left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right) y' \;-\; 2xy \;+\; 2x\left( 4 \;-\; x^2 \right)^2 \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 2$, passes through the point $(3, 15)$, then the local maximum value of $f$ is ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $\left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right)^2$ to write the equation as $\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y}{x^2 \;-\; 4} \right) \;=\; -2x$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $\left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right)^2$ gives $\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y}{x^2 \;-\; 4} \right) \;=\; -2x$. Integrating yields $\frac{y}{x^2 \;-\; 4} \;=\; -x^2 \;+\; C \;\implies\; y \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right)\left( C \;-\; x^2 \right)$. Passing through $(3, 15) \;\implies\; 15 \;=\; 5(C \;-\; 9) \;\implies\; C \;=\; 12$. Thus $f(x) \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right)\left( 12 \;-\; x^2 \right)$. Setting $f'(x) \;=\; 4x\left( 8 \;-\; x^2 \right) \;=\; 0$ for $x \;>\; 2$ gives $x \;=\; 2\sqrt{2}$, so the local maximum value is $f\left( 2\sqrt{2} \right) \;=\; (8 \;-\; 4)(12 \;-\; 8) \;=\; 16$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\sec y \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; 2x \sin y \;=\; x^3 \cos y$, $y(1) \;=\; 0$. Then $y\left( \sqrt{3} \right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Multiply by $\sec y$ and substitute $\tan y \;=\; t$ to reduce this Bernoulli equation to a linear differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Multiplying by $\sec y$ gives $\sec^2 y \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; 2x \tan y \;=\; x^3$. Let $\tan y \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dt}{dx} \;+\; 2x t \;=\; x^3$, which has $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{x^2}$. Integrating gives $t e^{x^2} \;=\; \int x^3 e^{x^2} \, dx \;=\; \frac{1}{2} e^{x^2} \left( x^2 \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; C \;\implies\; 2 \tan y \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; 2C e^{-x^2}$. Using $y(1) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; \sqrt{3}$, $2 \tan y \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; y\left( \sqrt{3} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.text: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable non-negative function such that $(f(x))^2 \;=\; 25 \;+\; \int_{0}^{x} \left( (f(t))^2 \;+\; (f'(t))^2 \right) dt$. Then the mean of $f(\log_e(1)), f(\log_e(2)), \dots, f(\log_e(625))$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate both sides using the Newton-Leibniz rule to form $(f(x) \;-\; f'(x))^2 \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives $2 f(x) f'(x) \;=\; (f(x))^2 \;+\; (f'(x))^2 \;\implies\; (f(x) \;-\; f'(x))^2 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; f'(x) \;=\; f(x) \;\implies\; f(x) \;=\; C e^x$. Since $(f(0))^2 \;=\; 25$ and $f \;\ge\; 0$, we have $f(0) \;=\; 5 \;\implies\; f(x) \;=\; 5 e^x$. Thus $f(\log_e k) \;=\; 5k$. The mean for $k \;=\; 1, 2, \dots, 625$ is $\frac{5(1 \;+\; 2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 625)}{625} \;=\; \frac{5 \;\times\; 625 \;\times\; 626}{2 \;\times\; 625} \;=\; 1565$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( x \;+\; y \;+\; 2 \right)^2 dx \;=\; dy$, $y(0) \;=\; -2$. Let the maximum and minimum values of the function $y \;=\; y(x)$ in $\left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{3} \right]$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$, respectively. If $\left( 3\alpha \;+\; \pi \right)^2 \;+\; \beta^2 \;=\; \gamma \;+\; \delta \sqrt{3}$, $\gamma, \delta \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$, then $\gamma \;+\; \delta$ equals ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \;+\; y \;+\; 2 \;=\; v$ to reduce the differential equation to a variable separable form. // 📝 Solution: Let $x \;+\; y \;+\; 2 \;=\; v \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; \frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{dv}{dx}$. The equation becomes $\frac{dv}{dx} \;=\; 1 \;+\; v^2 \;\implies\; \int \frac{dv}{1 \;+\; v^2} \;=\; \int dx \;\implies\; \tan^{-1}(x \;+\; y \;+\; 2) \;=\; x \;+\; C$. Since $y(0) \;=\; -2 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$, so $y(x) \;=\; \tan x \;-\; x \;-\; 2$. For $x \;\in\; \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{3} \right]$, $y'(x) \;=\; \sec^2 x \;-\; 1 \;\ge\; 0$, so $y(x)$ is increasing. Thus $\beta \;=\; y(0) \;=\; -2$ and $\alpha \;=\; y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; \sqrt{3} \;-\; \frac{\pi}{3} \;-\; 2$. Now $\left( 3\alpha \;+\; \pi \right)^2 \;+\; \beta^2 \;=\; \left( 3\sqrt{3} \;-\; 6 \right)^2 \;+\; 4 \;=\; 67 \;-\; 36\sqrt{3}$. Hence $\gamma \;=\; 67$ and $\delta \;=\; -36$, giving $\gamma \;+\; \delta \;=\; 31$.

questions.text: If $x \;=\; x(t)$ is the solution of the differential equation $(t \;+\; 1) dx \;=\; \left( 2x \;+\; (t \;+\; 1)^4 \right) dt$, $x(0) \;=\; 2$, then, $x(1)$ equals
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite as a linear differential equation in $x(t)$: $\frac{dx}{dt} \;-\; \frac{2}{t \;+\; 1} x \;=\; (t \;+\; 1)^3$. // 📝 Solution: Rearranging gives $\frac{dx}{dt} \;-\; \frac{2x}{t \;+\; 1} \;=\; (t \;+\; 1)^3$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-\int \frac{2}{t + 1} \, dt} \;=\; \frac{1}{(t \;+\; 1)^2}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $\frac{x}{(t \;+\; 1)^2} \;=\; \int (t \;+\; 1) \, dt \;=\; \frac{(t \;+\; 1)^2}{2} \;+\; C$. Using $x(0) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; 2 \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$. Thus $x(t) \;=\; \frac{(t \;+\; 1)^4}{2} \;+\; \frac{3}{2} (t \;+\; 1)^2$. Putting $t \;=\; 1$, we get $x(1) \;=\; 8 \;+\; 6 \;=\; 14$.

questions.text: Let the solution curve of the differential equation $x \, dy \;-\; y \, dx \;=\; \sqrt{x^2 \;+\; y^2} \, dx$, $x \;>\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; 0$, be $y \;=\; y(x)$. Then $y(3)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Put $y \;=\; vx$ in the homogeneous equation to get $\frac{dv}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; v^2}} \;=\; \frac{dx}{x}$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $y \;=\; vx$ gives $x^2 \, dv \;=\; x\sqrt{1 \;+\; v^2} \, dx \;\implies\; \int \frac{dv}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; v^2}} \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{x} \;\implies\; \ln\left( v \;+\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; v^2} \right) \;=\; \ln x \;+\; C$. Since $y(1) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; v \;=\; 0$ at $x \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Thus $v \;+\; \sqrt{1 \;+\; v^2} \;=\; x \;\implies\; y \;+\; \sqrt{x^2 \;+\; y^2} \;=\; x^2$. At $x \;=\; 3$, $y \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; y^2} \;=\; 9 \;\implies\; 9 \;+\; y^2 \;=\; (9 \;-\; y)^2 \;\implies\; 18y \;=\; 72 \;\implies\; y(3) \;=\; 4$.

questions.text: Let the solution $y \;=\; y(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; y \;=\; 1 \;+\; 4 \sin x$ satisfy $y(\pi) \;=\; 1$. Then $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;+\; 10$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: This is a first-order linear differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; P(x)y \;=\; Q(x)$ with integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-x}$. // 📝 Solution: The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int -1 \, dx} \;=\; e^{-x}$. Multiplying by $e^{-x}$ and integrating gives $y e^{-x} \;=\; \int e^{-x} \left( 1 \;+\; 4 \sin x \right) dx \;=\; -e^{-x} \;-\; 2 e^{-x} \left( \sin x \;+\; \cos x \right) \;+\; C$, so $y \;=\; -1 \;-\; 2 \left( \sin x \;+\; \cos x \right) \;+\; C e^x$. Since $y(\pi) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; 1 \;=\; -1 \;-\; 2(0 \;-\; 1) \;+\; C e^\pi \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Now, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; -1 \;-\; 2(1 \;+\; 0) \;=\; -3$. Therefore, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;+\; 10 \;=\; -3 \;+\; 10 \;=\; 7$.

questions.text: The solution curve, of the differential equation $2y \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; 3 \;=\; 5 \frac{dy}{dx}$, passing through the point $(0, 1)$ is a conic, whose vertex lies on the line:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables as $(2y \;-\; 5) dy \;=\; -3 \, dx$ and integrate to find the equation of the parabola. // 📝 Solution: Rearranging gives $(2y \;-\; 5) dy \;=\; -3 \, dx$. Integrating both sides yields $y^2 \;-\; 5y \;=\; -3x \;+\; \lambda$. Since the curve passes through $(0, 1)$, we get $1 \;-\; 5 \;=\; \lambda \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; -4$. Completing the square gives $\left( y \;-\; \frac{5}{2} \right)^2 \;=\; -3\left( x \;-\; \frac{3}{4} \right)$, whose vertex is $\left( \frac{3}{4}, \frac{5}{2} \right)$. Substituting into $2x \;+\; 3y$ gives $2\left( \frac{3}{4} \right) \;+\; 3\left( \frac{5}{2} \right) \;=\; 9$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x^3 \, dy \;+\; (xy \;-\; 1) dx \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 0$, $y\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \;=\; 3 \;-\; e$. Then $y(1)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{x^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{x^3}$ with integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-1/x}$. // 📝 Solution: The equation is $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{x^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{x^3}$, with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx} \;=\; e^{-1/x}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating with $-\frac{1}{x} \;=\; t$ gives $y e^{-1/x} \;=\; \int \frac{1}{x^3} e^{-1/x} \, dx \;=\; -\int t e^t \, dt \;=\; e^{-1/x} \left( \frac{1}{x} \;+\; 1 \right) \;+\; C \;\implies\; y \;=\; \frac{1}{x} \;+\; 1 \;+\; C e^{1/x}$. Using $y\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \;=\; 3 \;-\; e \;\implies\; 3 \;-\; e \;=\; 3 \;+\; C e^2 \;\implies\; C \;=\; -\frac{1}{e}$. At $x \;=\; 1$, $y(1) \;=\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 1$.

questions.text: Let $x \;=\; x(t)$ and $y \;=\; y(t)$ be solutions of the differential equations $\frac{dx}{dt} \;+\; ax \;=\; 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} \;+\; by \;=\; 0$ respectively, $a, b \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Given that $x(0) \;=\; 2$; $y(0) \;=\; 1$ and $3y(1) \;=\; 2x(1)$, the value of $t$, for which $x(t) \;=\; y(t)$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve both separable differential equations to get $x(t) \;=\; 2e^{-at}$ and $y(t) \;=\; e^{-bt}$. // 📝 Solution: Solving $\frac{dx}{dt} \;+\; ax \;=\; 0$ with $x(0) \;=\; 2$ gives $x(t) \;=\; 2e^{-at}$. Solving $\frac{dy}{dt} \;+\; by \;=\; 0$ with $y(0) \;=\; 1$ gives $y(t) \;=\; e^{-bt}$. Given $3y(1) \;=\; 2x(1) \;\implies\; 3e^{-b} \;=\; 4e^{-a} \;\implies\; e^{a - b} \;=\; \frac{4}{3}$. For $x(t) \;=\; y(t)$, we have $2e^{-at} \;=\; e^{-bt} \;\implies\; e^{(a - b)t} \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \left( \frac{4}{3} \right)^t \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; t \;=\; \log_{\frac{4}{3}} 2$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; 2x(x \;+\; y)^3 \;-\; x(x \;+\; y) \;-\; 1$, $y(0) \;=\; 1$. Then, $\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \;+\; y\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \right)^2$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \;+\; y \;=\; t$ and then $t^2 \;=\; z$ to reduce the equation to variable separable form. // 📝 Solution: Let $x \;+\; y \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dt}{dx} \;-\; 1 \;=\; 2xt^3 \;-\; xt \;-\; 1 \;\implies\; \frac{dt}{2t^3 \;-\; t} \;=\; x \, dx \;\implies\; \frac{t \, dt}{2t^4 \;-\; t^2} \;=\; x \, dx$. Let $t^2 \;=\; z \;\implies\; \int \frac{dz}{2\left( 2z^2 \;-\; z \right)} \;=\; \int x \, dx \;\implies\; \frac{1}{2} \ln\left\lvert \frac{2z \;-\; 1}{z} \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{x^2}{2} \;+\; C$. At $x \;=\; 0, y \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; z \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Thus $2 \;-\; \frac{1}{z} \;=\; e^{x^2}$. For $x \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, we get $2 \;-\; \frac{1}{z} \;=\; \sqrt{e} \;\implies\; z \;=\; \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \;+\; y\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \right)^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{2 \;-\; \sqrt{e}}$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(t)$ be a solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dt} \;+\; \alpha y \;=\; \gamma e^{-\beta t}$ where, $\alpha \;>\; 0$, $\beta \;>\; 0$ and $\gamma \;>\; 0$. Then $\lim_{t \to \infty} y(t)$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the linear differential equation using $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\alpha t}$ and take the limit as $t \;\to\; \infty$. // 📝 Solution: Multiplying by $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\alpha t}$ and integrating (for $\alpha \;\neq\; \beta$) gives $y(t) e^{\alpha t} \;=\; \frac{\gamma}{\alpha \;-\; \beta} e^{(\alpha - \beta)t} \;+\; C \;\implies\; y(t) \;=\; \frac{\gamma}{\alpha \;-\; \beta} e^{-\beta t} \;+\; C e^{-\alpha t}$ (and if $\alpha \;=\; \beta$, $y(t) \;=\; (\gamma t \;+\; C)e^{-\alpha t}$). Since $\alpha \;>\; 0$ and $\beta \;>\; 0$, as $t \;\to\; \infty$, both $e^{-\beta t} \;\to\; 0$ and $e^{-\alpha t} \;\to\; 0$. Hence, $\lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( x^2 \;-\; 3y^2 \right) dx \;+\; 3xy \, dy \;=\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; 1$. Then $6y^2(e)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Put $y \;=\; vx$ in the homogeneous differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{3y^2 \;-\; x^2}{3xy}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $y \;=\; vx \;\implies\; v \;+\; x \frac{dv}{dx} \;=\; v \;-\; \frac{1}{3v} \;\implies\; \int v \, dv \;=\; -\frac{1}{3} \int \frac{dx}{x}$. Integrating gives $\frac{y^2}{2x^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{3} \ln x \;+\; C$. Since $y(1) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. At $x \;=\; e$, $\frac{y^2(e)}{2e^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{3} \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{6} \;\implies\; 6y^2(e) \;=\; 2e^2$.

questions.text: If $\sin\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \log_e \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; \frac{\alpha}{2}$ is the solution of the differential equation $x \cos\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; y \cos\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;+\; x$ and $y(1) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{3}$, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rearrange the homogeneous equation to form $\cos\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) d\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \frac{dx}{x}$. // 📝 Solution: Rearranging gives $\cos\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \left( \frac{x \, dy \;-\; y \, dx}{x^2} \right) \;=\; \frac{dx}{x} \;\implies\; \cos\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) d\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \frac{dx}{x}$. Integrating both sides yields $\sin\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{3} \;\implies\; \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; 0 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Comparing with $\frac{\alpha}{2} \;=\; C$, we get $\alpha \;=\; \sqrt{3} \;\implies\; \alpha^2 \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: If $y \;=\; y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; 2y \;=\; \sin(2x)$, $y(0) \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$, then $y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{2x}$ and use the standard formula $\int e^{ax} \sin(bx) \, dx \;=\; \frac{e^{ax}}{a^2 \;+\; b^2} \left( a \sin bx \;-\; b \cos bx \right)$. // 📝 Solution: The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int 2 \, dx} \;=\; e^{2x}$. Multiplying by $e^{2x}$ and integrating gives $y e^{2x} \;=\; \int e^{2x} \sin(2x) \, dx \;=\; \frac{e^{2x} \left( 2 \sin 2x \;-\; 2 \cos 2x \right)}{8} \;+\; C$. Using $y(0) \;=\; \frac{3}{4} \;\implies\; \frac{3}{4} \;=\; -\frac{1}{4} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 1$. Thus, $y(x) \;=\; \frac{\sin 2x \;-\; \cos 2x}{4} \;+\; e^{-2x}$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{8}$, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) \;=\; \frac{\sin\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;-\; \cos\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}{4} \;+\; e^{-\pi/4} \;=\; e^{-\pi/4}$.

questions.text: If the solution of the differential equation $(2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 2) dx \;+\; (4x \;+\; 6y \;-\; 7) dy \;=\; 0$, $y(0) \;=\; 3$, is $\alpha x \;+\; \beta y \;+\; 3 \log_e \left\lvert 2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; \gamma \right\rvert \;=\; 6$, then $\alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;+\; 3\gamma$ is equal to _____
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 2 \;=\; t$ to reduce the equation to variable separable form. // 📝 Solution: Let $2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 2 \;=\; t \;\implies\; 2 \;+\; 3 \frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{dt}{dx}$. Since $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; -\frac{t}{2t \;-\; 3}$, we get $\frac{dt}{dx} \;=\; 2 \;-\; \frac{3t}{2t \;-\; 3} \;=\; \frac{t \;-\; 6}{2t \;-\; 3}$. Separating variables gives $\int \frac{2t \;-\; 3}{t \;-\; 6} \, dt \;=\; \int dx \;\implies\; 2t \;+\; 9 \ln\left\lvert t \;-\; 6 \right\rvert \;=\; x \;+\; C \;\implies\; 2(2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 2) \;+\; 9 \ln\left\lvert 2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 8 \right\rvert \;=\; x \;+\; C$. Using $y(0) \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 14$. Simplifying and dividing by $3$ gives $x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 3 \ln\left\lvert 2x \;+\; 3y \;-\; 8 \right\rvert \;=\; 6$. Thus $\alpha \;=\; 1, \beta \;=\; 2, \gamma \;=\; 8 \;\implies\; \alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;+\; 3\gamma \;=\; 29$.

questions.text: If the solution $y(x)$ of the given differential equation $\left( e^y \;+\; 1 \right) \cos x \, dx \;+\; e^y \sin x \, dy \;=\; 0$ passes through the point $\left( \frac{\pi}{2}, 0 \right)$, then the value of $e^{y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}$ is equal to _________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Notice that the left-hand side is the exact differential $d\left( \left( e^y \;+\; 1 \right) \sin x \right) \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: The given equation can be written as $d\left( \left( e^y \;+\; 1 \right) \sin x \right) \;=\; 0$. Integrating both sides gives $\left( e^y \;+\; 1 \right) \sin x \;=\; C$. Since it passes through $\left( \frac{\pi}{2}, 0 \right)$, we have $(1 \;+\; 1)(1) \;=\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6}$, $\left( e^{y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \;+\; 1 \right) \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; e^{y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \;+\; 1 \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; e^{y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: The temperature $T(t)$ of a body at time $t \;=\; 0$ is $160^\circ\text{F}$ and it decreases continuously as per the differential equation $\frac{dT}{dt} \;=\; -K(T \;-\; 80)$, where $K$ is positive constant. If $T(15) \;=\; 120^\circ\text{F}$, then $T(45)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables to integrate Newton's Law of Cooling: $\int_{160}^{T} \frac{dT}{T \;-\; 80} \;=\; -K \int_{0}^{t} dt$. // 📝 Solution: Integrating $\frac{dT}{T \;-\; 80} \;=\; -K \, dt$ with $T(0) \;=\; 160$ gives $T(t) \;-\; 80 \;=\; 80 e^{-Kt}$. Given $T(15) \;=\; 120 \;\implies\; 40 \;=\; 80 e^{-15K} \;\implies\; e^{-15K} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. For $t \;=\; 45$, $T(45) \;=\; 80 \;+\; 80 e^{-45K} \;=\; 80 \;+\; 80\left( e^{-15K} \right)^3 \;=\; 80 \;+\; 80\left( \frac{1}{8} \right) \;=\; 90^\circ\text{F}$.

questions.text: If $y \;=\; y(x)$ is the solution curve of the differential equation $\left( x^2 \;-\; 4 \right) dy \;-\; \left( y^2 \;-\; 3y \right) dx \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 2$, $y(4) \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$ and the slope of the curve is never zero, then the value of $y(10)$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables and use partial fractions to integrate $\frac{dy}{y(y \;-\; 3)} \;=\; \frac{dx}{x^2 \;-\; 4}$. // 📝 Solution: Separating variables gives $\int \frac{dy}{y(y \;-\; 3)} \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{x^2 \;-\; 4} \;\implies\; \frac{1}{3} \ln\left\lvert \frac{y \;-\; 3}{y} \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln\left\lvert \frac{x \;-\; 2}{x \;+\; 2} \right\rvert \;+\; C$. At $x \;=\; 4, y \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$, we get $0 \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln 3$. At $x \;=\; 10$, $\frac{1}{3} \ln\left\lvert \frac{y \;-\; 3}{y} \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \;+\; \frac{1}{4} \ln 3 \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln 2 \;\implies\; \left\lvert \frac{y \;-\; 3}{y} \right\rvert \;=\; 8^{1/4}$. Since $y(4) \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$ and slope is never zero, $y \;\in\; (0, 3)$, so $\frac{3 \;-\; y}{y} \;=\; 8^{1/4} \;\implies\; y(10) \;=\; \frac{3}{1 \;+\; (8)^{1/4}}$.

💡 Hint: Write the equation in standard linear form with respect to $x$: $\frac{dx}{dy} \;-\; \frac{x}{y} \;=\; \frac{1 \;-\; y^2}{y}$. // 📝 Solution: Rearranging gives $\frac{dx}{dy} \;-\; \frac{x}{y} \;=\; \frac{1 \;-\; y^2}{y}$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int -\frac{1}{y} \, dy} \;=\; \frac{1}{y}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $\frac{x}{y} \;=\; \int \frac{1 \;-\; y^2}{y^2} \, dy \;=\; -\frac{1}{y} \;-\; y \;+\; C \;\implies\; x \;=\; -1 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; Cy$. Given $x(1) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; 1 \;=\; -1 \;-\; 1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 3$. Thus $x(y) \;=\; -1 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 3y$. At $y \;=\; 2$, $5x(2) \;=\; 5(-1 \;-\; 4 \;+\; 6) \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{y}{x} \left( 1 \;+\; xy^2 \left( 1 \;+\; \log_e x \right) \right)$, $x \;>\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; 3$. Then $\frac{y^2(x)}{9}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $y^3$ and substitute $-\frac{1}{y^2} \;=\; t$ to convert this Bernoulli equation into a linear ODE. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $y^3$ gives $\frac{1}{y^3} \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \frac{1}{xy^2} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \log_e x$. Let $-\frac{1}{y^2} \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dt}{dx} \;+\; \frac{2t}{x} \;=\; 2\left( 1 \;+\; \log_e x \right)$, with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; x^2$. Integrating gives $-\frac{x^2}{y^2} \;=\; \int 2x^2\left( 1 \;+\; \log_e x \right) dx \;=\; \frac{2}{3} x^3\left( 1 \;+\; \log_e x \right) \;-\; \frac{2}{9} x^3 \;+\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; -\frac{1}{9} \;=\; \frac{4}{9} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; -\frac{5}{9}$. Rearranging gives $\frac{y^2(x)}{9} \;=\; \frac{x^2}{5 \;-\; 2x^3\left( 2 \;+\; \log_e x^3 \right)}$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha x \;=\; \exp\left( x^\beta y^\gamma \right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $2x^2 y \, dy \;-\; \left( 1 \;-\; xy^2 \right) dx \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 0$, $y(2) \;=\; \sqrt{\log_e 2}$. Then $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;-\; \gamma$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $y^2 \;=\; t$ to convert this Bernoulli equation into a linear differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting as $2y \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y^2}{x} \;=\; \frac{1}{x^2}$ and putting $y^2 \;=\; t$ gives $\frac{dt}{dx} \;+\; \frac{t}{x} \;=\; \frac{1}{x^2}$, with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; x$. Integrating gives $x y^2 \;=\; \int \frac{1}{x} \, dx \;=\; \ln x \;+\; C$. Using $y(2) \;=\; \sqrt{\ln 2} \;\implies\; 2 \ln 2 \;=\; \ln 2 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \ln 2$. Thus $x y^2 \;=\; \ln(2x) \;\implies\; 2x \;=\; \exp\left( x y^2 \right)$. Comparing with $\alpha x \;=\; \exp\left( x^\beta y^\gamma \right)$ gives $\alpha \;=\; 2, \beta \;=\; 1, \gamma \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \alpha \;+\; \beta \;-\; \gamma \;=\; 1$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{2x}{\left( 1 \;+\; x^2 \right)^2} y \;=\; x e^{\frac{1}{1 + x^2}}$; $y(0) \;=\; 0$. Then the area enclosed by the curve $f(x) \;=\; y(x) e^{-\frac{1}{1 + x^2}}$ and the line $y \;-\; x \;=\; 4$ is __________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the linear differential equation to find $f(x) \;=\; \frac{x^2}{2}$, and then integrate to find the area bounded by the parabola and the line. // 📝 Solution: The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{2x}{\left( 1 + x^2 \right)^2} \, dx} \;=\; e^{-\frac{1}{1 + x^2}}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $y(x) e^{-\frac{1}{1 + x^2}} \;=\; \int x e^{\frac{1}{1 + x^2}} \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{1 + x^2}} \, dx \;=\; \frac{x^2}{2} \;+\; C$. Since $y(0) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$, we have $f(x) \;=\; \frac{x^2}{2}$. [FIGURE] Solving $\frac{x^2}{2} \;=\; x \;+\; 4$ gives $x \;=\; -2, 4$. The enclosed area is $A \;=\; \int_{-2}^{4} \left( x \;+\; 4 \;-\; \frac{x^2}{2} \right) dx \;=\; 18$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha$ be a non-zero real number. Suppose $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable function such that $f(0) \;=\; 2$ and $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) \;=\; 1$. If $f'(x) \;=\; \alpha f(x) \;+\; 3$, for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, then $f\left( -\log_e 2 \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the linear differential equation $f'(x) \;-\; \alpha f(x) \;=\; 3$ using integrating factor $e^{-\alpha x}$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting as $f'(x) \;-\; \alpha f(x) \;=\; 3$, the integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-\alpha x}$. Integrating gives $f(x) e^{-\alpha x} \;=\; \int 3 e^{-\alpha x} \, dx \;=\; -\frac{3}{\alpha} e^{-\alpha x} \;+\; C \;\implies\; f(x) \;=\; -\frac{3}{\alpha} \;+\; C e^{\alpha x}$. Since $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) \;=\; 1$ (with $\alpha \;>\; 0$ wait: if $f(0) \;=\; 2$ and limit is $1$, $-\frac{3}{\alpha} \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; -3$, and from $f(0) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; C \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 1$, giving $f(x) \;=\; 1 \;+\; e^{-3x}$). Then $f\left( -\log_e 2 \right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; e^{3\log_e 2} \;=\; 1 \;+\; 8 \;=\; 9$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{(\tan x) \;+\; y}{\sin x (\sec x \;-\; \sin x \tan x)}$, $x \;\in\; \left( 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ satisfying the condition $y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; 2$. Then, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Simplify $\sin x(\sec x \;-\; \sin x \tan x) \;=\; \sin x \cos x$ to get a linear differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Since $\sec x \;-\; \sin x \tan x \;=\; \cos x$, the equation simplifies to $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \left( \frac{1}{\sin x \cos x} \right) y \;=\; \sec^2 x$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-\int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \, dx} \;=\; \frac{1}{\tan x}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $\frac{y}{\tan x} \;=\; \int \frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \, dx \;=\; \ln(\tan x) \;+\; C$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}, y \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{3}$, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; \sqrt{3}\left( 2 \;+\; \log_e \sqrt{3} \right)$.

questions.text: The solution curve of the differential equation $y \frac{dx}{dy} \;=\; x \left( \log_e x \;-\; \log_e y \;+\; 1 \right)$, $x \;>\; 0, y \;>\; 0$ passing through the point $(e, 1)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \;=\; ty$ in the homogeneous equation $\frac{dx}{dy} \;=\; \frac{x}{y} \left( \ln\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) \;+\; 1 \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Let $\frac{x}{y} \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dx}{dy} \;=\; t \;+\; y \frac{dt}{dy}$. The equation becomes $t \;+\; y \frac{dt}{dy} \;=\; t(\ln t \;+\; 1) \;\implies\; \int \frac{dt}{t \ln t} \;=\; \int \frac{dy}{y}$. Integrating gives $\ln\left\lvert \ln t \right\rvert \;=\; \ln y \;+\; C \;\implies\; \left\lvert \ln\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) \right\rvert \;=\; k y$. Since it passes through $(e, 1)$, we have $\left\lvert \ln e \right\rvert \;=\; k(1) \;\implies\; k \;=\; 1$. Therefore, $\left\lvert \log_e \frac{x}{y} \right\rvert \;=\; y$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be a differentiable function in the interval $(0, \infty)$ such that $y(1) \;=\; 2$, and $\lim_{t \to x} \left( \frac{t^2 y(x) \;-\; x^2 y(t)}{x \;-\; t} \right) \;=\; 3$ for each $x \;>\; 0$. Then $2y(2)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply L'Hôpital's rule with respect to $t$ to obtain the differential equation $x^2 y'(x) \;-\; 2x y(x) \;=\; 3$. // 📝 Solution: Applying L'Hôpital's rule with respect to $t$ gives $\lim_{t \to x} \frac{2t y(x) \;-\; x^2 y'(t)}{-1} \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; x^2 y'(x) \;-\; 2x y(x) \;=\; 3$. Dividing by $x^4$ gives $\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y(x)}{x^2} \right) \;=\; \frac{3}{x^4}$. Integrating yields $\frac{y(x)}{x^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{x^3} \;+\; C$. Since $y(1) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; 2 \;=\; -1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 3$, so $y(x) \;=\; -\frac{1}{x} \;+\; 3x^2$. For $x \;=\; 2$, $y(2) \;=\; -\frac{1}{2} \;+\; 12 \;=\; \frac{23}{2} \;\implies\; 2y(2) \;=\; 23$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( 3y^2 \;-\; 5x^2 \right) y \, dx \;+\; 2x\left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \right) dy \;=\; 0$ such that $y(1) \;=\; 1$. Then $\left\lvert (y(2))^3 \;-\; 12y(2) \right\rvert$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $y \;=\; mx$ in the homogeneous equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{y\left( 5x^2 \;-\; 3y^2 \right)}{2x\left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \right)}$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $y \;=\; mx$ gives $x \frac{dm}{dx} \;=\; \frac{m\left( 3 \;-\; m^2 \right)}{2\left( 1 \;-\; m^2 \right)} \;\implies\; \int \frac{dx}{x} \;=\; \int \left( \frac{2}{3m} \;+\; \frac{4m}{3\left( m^2 \;-\; 3 \right)} \right) dm$. Integrating gives $\ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{2}{3} \ln\left\lvert m \right\rvert \;+\; \frac{2}{3} \ln\left\lvert m^2 \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; -\frac{2}{3} \ln 2$, so $\left\lvert \left( \frac{y}{x} \right)^3 \;-\; 3\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \right\rvert \;=\; 2 x^{3/2}$. At $x \;=\; 2$, $\left\lvert \frac{y^3(2)}{8} \;-\; \frac{3y(2)}{2} \right\rvert \;=\; 4\sqrt{2} \;\implies\; \left\lvert (y(2))^3 \;-\; 12y(2) \right\rvert \;=\; 32\sqrt{2}$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha \left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert y \right\rvert e^{xy - \beta}$, $\alpha, \beta \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ be the solution of the differential equation $x \, dy \;-\; y \, dx \;+\; xy(x \, dy \;+\; y \, dx) \;=\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; 2$. Then $\alpha \;+\; \beta$ is equal to ________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide the equation by $xy$ to form exact differentials $\frac{dy}{y} \;-\; \frac{dx}{x} \;+\; d(xy) \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $xy$ gives $\frac{dy}{y} \;-\; \frac{dx}{x} \;+\; (x \, dy \;+\; y \, dx) \;=\; 0$. Integrating both sides yields $\ln\left\lvert y \right\rvert \;-\; \ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; xy \;=\; C$. Since $y(1) \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \ln 2 \;-\; 0 \;+\; 2 \;=\; C$. Thus $\ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \ln\left\lvert \frac{y}{2} \right\rvert \;+\; xy \;-\; 2 \;\implies\; 2\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert y \right\rvert e^{xy - 2}$. Comparing with $\alpha\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert y \right\rvert e^{xy - \beta}$, we get $\alpha \;=\; 2, \beta \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; \alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; 4$.

questions.text: The solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; -\left( \frac{x^2 \;+\; 3y^2}{3x^2 \;+\; y^2} \right)$, $y(1) \;=\; 0$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Put $y \;=\; vx$ in the homogeneous differential equation and use partial fractions to integrate $\frac{3 \;+\; v^2}{(v \;+\; 1)^3} \, dv \;+\; \frac{dx}{x} \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $y \;=\; vx$ gives $x \frac{dv}{dx} \;=\; -\frac{(v \;+\; 1)^3}{3 \;+\; v^2} \;\implies\; \int \left( \frac{1}{v \;+\; 1} \;-\; \frac{2}{(v \;+\; 1)^2} \;+\; \frac{4}{(v \;+\; 1)^3} \right) dv \;+\; \int \frac{dx}{x} \;=\; 0$. Integrating yields $\ln\left\lvert v \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; \frac{2}{v \;+\; 1} \;-\; \frac{2}{(v \;+\; 1)^2} \;+\; \ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;=\; C \;\implies\; \ln\left\lvert x \;+\; y \right\rvert \;+\; \frac{2xy}{(x \;+\; y)^2} \;=\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$, giving $\log_e \left\lvert x \;+\; y \right\rvert \;+\; \frac{2xy}{(x \;+\; y)^2} \;=\; 0$.

questions.text: Let $f : [1, \infty) \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function. If $6 \int_{1}^{x} f(t) \, dt \;=\; 3x f(x) \;+\; x^3 \;-\; 4$ for all $x \;\ge\; 1$, then the value of $f(2) \;-\; f(3)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ to form a linear differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Differentiating both sides gives $6f(x) \;=\; 3f(x) \;+\; 3x f'(x) \;+\; 3x^2 \;\implies\; \frac{x f'(x) \;-\; f(x)}{x^2} \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{f(x)}{x} \right) \;=\; -1$. Integrating gives $\frac{f(x)}{x} \;=\; -x \;+\; C \;\implies\; f(x) \;=\; -x^2 \;+\; Cx$. Putting $x \;=\; 1$ in the original equation gives $0 \;=\; 3f(1) \;-\; 3 \;\implies\; f(1) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2$. Thus $f(x) \;=\; -x^2 \;+\; 2x$, so $f(2) \;-\; f(3) \;=\; 0 \;-\; (-3) \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( 1 \;+\; y^2 \right) e^{\tan x} dx \;+\; \cos^2 x \left( 1 \;+\; e^{2\tan x} \right) dy \;=\; 0$, $y(0) \;=\; 1$. Then $y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables and substitute $u \;=\; e^{\tan x}$ to integrate with respect to $x$. // 📝 Solution: Separating variables gives $\int \frac{\sec^2 x \, e^{\tan x}}{1 \;+\; e^{2\tan x}} \, dx \;+\; \int \frac{dy}{1 \;+\; y^2} \;=\; C \;\implies\; \tan^{-1}\left( e^{\tan x} \right) \;+\; \tan^{-1} y \;=\; C$. For $x \;=\; 0, y \;=\; 1$, $\tan^{-1}(1) \;+\; \tan^{-1}(1) \;=\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}$, $\tan^{-1}(e) \;+\; \tan^{-1} y \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;\implies\; \tan^{-1} y \;=\; \cot^{-1}(e) \;\implies\; y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; \frac{1}{e}$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( 2x \log_e x \right) \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; 2y \;=\; \frac{3}{x} \log_e x$, $x \;>\; 0$ and $y\left( e^{-1} \right) \;=\; 0$. Then, $y(e)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $2x \log_e x$ to get a linear differential equation with integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \log_e x$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $2x \log_e x$ gives $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{x \log_e x} \;=\; \frac{3}{2x^2}$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{dx}{x \log_e x}} \;=\; \log_e x$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating by parts gives $y \log_e x \;=\; \int \frac{3 \log_e x}{2x^2} \, dx \;=\; -\frac{3 \log_e x}{2x} \;-\; \frac{3}{2x} \;+\; C$. Using $y\left( e^{-1} \right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;=\; \frac{3e}{2} \;-\; \frac{3e}{2} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; e$, $y(e) \;=\; -\frac{3}{2e} \;-\; \frac{3}{2e} \;=\; -\frac{3}{e}$.

questions.text: The solution of the differential equation $\left( x^2 \;+\; y^2 \right) dx \;-\; 5xy \, dy \;=\; 0$, $y(1) \;=\; 0$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: This is a homogeneous differential equation; substitute $y \;=\; vx$ and separate variables. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; y^2}{5xy}$ and putting $y \;=\; vx$ gives $v \;+\; x \frac{dv}{dx} \;=\; \frac{1 \;+\; v^2}{5v} \;\implies\; \int \frac{v}{1 \;-\; 4v^2} \, dv \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{5x}$. Integrating gives $-\frac{1}{8} \ln\left\lvert 1 \;-\; 4v^2 \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{5} \ln\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; \ln C \;\implies\; x^8 \left\lvert 1 \;-\; \frac{4y^2}{x^2} \right\rvert^5 \;=\; K \;\implies\; \left\lvert x^2 \;-\; 4y^2 \right\rvert^5 \;=\; K x^2$. Given $y(1) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; K \;=\; 1$, so $\left\lvert x^2 \;-\; 4y^2 \right\rvert^5 \;=\; x^2$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\left( 1 \;+\; x^2 \right) dy \;+\; \left( y \;-\; \tan^{-1} x \right) dx \;=\; 0$, $y(0) \;=\; 1$. Then the value of $y(1)$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;=\; \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{1 \;+\; x^2}$ with integrating factor $e^{\tan^{-1} x}$. // 📝 Solution: With $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\tan^{-1} x}$, multiplying and integrating gives $y e^{\tan^{-1} x} \;=\; \int \frac{\tan^{-1} x}{1 \;+\; x^2} e^{\tan^{-1} x} \, dx \;=\; e^{\tan^{-1} x} \left( \tan^{-1} x \;-\; 1 \right) \;+\; C \;\implies\; y \;=\; \tan^{-1} x \;-\; 1 \;+\; C e^{-\tan^{-1} x}$. Using $y(0) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; 1 \;=\; -1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 2$. At $x \;=\; 1$, $y(1) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;-\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{e^{\pi/4}}$.

questions.text: If the solution curve $y \;=\; y(x)$ of the differential equation $\left( 1 \;+\; y^2 \right)\left( 1 \;+\; \log_e x \right) dx \;+\; x \, dy \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 0$ passes through the point $(1, 1)$ and $y(e) \;=\; \frac{\alpha \;-\; \tan\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)}{\beta \;+\; \tan\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)}$, then $\alpha \;+\; 2\beta$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables as $\left( \frac{1 \;+\; \log_e x}{x} \right) dx \;+\; \frac{dy}{1 \;+\; y^2} \;=\; 0$ and integrate directly. // 📝 Solution: Separating variables and integrating gives $\int \left( \frac{1}{x} \;+\; \frac{\ln x}{x} \right) dx \;+\; \int \frac{dy}{1 \;+\; y^2} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \ln x \;+\; \frac{(\ln x)^2}{2} \;+\; \tan^{-1} y \;=\; C$. At $(1, 1)$, $0 \;+\; 0 \;+\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;=\; C$. At $x \;=\; e$, $1 \;+\; \frac{1}{2} \;+\; \tan^{-1} y(e) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;\implies\; y(e) \;=\; \tan\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \;-\; \frac{3}{2} \right) \;=\; \frac{1 \;-\; \tan\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)}{1 \;+\; \tan\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)}$. Comparing gives $\alpha \;=\; 1, \beta \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \alpha \;+\; 2\beta \;=\; 3$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; y \;=\; x^2 \cot x$, $x \;\in\; (0, \pi)$. If $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, then $6y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;-\; 8y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $x^2$ to form $\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \cot x$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $x^2$ gives $\frac{x \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; y}{x^2} \;=\; \cot x \;\implies\; \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \;=\; \cot x$. Integrating yields $\frac{y}{x} \;=\; \ln\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Using $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;\implies\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;+\; C \;\implies\; y(x) \;=\; x(1 \;+\; \ln(\sin x))$. Now $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6}(1 \;-\; \ln 2)$ and $y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}\left( 1 \;-\; \frac{\ln 2}{2} \right)$. Thus $6y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;-\; 8y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \;=\; \pi(1 \;-\; \ln 2) \;-\; 2\pi\left( 1 \;-\; \frac{\ln 2}{2} \right) \;=\; -\pi$.

questions.text: A function $y \;=\; f(x)$ satisfies $f(x) \sin 2x \;+\; \sin x \;-\; \left( 1 \;+\; \cos^2 x \right) f'(x) \;=\; 0$ with condition $f(0) \;=\; 0$. Then $f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite as a linear differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \left( \frac{\sin 2x}{1 \;+\; \cos^2 x} \right) y \;=\; \frac{\sin x}{1 \;+\; \cos^2 x}$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $1 \;+\; \cos^2 x$ gives $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \left( \frac{2 \sin x \cos x}{1 \;+\; \cos^2 x} \right) y \;=\; \frac{\sin x}{1 \;+\; \cos^2 x}$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{-2\sin x \cos x}{1 + \cos^2 x} \, dx} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \cos^2 x$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $y\left( 1 \;+\; \cos^2 x \right) \;=\; \int \sin x \, dx \;=\; -\cos x \;+\; C$. Using $f(0) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;=\; -1 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 1$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, $f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)(1 \;+\; 0) \;=\; 0 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 1$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x^4 \, dy \;+\; \left( 4x^3 y \;+\; 2 \sin x \right) dx \;=\; 0$, $x \;>\; 0$, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; 0$. Then $\pi^4 y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Group the terms as an exact differential $d\left( x^4 y \right) \;+\; 2 \sin x \, dx \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: The given equation can be written as $d\left( x^4 y \right) \;+\; 2 \sin x \, dx \;=\; 0$. Integrating both sides gives $x^4 y \;-\; 2 \cos x \;=\; C$. Using $y\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;-\; 0 \;=\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Thus $x^4 y \;=\; 2 \cos x$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{3}$, $\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)^4 y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; 2 \cos\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; \pi^4 y\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) \;=\; 3^4 \;=\; 81$.

questions.text: The differential equation of the family of circles passing through the origin and having centre at the line $y \;=\; x$ is :

options.text: $\left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dx \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;-\; 2xy \right) dy$
$\left( x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dx \;=\; \left( x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;-\; 2xy \right) dy$
$\left( x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;-\; 2xy \right) dx \;=\; \left( x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dy$
$\left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dx \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dy$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The equation of a circle passing through the origin with centre $\left( -\frac{g}{2}, -\frac{g}{2} \right)$ on $y \;=\; x$ is $x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;+\; gx \;+\; gy \;=\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Let the family of circles be $x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;+\; gx \;+\; gy \;=\; 0 \quad \text{...(1)}$. Differentiating with respect to $x$: $2x \;+\; 2y y' \;+\; g \;+\; g y' \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; g \;=\; -\frac{2x \;+\; 2y y'}{1 \;+\; y'}$. Substituting $g$ into (1) gives $x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;-\; \left( \frac{2x \;+\; 2y y'}{1 \;+\; y'} \right)(x \;+\; y) \;=\; 0$. Simplifying yields $\left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;-\; 2xy \right) \frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \;\implies\; \left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;+\; 2xy \right) dx \;=\; \left( x^2 \;-\; y^2 \;-\; 2xy \right) dy$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2 dy \;+\; \left( 2x^3 y \;+\; 8xy \;-\; 2 \right) dx \;=\; 0$. If $y(0) \;=\; 0$, then $y(2)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite the equation in the standard linear form $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{2x}{x^2 \;+\; 4} y \;=\; \frac{2}{\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2}$. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2 dx$, we get $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{2x \left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)}{\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2} y \;=\; \frac{2}{\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2} \;\implies\; \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \left( \frac{2x}{x^2 \;+\; 4} \right) y \;=\; \frac{2}{\left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right)^2}$. The integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{2x}{x^2 + 4} \, dx} \;=\; x^2 \;+\; 4$. The solution is $y \left( x^2 \;+\; 4 \right) \;=\; \int \frac{2}{x^2 \;+\; 4} \, dx \;=\; \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{x}{2} \right) \;+\; C$. Using $y(0) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; 2$, $y(2) \cdot (4 \;+\; 4) \;=\; \tan^{-1}(1) \;\implies\; 8 y(2) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;\implies\; y(2) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{32}$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \sin 2y \;=\; x^3 \left( 2 \;-\; x^3 \right) \cos^2 y$, $x \;\neq\; 0$. If $y(2) \;=\; 0$, then $\tan(y(1))$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $\cos^2 y$ and substitute $\tan y \;=\; v$ to get a linear differential equation. // 📝 Solution: Dividing by $\cos^2 y$ gives $x \sec^2 y \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; 2 \tan y \;=\; x^3\left( 2 \;-\; x^3 \right)$. Putting $v \;=\; \tan y$ and dividing by $x^3$ gives $\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{-2} v \right) \;=\; 2 \;-\; x^3$. Integrating yields $x^{-2} \tan y \;=\; 2x \;-\; \frac{x^4}{4} \;+\; C$. Using $y(2) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;=\; 4 \;-\; 4 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Thus $\tan y \;=\; 2x^3 \;-\; \frac{x^6}{4}$, so $\tan(y(1)) \;=\; 2 \;-\; \frac{1}{4} \;=\; \frac{7}{4}$.

questions.text: If the solution curve, of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{x \;+\; y \;-\; 2}{x \;-\; y}$ passing through the point $(2, 1)$ is $\tan^{-1}\left( \frac{y \;-\; 1}{x \;-\; 1} \right) \;-\; \frac{1}{\beta} \log_e \left( \alpha \;+\; \left( \frac{y \;-\; 1}{x \;-\; 1} \right)^2 \right) \;=\; \log_e \left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$, then $5\beta \;+\; \alpha$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Shift the origin to $(1, 1)$ by putting $x \;=\; X \;+\; 1$ and $y \;=\; Y \;+\; 1$ to make the equation homogeneous. // 📝 Solution: Let $x \;=\; X \;+\; 1$ and $y \;=\; Y \;+\; 1 \;\implies\; \frac{dY}{dX} \;=\; \frac{X \;+\; Y}{X \;-\; Y}$. Putting $Y \;=\; vX$ gives $v \;+\; X \frac{dv}{dX} \;=\; \frac{1 \;+\; v}{1 \;-\; v} \;\implies\; \int \frac{1 \;-\; v}{1 \;+\; v^2} \, dv \;=\; \int \frac{dX}{X}$. Integrating gives $\tan^{-1} v \;-\; \frac{1}{2} \ln\left( 1 \;+\; v^2 \right) \;=\; \ln\left\lvert X \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Passing through $(2, 1) \;\implies\; X \;=\; 1, Y \;=\; 0, v \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Comparing with the given solution yields $\alpha \;=\; 1$ and $\beta \;=\; 2 \;\implies\; 5\beta \;+\; \alpha \;=\; 11$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sec x \frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; 2y \;=\; 2 \;+\; 3 \sin x$, $x \;\in\; \left( -\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$, $y(0) \;=\; -\frac{7}{4}$. Then $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Multiply by $\cos x$ to get a linear ODE with integrating factor $\mu(x) \;=\; e^{-2\sin x}$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting the equation as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; 2 \cos x \cdot y \;=\; (2 \;+\; 3 \sin x) \cos x$, the integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-2\sin x}$. Multiplying and integrating by parts gives $y e^{-2\sin x} \;=\; \int (2 \;+\; 3 \sin x) \cos x \, e^{-2\sin x} \, dx \;=\; -e^{-2\sin x} \;+\; \frac{3}{4} e^{-2\sin x} (-2 \sin x \;-\; 1) \;+\; C \;\implies\; y \;=\; -\frac{7}{4} \;-\; \frac{3}{2} \sin x \;+\; C e^{2\sin x}$. Using $y(0) \;=\; -\frac{7}{4} \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Therefore, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; -\frac{7}{4} \;-\; \frac{3}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \;=\; -\frac{5}{2}$.

questions.text: Suppose the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;=\; \frac{(2 \;+\; \alpha)x \;-\; \beta y \;+\; 2}{\beta x \;-\; 2\alpha y \;-\; (\beta \gamma \;-\; 4\alpha)}$ represents a circle passing through origin. Then the radius of this circle is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Cross-multiply and integrate the exact differential equation, then apply the conditions for a second-degree curve to represent a circle. // 📝 Solution: Cross-multiplying and grouping gives $\beta(x \, dy \;+\; y \, dx) \;-\; 2\alpha y \, dy \;-\; (\beta \gamma \;-\; 4\alpha) dy \;=\; (2 \;+\; \alpha) x \, dx \;+\; 2 \, dx$. Integrating gives $\beta xy \;-\; \alpha y^2 \;-\; (\beta \gamma \;-\; 4\alpha) y \;=\; \frac{(2 \;+\; \alpha) x^2}{2} \;+\; 2x \;+\; C$. For a circle passing through the origin, $C \;=\; 0$, $\beta \;=\; 0$, and $\frac{2 \;+\; \alpha}{2} \;=\; \alpha \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; 2$. The circle equation is $2x^2 \;+\; 2y^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 8y \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; y^2 \;+\; x \;-\; 4y \;=\; 0$. Its radius is $r \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} \;+\; 4} \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}$.

questions.text: Let the solution curve $y \;=\; y(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \frac{3x^5 \tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right)}{\left( 1 \;+\; x^6 \right)^{3/2}} y \;=\; 2x \exp\left( \frac{x^3 \;-\; \tan^{-1} x^3}{\sqrt{\left( 1 \;+\; x^6 \right)}} \right)$ pass through the origin. Then $y(1)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x^3 \;=\; \tan \theta$ to find the integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \exp\left( \frac{\tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right) \;-\; x^3}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; x^6}} \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Computing $\int \frac{-3x^5 \tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right)}{\left( 1 \;+\; x^6 \right)^{3/2}} \, dx$ by putting $x^3 \;=\; \tan \theta$ gives $\frac{\tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right) \;-\; x^3}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; x^6}}$, so $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \exp\left( \frac{\tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right) \;-\; x^3}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; x^6}} \right)$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $y \cdot \exp\left( \frac{\tan^{-1}\left( x^3 \right) \;-\; x^3}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; x^6}} \right) \;=\; \int 2x \, dx \;=\; x^2 \;+\; C$. Passing through $(0, 0) \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; 1$, $y(1) \exp\left( \frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \;-\; 1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; y(1) \;=\; \exp\left( \frac{4 \;-\; \pi}{4\sqrt{2}} \right)$.

questions.text: If $y \;=\; y(x)$ is the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; y \tan x \;=\; x \sec x$, $0 \;\le\; x \;\le\; \frac{\pi}{3}$, $y(0) \;=\; 1$, then $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The integrating factor of the linear ODE is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \tan x \, dx} \;=\; \sec x$. // 📝 Solution: Multiplying by $\text{I.F.} \;=\; \sec x$ and integrating by parts gives $y \sec x \;=\; \int x \sec^2 x \, dx \;=\; x \tan x \;-\; \ln\left\lvert \sec x \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Given $y(0) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 1$. At $x \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6}$, $y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}} \;-\; \ln\left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right) \;+\; 1 \;\implies\; y\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{12} \;-\; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \log_e\left( \frac{2}{e\sqrt{3}} \right)$.

questions.text: If $y \;=\; y(x)$ satisfies the differential equation $16\left( \sqrt{x \;+\; 9\sqrt{x}} \right)\left( 4 \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}} \right) \cos y \, dy \;=\; (1 \;+\; 2 \sin y) dx$, $x \;>\; 0$ and $y(256) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2}$, $y(49) \;=\; \alpha$, then $2 \sin \alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables and substitute $t \;=\; 4 \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}}$ on the $x$-integral. // 📝 Solution: Separating variables gives $\int \frac{\cos y}{1 \;+\; 2 \sin y} \, dy \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{16\sqrt{x}\sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}}\left( 4 \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}} \right)}$. Let $4 \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}} \;=\; t \;\implies\; \frac{dx}{4\sqrt{x}\sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}}} \;=\; dt$. Integrating gives $\frac{1}{2} \ln\left\lvert 1 \;+\; 2 \sin y \right\rvert \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln\left\lvert 4 \;+\; \sqrt{9 \;+\; \sqrt{x}} \right\rvert \;+\; C$. Using $y(256) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{2} \;\implies\; \frac{1}{2} \ln 3 \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln 9 \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. At $x \;=\; 49, y \;=\; \alpha$, $\frac{1}{2} \ln(1 \;+\; 2 \sin \alpha) \;=\; \frac{1}{4} \ln 8 \;\implies\; 1 \;+\; 2 \sin \alpha \;=\; 2\sqrt{2} \;\implies\; 2 \sin \alpha \;=\; 2\sqrt{2} \;-\; 1$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( 1 \;-\; x^2 \right) dy \;=\; \left[ xy \;+\; \left( x^3 \;+\; 2 \right) \sqrt{3\left( 1 \;-\; x^2 \right)} \right] dx$, $-1 \;<\; x \;<\; 1$, $y(0) \;=\; 0$. If $y\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \;=\; \frac{m}{n}$, $m$ and $n$ are coprime numbers, then $m \;+\; n$ is equal to _____
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $\left( 1 \;-\; x^2 \right) dx$ to form a linear differential equation with integrating factor $\sqrt{1 \;-\; x^2}$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; \frac{x}{1 \;-\; x^2} y \;=\; \frac{\left( x^3 \;+\; 2 \right)\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1 \;-\; x^2}}$, the integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{-x}{1 - x^2} \, dx} \;=\; \sqrt{1 \;-\; x^2}$. Multiplying by $\text{I.F.}$ and integrating gives $y \sqrt{1 \;-\; x^2} \;=\; \sqrt{3} \int \left( x^3 \;+\; 2 \right) dx \;=\; \sqrt{3} \left( \frac{x^4}{4} \;+\; 2x \right) \;+\; C$. Since $y(0) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. For $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$, $y\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \;=\; \sqrt{3} \left( \frac{1}{64} \;+\; 1 \right) \;\implies\; y\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \;=\; \frac{65}{32} \;=\; \frac{m}{n}$. Thus $m \;+\; n \;=\; 65 \;+\; 32 \;=\; 97$.

questions.text: For a differentiable function $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$, suppose $f'(x) \;=\; 3f(x) \;+\; \alpha$, where $\alpha \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, $f(0) \;=\; 1$ and $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) \;=\; 7$. Then $9f\left( -\log_e 3 \right)$ is equal to _________
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the first-order linear differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; 3y \;=\; \alpha$ and use the given boundary conditions. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;-\; 3y \;=\; \alpha$ with $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{-3x}$, we get $y e^{-3x} \;=\; \int \alpha e^{-3x} \, dx \;=\; -\frac{\alpha}{3} e^{-3x} \;+\; C \;\implies\; f(x) \;=\; -\frac{\alpha}{3} \;+\; C e^{3x}$. As $x \;\to\; -\infty$, $f(x) \;\to\; 7 \;\implies\; -\frac{\alpha}{3} \;=\; 7$. Using $f(0) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; 7 \;+\; C \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; C \;=\; -6$. Thus $f(x) \;=\; 7 \;-\; 6 e^{3x}$, so $9f\left( -\log_e 3 \right) \;=\; 9\left( 7 \;-\; \frac{6}{27} \right) \;=\; 61$.

questions.text: Let $y \;=\; y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left( 1 \;+\; x^2 \right) \frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; y \;=\; e^{\tan^{-1} x}$, $y(1) \;=\; 0$. Then $y(0)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $1 \;+\; x^2$ to put the equation in linear form with integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\tan^{-1} x}$. // 📝 Solution: Rewriting the equation as $\frac{dy}{dx} \;+\; \frac{y}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;=\; \frac{e^{\tan^{-1} x}}{1 \;+\; x^2}$, the integrating factor is $\text{I.F.} \;=\; e^{\int \frac{1}{1 + x^2} \, dx} \;=\; e^{\tan^{-1} x}$. The solution is $y e^{\tan^{-1} x} \;=\; \int \frac{e^{2\tan^{-1} x}}{1 \;+\; x^2} \, dx \;=\; \frac{e^{2\tan^{-1} x}}{2} \;+\; C$. Using $y(1) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 0 \;=\; \frac{e^{\pi/2}}{2} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; -\frac{e^{\pi/2}}{2}$. At $x \;=\; 0$, $y(0) \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 \;-\; e^{\pi/2} \right)$.

questions.text: If the solution $y \;=\; y(x)$ of the differential equation $\left( x^4 \;+\; 2x^3 \;+\; 3x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2 \right) dy \;-\; \left( 2x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 3 \right) dx \;=\; 0$ satisfies $y(-1) \;=\; -\frac{\pi}{4}$, then $y(0)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Separate the variables and factorize the quartic polynomial in the denominator as $\left( x^2 \;+\; 1 \right)\left( x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2 \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Separating the variables and integrating, we get $\int dy \;=\; \int \frac{2x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 3}{x^4 \;+\; 2x^3 \;+\; 3x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2} \, dx \;=\; \int \frac{\left( x^2 \;+\; 1 \right) \;+\; \left( x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2 \right)}{\left( x^2 \;+\; 1 \right)\left( x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2 \right)} \, dx \;=\; \int \frac{dx}{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 2} \;+\; \int \frac{dx}{x^2 \;+\; 1}$. Integrating both sides gives $y \;=\; \tan^{-1}(x \;+\; 1) \;+\; \tan^{-1} x \;+\; C$. Given $y(-1) \;=\; -\frac{\pi}{4} \;\implies\; -\frac{\pi}{4} \;=\; 0 \;-\; \frac{\pi}{4} \;+\; C \;\implies\; C \;=\; 0$. Thus, $y(x) \;=\; \tan^{-1}(x \;+\; 1) \;+\; \tan^{-1} x$. Putting $x \;=\; 0$, we get $y(0) \;=\; \tan^{-1}(1) \;+\; \tan^{-1}(0) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.text: The number of functions $f : \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\} \;\to\; \left\{a \;\in\; \mathbb{Z} : \left\lvert a \right\rvert \;\le\; 8\right\}$ satisfying $f\left(n\right) \;+\; \frac{1}{n}f\left(n \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 1, \forall n \;\in\; \left\{1, 2, 3\right\}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express $f\left(3\right), f\left(2\right), f\left(1\right)$ in terms of $f\left(4\right)$ and apply divisibility and range constraints $\left\lvert f\left(n\right) \right\rvert \;\le\; 8$. // 📝 Solution: From $f\left(n\right) \;+\; \frac{1}{n}f\left(n \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 1$, $f\left(n \;+\; 1\right)$ must be divisible by $n$. For $n \;=\; 3$, $f\left(3\right) \;=\; 1 \;-\; \frac{f\left(4\right)}{3}$, so $f\left(4\right) \;\in\; \left\{-6, -3, 0, 3, 6\right\}$. Also, for $n \;=\; 2$, $f\left(2\right) \;=\; 1 \;-\; \frac{f\left(3\right)}{2}$, which requires $f\left(3\right)$ to be even, meaning $\frac{f\left(4\right)}{3}$ must be odd. Thus, $f\left(4\right) \;\in\; \left\{-3, 3\right\}$. If $f\left(4\right) \;=\; -3$, then $f\left(3\right) \;=\; 2, f\left(2\right) \;=\; 0, f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$. If $f\left(4\right) \;=\; 3$, then $f\left(3\right) \;=\; 0, f\left(2\right) \;=\; 1, f\left(1\right) \;=\; 0$. Both tuples lie within $\left[-8, 8\right]$, so $2$ functions are possible.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{x^2 \;-\; 25}}{\left(4 \;-\; x^2\right)} \;+\; \log_{10}\left(x^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 15\right)$ is $\left(-\infty, \alpha\right) \;\cup\; \left[\beta, \infty\right)$, then $\alpha^2 \;+\; \beta^3$ is equal to:
The equation $x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; \left[x\right] \;+\; 3 \;=\; x\left[x\right]$, where $\left[x\right]$ denotes the greatest integer function, has:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rearrange the equation to factor out $\left(x \;-\; 1\right)$ on both sides. // 📝 Solution: Given $x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; \left[x\right] \;+\; 3 \;=\; x\left[x\right] \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; 3 \;=\; x\left[x\right] \;-\; \left[x\right] \;\implies\; \left(x \;-\; 1\right)\left(x \;-\; 3\right) \;=\; \left[x\right]\left(x \;-\; 1\right)$. This gives either $x \;=\; 1$ or $x \;-\; 3 \;=\; \left[x\right] \;\implies\; x \;-\; \left[x\right] \;=\; 3 \;\implies\; \left\{x\right\} \;=\; 3$, which is impossible since $0 \;\le\; \left\{x\right\} \;<\; 1$. Therefore, there is only one unique solution $x \;=\; 1$ in $\left(-\infty, \infty\right)$.

questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \left\{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9\right\}$. Then the number of possible functions $f : A \;\to\; A$ such that $f\left(m \cdot n\right) \;=\; f\left(m\right) \cdot f\left(n\right)$ for every $m, n \;\in\; A$ with $m \cdot n \;\in\; A$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Identify all pairs $\left(m, n\right)$ in $A$ whose product belongs to $A$: $1 \cdot m \;\in\; A$ and $3 \cdot 3 \;=\; 9 \;\in\; A$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $m \;=\; n \;=\; 1$ gives $f\left(1\right) \;=\; \left(f\left(1\right)\right)^2 \;\implies\; f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$. The only other product of elements in $A$ that remains in $A$ is $3 \times 3 \;=\; 9$, which requires $f\left(9\right) \;=\; \left(f\left(3\right)\right)^2$. Since $f\left(9\right) \;\in\; A$, $f\left(3\right)$ can only be $1$ or $3$ ($2$ choices), which uniquely fixes $f\left(9\right)$ ($1$ choice). The remaining $3$ elements $\left\{2, 5, 8\right\}$ can each be mapped to any of the $6$ elements of $A$ ($6^3$ choices). Thus, the total number of functions is $1 \times 2 \times 1 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6 \;=\; 432$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{5 \;-\; x}{3 \;+\; 2x}\right) \;+\; \frac{1}{\log_e\left(10 \;-\; x\right)}$ is $\left(-\infty, \alpha\right] \;\cup\; \left[\beta, \gamma\right) \;-\; \left\{\delta\right\}$, then $6\left(\alpha \;+\; \beta \;+\; \gamma \;+\; \delta\right)$ is equal to

For some $a, b, c \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; ax \;-\; 3$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; x^b \;+\; c, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $\left(f \circ g\right)^{-1}\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{x \;-\; 7}{2}\right)^{1/3}$ then $\left(f \circ g\right)\left(ac\right) \;+\; \left(g \circ f\right)\left(b\right)$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $\left(f \circ g\right)\left(x\right)$ by inverting $\left(\frac{x \;-\; 7}{2}\right)^{1/3}$ and compare coefficients with $a\left(x^b \;+\; c\right) \;-\; 3$. // 📝 Solution: Let $h\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(f \circ g\right)\left(x\right)$. Since $h^{-1}\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(\frac{x \;-\; 7}{2}\right)^{1/3}$, inverting gives $h\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(f \circ g\right)\left(x\right) \;=\; 2x^3 \;+\; 7$. Also, $\left(f \circ g\right)\left(x\right) \;=\; a\left(x^b \;+\; c\right) \;-\; 3 \;=\; ax^b \;+\; ac \;-\; 3$. Comparing the two expressions gives $a \;=\; 2, b \;=\; 3$, and $2c \;-\; 3 \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; c \;=\; 5$. Then $\left(f \circ g\right)\left(ac\right) \;=\; \left(f \circ g\right)\left(10\right) \;=\; 2\left(10\right)^3 \;+\; 7 \;=\; 2007$, and $\left(g \circ f\right)\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(2x \;-\; 3\right)^3 \;+\; 5 \;\implies\; \left(g \circ f\right)\left(3\right) \;=\; 3^3 \;+\; 5 \;=\; 32$. Thus, the required sum is $2007 \;+\; 32 \;=\; 2039$.

questions.text: Let $\left[t\right]$ be the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Let $A$ be the set of all prime factors of $2310$ and $f : A \;\to\; \mathbb{Z}$ be the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(x^2 \;+\; \left[\frac{x^3}{5}\right]\right)\right]$. The number of one-to-one functions from $A$ to the range of $f$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the prime factorization of $2310$ to determine the elements of set $A$, then check the cardinality of the range of $f$. // 📝 Solution: We have $2310 \;=\; 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11$, so $A \;=\; \left\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11\right\}$. Evaluating $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(x^2 \;+\; \left[\frac{x^3}{5}\right]\right)\right]$ at each element of $A$: $f\left(2\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(5\right)\right] \;=\; 2$, $f\left(3\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(14\right)\right] \;=\; 3$, $f\left(5\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(25 \;+\; 25\right)\right] \;=\; 5$, $f\left(7\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(117\right)\right] \;=\; 6$, and $f\left(11\right) \;=\; \left[\log_2\left(387\right)\right] \;=\; 8$. Thus, the range of $f$ is $B \;=\; \left\{2, 3, 5, 6, 8\right\}$. Since both $A$ and $B$ have $5$ elements, the number of one-to-one functions from $A$ to $B$ is $5! \;=\; 120$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_e\left(\frac{2x \;+\; 3}{4x^2 \;+\; x \;-\; 3}\right) \;+\; \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2x \;-\; 1}{x \;+\; 2}\right)$ is $\left(\alpha, \beta\right]$, then the value of $5\beta \;-\; 4\alpha$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve $\frac{2x \;+\; 3}{4x^2 \;+\; x \;-\; 3} \;>\; 0$ and $-1 \;\le\; \frac{2x \;-\; 1}{x \;+\; 2} \;\le\; 1$, then take their intersection. // 📝 Solution: First, $\frac{2x \;+\; 3}{4x^2 \;+\; x \;-\; 3} \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{2x \;+\; 3}{\left(4x \;-\; 3\right)\left(x \;+\; 1\right)} \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(-\frac{3}{2}, -1\right) \;\cup\; \left(\frac{3}{4}, \infty\right)$. Second, $-1 \;\le\; \frac{2x \;-\; 1}{x \;+\; 2} \;\le\; 1 \;\implies\; \frac{3x \;+\; 1}{x \;+\; 2} \;\ge\; 0$ and $\frac{x \;-\; 3}{x \;+\; 2} \;\le\; 0$, which gives $x \;\in\; \left(-\infty, -2\right) \;\cup\; \left[-\frac{1}{3}, \infty\right)$ and $x \;\in\; \left(-2, 3\right]$, whose intersection is $\left[-\frac{1}{3}, 3\right]$. Intersecting with the first condition gives $x \;\in\; \left(\frac{3}{4}, 3\right]$. Thus, $\alpha \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$ and $\beta \;=\; 3$, so $5\beta \;-\; 4\alpha \;=\; 15 \;-\; 3 \;=\; 12$.

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; x^5 \;+\; 2x^3 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 1, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, and $g\left(x\right)$ be a function such that $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; x$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. Then $\frac{g\left(7\right)}{g'\left(7\right)}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the derivative of an inverse function relation $g'\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \cdot f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x\right) \;=\; x^5 \;+\; 2x^3 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 1$, differentiating gives $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 5x^4 \;+\; 6x^2 \;+\; 3$. Setting $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; x^5 \;+\; 2x^3 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 1 \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 1$. Thus, $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 7 \;\implies\; g\left(7\right) \;=\; 1$, and $f'\left(1\right) \;=\; 5 \;+\; 6 \;+\; 3 \;=\; 14$. Differentiating $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; x$ gives $g'\left(f\left(x\right)\right)f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 1$. Putting $x \;=\; 1$, we get $g'\left(7\right)f'\left(1\right) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; g'\left(7\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'\left(1\right)} \;=\; \frac{1}{14}$. Therefore, $\frac{g\left(7\right)}{g'\left(7\right)} \;=\; \frac{1}{\frac{1}{14}} \;=\; 14$.

questions.text: Let the range of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{2 \;+\; \sin 3x \;+\; \cos 3x}, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ be $\left[a, b\right]$. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are respectively the A.M. and the G.M. of $a$ and $b$, then $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $-\sqrt{2} \;\le\; \sin 3x \;+\; \cos 3x \;\le\; \sqrt{2}$ to find $a$ and $b$, then compute $\frac{\alpha}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{2\sqrt{ab}}$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\sin 3x \;+\; \cos 3x \;\in\; \left[-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}\right]$, the range of $f\left(x\right)$ is $\left[a, b\right] \;=\; \left[\frac{1}{2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{2 \;-\; \sqrt{2}}\right]$. Then $\frac{\alpha}{\beta} \;=\; \frac{a \;+\; b}{2\sqrt{ab}} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}} \;+\; \sqrt{\frac{b}{a}}\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 \;-\; \sqrt{2}}{2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}}} \;+\; \sqrt{\frac{2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}}{2 \;-\; \sqrt{2}}}\right) \;=\; \frac{\left(2 \;-\; \sqrt{2}\right) \;+\; \left(2 \;+\; \sqrt{2}\right)}{2\sqrt{2}} \;=\; \sqrt{2}$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ and $g : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} \log_e x, & x \;>\; 0 \\ e^{-x}, & x \;\le\; 0 \end{cases}$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} x, & x \;\ge\; 0 \\ e^x, & x \;<\; 0 \end{cases}$. Then, $g \circ f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Construct the piecewise definition of $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ based on the sign of $f\left(x\right)$ over the intervals $\left(-\infty, 0\right]$, $\left(0, 1\right)$, and $\left[1, \infty\right)$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] By definition, $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} f\left(x\right), & f\left(x\right) \;\ge\; 0 \\ e^{f\left(x\right)}, & f\left(x\right) \;<\; 0 \end{cases}$. Evaluating on each interval gives $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} e^{-x}, & x \;\in\; \left(-\infty, 0\right] \\ e^{\ln x} \;=\; x, & x \;\in\; \left(0, 1\right) \\ \ln x, & x \;\in\; \left[1, \infty\right) \end{cases}$. From the graph of $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$, its range is $\left[0, \infty\right) \;\neq\; \mathbb{R}$ and multiple inputs yield the same output. Thus, $g \circ f$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.text: Let $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three non-zero non-coplanar vectors. Let the position vectors of four points $A, B, C$ and $D$ be $\vec{a} \;-\; \vec{b} \;+\; \vec{c}, \lambda\vec{a} \;-\; 3\vec{b} \;+\; 4\vec{c}, -\vec{a} \;+\; 2\vec{b} \;-\; 3\vec{c}$ and $2\vec{a} \;-\; 4\vec{b} \;+\; 6\vec{c}$ respectively. If $\overrightarrow{AB}, \overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD}$ are coplanar, then $\lambda$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Three vectors expressed in terms of non-coplanar vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are coplanar if the determinant of their coefficients is zero. // 📝 Solution: We compute $\overrightarrow{AB} \;=\; \left(\lambda \;-\; 1\right)\vec{a} \;-\; 2\vec{b} \;+\; 3\vec{c}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} \;=\; -2\vec{a} \;+\; 3\vec{b} \;-\; 4\vec{c}$, and $\overrightarrow{AD} \;=\; \vec{a} \;-\; 3\vec{b} \;+\; 5\vec{c}$. Since $\overrightarrow{AB}, \overrightarrow{AC}, \overrightarrow{AD}$ are coplanar, the determinant of their scalar components must vanish: $\begin{vmatrix} \lambda \;-\; 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(\lambda \;-\; 1\right)\left(15 \;-\; 12\right) \;+\; 2\left(-10 \;+\; 4\right) \;+\; 3\left(6 \;-\; 3\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 3\left(\lambda \;-\; 1\right) \;-\; 12 \;+\; 9 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \lambda \;=\; 2$.

questions.text: Consider a function $f : \mathbb{N} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$, satisfying $f\left(1\right) \;+\; 2f\left(2\right) \;+\; 3f\left(3\right) \;+\; \dots \;+\; xf\left(x\right) \;=\; x\left(x \;+\; 1\right)f\left(x\right); x \;\ge\; 2$ with $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$. Then $\frac{1}{f\left(2022\right)} \;+\; \frac{1}{f\left(2028\right)}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Subtract the relation for $x$ from the relation for $x \;+\; 1$ to obtain a recurrence relation for $f\left(x\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(1\right) \;+\; 2f\left(2\right) \;+\; \dots \;+\; xf\left(x\right) \;=\; x\left(x \;+\; 1\right)f\left(x\right)$ for $x \;\ge\; 2$. Replacing $x$ by $x \;+\; 1$ and substituting the original sum gives $x\left(x \;+\; 1\right)f\left(x\right) \;+\; \left(x \;+\; 1\right)f\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 1\right)\left(x \;+\; 2\right)f\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;\implies\; xf\left(x\right) \;=\; \left(x \;+\; 1\right)f\left(x \;+\; 1\right)$ for $x \;\ge\; 2$. For $x \;=\; 2$, $f\left(1\right) \;+\; 2f\left(2\right) \;=\; 6f\left(2\right) \;\implies\; 4f\left(2\right) \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; f\left(2\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{4}$. Thus, $xf\left(x\right) \;=\; 2f\left(2\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{2x}$ for all $x \;\ge\; 2$. Hence, $\frac{1}{f\left(2022\right)} \;+\; \frac{1}{f\left(2028\right)} \;=\; 4044 \;+\; 4056 \;=\; 8100$.

questions.text: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{1 \;+\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert}$ is one-one. Statement II: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 4x \;-\; 30}{x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 18}$ is many-one. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the sign of $f'\left(x\right)$ for both functions to determine whether they are strictly monotonic or change direction. // 📝 Solution: Statement I: For $x \;\ge\; 0$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{1 \;+\; x}$ has $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{\left(1 \;+\; x\right)^2} \;>\; 0$. For $x \;<\; 0$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{1 \;-\; x}$ has $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{\left(1 \;-\; x\right)^2} \;>\; 0$. Since $f$ is continuous at $x \;=\; 0$ and strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$, it is one-one. Statement I is true. Statement II: For $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 4x \;-\; 30}{x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 18}$, the denominator $\left(x \;-\; 4\right)^2 \;+\; 2 \;>\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, and $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{-12\left(x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 14\right)}{\left(x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 18\right)^2}$. Since $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 0$ at $x \;=\; 4 \;\pm\; \sqrt{2}$ and changes sign, $f$ is many-one. Both statements are true.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$. Then the number of one-one functions $f : S \;\to\; P\left(S\right)$, where $P\left(S\right)$ denote the power set of $S$, such that $f\left(n\right) \;\subset\; f\left(m\right)$ where $n \;<\; m$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A strictly increasing chain of $6$ subsets of a $6$-element set $S$ is obtained by omitting exactly one subset size from $\left\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$. // 📝 Solution: The chain $f\left(1\right) \;\subset\; f\left(2\right) \;\subset\; f\left(3\right) \;\subset\; f\left(4\right) \;\subset\; f\left(5\right) \;\subset\; f\left(6\right)$ consists of $6$ subsets of $S$ of strictly increasing cardinalities chosen from $\left\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$. If cardinality $6$ or $0$ is omitted, there are $6! \;=\; 720$ chains each ($2 \times 720 \;=\; 1440$). If any of the $5$ intermediate cardinalities $k \;\in\; \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}$ is omitted, there is one step where the subset size jumps by $2$, giving $\frac{6!}{2!} \;=\; 360$ chains for each of the $5$ cases ($5 \times 360 \;=\; 1800$). Thus, the total number of such functions is $1440 \;+\; 1800 \;=\; 3240$.

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 2x^n \;+\; \lambda, \lambda \;\in\; \mathbb{R}, n \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, and $f\left(4\right) \;=\; 133, f\left(5\right) \;=\; 255$. Then the sum of all the positive integer divisors of $\left(f\left(3\right) \;-\; f\left(2\right)\right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Subtract $f\left(4\right) \;=\; 133$ from $f\left(5\right) \;=\; 255$ to eliminate $\lambda$ and find $n$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(4\right) \;=\; 2 \cdot 4^n \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 133$ and $f\left(5\right) \;=\; 2 \cdot 5^n \;+\; \lambda \;=\; 255$. Subtracting the two equations gives $2\left(5^n \;-\; 4^n\right) \;=\; 122 \;\implies\; 5^n \;-\; 4^n \;=\; 61 \;\implies\; n \;=\; 3$ (and $\lambda \;=\; 5$). Then $f\left(3\right) \;-\; f\left(2\right) \;=\; 2\left(3^3 \;-\; 2^3\right) \;=\; 2\left(27 \;-\; 8\right) \;=\; 38$. The positive integer divisors of $38$ are $1, 2, 19, 38$, and their sum is $1 \;+\; 2 \;+\; 19 \;+\; 38 \;=\; 60$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \;-\; \left\lvert x \right\rvert}{4}\right) \;+\; \left(\log_e\left(3 \;-\; x\right)\right)^{-1}$ is $\left[-\alpha, \beta\right) \;-\; \left\{\gamma\right\}$, then $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;+\; \gamma$ is equal to:

The sum of all the elements in the range of $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \text{Sgn}\left(\sin x\right) \;+\; \text{Sgn}\left(\cos x\right) \;+\; \text{Sgn}\left(\tan x\right) \;+\; \text{Sgn}\left(\cot x\right)$, $x \;\neq\; \frac{n\pi}{2}, n \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$, where $\text{Sgn}\left(t\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } t \;>\; 0 \\ -1, & \text{if } t \;<\; 0 \end{cases}$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the signs of $\sin x, \cos x, \tan x, \cot x$ in each of the four quadrants. // 📝 Solution: Checking each quadrant: For $x \;\in\; \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 4$. For $x \;\in\; \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; -2$. For $x \;\in\; \left(\pi, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; -1 \;-\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 0$. For $x \;\in\; \left(\frac{3\pi}{2}, 2\pi\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; -1 \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;-\; 1 \;=\; -2$. Thus, the range of $f$ is $\left\{-2, 0, 4\right\}$, and the sum of its elements is $-2 \;+\; 0 \;+\; 4 \;=\; 2$.

questions.text: If $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2^{2x}}{2^{2x} \;+\; 2}, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, then $f\left(\frac{1}{2023}\right) \;+\; f\left(\frac{2}{2023}\right) \;+\; \dots \;+\; f\left(\frac{2022}{2023}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the symmetry property $f\left(x\right) \;+\; f\left(1 \;-\; x\right)$ by writing $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{4^x}{4^x \;+\; 2}$. // 📝 Solution: We have $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{4^x}{4^x \;+\; 2}$. Then $f\left(x\right) \;+\; f\left(1 \;-\; x\right) \;=\; \frac{4^x}{4^x \;+\; 2} \;+\; \frac{4^{1-x}}{4^{1-x} \;+\; 2} \;=\; \frac{4^x}{4^x \;+\; 2} \;+\; \frac{4}{4 \;+\; 2 \cdot 4^x} \;=\; \frac{4^x}{4^x \;+\; 2} \;+\; \frac{2}{2 \;+\; 4^x} \;=\; 1$. Pairing the $2022$ terms equidistant from the beginning and the end into $1011$ pairs of the form $f\left(\frac{k}{2023}\right) \;+\; f\left(1 \;-\; \frac{k}{2023}\right) \;=\; 1$, the required sum is $1 \;+\; 1 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 1 \;\left(1011 \text{ times}\right) \;=\; 1011$.
