questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 2^x \;-\; x^2, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $m$ and $n$ are respectively the number of points at which the curves $y \;=\; f\left(x\right)$ and $y \;=\; f'\left(x\right)$ intersects the $x$-axis, then the value of $m \;+\; n$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Sketch the graphs of $y \;=\; 2^x$ and $y \;=\; x^2$ to find $m$, and the graphs of $y \;=\; 2^x \ln 2$ and $y \;=\; 2x$ to find $n$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Setting $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 2^x \;=\; x^2$. From the graphs of $y \;=\; 2^x$ and $y \;=\; x^2$, they intersect at $3$ points ($x \;=\; 2, x \;=\; 4$, and one negative root), so $m \;=\; 3$. [FIGURE] Next, $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 2^x \ln 2 \;-\; 2x \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; 2^x \ln 2 \;=\; 2x$. The exponential curve $y \;=\; 2^x \ln 2$ and the line $y \;=\; 2x$ intersect at $2$ points, so $n \;=\; 2$. Therefore, $m \;+\; n \;=\; 3 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: Consider the function $f : \left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right] \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 4\sqrt{2}x^3 \;-\; 3\sqrt{2}x \;-\; 1$. Consider the statements (I) The curve $y \;=\; f\left(x\right)$ intersects the $x$-axis exactly at one point (II) The curve $y \;=\; f\left(x\right)$ intersects the $x$-axis at $x \;=\; \cos \frac{\pi}{12}$. Then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check monotonicity using $f'\left(x\right)$ on $\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$ and substitute $x \;=\; \cos \alpha$ into $4x^3 \;-\; 3x \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. // 📝 Solution: Differentiating gives $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; 12\sqrt{2}x^2 \;-\; 3\sqrt{2} \;\ge\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$. Since $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \;=\; -\sqrt{2} \;-\; 1 \;<\; 0$ and $f\left(1\right) \;=\; \sqrt{2} \;-\; 1 \;>\; 0$, the strictly increasing curve intersects the $x$-axis at exactly one point, so (I) is correct. Next, setting $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \sqrt{2}\left(4x^3 \;-\; 3x\right) \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ and letting $x \;=\; \cos \alpha$, we get $\cos 3\alpha \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \;=\; \cos \frac{\pi}{4} \;\implies\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{\pi}{12} \;\implies\; x \;=\; \cos \frac{\pi}{12} \;\in\; \left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$. Thus, both (I) and (II) are correct.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{2, 6\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be real valued function defined as $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 1}{x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 12}$. Then range of $f$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $y \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 1}{x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 12}$, form a quadratic in $x$, and apply $D \;\ge\; 0$ while checking $y \;=\; 1$ separately. // 📝 Solution: Let $y \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 1}{x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 12} \;\implies\; x^2\left(y \;-\; 1\right) \;-\; x\left(8y \;+\; 2\right) \;+\; \left(12y \;-\; 1\right) \;=\; 0$. Case 1: $y \;\neq\; 1$. For real $x$, $D \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(8y \;+\; 2\right)^2 \;-\; 4\left(y \;-\; 1\right)\left(12y \;-\; 1\right) \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; 16y^2 \;+\; 84y \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; y\left(4y \;+\; 21\right) \;\ge\; 0$. [FIGURE] This gives $y \;\in\; \left(-\infty, -\frac{21}{4}\right] \;\cup\; \left[0, \infty\right) \;-\; \left\{1\right\}$. Case 2: $y \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 1 \;=\; x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 12 \;\implies\; 10x \;=\; 11 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{11}{10} \;\notin\; \left\{2, 6\right\}$, so $y \;=\; 1$ is also attained. Hence, the range of $f$ is $\left(-\infty, -\frac{21}{4}\right] \;\cup\; \left[0, \infty\right)$.

questions.text: Let $f$ and $g$ be functions satisfying $f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right), f\left(1\right) \;=\; 7$ and $g\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; g\left(xy\right), g\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$, for all $x, y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. If $\sum_{x=1}^n \left(\frac{f\left(x\right)}{g\left(x\right)}\right) \;=\; 19607$, then $n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Put $y \;=\; 1$ in both functional equations to deduce $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 7^x$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: From $f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right)$ and $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 7$, we get $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 7^x$. Putting $y \;=\; 1$ in $g\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; g\left(xy\right)$ gives $g\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; g\left(x\right) \;\implies\; g\left(x\right) \;=\; g\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. Then $\sum_{x=1}^n \frac{f\left(x\right)}{g\left(x\right)} \;=\; \sum_{x=1}^n 7^x \;=\; \frac{7\left(7^n \;-\; 1\right)}{6} \;=\; 19607 \;\implies\; 7^{n+1} \;-\; 7 \;=\; 117642 \;\implies\; 7^{n+1} \;=\; 117649 \;=\; 7^6 \;\implies\; n \;+\; 1 \;=\; 6 \;\implies\; n \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_{\left(10x^2 \;-\; 17x \;+\; 7\right)}\left(18x^2 \;-\; 11x \;+\; 1\right)$ is $\left(-\infty, a\right) \;\cup\; \left(b, c\right) \;\cup\; \left(d, \infty\right) \;-\; \left\{e\right\}$, then $90\left(a \;+\; b \;+\; c \;+\; d \;+\; e\right)$ equals:

If the domain of the function $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3x \;-\; 22}{2x \;-\; 19}\right) \;+\; \log_{e}\left(\frac{3x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 5}{x^2 \;-\; 3x \;-\; 10}\right)$ is $\left(\alpha, \beta\right]$, then $3\alpha \;+\; 10\beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $\sin^{-1}\left(u\right)$, the argument must satisfy $-1 \;\le\; u \;\le\; 1$, and for $\log_{e}\left(v\right)$, the argument must satisfy $v \;>\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: For $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3x \;-\; 22}{2x \;-\; 19}\right)$ to be defined, we require $-1 \;\le\; \frac{3x \;-\; 22}{2x \;-\; 19} \;\le\; 1$. Solving $\frac{3x \;-\; 22}{2x \;-\; 19} \;+\; 1 \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{5x \;-\; 41}{2x \;-\; 19} \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(-\infty, \frac{41}{5}\right] \;\cup\; \left(\frac{19}{2}, \infty\right)$, and solving $\frac{3x \;-\; 22}{2x \;-\; 19} \;-\; 1 \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{x \;-\; 3}{2x \;-\; 19} \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left[3, \frac{19}{2}\right)$. The intersection of these two intervals gives $x \;\in\; \left[3, \frac{41}{5}\right]$. For $\log_{e}\left(\frac{3x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 5}{x^2 \;-\; 3x \;-\; 10}\right)$ to be defined, we require $\frac{3x^2 \;-\; 8x \;+\; 5}{x^2 \;-\; 3x \;-\; 10} \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; \frac{\left(3x \;-\; 5\right)\left(x \;-\; 1\right)}{\left(x \;-\; 5\right)\left(x \;+\; 2\right)} \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(-\infty, -2\right) \;\cup\; \left(1, \frac{5}{3}\right) \;\cup\; \left(5, \infty\right)$. Taking the intersection of both conditions yields $x \;\in\; \left(5, \frac{41}{5}\right]$. Thus, $\alpha \;=\; 5$ and $\beta \;=\; \frac{41}{5}$, which gives $3\alpha \;+\; 10\beta \;=\; 3\left(5\right) \;+\; 10\left(\frac{41}{5}\right) \;=\; 15 \;+\; 82 \;=\; 97$.

questions.text: Let $f^1\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{3x \;+\; 2}{2x \;+\; 3}, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{\frac{-3}{2}\right\}$. For $n \;\ge\; 2$, define $f^n\left(x\right) \;=\; f^1 \circ f^{n-1}\left(x\right)$. If $f^5\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{ax \;+\; b}{bx \;+\; a}, \text{gcd}\left(a, b\right) \;=\; 1$, then $a \;+\; b$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute $f^2\left(x\right)$ and $f^3\left(x\right)$ to observe that the sum of the coefficients $a \;+\; b$ in $f^n\left(x\right)$ equals $5^n$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f^1\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{3x \;+\; 2}{2x \;+\; 3}$, we compute $f^2\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{13x \;+\; 12}{12x \;+\; 13}$ and $f^3\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{63x \;+\; 62}{62x \;+\; 63}$. Observing the pattern, for $f^n\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{ax \;+\; b}{bx \;+\; a}$ with $\text{gcd}\left(a, b\right) \;=\; 1$, we have $a \;-\; b \;=\; 1$ and $a \;+\; b \;=\; 5^n$. For $n \;=\; 5$, $f^5\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1563x \;+\; 1562}{1562x \;+\; 1563}$, so $a \;+\; b \;=\; 1563 \;+\; 1562 \;=\; 5^5 \;=\; 3125$.

questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \left\{1, 3, 7, 9, 11\right\}$ and $B \;=\; \left\{2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12\right\}$. Then the total number of one-one maps $f : A \;\to\; B$, such that $f\left(1\right) \;+\; f\left(3\right) \;=\; 14$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Identify all pairs of distinct elements in $B$ whose sum is $14$, and arrange the remaining elements using permutations. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Given $A \;=\; \left\{1, 3, 7, 9, 11\right\}$ and $B \;=\; \left\{2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12\right\}$. Since $f$ is one-one, $f\left(1\right) \;\neq\; f\left(3\right)$. The pairs of distinct elements in $B$ satisfying $f\left(1\right) \;+\; f\left(3\right) \;=\; 14$ are: (i) $2 \;+\; 12 \;=\; 14$ and (ii) $4 \;+\; 10 \;=\; 14$. There are $2$ ways to choose the pair, $2!$ ways to assign images to $1$ and $3$, and $5 \times 4 \times 3$ ways to map the remaining $3$ elements of $A$ to the remaining $5$ elements of $B$. Thus, the total number of one-one maps is $2 \times \left(2 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3\right) \;=\; 240$.

questions.text: Let the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_3 \log_5 \left(7 \;-\; \log_2\left(x^2 \;-\; 10x \;+\; 85\right)\right) \;+\; \sin^{-1}\left(\left\lvert \frac{3x \;-\; 7}{17 \;-\; x} \right\rvert\right)$ be $\left(\alpha, \beta\right]$. Then $\alpha \;+\; \beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $\log_3 \log_5\left(u\right)$ to be defined, we require $u \;>\; 1$, and for $\sin^{-1}\left(\left\lvert v \right\rvert\right)$, we require $\left\lvert v \right\rvert \;\le\; 1$. // 📝 Solution: For the logarithmic term, we need $\log_5\left(7 \;-\; \log_2\left(x^2 \;-\; 10x \;+\; 85\right)\right) \;>\; 0 \;\implies\; 7 \;-\; \log_2\left(x^2 \;-\; 10x \;+\; 85\right) \;>\; 1 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 10x \;+\; 85 \;<\; 2^6 \;=\; 64 \;\implies\; \left(x \;-\; 3\right)\left(x \;-\; 7\right) \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left(3, 7\right)$. For the inverse sine term, $\left\lvert 3x \;-\; 7 \right\rvert \;\le\; \left\lvert 17 \;-\; x \right\rvert \;\implies\; \left(3x \;-\; 7\right)^2 \;-\; \left(17 \;-\; x\right)^2 \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(x \;-\; 6\right)\left(x \;+\; 5\right) \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left[-5, 6\right]$. Taking the intersection gives $\left(3, 6\right]$, so $\alpha \;=\; 3$ and $\beta \;=\; 6$, which gives $\alpha \;+\; \beta \;=\; 9$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \log_{\sqrt{m}}\left\{\sqrt{2}\left(\sin x \;-\; \cos x\right) \;+\; m \;-\; 2\right\}$, for some $m$, such that the range of $f$ is $\left[0, 2\right]$. Then the value of $m$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the bound $-2 \;\le\; \sqrt{2}\left(\sin x \;-\; \cos x\right) \;\le\; 2$ and equate the extremes of the logarithm argument to $\left(\sqrt{m}\right)^0 \;=\; 1$ and $\left(\sqrt{m}\right)^2 \;=\; m$. // 📝 Solution: Since $-\sqrt{2} \;\le\; \sin x \;-\; \cos x \;\le\; \sqrt{2}$, we have $-2 \;\le\; \sqrt{2}\left(\sin x \;-\; \cos x\right) \;\le\; 2$. Let $k \;=\; \sqrt{2}\left(\sin x \;-\; \cos x\right) \;\in\; \left[-2, 2\right]$. Given $0 \;\le\; \log_{\sqrt{m}}\left(k \;+\; m \;-\; 2\right) \;\le\; 2 \;\implies\; 1 \;\le\; k \;+\; m \;-\; 2 \;\le\; m \;\implies\; 3 \;-\; m \;\le\; k \;\le\; 2$. Comparing with $-2 \;\le\; k \;\le\; 2$ gives $3 \;-\; m \;=\; -2 \;\implies\; m \;=\; 5$.

questions.text: The domain of $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\log_{\left(x+1\right)}\left(x \;-\; 2\right)}{e^{2\log_e x} \;-\; \left(2x \;+\; 3\right)}, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ is

Consider the function $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9x^2}}$. If the composition of $f$, $\underbrace{\left(f \circ f \circ f \circ \dots \circ f\right)}_{10 \text{ times}}\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2^{10}x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9\alpha x^2}}$, then the value of $\sqrt{3\alpha \;+\; 1}$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute $f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ and $f\left(f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)\right)$ to identify the geometric progression pattern in the denominator. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9x^2}}$, we find $f\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \frac{2f\left(x\right)}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9\left(f\left(x\right)\right)^2}} \;=\; \frac{2^2 x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9x^2 \;+\; 9 \cdot 2^2 x^2}} \;=\; \frac{2^2 x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9x^2\left(1 \;+\; 2^2\right)}}$. Similarly, $f\left(f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)\right) \;=\; \frac{2^3 x}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; 9x^2\left(1 \;+\; 2^2 \;+\; 2^4\right)}}$. By pattern observation for $10$ compositions, we obtain $\alpha \;=\; 1 \;+\; 2^2 \;+\; 2^4 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 2^{18} \;=\; \frac{\left(2^2\right)^{10} \;-\; 1}{2^2 \;-\; 1} \;=\; \frac{2^{20} \;-\; 1}{3}$. Therefore, $3\alpha \;+\; 1 \;=\; 2^{20} \;\implies\; \sqrt{3\alpha \;+\; 1} \;=\; 2^{10} \;=\; 1024$.

questions.text: If the function $f : \left(-\infty, -1\right] \;\to\; \left(a, b\right]$ defined by $f\left(x\right) \;=\; e^{x^3 \;-\; 3x \;+\; 1}$ is one-one and onto, then the distance of the point $P\left(2b \;+\; 4, a \;+\; 2\right)$ from the line $x \;+\; e^{-3}y \;=\; 4$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since $f$ is onto, $\left(a, b\right]$ is the range of $f$ on $\left(-\infty, -1\right]$; find $a$ and $b$ using monotonicity. // 📝 Solution: Differentiating gives $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; e^{x^3 \;-\; 3x \;+\; 1} \cdot 3\left(x \;-\; 1\right)\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;\ge\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \left(-\infty, -1\right]$, so $f\left(x\right)$ is increasing on $\left(-\infty, -1\right]$. Thus, $a \;=\; \lim_{x \to -\infty} f\left(x\right) \;=\; e^{-\infty} \;=\; 0$ and $b \;=\; f\left(-1\right) \;=\; e^{-1 \;+\; 3 \;+\; 1} \;=\; e^3$. The point is $P\left(2b \;+\; 4, a \;+\; 2\right) \;=\; P\left(2e^3 \;+\; 4, 2\right)$. [FIGURE] Its perpendicular distance from the line $x \;+\; e^{-3}y \;-\; 4 \;=\; 0$ is $d \;=\; \frac{\left\lvert \left(2e^3 \;+\; 4\right) \;+\; 2e^{-3} \;-\; 4 \right\rvert}{\sqrt{1 \;+\; e^{-6}}} \;=\; \frac{2\left(e^3 \;+\; e^{-3}\right)}{e^{-3}\sqrt{e^6 \;+\; 1}} \;=\; \frac{2\left(e^6 \;+\; 1\right)}{\sqrt{e^6 \;+\; 1}} \;=\; 2\sqrt{1 \;+\; e^6}$.

questions.text: If the range of $f\left(\theta\right) \;=\; \frac{\sin^4\theta \;+\; 3\cos^2\theta}{\sin^4\theta \;+\; \cos^2\theta}, \theta \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ is $\left[\alpha, \beta\right]$, then the sum of the infinite G.P., whose first term is $64$ and the common ratio is $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$, is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite $f\left(\theta\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2\cos^2\theta}{\sin^4\theta \;+\; \cos^2\theta}$ and use the AM-GM inequality on $\cos^2\theta \;+\; \sec^2\theta$. // 📝 Solution: We write $f\left(\theta\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2\cos^2\theta}{\sin^4\theta \;+\; \cos^2\theta} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2\cos^2\theta}{\cos^4\theta \;-\; \cos^2\theta \;+\; 1}$. At $\cos\theta \;=\; 0$, $f\left(\theta\right)_{\min} \;=\; 1$. For $\cos\theta \;\neq\; 0$, $f\left(\theta\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{\cos^2\theta \;+\; \sec^2\theta \;-\; 1}$. Since $\cos^2\theta \;+\; \sec^2\theta \;\ge\; 2$, the maximum value is $f\left(\theta\right)_{\max} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2}{2 \;-\; 1} \;=\; 3$. Thus, $\alpha \;=\; 1$ and $\beta \;=\; 3$. The sum of the infinite G.P. is $S \;=\; \frac{64}{1 \;-\; \frac{1}{3}} \;=\; 96$.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x \;-\; 1}{2x \;+\; 3}\right)$ is $\mathbb{R} \;-\; \left(\alpha, \beta\right)$, then $12\alpha\beta$ is equal to:

Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be a function defined $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{\left(1 \;+\; x^4\right)^{1/4}}$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; f\left(f\left(f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)\right)\right)$ then $18 \int_0^{\sqrt{2\sqrt{5}}} x^2 g\left(x\right) dx$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Simplify $f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ to see the pattern for $4$ compositions, then use the substitution $1 \;+\; 4x^4 \;=\; t^4$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{\left(1 \;+\; x^4\right)^{1/4}}$, we find $f\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{\left(1 \;+\; 2x^4\right)^{1/4}}$, and after $4$ compositions, $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{\left(1 \;+\; 4x^4\right)^{1/4}}$. Then $I \;=\; 18 \int_0^{\sqrt{2\sqrt{5}}} \frac{x^3}{\left(1 \;+\; 4x^4\right)^{1/4}} dx$. Let $1 \;+\; 4x^4 \;=\; t^4 \;\implies\; 16x^3 dx \;=\; 4t^3 dt \;\implies\; x^3 dx \;=\; \frac{1}{4}t^3 dt$. As $x$ goes from $0$ to $\sqrt{2\sqrt{5}}$, $t$ goes from $1$ to $3$. Thus, $I \;=\; \frac{18}{4} \int_1^3 t^2 dt \;=\; \frac{9}{2}\left[\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_1^3 \;=\; \frac{3}{2}\left(27 \;-\; 1\right) \;=\; 39$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{0, 1\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f\left(x\right) \;+\; f\left(\frac{1}{1 \;-\; x}\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; x$. Then $f\left(2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \;=\; 2$, $x \;=\; -1$, and $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$ into the functional equation to form a cyclic system of three linear equations. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x\right) \;+\; f\left(\frac{1}{1 \;-\; x}\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; x$. Substituting $x \;=\; 2$ gives $f\left(2\right) \;+\; f\left(-1\right) \;=\; 3$ ...(1). Substituting $x \;=\; -1$ gives $f\left(-1\right) \;+\; f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \;=\; 0$ ...(2). Substituting $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$ gives $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \;+\; f\left(2\right) \;=\; \frac{3}{2}$ ...(3). Computing $\left(1\right) \;+\; \left(3\right) \;-\; \left(2\right)$ yields $2f\left(2\right) \;=\; 3 \;+\; \frac{3}{2} \;-\; 0 \;=\; \frac{9}{2} \;\implies\; f\left(2\right) \;=\; \frac{9}{4}$.

questions.text: Let the sum of the maximum and the minimum values of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2x^2 \;-\; 3x \;+\; 8}{2x^2 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 8}$ be $\frac{m}{n}$, where $\text{gcd}\left(m, n\right) \;=\; 1$. Then $m \;+\; n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Set $y \;=\; f\left(x\right)$, form a quadratic equation in $x$, and apply the condition $D \;\ge\; 0$ since $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. // 📝 Solution: Let $y \;=\; \frac{2x^2 \;-\; 3x \;+\; 8}{2x^2 \;+\; 3x \;+\; 8}$. Cross-multiplying and rearranging terms in powers of $x$ gives $x^2\left(2y \;-\; 2\right) \;+\; x\left(3y \;+\; 3\right) \;+\; \left(8y \;-\; 8\right) \;=\; 0$. Since $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, the discriminant must be non-negative: $D \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(3y \;+\; 3\right)^2 \;-\; 4\left(2y \;-\; 2\right)\left(8y \;-\; 8\right) \;\ge\; 0$. Simplifying gives $9\left(y \;+\; 1\right)^2 \;-\; 64\left(y \;-\; 1\right)^2 \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(11y \;-\; 5\right)\left(5y \;-\; 11\right) \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; y \;\in\; \left[\frac{5}{11}, \frac{11}{5}\right]$ (with $y \;=\; 1$ included at $x \;=\; 0$). Thus, the minimum value is $\frac{5}{11}$ and the maximum value is $\frac{11}{5}$. Their sum is $\frac{m}{n} \;=\; \frac{5}{11} \;+\; \frac{11}{5} \;=\; \frac{146}{55}$. Since $\text{gcd}\left(146, 55\right) \;=\; 1$, we have $m \;=\; 146$ and $n \;=\; 55$, so $m \;+\; n \;=\; 146 \;+\; 55 \;=\; 201$.

questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \left\{\left(x, y\right) : 2x \;+\; 3y \;=\; 23, x, y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}\right\}$ and $B \;=\; \left\{x : \left(x, y\right) \;\in\; A\right\}$. Then the number of one-one functions from $A$ to $B$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find all natural number solutions $\left(x, y\right)$ to $2x \;+\; 3y \;=\; 23$ to determine the number of elements in $A$ and $B$. // 📝 Solution: The natural number solutions $\left(x, y\right)$ to $2x \;+\; 3y \;=\; 23$ are $\left(1, 7\right), \left(4, 5\right), \left(7, 3\right), \left(10, 1\right)$. Thus, $A \;=\; \left\{\left(1, 7\right), \left(4, 5\right), \left(7, 3\right), \left(10, 1\right)\right\}$ and $B \;=\; \left\{1, 4, 7, 10\right\}$. Since $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; \left\lvert B \right\rvert \;=\; 4$, the number of one-one functions from $A$ to $B$ is $4! \;=\; 24$.

questions.text: If $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} 2 \;+\; 2x, & -1 \;\le\; x \;<\; 0 \\ 1 \;-\; \frac{x}{3}, & 0 \;\le\; x \;\le\; 3 \end{cases}$; $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} -x, & -3 \;\le\; x \;\le\; 0 \\ x, & 0 \;<\; x \;\le\; 1 \end{cases}$ then range of $\left(f \circ g\left(x\right)\right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the range of $g\left(x\right)$ first, and then evaluate $f$ on that set of values. // 📝 Solution: We have $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} 2 \;+\; 2g\left(x\right), & -1 \;\le\; g\left(x\right) \;<\; 0 \\ 1 \;-\; \frac{g\left(x\right)}{3}, & 0 \;\le\; g\left(x\right) \;\le\; 3 \end{cases}$. [FIGURE] Since $g\left(x\right) \;\ge\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \left[-3, 1\right]$, the first branch $-1 \;\le\; g\left(x\right) \;<\; 0$ yields $x \;\in\; \phi$. For the second branch $0 \;\le\; g\left(x\right) \;\le\; 3$, the range of $g\left(x\right)$ over $x \;\in\; \left[-3, 1\right]$ is $\left[0, 3\right]$. [FIGURE] As $g\left(x\right)$ varies over $\left[0, 3\right]$, $1 \;-\; \frac{g\left(x\right)}{3}$ varies over $\left[0, 1\right]$. Thus, the range of $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)$ is $\left[0, 1\right]$.

questions.text: Suppose $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \left(0, \infty\right)$ be a differentiable function such that $5f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right), \forall x, y \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. If $f\left(3\right) \;=\; 320$, then $\sum_{n=0}^5 f\left(n\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Put $x \;=\; y \;=\; 0$ to find $f\left(0\right) \;=\; 5$, and use $f\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; \frac{f\left(1\right)}{5}f\left(x\right)$ to show $f\left(n\right)$ forms a G.P. // 📝 Solution: Given $5f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right)$. Putting $x \;=\; y \;=\; 0$ gives $5f\left(0\right) \;=\; \left(f\left(0\right)\right)^2 \;\implies\; f\left(0\right) \;=\; 5$ (since $f\left(x\right) \;>\; 0$). Also, $\frac{f\left(x \;+\; 1\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \;=\; \frac{f\left(1\right)}{5}$. Then $\frac{f\left(3\right)}{f\left(0\right)} \;=\; \left(\frac{f\left(1\right)}{5}\right)^3 \;\implies\; \frac{320}{5} \;=\; \frac{\left(f\left(1\right)\right)^3}{5^3} \;\implies\; f\left(1\right) \;=\; 20$, so $f\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 4f\left(x\right)$. Therefore, $\sum_{n=0}^5 f\left(n\right) \;=\; 5 \;+\; 5 \cdot 4 \;+\; 5 \cdot 4^2 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 5 \cdot 4^5 \;=\; \frac{5\left(4^6 \;-\; 1\right)}{4 \;-\; 1} \;=\; 6825$.

questions.text: If a function $f$ satisfies $f\left(m \;+\; n\right) \;=\; f\left(m\right) \;+\; f\left(n\right)$ for all $m, n \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ and $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$, then the largest natural number $\lambda$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{2022} f\left(\lambda \;+\; k\right) \;\le\; \left(2022\right)^2$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Cauchy's functional equation $f\left(m \;+\; n\right) \;=\; f\left(m\right) \;+\; f\left(n\right)$ with $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$ implies $f\left(x\right) \;=\; x$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(m \;+\; n\right) \;=\; f\left(m\right) \;+\; f\left(n\right)$ and $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 1$, we get $f\left(x\right) \;=\; x$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. Substituting into the inequality gives $\sum_{k=1}^{2022} \left(\lambda \;+\; k\right) \;\le\; \left(2022\right)^2 \;\implies\; 2022\lambda \;+\; \frac{2022 \times 2023}{2} \;\le\; \left(2022\right)^2$. Dividing by $2022$, we get $\lambda \;\le\; 2022 \;-\; \frac{2023}{2} \;=\; 1010.5$. Thus, the largest natural number $\lambda$ is $1010$.

questions.text: The function $f : \mathbb{N} \;-\; \left\{1\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{N}$; defined by $f\left(n\right) \;=\;$ the highest prime factor of $n$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check if two distinct numbers share the same highest prime factor and whether composite numbers in the codomain have pre-images. // 📝 Solution: For $f : \mathbb{N} \;-\; \left\{1\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{N}$, we have $f\left(2\right) \;=\; 2$ and $f\left(4\right) \;=\; 2$, so $f$ is many-one. Also, non-prime numbers like $1$ and $4$ in the codomain $\mathbb{N}$ are not the image of any element, so $f$ is into. Hence, $f$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.text: If $S \;=\; \left\{a \;\in\; \mathbb{R} : \left\lvert 2a \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; 3\left[a\right] \;+\; 2\left\{a\right\}\right\}$, where $\left[t\right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$ and $\left\{t\right\}$ represents the fractional part of $t$, then $72\sum_{a \in S} a$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $\left\{a\right\} \;=\; a \;-\; \left[a\right]$ so that $3\left[a\right] \;+\; 2\left\{a\right\} \;=\; \left[a\right] \;+\; 2a$. // 📝 Solution: Given $\left\lvert 2a \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; 3\left[a\right] \;+\; 2\left\{a\right\} \;=\; \left[a\right] \;+\; 2a$. Case 1: $a \;\ge\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; 2a \;-\; 1 \;=\; \left[a\right] \;+\; 2a \;\implies\; \left[a\right] \;=\; -1 \;\implies\; a \;\in\; \left[-1, 0\right)$, which is rejected. Case 2: $a \;<\; \frac{1}{2} \;\implies\; -2a \;+\; 1 \;=\; \left[a\right] \;+\; 2a$. Let $a \;=\; I \;+\; f$, where $I \;=\; \left[a\right] \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}$ and $f \;=\; \left\{a\right\} \;\in\; \left[0, 1\right)$. Then $-2\left(I \;+\; f\right) \;+\; 1 \;=\; I \;+\; 2\left(I \;+\; f\right) \;\implies\; 5I \;+\; 4f \;=\; 1$. This holds only when $I \;=\; 0$ and $f \;=\; \frac{1}{4}$, giving $a \;=\; \frac{1}{4}$. Therefore, $72\sum_{a \in S} a \;=\; 72 \times \frac{1}{4} \;=\; 18$.
questions.topic: Greatest Integer and Fractional Part Functions

questions.text: The number of distinct real roots of the equation $\left\lvert x \right\rvert\left\lvert x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert \;-\; 5\left\lvert x \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Split the real line into four intervals based on the critical points $x \;=\; -2, -1, 0$ of the modulus expressions. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] Case 1: $x \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 5x \;-\; 5 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 3x \;-\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{3 \;\pm\; \sqrt{33}}{2}$, which gives one positive root $x \;=\; \frac{3 \;+\; \sqrt{33}}{2}$. Case 2: $-1 \;\le\; x \;<\; 0 \;\implies\; -x^2 \;-\; 2x \;-\; 5x \;-\; 5 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7x \;+\; 6 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(x \;+\; 6\right)\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; -1$ (one root in range). Case 3: $-2 \;\le\; x \;<\; -1 \;\implies\; -x^2 \;-\; 2x \;+\; 5x \;+\; 5 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;-\; 3x \;-\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(x \;-\; 4\right)\left(x \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 0$ (no root in range). Case 4: $x \;<\; -2 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 5x \;+\; 5 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7x \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{-7 \;\pm\; \sqrt{33}}{2}$, which gives one root $x \;=\; \frac{-7 \;-\; \sqrt{33}}{2}$ in range. Hence, the total number of distinct real roots is $3$.

questions.text: If $g\left(x\right) \;=\; 3x^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 3, f\left(0\right) \;=\; -3$ and $4g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; 3x^2 \;-\; 32x \;+\; 72$, then $f\left(g\left(2\right)\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Assume $f\left(x\right) \;=\; ax \;+\; b$ is linear since $g\left(x\right)$ and $g\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ are both quadratic of degree $2$. // 📝 Solution: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; ax \;+\; b$. Since $f\left(0\right) \;=\; -3$, we have $b \;=\; -3$, so $f\left(x\right) \;=\; ax \;-\; 3$. Substituting into $4g\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; 12\left(ax \;-\; 3\right)^2 \;+\; 8\left(ax \;-\; 3\right) \;-\; 12 \;=\; 12a^2 x^2 \;-\; 64ax \;+\; 72$. Comparing with $3x^2 \;-\; 32x \;+\; 72$ gives $-64a \;=\; -32 \;\implies\; a \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x}{2} \;-\; 3$. Now, $g\left(2\right) \;=\; 3\left(4\right) \;+\; 4 \;-\; 3 \;=\; 13$, so $f\left(g\left(2\right)\right) \;=\; f\left(13\right) \;=\; \frac{13}{2} \;-\; 3 \;=\; \frac{7}{2}$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{-\frac{1}{2}\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ and $g : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{-\frac{5}{2}\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2x \;+\; 3}{2x \;+\; 1}$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\left\lvert x \right\rvert \;+\; 1}{2x \;+\; 5}$. Then the domain of the function $f \circ g$ is:

Let $f\left(x\right)$ be a function such that $f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right)$ for all $x, y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. If $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 3$ and $\sum_{k=1}^n f\left(k\right) \;=\; 3279$, then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The functional equation $f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right)$ with $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 3$ gives $f\left(k\right) \;=\; 3^k$. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x \;+\; y\right) \;=\; f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right)$ for all $x, y \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ and $f\left(1\right) \;=\; 3$, we get $f\left(2\right) \;=\; 3^2, f\left(3\right) \;=\; 3^3, \dots, f\left(k\right) \;=\; 3^k$. Then $\sum_{k=1}^n f\left(k\right) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 3^2 \;+\; 3^3 \;+\; \dots \;+\; 3^n \;=\; 3279 \;\implies\; \frac{3\left(3^n \;-\; 1\right)}{3 \;-\; 1} \;=\; 3279 \;\implies\; \frac{3^n \;-\; 1}{2} \;=\; 1093 \;\implies\; 3^n \;-\; 1 \;=\; 2186 \;\implies\; 3^n \;=\; 2187 \;=\; 3^7 \;\implies\; n \;=\; 7$.

questions.text: The number of distinct real solutions of the equation $x\left\lvert x \;+\; 4 \right\rvert \;+\; 3\left\lvert x \;+\; 2 \right\rvert \;+\; 10 \;=\; 0$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Analyze the equation across three intervals determined by the critical points $x \;=\; -4$ and $x \;=\; -2$. // 📝 Solution: The critical points are $x \;=\; -4, -2$. Case 1: $x \;\ge\; -2 \;\implies\; x\left(x \;+\; 4\right) \;+\; 3\left(x \;+\; 2\right) \;+\; 10 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7x \;+\; 16 \;=\; 0$, which has discriminant $D \;=\; 49 \;-\; 64 \;=\; -15 \;<\; 0$ (no real roots). Case 2: $-4 \;\le\; x \;<\; -2 \;\implies\; x\left(x \;+\; 4\right) \;-\; 3\left(x \;+\; 2\right) \;+\; 10 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; x \;+\; 4 \;=\; 0$, which has $D \;=\; 1 \;-\; 16 \;=\; -15 \;<\; 0$ (no real roots). Case 3: $x \;<\; -4 \;\implies\; -x\left(x \;+\; 4\right) \;-\; 3\left(x \;+\; 2\right) \;+\; 10 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x^2 \;+\; 7x \;-\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; \frac{-7 \;\pm\; \sqrt{65}}{2}$. Only $x \;=\; \frac{-7 \;-\; \sqrt{65}}{2} \;\approx\; -7.53$ lies in $x \;<\; -4$. Thus, there is $1$ distinct real solution.

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} -a & \text{if } -a \;\le\; x \;\le\; 0 \\ x \;+\; a & \text{if } 0 \;<\; x \;\le\; a \end{cases}$ where $a \;>\; 0$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{f\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert\right) \;-\; \left\lvert f\left(x\right) \right\rvert}{2}$. Then the function $g : \left[-a, a\right] \;\to\; \left[-a, a\right]$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate $f\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert\right)$ and $\left\lvert f\left(x\right) \right\rvert$ separately on $\left[-a, 0\right]$ and $\left(0, a\right]$ to obtain $g\left(x\right)$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] From the definition of $f\left(x\right)$, for $0 \;<\; x \;\le\; a$, we have $f\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert\right) \;=\; x \;+\; a$ and $\left\lvert f\left(x\right) \right\rvert \;=\; x \;+\; a$, so $g\left(x\right) \;=\; 0$. For $-a \;\le\; x \;<\; 0$, $f\left(\left\lvert x \right\rvert\right) \;=\; -x \;+\; a$ and $\left\lvert f\left(x\right) \right\rvert \;=\; a$, so $g\left(x\right) \;=\; -\frac{x}{2}$. At $x \;=\; 0$, $g\left(0\right) \;=\; \frac{-a \;-\; a}{2} \;=\; -a$. Since $g\left(x\right) \;=\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \left(0, a\right]$ and its range is $\left\{-a\right\} \;\cup\; \left[0, \frac{a}{2}\right] \;\neq\; \left[-a, a\right]$, $g$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.text: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\left[x\right]}{1 \;+\; x^2}$, where $\left[x\right]$ is greatest integer $\;\le\; x$, is $\left[2, 6\right)$, then its range is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Break the interval $\left[2, 6\right)$ into unit sub-intervals $\left[2, 3\right), \left[3, 4\right), \left[4, 5\right), \left[5, 6\right)$ and take the union of the ranges on each piece. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] On each unit interval, $\left[x\right]$ is constant and $\frac{1}{1 \;+\; x^2}$ is strictly decreasing: For $x \;\in\; \left[2, 3\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;\in\; \left(\frac{2}{10}, \frac{2}{5}\right]$. For $x \;\in\; \left[3, 4\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{3}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;\in\; \left(\frac{3}{17}, \frac{3}{10}\right]$. For $x \;\in\; \left[4, 5\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{4}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;\in\; \left(\frac{4}{26}, \frac{4}{17}\right]$. For $x \;\in\; \left[5, 6\right)$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{5}{1 \;+\; x^2} \;\in\; \left(\frac{5}{37}, \frac{5}{26}\right]$. Since these overlapping intervals cover all values continuously from $\frac{5}{37}$ to $\frac{2}{5}$, the union is $\left(\frac{5}{37}, \frac{2}{5}\right]$.

questions.text: Let $A \;=\; \left\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 7\right\}$ and let $P\left(A\right)$ denote the power set of $A$. If the number of functions $f : A \;\to\; P\left(A\right)$ such that $a \;\in\; f\left(a\right), \forall a \;\in\; A$ is $m^n, m$ and $n \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ and $m$ is least, then $m \;+\; n$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the number of subsets of $A$ that contain a specific element $a \;\in\; A$. // 📝 Solution: For each element $a \;\in\; A$, $f\left(a\right)$ must be a subset of $A$ containing $a$. Since $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 7$, the number of subsets of $A$ that contain a fixed element $a$ is $2^{7-1} \;=\; 2^6$. Since this holds independently for each of the $7$ elements of $A$, the total number of such functions is $\left(2^6\right)^7 \;=\; 2^{42}$. For $m \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ to be least, $m \;=\; 2$ and $n \;=\; 42$, giving $m \;+\; n \;=\; 2 \;+\; 42 \;=\; 44$.

questions.text: If $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{4x \;+\; 3}{6x \;-\; 4}, x \;\neq\; \frac{2}{3}$ and $\left(f \circ f\right)\left(x\right) \;=\; g\left(x\right)$, where $g : \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{\frac{2}{3}\right\} \;\to\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{\frac{2}{3}\right\}$, then $\left(g \circ g \circ g\right)\left(4\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compute $g\left(x\right) \;=\; f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ directly; functions of the form $\frac{ax \;+\; b}{cx \;-\; a}$ are self-inverse. // 📝 Solution: Given $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{4x \;+\; 3}{6x \;-\; 4}$, we have $g\left(x\right) \;=\; f\left(f\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \frac{4\left(\frac{4x \;+\; 3}{6x \;-\; 4}\right) \;+\; 3}{6\left(\frac{4x \;+\; 3}{6x \;-\; 4}\right) \;-\; 4} \;=\; \frac{16x \;+\; 12 \;+\; 18x \;-\; 12}{24x \;+\; 18 \;-\; 24x \;+\; 16} \;=\; \frac{34x}{34} \;=\; x$. Since $g\left(x\right) \;=\; x$ is the identity function, $\left(g \circ g \circ g\right)\left(4\right) \;=\; 4$.

questions.text: The range of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \sqrt{3 \;-\; x} \;+\; \sqrt{2 \;+\; x}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Square $y \;=\; \sqrt{3 \;-\; x} \;+\; \sqrt{2 \;+\; x} \;>\; 0$ to express $y^2$ in terms of a completed square on the domain $x \;\in\; \left[-2, 3\right]$. // 📝 Solution: The domain of $f\left(x\right)$ is $x \;\in\; \left[-2, 3\right]$ and $y \;=\; f\left(x\right) \;>\; 0$. Squaring gives $y^2 \;=\; 3 \;-\; x \;+\; 2 \;+\; x \;+\; 2\sqrt{\left(3 \;-\; x\right)\left(2 \;+\; x\right)} \;=\; 5 \;+\; 2\sqrt{6 \;+\; x \;-\; x^2} \;=\; 5 \;+\; 2\sqrt{\frac{25}{4} \;-\; \left(x \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\right)^2}$. On $x \;\in\; \left[-2, 3\right]$, the maximum occurs at $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$, giving $y_{\max} \;=\; \sqrt{5 \;+\; 5} \;=\; \sqrt{10}$, and the minimum occurs at $x \;=\; -2$ or $3$, giving $y_{\min} \;=\; \sqrt{5}$. Thus, the range is $\left[\sqrt{5}, \sqrt{10}\right]$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;+\; 1}{x^2 \;+\; 1}$. Then

options.text: $f\left(x\right)$ is one-one in $\left[1, \infty\right)$ but not in $\left(-\infty, \infty\right)$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $f\left(x\right) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2x}{x^2 \;+\; 1}$ and find the intervals of monotonicity using $f'\left(x\right)$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] We have $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\left(x \;+\; 1\right)^2}{x^2 \;+\; 1} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{2x}{x^2 \;+\; 1}$. Differentiating gives $f'\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{2\left(1 \;-\; x^2\right)}{\left(x^2 \;+\; 1\right)^2}$. Thus, $f\left(x\right)$ has local extrema at $x \;=\; -1$ and $x \;=\; 1$, and is strictly decreasing on $\left[1, \infty\right)$. Therefore, $f\left(x\right)$ is one-one in $\left[1, \infty\right)$ but not in $\left(-\infty, \infty\right)$.

questions.text: The absolute minimum value, of the function $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \left\lvert x^2 \;-\; x \;+\; 1 \right\rvert \;+\; \left[x^2 \;-\; x \;+\; 1\right]$, where $\left[t\right]$ denotes the greatest integer function, in the interval $\left[-1, 2\right]$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Complete the square in $g\left(x\right) \;=\; x^2 \;-\; x \;+\; 1 \;=\; \left(x \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \;+\; \frac{3}{4}$ to find its minimum on $\left[-1, 2\right]$. // 📝 Solution: Let $g\left(x\right) \;=\; x^2 \;-\; x \;+\; 1 \;=\; \left(x \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \;+\; \frac{3}{4}$. On the interval $\left[-1, 2\right]$, both $\left\lvert g\left(x\right) \right\rvert$ and $\left[g\left(x\right)\right]$ attain their minimum value simultaneously at $x \;=\; \frac{1}{2}$, where $g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$. Thus, the minimum value of $f\left(x\right)$ is $\left\lvert \frac{3}{4} \right\rvert \;+\; \left[\frac{3}{4}\right] \;=\; \frac{3}{4} \;+\; 0 \;=\; \frac{3}{4}$.

questions.text: Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$ be defined as: $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \left\lvert x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$ and $g\left(x\right) \;=\; \begin{cases} e^x, & x \;\ge\; 0 \\ x \;+\; 1, & x \;\le\; 0 \end{cases}$. Then the function $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Construct the piecewise expression for $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \left\lvert g\left(x\right) \;-\; 1 \right\rvert$ for $x \;\ge\; 0$ and $x \;\le\; 0$. // 📝 Solution: We have $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) \;=\; \left\lvert g\left(x\right) \;-\; 1 \right\rvert \;=\; \begin{cases} \left\lvert e^x \;-\; 1 \right\rvert, & x \;\ge\; 0 \\ \left\lvert x \;+\; 1 \;-\; 1 \right\rvert, & x \;\le\; 0 \end{cases} \;=\; \begin{cases} e^x \;-\; 1, & x \;\ge\; 0 \\ -x, & x \;\le\; 0 \end{cases}$. [FIGURE] From the graph of $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)$, it is decreasing for $x \;\le\; 0$ and increasing for $x \;\ge\; 0$, and its range is $\left[0, \infty\right) \;\neq\; \mathbb{R}$. Hence, $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.text: Let $f$ be a function such that $3f\left(x\right) \;+\; 2f\left(\frac{m}{19x}\right) \;=\; 5x, x \;\neq\; 0$, where $m \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^9 \left(i\right)^2$. Then $f\left(5\right) \;-\; f\left(2\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Calculate $m \;=\; \frac{9 \cdot 10 \cdot 19}{6} \;=\; 285$, then replace $x$ by $\frac{15}{x}$ to eliminate $f\left(\frac{15}{x}\right)$. // 📝 Solution: We have $m \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^9 i^2 \;=\; \frac{9 \cdot 10 \cdot 19}{6} \;=\; 285$, so $\frac{m}{19} \;=\; 15$. The given equation is $3f\left(x\right) \;+\; 2f\left(\frac{15}{x}\right) \;=\; 5x$ ...(i). Replacing $x$ by $\frac{15}{x}$ gives $3f\left(\frac{15}{x}\right) \;+\; 2f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{75}{x}$ ...(ii). Taking $3 \times \text{(i)} \;-\; 2 \times \text{(ii)}$ yields $5f\left(x\right) \;=\; 15x \;-\; \frac{150}{x} \;\implies\; f\left(x\right) \;=\; 3x \;-\; \frac{30}{x}$. Thus, $f\left(5\right) \;=\; 15 \;-\; 6 \;=\; 9$ and $f\left(2\right) \;=\; 6 \;-\; 15 \;=\; -9$, giving $f\left(5\right) \;-\; f\left(2\right) \;=\; 9 \;-\; \left(-9\right) \;=\; 18$.

questions.text: Consider two sets $A \;=\; \left\{x \;\in\; \mathbb{Z} : \left\lvert \left(\left\lvert x \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;-\; 3\right) \right\rvert \;\le\; 1\right\}$ and $B \;=\; \left\{x \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{1, 2\right\} : \frac{\left(x \;-\; 2\right)\left(x \;-\; 4\right)}{x \;-\; 1}\log_e\left(\left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert\right) \;=\; 0\right\}$. Then the number of onto functions $f : A \;\to\; B$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the number of elements in $A$ and $B$; if $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; m$ and $\left\lvert B \right\rvert \;=\; 2$, the number of onto functions is $2^m \;-\; 2$. // 📝 Solution: For set $A$: $\left\lvert \left\lvert x \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;\le\; 1 \;\implies\; 2 \;\le\; \left\lvert x \;-\; 3 \right\rvert \;\le\; 4$. For $x \;\ge\; 3$, $5 \;\le\; x \;\le\; 7 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left\{5, 6, 7\right\}$. For $x \;<\; 3$, $-1 \;\le\; x \;\le\; 1 \;\implies\; x \;\in\; \left\{-1, 0, 1\right\}$. Thus, $A \;=\; \left\{-1, 0, 1, 5, 6, 7\right\}$ and $\left\lvert A \right\rvert \;=\; 6$. For set $B$: With $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R} \;-\; \left\{1, 2\right\}$, either $x \;-\; 4 \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 4$ or $\log_e\left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert \;=\; 0 \;\implies\; \left\lvert x \;-\; 2 \right\rvert \;=\; 1 \;\implies\; x \;=\; 3$ (since $x \;\neq\; 1$). Thus, $B \;=\; \left\{3, 4\right\}$ and $\left\lvert B \right\rvert \;=\; 2$. The number of onto functions from $A$ to $B$ is $2^6 \;-\; 2 \;=\; 62$.

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{7 \;-\; \sin 5x}$ be a function defined on $\mathbb{R}$. Then the range of the function $f\left(x\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the standard bound $-1 \;\le\; \sin 5x \;\le\; 1$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. // 📝 Solution: Since $\sin 5x \;\in\; \left[-1, 1\right]$, we have $-\sin 5x \;\in\; \left[-1, 1\right]$. Adding $7$ gives $7 \;-\; \sin 5x \;\in\; \left[6, 8\right]$. Taking the reciprocal yields $\frac{1}{7 \;-\; \sin 5x} \;\in\; \left[\frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{6}\right]$.

questions.text: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \;\to\; \mathbb{R}$, $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 15}{x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; 9}, x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Check the roots of the numerator for injectivity and find the range using the discriminant condition $D \;\ge\; 0$ for surjectivity. // 📝 Solution: Factoring the numerator gives $f\left(x\right) \;=\; \frac{\left(x \;+\; 5\right)\left(x \;-\; 3\right)}{x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; 9}$. Note that $x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; 9 \;>\; 0$ for all $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$. [FIGURE] Since $f\left(-5\right) \;=\; 0$ and $f\left(3\right) \;=\; 0$, $f\left(x\right)$ is many-one. Again, let $y \;=\; \frac{x^2 \;+\; 2x \;-\; 15}{x^2 \;-\; 4x \;+\; 9} \;\implies\; x^2\left(y \;-\; 1\right) \;-\; 2x\left(2y \;+\; 1\right) \;+\; \left(9y \;+\; 15\right) \;=\; 0$. Since $x \;\in\; \mathbb{R}$, $D \;=\; 4\left(2y \;+\; 1\right)^2 \;-\; 4\left(y \;-\; 1\right)\left(9y \;+\; 15\right) \;\ge\; 0 \;\implies\; 5y^2 \;+\; 2y \;-\; 16 \;\le\; 0 \;\implies\; \left(5y \;-\; 8\right)\left(y \;+\; 2\right) \;\le\; 0$. [FIGURE] Thus, the range is $y \;\in\; \left[-2, \frac{8}{5}\right] \;\neq\; \mathbb{R}$. Therefore, $f\left(x\right)$ is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.text: Number of solutions of $\sqrt{3} \cos 2\theta \; + \; 8 \cos \theta \; + \; 3\sqrt{3} \; = \; 0$, $\theta \; \in \; \left[ -3\pi, 2\pi \right]$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\cos 2\theta \; = \; 2\cos^{2} \theta \; - \; 1$ to get a quadratic in $\cos \theta$ and reject values outside $\left[ -1, 1 \right]$. // 📝 Solution: $\sqrt{3} \left( 2\cos^{2} \theta \; - \; 1 \right) \; + \; 8\cos \theta \; + \; 3\sqrt{3} \; = \; 0 \implies \sqrt{3} \cos^{2} \theta \; + \; 4\cos \theta \; + \; \sqrt{3} \; = \; 0$. So $\cos \theta \; = \; \frac{-4 \; \pm \; 2}{2\sqrt{3}}$, giving $\cos \theta \; = \; -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ or $\cos \theta \; = \; -\sqrt{3}$ (rejected). Let $\alpha \; = \; \cos^{-1} \left( -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) \; \approx \; 2.186$ rad. The general solution is $\theta \; = \; 2n\pi \; \pm \; \alpha$. In $\left[ -3\pi, 2\pi \right]$ the solutions are $\alpha, \; -\alpha, \; 2\pi \; - \; \alpha, \; -2\pi \; + \; \alpha, \; -2\pi \; - \; \alpha$. Hence there are $5$ solutions.

questions.text: If $\alpha$, $-\frac{\pi}{2} \; < \; \alpha \; < \; \frac{\pi}{2}$ is the solution of $4 \cos \theta \; + \; 5 \sin \theta \; = \; 1$, then the value of $\tan \alpha$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Divide by $\cos \theta$ to get $4 \; + \; 5\tan \theta \; = \; \sec \theta$, square it, and reject the root that makes $\sec \theta$ negative. // 📝 Solution: Divide by $\cos \theta$: $4 \; + \; 5\tan \theta \; = \; \sec \theta$. Squaring gives $16 \; + \; 40\tan \theta \; + \; 25\tan^{2} \theta \; = \; 1 \; + \; \tan^{2} \theta \implies 24\tan^{2} \theta \; + \; 40\tan \theta \; + \; 15 \; = \; 0$. So $\tan \theta \; = \; \frac{-40 \; \pm \; \sqrt{160}}{48} \; = \; \frac{-10 \; \pm \; \sqrt{10}}{12}$. For $\theta \; \in \; \left( -\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$, $\sec \theta \; > \; 0$. For $\tan \theta \; = \; -\frac{10 \; + \; \sqrt{10}}{12}$, $\sec \theta \; = \; 4 \; + \; 5\tan \theta \; = \; \frac{-2 \; - \; 5\sqrt{10}}{12} \; < \; 0$, so it is rejected. Hence $\tan \alpha \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{10} \; - \; 10}{12}$.

questions.text: Let the set of all $a \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$ such that the equation $\cos 2x \; + \; a \sin x \; = \; 2a \; - \; 7$ has a solution be $\left[ p, q \right]$ and $r \; = \; \tan 9^{\circ} \; - \; \tan 27^{\circ} \; - \; \frac{1}{\cot 63^{\circ}} \; + \; \tan 81^{\circ}$, then $pqr$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $\cos 2x \; = \; 1 \; - \; 2\sin^{2} x$ and factor out $\left( \sin x \; - \; 2 \right)$; for $r$ use $\tan \theta \; + \; \cot \theta \; = \; \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}$. // 📝 Solution: $\cos 2x \; + \; a \sin x \; = \; 2a \; - \; 7$ becomes $8 \; - \; 2\sin^{2} x \; + \; a \left( \sin x \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; 0$. So $a \left( \sin x \; - \; 2 \right) \; = \; 2 \left( \sin x \; - \; 2 \right) \left( \sin x \; + \; 2 \right)$. Since $\sin x \; \ne \; 2$, $a \; = \; 2 \left( \sin x \; + \; 2 \right)$. With $\sin x \; \in \; \left[ -1, 1 \right]$ we get $a \; \in \; \left[ 2, 6 \right]$, so $p \; = \; 2$ and $q \; = \; 6$. Next, $\frac{1}{\cot 63^{\circ}} \; = \; \tan 63^{\circ} \; = \; \cot 27^{\circ}$ and $\tan 81^{\circ} \; = \; \cot 9^{\circ}$. So $r \; = \; \left( \tan 9^{\circ} \; + \; \cot 9^{\circ} \right) \; - \; \left( \tan 27^{\circ} \; + \; \cot 27^{\circ} \right) \; = \; \frac{2}{\sin 18^{\circ}} \; - \; \frac{2}{\sin 54^{\circ}}$. Using $\sin 18^{\circ} \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{5} \; - \; 1}{4}$ and $\sin 54^{\circ} \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{5} \; + \; 1}{4}$: $r \; = \; 2 \left( \sqrt{5} \; + \; 1 \right) \; - \; 2 \left( \sqrt{5} \; - \; 1 \right) \; = \; 4$. Therefore $pqr \; = \; 2 \; \times \; 6 \; \times \; 4 \; = \; 48$.

questions.text: If $2 \sin^{3} x \; + \; \sin 2x \cos x \; + \; 4 \sin x \; - \; 4 \; = \; 0$ has exactly 3 solutions in the interval $\left[ 0, \frac{n\pi}{2} \right]$, $n \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$, then the roots of the equation $x^{2} \; + \; nx \; + \; \left( n \; - \; 3 \right) \; = \; 0$ belong to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sin 2x \; = \; 2\sin x \cos x$ and $\cos^{2} x \; = \; 1 \; - \; \sin^{2} x$ to reduce the equation to a linear one in $\sin x$. // 📝 Solution: $2\sin^{3} x \; + \; 2\sin x \left( 1 \; - \; \sin^{2} x \right) \; + \; 4\sin x \; - \; 4 \; = \; 0 \implies 6\sin x \; - \; 4 \; = \; 0 \implies \sin x \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$. The solutions are $\alpha, \; \pi \; - \; \alpha, \; 2\pi \; + \; \alpha, \; 3\pi \; - \; \alpha, \ldots$ where $\alpha \; \approx \; 0.73$. For exactly 3 solutions we need $2\pi \; + \; \alpha \; \le \; \frac{n\pi}{2} \; < \; 3\pi \; - \; \alpha$, which gives $n \; = \; 5$. The equation becomes $x^{2} \; + \; 5x \; + \; 2 \; = \; 0$, so $x \; = \; \frac{-5 \; \pm \; \sqrt{17}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{17} \; < \; 5$, both roots are negative, so the roots lie in $\left( -\infty, 0 \right)$.

questions.text: Suppose $\theta \in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{4} \right]$ is a solution of $4 \cos \theta \; - \; 3 \sin \theta \; = \; 1$. Then $\cos \theta$ is equal to :
The number of solutions of $\sin^{2} x \; + \; \left( 2 \; + \; 2x \; - \; x^{2} \right) \sin x \; - \; 3 \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \; = \; 0$, where $-\pi \; \le \; x \; \le \; \pi$, is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Treat the equation as a quadratic in $\sin x$ and factorise it, then compare $\sin x$ with $\left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2}$ graphically. // 📝 Solution: Write $2 \; + \; 2x \; - \; x^{2} \; = \; 3 \; - \; \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2}$. The equation becomes $\sin^{2} x \; + \; \left( 3 \; - \; \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \right) \sin x \; - \; 3 \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \; = \; 0$. It factorises as $\left( \sin x \; + \; 3 \right) \left( \sin x \; - \; \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \right) \; = \; 0$. Since $\sin x \; = \; -3$ is impossible, we need $\sin x \; = \; \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2}$. [FIGURE] Graph of $y \; = \; \sin x$ and $y \; = \; \left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2}$ for $x \; \in \; \left[ -\pi, \pi \right]$. For $x \; < \; 0$ or $x \; > \; 2$, $\left( x \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \; > \; 1 \; \ge \; \sin x$, so there is no solution. In $\left[ 0, 2 \right]$, the parabola (vertex at $\left( 1, 0 \right)$) cuts the sine curve once in $\left( 0, 1 \right)$ and once in $\left( 1, 2 \right)$. So the number of solutions is $2$.

questions.text: If $m$ and $n$ respectively are the numbers of positive and negative values of $\theta$ in the interval $\left[ -\pi, \pi \right]$ that satisfy the equation $\cos 2\theta \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \; = \; \cos 3\theta \cos \frac{9\theta}{2}$, then $mn$ is equal to ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Multiply by 2 and use $2\cos A \cos B \; = \; \cos \left( A + B \right) \; + \; \cos \left( A - B \right)$ on both sides. // 📝 Solution: $2\cos 2\theta \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \; = \; 2\cos \frac{9\theta}{2} \cos 3\theta$ gives $\cos \frac{5\theta}{2} \; + \; \cos \frac{3\theta}{2} \; = \; \cos \frac{15\theta}{2} \; + \; \cos \frac{3\theta}{2}$. So $\cos \frac{15\theta}{2} \; = \; \cos \frac{5\theta}{2}$, hence $\frac{15\theta}{2} \; = \; 2k\pi \; \pm \; \frac{5\theta}{2}$. This gives $5\theta \; = \; 2k\pi$ or $10\theta \; = \; 2k\pi$, i.e. $\theta \; = \; \frac{2k\pi}{5}$ or $\theta \; = \; \frac{k\pi}{5}$. Together, $\theta \; = \; \frac{k\pi}{5}$. In $\left[ -\pi, \pi \right]$: $\theta \; = \; -\pi, -\frac{4\pi}{5}, -\frac{3\pi}{5}, -\frac{2\pi}{5}, -\frac{\pi}{5}, 0, \frac{\pi}{5}, \frac{2\pi}{5}, \frac{3\pi}{5}, \frac{4\pi}{5}, \pi$. So $m \; = \; 5$ and $n \; = \; 5$, and $mn \; = \; 25$.

questions.text: If $2 \tan^{2} \theta \; - \; 5 \sec \theta \; = \; 1$ has exactly 7 solutions in the interval $\left[ 0, \frac{n\pi}{2} \right]$, for the least value of $n \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$, then $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k}{2^{k}}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Reduce to a quadratic in $\sec \theta$, find $n$ by counting solutions, then use the arithmetico-geometric series trick $S \; - \; \frac{S}{2}$. // 📝 Solution: $2 \tan^{2} \theta \; - \; 5 \sec \theta \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies 2\sec^{2} \theta \; - \; 5\sec \theta \; - \; 3 \; = \; 0 \implies \left( 2\sec \theta \; + \; 1 \right) \left( \sec \theta \; - \; 3 \right) \; = \; 0$. So $\sec \theta \; = \; -\frac{1}{2}$ (rejected, as $\cos \theta \; = \; -2$) or $\sec \theta \; = \; 3$, i.e. $\cos \theta \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. The solutions are $\theta \; = \; 2m\pi \; \pm \; \alpha$ with $\alpha \; \in \; \left( 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$: $\alpha, \; 2\pi \; - \; \alpha, \; 2\pi \; + \; \alpha, \; 4\pi \; - \; \alpha, \; 4\pi \; + \; \alpha, \; 6\pi \; - \; \alpha, \; 6\pi \; + \; \alpha$. The 7th solution $6\pi \; + \; \alpha$ first lies in $\left[ 0, \frac{n\pi}{2} \right]$ when $\frac{n\pi}{2} \; \ge \; 6\pi \; + \; \alpha$, i.e. $n \; = \; 13$. Let $S \; = \; \sum_{k=1}^{13} \frac{k}{2^{k}}$. Then $\frac{S}{2} \; = \; \sum_{k=1}^{13} \frac{1}{2^{k}} \; - \; \frac{13}{2^{14}} \; = \; \left( 1 \; - \; \frac{1}{2^{13}} \right) \; - \; \frac{13}{2^{14}}$. So $S \; = \; 2 \; - \; \frac{2}{2^{13}} \; - \; \frac{13}{2^{13}} \; = \; 2 \; - \; \frac{15}{2^{13}} \; = \; \frac{1}{2^{13}} \left( 2^{14} \; - \; 15 \right)$.

questions.text: The sum of the solutions $x \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$ of the equation $\frac{3\cos 2x \; + \; \cos^{3} 2x}{\cos^{6} x \; - \; \sin^{6} x} \; = \; x^{3} \; - \; x^{2} \; + \; 6$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor $\cos^{6} x \; - \; \sin^{6} x \; = \; \left( \cos^{2} x \; - \; \sin^{2} x \right) \left( \cos^{4} x \; + \; \sin^{2} x \cos^{2} x \; + \; \sin^{4} x \right)$ to simplify the left side to a constant. // 📝 Solution: $\cos^{6} x \; - \; \sin^{6} x \; = \; \cos 2x \left( 1 \; - \; \sin^{2} x \cos^{2} x \right) \; = \; \cos 2x \cdot \frac{4 \; - \; \sin^{2} 2x}{4}$. The numerator is $\cos 2x \left( 3 \; + \; \cos^{2} 2x \right)$. Since $4 \; - \; \sin^{2} 2x \; = \; 3 \; + \; \cos^{2} 2x$, the left side equals $\frac{4 \cos 2x \left( 3 \; + \; \cos^{2} 2x \right)}{\cos 2x \left( 3 \; + \; \cos^{2} 2x \right)} \; = \; 4$. So $x^{3} \; - \; x^{2} \; + \; 6 \; = \; 4 \implies x^{3} \; - \; x^{2} \; + \; 2 \; = \; 0 \implies \left( x \; + \; 1 \right) \left( x^{2} \; - \; 2x \; + \; 2 \right) \; = \; 0$. The quadratic has discriminant $-4 \; < \; 0$, so the only real solution is $x \; = \; -1$ (valid, as $\cos \left( -2 \right) \; \ne \; 0$). Hence the sum of solutions is $-1$.

questions.text: Let $f \left( \theta \right) \; = \; 3 \left( \sin^{4} \left( \frac{3\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta \right) \; + \; \sin^{4} \left( 3\pi \; + \; \theta \right) \right) \; - \; 2 \left( 1 \; - \; \sin^{2} 2\theta \right)$ and $S \; = \; \left\{ \theta \; \in \; \left[ 0, \pi \right] \; : \; f' \left( \theta \right) \; = \; -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right\}$. If $4\beta \; = \; \sum_{\theta \in S} \theta$, then $f \left( \beta \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Reduce $f \left( \theta \right)$ to the form $\frac{5}{4} \; - \; \frac{\cos 4\theta}{4}$ using $\sin^{4} \theta \; + \; \cos^{4} \theta \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \sin^{2} 2\theta$. // 📝 Solution: $\sin \left( \frac{3\pi}{2} \; - \; \theta \right) \; = \; - \cos \theta$ and $\sin \left( 3\pi \; + \; \theta \right) \; = \; - \sin \theta$. So $f \left( \theta \right) \; = \; 3 \left( \cos^{4} \theta \; + \; \sin^{4} \theta \right) \; - \; 2\cos^{2} 2\theta \; = \; 3 \left( 1 \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \sin^{2} 2\theta \right) \; - \; 2\cos^{2} 2\theta \; = \; \frac{3}{2} \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \cos^{2} 2\theta \; = \; \frac{5}{4} \; - \; \frac{\cos 4\theta}{4}$. Then $f' \left( \theta \right) \; = \; \sin 4\theta$. Solving $\sin 4\theta \; = \; -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $4\theta \; \in \; \left[ 0, 4\pi \right]$ gives $4\theta \; = \; \frac{4\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}, \frac{10\pi}{3}, \frac{11\pi}{3}$, i.e. $\theta \; = \; \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{12}, \frac{5\pi}{6}, \frac{11\pi}{12}$. Their sum is $\frac{30\pi}{12} \; = \; \frac{5\pi}{2}$, so $4\beta \; = \; \frac{5\pi}{2}$ and $\beta \; = \; \frac{5\pi}{8}$. Then $f \left( \beta \right) \; = \; \frac{5}{4} \; - \; \frac{\cos \frac{5\pi}{2}}{4} \; = \; \frac{5}{4} \; - \; 0 \; = \; \frac{5}{4}$.

questions.text: The number of solutions of the equation $4 \sin^{2} x \; - \; 4 \cos^{3} x \; + \; 9 \; - \; 4 \cos x \; = \; 0$; $x \; \in \; \left[ -2\pi, 2\pi \right]$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert to a cubic in $\cos x$ using $\sin^{2} x \; = \; 1 \; - \; \cos^{2} x$ and use the bound $-1 \; \le \; \cos x \; \le \; 1$. // 📝 Solution: Using $\sin^{2} x \; = \; 1 \; - \; \cos^{2} x$: $4 \; - \; 4\cos^{2} x \; - \; 4\cos^{3} x \; + \; 9 \; - \; 4\cos x \; = \; 0$. This gives $4\cos^{3} x \; + \; 4\cos^{2} x \; + \; 4\cos x \; = \; 13$. Let $g \left( c \right) \; = \; 4c^{3} \; + \; 4c^{2} \; + \; 4c$ with $c \; = \; \cos x \; \in \; \left[ -1, 1 \right]$. Then $g' \left( c \right) \; = \; 12c^{2} \; + \; 8c \; + \; 4 \; > \; 0$ (since the discriminant is negative), so $g$ is increasing. Hence $g_{max} \; = \; g \left( 1 \right) \; = \; 12 \; < \; 13$. So the equation has no solution and the number of solutions is $0$.

questions.text: The number of elements in the set $\left\{ x \; \in \; \left[ 0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ} \right] \; : \; \tan \left( x \; + \; 100^{\circ} \right) \; = \; \tan \left( x \; + \; 50^{\circ} \right) \tan x \tan \left( x \; - \; 50^{\circ} \right) \right\}$ is ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write it as $\frac{\tan \left( x + 100^{\circ} \right)}{\tan x} \; = \; \tan \left( x + 50^{\circ} \right) \tan \left( x - 50^{\circ} \right)$ and apply componendo and dividendo. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\sin \left( x + 100^{\circ} \right) \cos x}{\cos \left( x + 100^{\circ} \right) \sin x} \; = \; \frac{\sin \left( x + 50^{\circ} \right) \sin \left( x - 50^{\circ} \right)}{\cos \left( x + 50^{\circ} \right) \cos \left( x - 50^{\circ} \right)}$. Applying componendo and dividendo: $\frac{\sin \left( 2x + 100^{\circ} \right)}{\sin 100^{\circ}} \; = \; \frac{\cos 100^{\circ}}{- \cos 2x}$. So $2\sin \left( 2x + 100^{\circ} \right) \cos 2x \; + \; \sin 200^{\circ} \; = \; 0$, i.e. $\sin \left( 4x + 100^{\circ} \right) \; + \; \sin 100^{\circ} \; + \; \sin 200^{\circ} \; = \; 0$. Since $\sin 100^{\circ} \; + \; \sin 200^{\circ} \; = \; 2\sin 150^{\circ} \cos 50^{\circ} \; = \; \cos 50^{\circ}$, we get $\sin \left( 4x + 100^{\circ} \right) \; = \; - \cos 50^{\circ} \; = \; \sin \left( -40^{\circ} \right)$. Then $4x \; + \; 100^{\circ} \; = \; n\pi \; + \; \left( -1 \right)^{n} \left( -40^{\circ} \right)$, so $x \; = \; \frac{n\pi \; + \; \left( -1 \right)^{n+1} 40^{\circ} \; - \; 100^{\circ}}{4}$. The values in $\left[ 0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ} \right]$ are $x \; = \; 30^{\circ}, \; 55^{\circ}, \; 120^{\circ}, \; 145^{\circ}$, and none of them makes a tangent undefined. Hence the number of elements is $4$.

questions.text: Let $S \; = \; \left\{ \sin^{2} 2\theta \; : \; \left( \sin^{4} \theta \; + \; \cos^{4} \theta \right) x^{2} \; + \; \left( \sin 2\theta \right) x \; + \; \left( \sin^{6} \theta \; + \; \cos^{6} \theta \right) \; = \; 0 \text{ has real roots} \right\}$. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the smallest and largest elements of the set $S$, respectively, then $3 \left( \left( \alpha \; - \; 2 \right)^{2} \; + \; \left( \beta \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \right)$ equals ______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sin^{4} \theta \; + \; \cos^{4} \theta \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \sin^{2} 2\theta$ and $\sin^{6} \theta \; + \; \cos^{6} \theta \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{3}{4} \sin^{2} 2\theta$, then apply $D \; \ge \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Let $s \; = \; \sin^{2} 2\theta$. Then the equation is $\left( 1 \; - \; \frac{s}{2} \right) x^{2} \; + \; \left( \sin 2\theta \right) x \; + \; \left( 1 \; - \; \frac{3s}{4} \right) \; = \; 0$. For real roots, $D \; = \; s \; - \; 4 \left( 1 \; - \; \frac{s}{2} \right) \left( 1 \; - \; \frac{3s}{4} \right) \; = \; - \frac{3}{2} s^{2} \; + \; 6s \; - \; 4 \; \ge \; 0$. So $3s^{2} \; - \; 12s \; + \; 8 \; \le \; 0 \implies s \; \in \; \left[ 2 \; - \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \; 2 \; + \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right]$. Since $s \; \in \; \left[ 0, 1 \right]$, we get $S \; = \; \left[ 2 \; - \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \; 1 \right]$. Hence $\alpha \; = \; 2 \; - \; \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\beta \; = \; 1$. So $\left( \alpha \; - \; 2 \right)^{2} \; = \; \frac{4}{3}$ and $\left( \beta \; - \; 1 \right)^{2} \; = \; 0$. Therefore $3 \left( \frac{4}{3} \; + \; 0 \right) \; = \; 4$.
