questions.text: The mean and variance of $7$ observations are $8$ and $16$ respectively. If one observation $14$ is omitted, and $a$ and $b$ are respectively the mean and variance of the remaining $6$ observations, then $a \; + \; 3b \; - \; 5$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\sum x_i \; = \; n\bar{x}$ and $\sum x_i^2 \; = \; n\left( \sigma^2 \; + \; \bar{x}^2 \right)$, then remove the omitted observation from both sums. // 📝 Solution: $\sum x_i \; = \; 7 \times 8 \; = \; 56$, so for the remaining six $\sum x_i \; = \; 56 \; - \; 14 \; = \; 42$ and $a \; = \; \frac{42}{6} \; = \; 7$. $\sum x_i^2 \; = \; 7\left( 16 \; + \; 64 \right) \; = \; 560$, so the remaining sum of squares is $560 \; - \; 196 \; = \; 364$. Then $b \; = \; \frac{364}{6} \; - \; 49 \; = \; \frac{70}{6} \; = \; \frac{35}{3}$. Therefore $a \; + \; 3b \; - \; 5 \; = \; 7 \; + \; 35 \; - \; 5 \; = \; 37$.
questions.topic: Mean and variance after removing an observation

questions.text: Let $a,\; b,\; c \in N$ and $a \; < \; b \; < \; c$. Let the mean, the mean deviation about the mean and the variance of the $5$ observations $9,\; 25,\; a,\; b,\; c$ be $18$, $4$ and $\frac{136}{5}$, respectively. Then $2a \; + \; b \; - \; c$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the mean to get $a + b + c$, then use the mean deviation and variance conditions on $\left( 18 - a \right)$, $\left( 18 - b \right)$, $\left( 18 - c \right)$. // 📝 Solution: Mean: $\frac{9 + 25 + a + b + c}{5} \; = \; 18 \implies a \; + \; b \; + \; c \; = \; 56$. Mean deviation: $\frac{9 + 7 + \left\lvert 18 - a \right\rvert + \left\lvert 18 - b \right\rvert + \left\lvert 18 - c \right\rvert}{5} \; = \; 4 \implies \left\lvert 18 - a \right\rvert + \left\lvert 18 - b \right\rvert + \left\lvert 18 - c \right\rvert \; = \; 4$. Variance: $\frac{81 + 49 + \left( 18 - a \right)^2 + \left( 18 - b \right)^2 + \left( 18 - c \right)^2}{5} \; = \; \frac{136}{5} \implies \left( 18 - a \right)^2 + \left( 18 - b \right)^2 + \left( 18 - c \right)^2 \; = \; 6$. With absolute values summing to $4$ and squares summing to $6$, the squares are $1,\; 1,\; 4$. Since $a < b < c$ and the deviations sum to zero, $18 - a \; = \; 1$, $18 - b \; = \; -1$, $18 - c \; = \; -2$, giving $a \; = \; 17$, $b \; = \; 19$, $c \; = \; 20$. Then $2a \; + \; b \; - \; c \; = \; 34 \; + \; 19 \; - \; 20 \; = \; 33$.

questions.text: For a statistical data $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{10}$ of $10$ values, a student obtained the mean as $5.5$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{10}x_i^2=371$. He later found that he had noted two values in the data incorrectly as $4$ and $5$, instead of the correct values $6$ and $8$, respectively. The variance of the corrected data is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Correct $\sum x_i$ and $\sum x_i^2$ first, then use $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}-\left(\text{mean}\right)^2$. // 📝 Solution: $\sum x_i=55-9+14=60\;;\;\sum x_i^2=371-41+100=430\;\implies\;\sigma^2=\frac{430}{10}-\left(\frac{60}{10}\right)^2=43-36=7$

questions.text: Let the Mean and Variance of five observations $x_{1}=1,\ x_{2}=3,\ x_{3}=a,\ x_{4}=7$ and $x_{5}=b,\ a>b$, be $5$ and $10$ respectively. Then the Variance of the observations $n+x_{n},\ n=1,2,\ldots,5$, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\bar{x}=5$ gives $a+b=14$, and the variance gives $a^{2}+b^{2}=116$ // 📝 Solution: $\{a,b\}=\{10,4\}$ with $a>b$, so the new observations are $2,5,13,11,9$; variance $=\dfrac{400}{5}-8^{2}\implies16$

questions.text: If the mean and the variance of $6,4,a,8,b,12,10,13$ are $9$ and $9.25$ respectively, then $a+b+ab$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: mean gives $a+b=19$; variance gives $a^{2}+b^{2}=193$ // 📝 Solution: $ab=\dfrac{361-193}{2}=84\implies a+b+ab=103$

questions.text: If the variance of the frequency distribution $x_i$ : $2,\; 3,\; 4,\; 5,\; 6,\; 7,\; 8$ with frequency $f_i$ : $3,\; 6,\; 16,\; \alpha,\; 9,\; 5,\; 6$ [FIGURE] is $3$, then $\alpha$ is equal to

Let the mean and variance of $7$ observations $2,\; 4,\; 10,\; x,\; 12,\; 14,\; y,\; x > y$, be $8$ and $16$ respectively. Two numbers are chosen from $\left\{ 1,\; 2,\; 3,\; x - 4,\; y,\; 5 \right\}$ one after another without replacement, then the probability that the smaller number among the two chosen numbers is less than $4$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Mean gives $x + y$, variance gives $\left( x - 8 \right)^2 + \left( y - 8 \right)^2$; then use the complement (both numbers at least $4$). // 📝 Solution: Mean $\; = \; 8 \implies 42 + x + y \; = \; 56 \implies x \; + \; y \; = \; 14$. Variance $\; = \; 16 \implies \sum x_i^2 \; = \; 7\left( 16 + 64 \right) \; = \; 560$, and the known squares sum to $460$, so $x^2 + y^2 \; = \; 100$, i.e. $\left( x - 8 \right)^2 + \left( y - 8 \right)^2 \; = \; 4$. Solving, $x \; = \; 8$, $y \; = \; 6$ (as $x > y$). The set becomes $\left\{ 1,\; 2,\; 3,\; 4,\; 6,\; 5 \right\}$. Total pairs $\; = \; \binom{6}{2} \; = \; 15$. The smaller number is not less than $4$ only if both numbers come from $\left\{ 4,\; 5,\; 6 \right\}$, giving $\binom{3}{2} \; = \; 3$ pairs. Required probability $\; = \; \frac{15 - 3}{15} \; = \; \frac{4}{5}$.

questions.text: Let $9 \; = \; x_1 \; < \; x_2 \; < \; \ldots \; < \; x_7$ be in an A.P. with common difference $d$. If the standard deviation of $x_1,\; x_2,\; \ldots,\; x_7$ is $4$ and the mean is $\bar{x}$, then $\bar{x} \; + \; x_6$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Variance is unchanged by shifting, so subtract $9$ from every term to get $0,\; d,\; 2d,\; \ldots,\; 6d$. // 📝 Solution: For $0,\; d,\; \ldots,\; 6d$ the mean is $\frac{21d}{7} \; = \; 3d$. Variance: $16 \; = \; \frac{1}{7}\left( 0^2 + 1^2 + \ldots + 6^2 \right)d^2 \; - \; 9d^2 \; = \; \frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{6 \cdot 7 \cdot 13}{6}\, d^2 \; - \; 9d^2 \; = \; 4d^2$. So $d^2 \; = \; 4$ and $d \; = \; 2$ (since $x_1 < x_2$). Mean $\bar{x} \; = \; 9 \; + \; 3d \; = \; 15$ and $x_6 \; = \; 9 \; + \; 5d \; = \; 19$. Therefore $\bar{x} \; + \; x_6 \; = \; 34$.

questions.text: Let $A=\left\{\theta\in[0,2\pi]:1+10\,\mathrm{Re}\left(\dfrac{2\cos\theta+i\sin\theta}{\cos\theta-3i\sin\theta}\right)=0\right\}$. Then $\sum_{\theta\in A}\theta^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: write the real part as $\dfrac{2\cos^{2}\theta-3\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta+9\sin^{2}\theta}$ // 📝 Solution: $21\cos^{2}\theta-21\sin^{2}\theta=0\implies\cos2\theta=0\implies\theta\in\left\{\tfrac\pi4,\tfrac{3\pi}4,\tfrac{5\pi}4,\tfrac{7\pi}4\right\}$; $\sum\theta^{2}=\tfrac{\pi^{2}}{16}(1+9+25+49)=\tfrac{21\pi^{2}}{4}$

questions.text: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1$. If $\dfrac{2+k^{2}z}{k+\bar z}=kz$, $k\in\mathbb{R}$, then the maximum distance of $k+ik^{2}$ from the circle $\left\lvert z-(1+2i)\right\rvert=1$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: use $\bar z=1/z$ on the unit circle to find $k$, then measure the distance to the centre // 📝 Solution: $2+k^{2}z=k^{2}z+k\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}\implies k=2$; point $2+4i=(2,4)$ is at distance $\sqrt{5}$ from centre $(1,2)$, so maximum $=\sqrt5+1$
questions.topic: Locus, modulus and distance from circle

questions.text: Let the product of $\omega_1=(8+i)\sin\theta+(7+4i)\cos\theta$ and $\omega_2=(1+8i)\sin\theta+(4+7i)\cos\theta$ be $\alpha+i\beta$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Let $p$ and $q$ be the maximum and the minimum values of $\alpha+\beta$ respectively. Then $p+q$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: the real part of $\omega_1\omega_2$ vanishes, so $\alpha=0$ and $\beta$ is a function of $2\theta$ // 📝 Solution: $\omega_1\omega_2=i\left(65\sin^{2}\theta+120\sin\theta\cos\theta+65\cos^{2}\theta\right)\implies\alpha+\beta=65+60\sin2\theta\in[5,125]\implies p+q=130$

questions.text: Let $z_1,z_2$ and $z_3$ be three complex numbers on the circle $\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1$ with $\arg(z_1)=-\frac{\pi}{4}$, $\arg(z_2)=0$ and $\arg(z_3)=\frac{\pi}{4}$. If $\left\lvert z_1\bar z_2+z_2\bar z_3+z_3\bar z_1\right\rvert^{2}=\alpha+\beta\sqrt{2}$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{Z}$, then the value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: On the unit circle $\bar z_k=\frac{1}{z_k}$, so each product is a unit complex number. // 📝 Solution: $z_1=\frac{1-i}{\sqrt2}$, $z_2=1$, $z_3=\frac{1+i}{\sqrt2}$ $\implies z_1\bar z_2+z_2\bar z_3+z_3\bar z_1=\sqrt{2}+i(1-\sqrt{2})$ $\implies \left\lvert\cdot\right\rvert^{2}=5-2\sqrt{2}$ $\implies \alpha=5,\beta=-2 \implies \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=29$

questions.text: Let the curve $z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)=4$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$, divide the region $\left\lvert z-3 \right\rvert\le 1$ into two parts of areas $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Then $\left\lvert\alpha-\beta\right\rvert$ equals :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert the curve to a Cartesian line and identify the chord of the disc. // 📝 Solution: $z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)=2(x-y)=4 \implies x-y=2$ $\implies$ chord of disc centre $(3,0)$, radius $1$ with endpoints $(2,0),(3,1)$ $\implies$ subtended angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$, minor segment $=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}$ $\implies$ difference $=\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right)=1+\frac{\pi}{2}$
questions.topic: Locus in complex plane and area of circular segment

questions.text: If the locus of $z\in\mathbb{C}$, such that $\mathrm{Re}\left(\dfrac{z-1}{2z+i}\right)+\mathrm{Re}\left(\dfrac{\bar z-1}{2\bar z-i}\right)=2$ is a circle of radius $r$ and centre $(a,b)$, then $\dfrac{15ab}{r^{2}}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\mathrm{Re}(w)+\mathrm{Re}(\bar w)$ here equals $2\mathrm{Re}(w)$; rationalise the denominator // 📝 Solution: $\mathrm{Re}\dfrac{z-1}{2z+i}=1\implies x^{2}+y^{2}+x+\tfrac32y+\tfrac12=0\implies(a,b)=\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac34\right),\ r^{2}=\tfrac5{16}\implies\dfrac{15ab}{r^{2}}=18$

questions.text: Let $O$ be the origin, the point $A$ be $z_1=\sqrt{3}+2\sqrt{2}\,i$, the point $B(z_2)$ be such that $\sqrt{3}\,\left\lvert z_2 \right\rvert=\left\lvert z_1 \right\rvert$ and $\arg(z_2)=\arg(z_1)+\frac{\pi}{6}$. Then :

options.text: $ABO$ is an obtuse angled isosceles triangle

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $\lvert z_1\rvert$, $\lvert z_2\rvert$ and the angle $\angle AOB$, then apply the cosine rule. // 📝 Solution: $OA=\sqrt{11}$, $OB=\sqrt{\frac{11}{3}}$, $\angle AOB=\frac{\pi}{6}$ $\implies AB^{2}=11+\frac{11}{3}-11=\frac{11}{3}$ $\implies AB=OB$ $\implies$ isosceles with obtuse apex angle $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ at $B$
questions.topic: Complex numbers as vectors, triangle classification

questions.text: If $\alpha$ is a root of the equation $x^{2}+x+1=0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\alpha^{k}+\dfrac{1}{\alpha^{k}}\right)^{2}=20$, then $n$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\alpha^{3}=1$, so each term reduces to $\alpha^{2k}+\alpha^{k}+2$ and the partial sums have period 3 // 📝 Solution: $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\alpha^{2k}+\alpha^{k}+2)=2n+S_n$ with $S_9=0,\ S_{10}=-1,\ S_{11}=-2\implies 2n+S_n=20\implies n=11$
questions.topic: Roots of unity and power sums

questions.text: Let $\left\lvert z_1-8-2i \right\rvert\le 1$ and $\left\lvert z_2-2+6i \right\rvert\le 2$, $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb{C}$. Then the minimum value of $\left\lvert z_1-z_2 \right\rvert$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The minimum distance between two discs is the distance between centres minus the sum of radii. // 📝 Solution: Centres $A(8,2)$ and $B(2,-6)$ $\implies AB=\sqrt{36+64}=10$ $\implies \min\left\lvert z_1-z_2\right\rvert=10-1-2=7$
questions.topic: Locus of complex numbers, discs and distance

questions.text: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^{2}-ax-b=0$ with $\operatorname{Im}(\alpha)<\operatorname{Im}(\beta)$. Let $P_n=\alpha^{n}-\beta^{n}$. If $P_3=-5\sqrt{7}\,i$, $P_4=-3\sqrt{7}\,i$, $P_5=11\sqrt{7}\,i$ and $P_6=45\sqrt{7}\,i$, then $\left\lvert\alpha^{4}+\beta^{4}\right\rvert$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $P_n$ obeys the recurrence $P_n=aP_{n-1}+bP_{n-2}$ with $a=\alpha+\beta$ and $b=-\alpha\beta$. // 📝 Solution: $11=-3a-5b$ and $45=11a-3b$ $\implies a=3,\; b=-4$ $\implies \alpha+\beta=3,\; \alpha\beta=4$ $\implies \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=1$ $\implies \alpha^{4}+\beta^{4}=1-2(16)=-31$ $\implies \left\lvert\alpha^{4}+\beta^{4}\right\rvert=31$

questions.text: Among the statements (S1): the set $\{z\in\mathbb{C}-\{-i\}:\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1\text{ and }\frac{z-i}{z+i}\text{ is purely real}\}$ contains exactly two elements, and (S2): the set $\{z\in\mathbb{C}-\{-1\}:\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1\text{ and }\frac{z-1}{z+1}\text{ is purely imaginary}\}$ contains infinitely many elements. Then
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: for $\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1$, use $\bar z=1/z$ to test each ratio // 📝 Solution: $\dfrac{z-i}{z+i}$ real with $\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1\implies z^{2}=-1$, and $z=-i$ is excluded, so only $z=i$ (one element); $\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ is purely imaginary for all $\left\lvert z\right\rvert=1$, $z\ne-1$, so infinitely many

questions.text: Let $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\left\lvert z-2-i\right\rvert=3\}$, $B=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(z-iz)=2\}$ and $S=A\cap B$. Then $\sum_{z\in S}\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: write $z=x+iy$; $B$ is the line $x+y=2$ and $A$ is a circle // 📝 Solution: $(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=9$ with $x+y=2\implies x^{2}-3x-2=0$, giving $x^{2}+y^{2}=11\pm\sqrt{17}$ at the two points; $\sum\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}=22$

questions.text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation $2z^{2}-3z-2i=0$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then $16\cdot\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right)\cdot\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Each root satisfies $\alpha-\frac{i}{\alpha}=\frac{3}{2}$; find $\alpha^{4}+\frac{1}{\alpha^{4}}$. // 📝 Solution: $\alpha^{4}+\frac{1}{\alpha^{4}}=\frac{49}{16}+9i$ (same for $\beta$) $\implies \frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}=\frac{49}{16}+9i$ $\implies 16\cdot\frac{49}{16}\cdot9=441$
questions.topic: Powers of roots of quadratic with complex coefficients

questions.text: The number of complex numbers $z$, satisfying $\left\lvert z \right\rvert=1$ and $\left\lvert \frac{z}{\bar{z}}+\frac{\bar{z}}{z} \right\rvert=1$, is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: On $\lvert z\rvert=1$ we have $\bar z=\frac{1}{z}$, so $\frac{z}{\bar z}+\frac{\bar z}{z}=z^{2}+\bar z^{2}$. // 📝 Solution: $z=e^{i\theta} \implies z^{2}+\bar z^{2}=2\cos 2\theta$ $\implies \left\lvert\cos 2\theta\right\rvert=\frac{1}{2}$ $\implies 2\theta\in[0,4\pi)$ has $4+4=8$ solutions $\implies 8$ complex numbers
questions.topic: Unit circle and modulus of complex expressions

questions.text: Let $\left\lvert \frac{\bar z-i}{2\bar z+i} \right\rvert=\frac{1}{3}$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$, be the equation of a circle with centre at $C$. If the area of the triangle whose vertices are at $(0,0)$, $C$ and $(\alpha,0)$ is $11$ square units, then $\alpha^{2}$ equals:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Convert the condition to $3\lvert\bar z-i\rvert=\lvert 2\bar z+i\rvert$ and find the centre. // 📝 Solution: With $z=x+iy$: $9\left(x^{2}+(y+1)^{2}\right)=4x^{2}+(1-2y)^{2}$ $\implies 5x^{2}+5y^{2}+22y+8=0$ $\implies C=\left(0,-\frac{11}{5}\right)$ $\implies \frac{1}{2}\lvert\alpha\rvert\cdot\frac{11}{5}=11 \implies \lvert\alpha\rvert=10 \implies \alpha^{2}=100$
questions.topic: Apollonius circle and centre of locus

questions.text: Let integers $a,b\in[-3,3]$ be such that $a+b\neq0$. Then the number of all possible ordered pairs $(a,b)$, for which $\left\lvert \frac{z-a}{z+b} \right\rvert=1$ and the determinant of the matrix with rows $(z+1,\;\omega,\;\omega^{2})$, $(\omega,\;z+\omega^{2},\;1)$, $(\omega^{2},\;1,\;z+\omega)$ equals $1$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$, where $\omega$ and $\omega^{2}$ are the roots of $x^{2}+x+1=0$, is equal to ________.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The matrix equals $zI+B$ with $B$ of rank one and trace zero, so its determinant is $z^{3}$. // 📝 Solution: $z^{3}=1 \implies z\in\{1,\omega,\omega^{2}\}$ $\implies z=1$: $(a-1)^{2}=(b+1)^{2} \implies a=b+2$ (as $a+b\neq0$), giving $4$ pairs $\implies z=\omega,\omega^{2}$: $a^{2}+a=b^{2}-b \implies (a+b)(a-b+1)=0 \implies b=a+1$, giving $6$ pairs $\implies$ total $=10$
questions.topic: Cube roots of unity, determinant and modulus conditions

questions.text: Let $z\in\mathbb{C}$ be such that $\dfrac{z^{2}+3i}{z-2+i}=2+3i$. Then the sum of all possible values of $z^{2}$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: clear the denominator to get a quadratic in $z$ and apply Vieta // 📝 Solution: $z^{2}-(2+3i)z+(7+7i)=0\implies z_1+z_2=2+3i,\ z_1z_2=7+7i$; $z_1^{2}+z_2^{2}=(2+3i)^{2}-2(7+7i)=-19-2i$

questions.text: If $z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}\in\mathbb{C}$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle, whose centroid is $z_{0}$, then $\sum_{k=1}^{3}(z_{k}-z_{0})^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: equilateral condition is $\sum z_k^{2}=\sum z_iz_j$ // 📝 Solution: $\sum z_k=3z_0$ and $(\sum z_k)^{2}=3\sum z_k^{2}\implies\sum z_k^{2}=3z_0^{2}\implies\sum(z_k-z_0)^{2}=3z_0^{2}-6z_0^{2}+3z_0^{2}=0$

questions.text: If $\alpha+i\beta$ and $\gamma+i\delta$ are the roots of $x^{2}-(3-2i)x-(2i-2)=0$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then $\alpha\gamma+\beta\delta$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve the quadratic directly using the complex discriminant. // 📝 Solution: Roots are $2-2i$ and $1$ (sum $3-2i$, product $2-2i$) $\implies \alpha=2,\beta=-2,\gamma=1,\delta=0$ $\implies \alpha\gamma+\beta\delta=2$

questions.text: The value of $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\log_e\left(\sec\left(ex\right) \cdot \sec\left(e^2 x\right) \cdots \sec\left(e^{10} x\right)\right)}{e^2 \; - \; e^{2\cos x}}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\log_e\left(\sec u\right) \; \approx \; \frac{u^2}{2}$ for small $u$ to convert the numerator into a geometric series and approximate $e^2 \; - \; e^{2\cos x} \; \approx \; e^2 x^2$. // 📝 Solution: Using $\sec u \; = \; 1 \; + \; \frac{u^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(u^4\right)$ and $\log_e\left(1 \; + \; t\right) \; \approx \; t$ as $t \; \to \; 0$, we have $\log_e\left(\sec\left(e^k x\right)\right) \; \approx \; \frac{e^{2k} x^2}{2}$. Thus, the numerator is $\sum_{k=1}^{10} \log_e\left(\sec\left(e^k x\right)\right) \; \approx \; \frac{x^2}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{10} e^{2k} \; = \; \frac{x^2 e^2\left(e^{20} \; - \; 1\right)}{2\left(e^2 \; - \; 1\right)}$. For the denominator, as $x \; \to \; 0$, $e^2 \; - \; e^{2\cos x} \; = \; e^2\left(1 \; - \; e^{2\left(\cos x \; - \; 1\right)}\right) \; \approx \; e^2 \cdot 2\left(1 \; - \; \cos x\right) \; \approx \; e^2 x^2$. Therefore, the required limit is $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{x^2 e^2\left(e^{20} \; - \; 1\right)}{2\left(e^2 \; - \; 1\right)}}{e^2 x^2} \; = \; \frac{e^{20} \; - \; 1}{2\left(e^2 \; - \; 1\right)}$.

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \; = \; x \; - \; 1$ when $x$ is even, and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; 2x$ when $x$ is odd, for $x \; \in \; \mathbb{N}$. If for some $a \; \in \; \mathbb{N}, \; f\left(f\left(f\left(a\right)\right)\right) \; = \; 21$, then $\lim_{x \to a^-} \left\{\frac{\left\lvert x \right\rvert^3}{a} \; - \; \left[\frac{x}{a}\right]\right\}$, where $\left[t\right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$, is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Determine $a$ by considering two cases ($a$ is even or $a$ is odd), and then evaluate the left-hand limit as $x \; \to \; a^-$. // 📝 Solution: Case 1: If $a$ is even, then $f\left(a\right) \; = \; a \; - \; 1$ (odd), so $f\left(f\left(a\right)\right) \; = \; 2\left(a \; - \; 1\right)$ (even), and $f\left(f\left(f\left(a\right)\right)\right) \; = \; 2\left(a \; - \; 1\right) \; - \; 1 \; = \; 2a \; - \; 3$. Setting $2a \; - \; 3 \; = \; 21$ gives $a \; = \; 12$ (even, valid). Case 2: If $a$ is odd, $f\left(a\right) \; = \; 2a$ (even), $f\left(f\left(a\right)\right) \; = \; 2a \; - \; 1$ (odd), and $f\left(f\left(f\left(a\right)\right)\right) \; = \; 4a \; - \; 2 \; = \; 21$, which gives no integer solution. Thus $a \; = \; 12$. Now, as $x \; \to \; 12^-$, $\frac{x}{12} \; \to \; 1^-$, so $\left[\frac{x}{12}\right] \; = \; 0$. Hence, $\lim_{x \to 12^-} \left\{\frac{\left\lvert x \right\rvert^3}{12} \; - \; \left[\frac{x}{12}\right]\right\} \; = \; \frac{12^3}{12} \; - \; 0 \; = \; 144$.

questions.text: If $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{\left(a \; - \; 1\right)x} \; + \; 2\cos bx \; + \; \left(c \; - \; 2\right)e^{-x}}{x\cos x \; - \; \log_e\left(1 \; + \; x\right)} \; = \; 2$, then $a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand both the numerator and denominator in Maclaurin series up to $x^2$ and equate the coefficients of $1$ and $x$ in the numerator to zero. // 📝 Solution: Expanding the denominator using Maclaurin series gives $x\left(1 \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; + \; \cdots\right) \; - \; \left(x \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; + \; \frac{x^3}{3} \; - \; \cdots\right) \; = \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(x^3\right)$. Expanding the numerator up to $x^2$ gives $\left(1 \; + \; \left(a \; - \; 1\right)x \; + \; \frac{\left(a \; - \; 1\right)^2 x^2}{2}\right) \; + \; 2\left(1 \; - \; \frac{b^2 x^2}{2}\right) \; + \; \left(c \; - \; 2\right)\left(1 \; - \; x \; + \; \frac{x^2}{2}\right) \; + \; O\left(x^3\right) \; = \; \left(c \; + \; 1\right) \; + \; \left(a \; - \; c \; + \; 1\right)x \; + \; \left(\frac{\left(a \; - \; 1\right)^2}{2} \; - \; b^2 \; + \; \frac{c \; - \; 2}{2}\right)x^2 \; + \; O\left(x^3\right)$. Since the limit as $x \; \to \; 0$ is $2$, we must have $c \; + \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies c \; = \; -1$, $a \; - \; c \; + \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies a \; = \; -2$, and $\frac{\frac{\left(a \; - \; 1\right)^2}{2} \; - \; b^2 \; + \; \frac{c \; - \; 2}{2}}{1/2} \; = \; 2 \implies \frac{9}{2} \; - \; b^2 \; - \; \frac{3}{2} \; = \; 1 \implies b^2 \; = \; 2$. Hence, $a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2 \; = \; 4 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 1 \; = \; 7$.
questions.topic: Finding Unknown Constants Using Series Expansion

questions.text: If $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{ax^2 e^x \; - \; b\log_e\left(1 \; + \; x\right) \; + \; cxe^{-x}}{x^2\sin x} \; = \; 1$, then $16\left(a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2\right)$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand $e^x$, $\log_e\left(1 \; + \; x\right)$, and $e^{-x}$ using Maclaurin series up to $x^3$ and equate the coefficients of $x$ and $x^2$ in the numerator to zero. // 📝 Solution: Using $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} \; = \; 1$, the denominator behaves as $x^3$. Expanding the numerator using Maclaurin series gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{ax^2\left(1 \; + \; x \; + \; \cdots\right) \; - \; b\left(x \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; + \; \frac{x^3}{3} \; - \; \cdots\right) \; + \; cx\left(1 \; - \; x \; + \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; - \; \cdots\right)}{x^3} \; = \; 1$. Grouping powers of $x$, we get $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left(c \; - \; b\right)x \; + \; \left(a \; + \; \frac{b}{2} \; - \; c\right)x^2 \; + \; \left(a \; - \; \frac{b}{3} \; + \; \frac{c}{2}\right)x^3 \; + \; O\left(x^4\right)}{x^3} \; = \; 1$. For this limit to be finite and equal to $1$, we must have $c \; - \; b \; = \; 0 \implies b \; = \; c$, $a \; + \; \frac{b}{2} \; - \; c \; = \; 0 \implies a \; = \; \frac{c}{2}$, and $a \; - \; \frac{b}{3} \; + \; \frac{c}{2} \; = \; 1$. Solving these gives $\frac{c}{2} \; - \; \frac{c}{3} \; + \; \frac{c}{2} \; = \; 1 \implies \frac{2c}{3} \; = \; 1 \implies c \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$, $b \; = \; \frac{3}{2}$, and $a \; = \; \frac{3}{4}$. Thus, $16\left(a^2 \; + \; b^2 \; + \; c^2\right) \; = \; 16\left(\frac{9}{16} \; + \; \frac{9}{4} \; + \; \frac{9}{4}\right) \; = \; 9 \; + \; 36 \; + \; 36 \; = \; 81$.
questions.topic: Finding Unknown Constants Using Series Expansion

questions.text: Let $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \int_{0}^{x} \left(t \; + \; \sin\left(1 \; - \; e^t\right)\right) \, dt, \; x \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$. Then, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f\left(x\right)}{x^3}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the Newton-Leibniz integral rule to differentiate $f\left(x\right)$ along with L'Hôpital's rule as $x \; \to \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Since $f\left(0\right) \; = \; 0$, the limit $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f\left(x\right)}{x^3}$ is in the $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule and the Leibniz rule, we get $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f'\left(x\right)}{3x^2} \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x \; + \; \sin\left(1 \; - \; e^x\right)}{3x^2}$. This is still in the $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule again gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 \; - \; e^x\cos\left(1 \; - \; e^x\right)}{6x}$, which is also $\frac{0}{0}$. Applying L'Hôpital's rule a third time, we obtain $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-\left[e^x\cos\left(1 \; - \; e^x\right) \; + \; e^{2x}\sin\left(1 \; - \; e^x\right)\right]}{6} \; = \; -\frac{1 \; + \; 0}{6} \; = \; -\frac{1}{6}$.
questions.topic: Limits with Definite Integrals & Leibniz Rule

questions.text: Let $\left\{x\right\}$ denote the fractional part of $x$ and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{\cos^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; \left\{x\right\}^2\right)\sin^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; \left\{x\right\}\right)}{\left\{x\right\} \; - \; \left\{x\right\}^3}, \; x \; \neq \; 0$. If $L$ and $R$ respectively denote the left hand limit and the right hand limit of $f\left(x\right)$ at $x \; = \; 0$, then $\frac{32}{\pi^2}\left(L^2 \; + \; R^2\right)$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For the right-hand limit ($x \; = \; 0 \; + \; h$), $\left\{h\right\} \; = \; h$, and for the left-hand limit ($x \; = \; 0 \; - \; h$), $\left\{-h\right\} \; = \; 1 \; - \; h$ where $h \; \to \; 0^+$. // 📝 Solution: To find $R \; = \; \lim_{h \to 0^+} f\left(h\right)$, since $\left\{h\right\} \; = \; h$, we have $R \; = \; \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\cos^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; h^2\right)\sin^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; h\right)}{h\left(1 \; - \; h^2\right)} \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\cos^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; h^2\right)}{h}$. Let $\cos^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; h^2\right) \; = \; \theta \implies h \; = \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; \cos\theta} \; = \; \sqrt{2}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$, so $R \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \lim_{\theta \to 0^+} \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{2}\sin\left(\theta/2\right)} \; = \; \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}$. For $L \; = \; \lim_{h \to 0^+} f\left(-h\right)$, since $\left\{-h\right\} \; = \; 1 \; - \; h$, we get $L \; = \; \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\cos^{-1}\left(1 \; - \; \left(1 \; - \; h\right)^2\right)\sin^{-1}\left(h\right)}{\left(1 \; - \; h\right)\left(1 \; - \; \left(1 \; - \; h\right)^2\right)} \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2} \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{\sin^{-1}h}{h\left(2 \; - \; h\right)} \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$. Therefore, $\frac{32}{\pi^2}\left(L^2 \; + \; R^2\right) \; = \; \frac{32}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{16} \; + \; \frac{\pi^2}{2}\right) \; = \; 2 \; + \; 16 \; = \; 18$.

questions.text: Let $\left[\cdot\right]$ denote the greatest integer function and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^3} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[\frac{k^2}{3^x}\right]$. Then $12 \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} f\left(j\right)$ is equal to ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Bound $\left[\frac{k^2}{3^x}\right]$ using $y \; - \; 1 \; < \; \left[y\right] \; \le \; y$, evaluate $f\left(x\right)$ via the Squeeze Theorem, and sum the resulting infinite geometric series. // 📝 Solution: Using $y \; - \; 1 \; < \; \left[y\right] \; \le \; y$, we have $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \left(\frac{k^2}{3^x} \; - \; 1\right) \; < \; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[\frac{k^2}{3^x}\right] \; \le \; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k^2}{3^x}$. Dividing by $n^3$ and taking $\lim_{n \to \infty}$, by the Squeeze Theorem we get $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^3 \cdot 3^x} \cdot \frac{n\left(n \; + \; 1\right)\left(2n \; + \; 1\right)}{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{3 \cdot 3^x} \; = \; \frac{1}{3^{x+1}}$. Now, $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} f\left(j\right) \; = \; \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{3^{j+1}} \; = \; \frac{1}{3^2} \; + \; \frac{1}{3^3} \; + \; \frac{1}{3^4} \; + \; \cdots \; = \; \frac{1/9}{1 \; - \; 1/3} \; = \; \frac{1}{6}$. Therefore, $12 \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} f\left(j\right) \; = \; 12 \times \frac{1}{6} \; = \; 2$.
questions.topic: Limit of a Sum & Greatest Integer Function

questions.text: Let $f : \left(-\infty, \; \infty\right) \; - \; \left\{0\right\} \; \to \; \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $f'\left(1\right) \; = \; \lim_{a \to \infty} a^2 f\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)$. Then $\lim_{a \to \infty} \frac{a\left(a \; + \; 1\right)}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{a}\right) \; + \; a^2 \; - \; 2\log_e a$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rewrite the given expression in the form $\lim_{a \to \infty} a^2 f\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)$ by factoring out $a^2$ and setting $x \; = \; \frac{1}{a}$. // 📝 Solution: Factoring out $a^2$ from the given expression, we get $\lim_{a \to \infty} a^2 \left[\frac{1}{2}\left(1 \; + \; \frac{1}{a}\right)\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{a}\right) \; + \; 1 \; + \; \frac{2}{a^2}\log_e\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)\right]$. Comparing this with $\lim_{a \to \infty} a^2 f\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)$, we identify $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \; + \; x\right)\tan^{-1}x \; + \; 1 \; + \; 2x^2\log_e x$. Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $f'\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x \; + \; \frac{1 \; + \; x}{2\left(1 \; + \; x^2\right)} \; + \; 4x\log_e x \; + \; 2x$. Substituting $x \; = \; 1$, the required limit is $f'\left(1\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \; + \; \frac{2}{4} \; + \; 0 \; + \; 2 \; = \; \frac{5}{2} \; + \; \frac{\pi}{8}$.

questions.text: Let $\lim_{n \to \infty} \left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; 1}} \; - \; \frac{2n}{\left(n^2 \; + \; 1\right)\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; 1}} \; + \; \frac{n}{\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; 16}} \; - \; \frac{8n}{\left(n^2 \; + \; 4\right)\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; 16}} \; + \; \cdots \; + \; \frac{n}{\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; n^4}} \; - \; \frac{2n \cdot n^2}{\left(n^2 \; + \; n^2\right)\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; n^4}}\right)$ be $\frac{\pi}{k}$, using only the principal values of the inverse trigonometric functions. Then $k^2$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write the general $r$-th term of the series and convert the limit of the sum into a definite integral by substituting $\frac{r}{n} \; = \; x$. // 📝 Solution: The given limit can be written as $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; r^4}} \; - \; \frac{2nr^2}{\left(n^2 \; + \; r^2\right)\sqrt{n^4 \; + \; r^4}}\right) \; = \; \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{1 \; - \; \left(\frac{r}{n}\right)^2}{\left(1 \; + \; \left(\frac{r}{n}\right)^2\right)\sqrt{1 \; + \; \left(\frac{r}{n}\right)^4}}$. Converting to a definite integral with $\frac{r}{n} \; = \; x$, we get $I \; = \; \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1 \; - \; x^2}{\left(1 \; + \; x^2\right)\sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4}} \, dx$. Dividing the numerator and denominator by $x^2$, we have $I \; = \; -\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{x^2}}{\left(x \; + \; \frac{1}{x}\right)\sqrt{\left(x \; + \; \frac{1}{x}\right)^2 \; - \; 2}} \, dx$. Let $x \; + \; \frac{1}{x} \; = \; t$ and $t^2 \; - \; 2 \; = \; \alpha^2 \implies t \, dt \; = \; \alpha \, d\alpha$. The integral becomes $\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\infty} \frac{d\alpha}{\alpha^2 \; + \; 2} \; = \; \left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]_{\sqrt{2}}^{\infty} \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \; - \; \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}$. Comparing with $\frac{\pi}{k}$, we get $k \; = \; 4\sqrt{2} \implies k^2 \; = \; 32$.
questions.topic: Limit of a Sum as Definite Integral

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor out $\left(\sqrt{x}\right)^6 \; = \; x^3$ from the numerator and $x^6$ from the denominator to evaluate the limit as $x \; \to \; \infty$. // 📝 Solution: Factoring out $\sqrt{x}$ from inside the brackets in the numerator and $x$ from inside the brackets in the denominator, we get $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^3 \left[\left(\sqrt{3 \; + \; \frac{1}{x}} \; + \; \sqrt{3 \; - \; \frac{1}{x}}\right)^6 \; + \; \left(\sqrt{3 \; + \; \frac{1}{x}} \; - \; \sqrt{3 \; - \; \frac{1}{x}}\right)^6\right] \cdot x^3}{x^6 \left[\left(1 \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{x^2}}\right)^6 \; + \; \left(1 \; - \; \sqrt{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{x^2}}\right)^6\right]}$. Canceling $x^6$ from the numerator and denominator and taking the limit as $x \; \to \; \infty$ (where $\frac{1}{x} \; \to \; 0$), we obtain $\frac{\left(2\sqrt{3}\right)^6 \; + \; 0}{2^6 \; + \; 0} \; = \; \left(\sqrt{3}\right)^6 \; = \; 3^3 \; = \; 27$.

questions.text: The set of all values of $a$ for which $\lim_{x \to a} \left(\left[x \; - \; 5\right] \; - \; \left[2x \; + \; 2\right]\right) \; = \; 0$, where $\left[\alpha\right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $\alpha$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the property $\left[x \; + \; n\right] \; = \; \left[x\right] \; + \; n$ for $n \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$ to simplify the equation to $\lim_{x \to a} \left(\left[x\right] \; - \; \left[2x\right]\right) \; = \; 7$. // 📝 Solution: Using $\left[x \; + \; n\right] \; = \; \left[x\right] \; + \; n$ for $n \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$, we get $\lim_{x \to a} \left(\left[x\right] \; - \; 5 \; - \; \left[2x\right] \; - \; 2\right) \; = \; 0 \implies \lim_{x \to a} \left(\left[x\right] \; - \; \left[2x\right]\right) \; = \; 7$. Let $a \; = \; I \; + \; f$, where $I \; = \; \left[a\right] \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$ and $f \; = \; \left\{a\right\} \; \in \; \left[0, \; 1\right)$. For non-integer and non-half-integer $a$, the function is continuous near $a$, so $I \; - \; \left(2I \; + \; \left[2f\right]\right) \; = \; 7 \implies -I \; - \; \left[2f\right] \; = \; 7$. Case 1: If $f \; \in \; \left(0, \; \frac{1}{2}\right)$, then $\left[2f\right] \; = \; 0 \implies I \; = \; -7 \implies a \; \in \; \left(-7, \; -6.5\right)$. Case 2: If $f \; \in \; \left(\frac{1}{2}, \; 1\right)$, then $\left[2f\right] \; = \; 1 \implies -I \; - \; 1 \; = \; 7 \implies I \; = \; -8 \implies a \; \in \; \left(-7.5, \; -7\right)$. Also, at $a \; = \; -7$, both the left-hand limit ($-8 \; - \; \left(-15\right) \; = \; 7$) and right-hand limit ($-7 \; - \; \left(-14\right) \; = \; 7$) equal $7$, whereas at $a \; = \; -7.5$ and $a \; = \; -6.5$ the limit does not exist. Hence, $a \; \in \; \left(-7.5, \; -6.5\right)$.
questions.topic: Greatest Integer Function & Existence of Limit

questions.text: If $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\left(5x \; + \; 1\right)^{1/3} \; - \; \left(x \; + \; 5\right)^{1/3}}{\left(2x \; + \; 3\right)^{1/2} \; - \; \left(x \; + \; 4\right)^{1/2}} \; = \; \frac{m\sqrt{5}}{n\left(2n\right)^{2/3}}$, where $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, then $8m \; + \; 12n$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply L'Hôpital's rule to evaluate the $\frac{0}{0}$ indeterminate form as $x \; \to \; 1$. // 📝 Solution: As $x \; \to \; 1$, the limit is of the $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule, we get $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\frac{1}{3}\left(5x \; + \; 1\right)^{-2/3} \cdot 5 \; - \; \frac{1}{3}\left(x \; + \; 5\right)^{-2/3} \cdot 1}{\frac{1}{2}\left(2x \; + \; 3\right)^{-1/2} \cdot 2 \; - \; \frac{1}{2}\left(x \; + \; 4\right)^{-1/2} \cdot 1} \; = \; \frac{\frac{5}{3}\left(6\right)^{-2/3} \; - \; \frac{1}{3}\left(6\right)^{-2/3}}{\left(5\right)^{-1/2} \; - \; \frac{1}{2}\left(5\right)^{-1/2}} \; = \; \frac{\frac{4}{3} \cdot 6^{-2/3}}{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 5^{-1/2}} \; = \; \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3\left(6\right)^{2/3}} \; = \; \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3\left(2 \cdot 3\right)^{2/3}}$. Comparing this with $\frac{m\sqrt{5}}{n\left(2n\right)^{2/3}}$, where $\gcd\left(m, \; n\right) \; = \; 1$, we obtain $m \; = \; 8$ and $n \; = \; 3$. Therefore, $8m \; + \; 12n \; = \; 8\left(8\right) \; + \; 12\left(3\right) \; = \; 64 \; + \; 36 \; = \; 100$.

questions.text: Let $a$ be the sum of all coefficients in the expansion of $\left(1 \; - \; 2x \; + \; 2x^2\right)^{2023}\left(3 \; - \; 4x^2 \; + \; 2x^3\right)^{2024}$ and $b \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \left(\frac{\int_{0}^{x} \frac{\log\left(1 \; + \; t\right)}{t^{2024} \; + \; 1} \, dt}{x^2}\right)$. If the equations $cx^2 \; + \; dx \; + \; e \; = \; 0$ and $2bx^2 \; + \; ax \; + \; 4 \; = \; 0$ have a common root, where $c, \; d, \; e \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$, then $d : c : e$ equals
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Substitute $x \; = \; 1$ to find the sum of coefficients $a$, apply L'Hôpital's rule to find $b$, and check the discriminant of $2bx^2 \; + \; ax \; + \; 4 \; = \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Putting $x \; = \; 1$ in the polynomial gives the sum of all coefficients: $a \; = \; \left(1 \; - \; 2 \; + \; 2\right)^{2023}\left(3 \; - \; 4 \; + \; 2\right)^{2024} \; = \; 1$. Applying L'Hôpital's rule to $b$, we get $b \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\log\left(1 \; + \; x\right)}{2x\left(x^{2024} \; + \; 1\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. Substituting $a \; = \; 1$ and $b \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$ into $2bx^2 \; + \; ax \; + \; 4 \; = \; 0$ gives $x^2 \; + \; x \; + \; 4 \; = \; 0$. Since its discriminant $D \; = \; 1 \; - \; 16 \; = \; -15 \; < \; 0$, its roots are non-real complex conjugates. Since $c, \; d, \; e \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$, both quadratic equations must have both roots in common, so $\frac{c}{1} \; = \; \frac{d}{1} \; = \; \frac{e}{4} \implies d : c : e \; = \; 1 : 1 : 4$.
questions.topic: Limits with Definite Integrals & Quadratic Equations

questions.text: If $\alpha \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0^+} \left(\frac{e^{\sqrt{\tan x}} \; - \; e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{\tan x} \; - \; \sqrt{x}}\right)$ and $\beta \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \left(1 \; + \; \sin x\right)^{\frac{1}{2}\cot x}$ are the roots of the quadratic equation $ax^2 \; + \; bx \; - \; \sqrt{e} \; = \; 0$, then $12\log_e\left(a \; + \; b\right)$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor out $e^{\sqrt{x}}$ to evaluate $\alpha$ using $\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{e^t \; - \; 1}{t} \; = \; 1$, and use the $1^\infty$ standard limit form for $\beta$. // 📝 Solution: We have $\alpha \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0^+} e^{\sqrt{x}} \left(\frac{e^{\sqrt{\tan x} \; - \; \sqrt{x}} \; - \; 1}{\sqrt{\tan x} \; - \; \sqrt{x}}\right) \; = \; e^0 \cdot 1 \; = \; 1$. For $\beta$, since it is a $1^\infty$ form, $\beta \; = \; e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{2}\cot x \cdot \sin x} \; = \; e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{2}\cos x} \; = \; e^{1/2} \; = \; \sqrt{e}$. Since $\alpha \; = \; 1$ and $\beta \; = \; \sqrt{e}$ are the roots of $ax^2 \; + \; bx \; - \; \sqrt{e} \; = \; 0$, the quadratic equation with constant term $-\sqrt{e}$ is $-x^2 \; + \; \left(1 \; + \; \sqrt{e}\right)x \; - \; \sqrt{e} \; = \; 0$. Comparing coefficients gives $a \; = \; -1$ and $b \; = \; 1 \; + \; \sqrt{e}$. Thus $a \; + \; b \; = \; \sqrt{e}$, and $12\log_e\left(a \; + \; b\right) \; = \; 12\log_e\left(e^{1/2}\right) \; = \; 12 \times \frac{1}{2} \; = \; 6$.

questions.text: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e \; - \; \left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)^{\frac{1}{2x}}}{x}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write $\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)^{\frac{1}{2x}} \; = \; e^{\frac{\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)}{2x}}$ and use the Maclaurin series expansion of $\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)$ around $x \; = \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: We can rewrite the limit as $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e \; - \; e^{\frac{\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)}{2x}}}{x} \; = \; -e \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{\frac{\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right)}{2x} \; - \; 1} \; - \; 1}{x}$. Using $\lim_{u \to 0} \frac{e^u \; - \; 1}{u} \; = \; 1$, this simplifies to $-e \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right) \; - \; 2x}{2x^2}$. Substituting the expansion $\ln\left(1 \; + \; 2x\right) \; = \; 2x \; - \; \frac{\left(2x\right)^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(x^3\right)$, we get $-e \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-2x^2}{2x^2} \; = \; -e \cdot \left(-1\right) \; = \; e$.

questions.text: The value of $\lim_{x \to 0} 2\left(\frac{1 \; - \; \cos x \sqrt{\cos 2x} \sqrt[3]{\cos 3x} \cdots \sqrt[10]{\cos 10x}}{x^2}\right)$ is _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the binomial and Maclaurin series approximation $\left(\cos kx\right)^{1/k} \; \approx \; \left(1 \; - \; \frac{k^2 x^2}{2}\right)^{1/k} \; \approx \; 1 \; - \; \frac{k x^2}{2}$ as $x \; \to \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Using the expansion $\cos\left(kx\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{k^2 x^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(x^4\right)$, we have $\left(\cos kx\right)^{1/k} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{1}{k} \cdot \frac{k^2 x^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(x^4\right) \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{kx^2}{2} \; + \; O\left(x^4\right)$. Taking the product for $k \; = \; 1, \; 2, \; \dots, \; 10$, we get $\prod_{k=1}^{10} \left(\cos kx\right)^{1/k} \; = \; 1 \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2}\left(1 \; + \; 2 \; + \; 3 \; + \; \cdots \; + \; 10\right) \; + \; O\left(x^4\right)$. Substituting this into the limit gives $\lim_{x \to 0} 2\left(\frac{\frac{x^2}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{10} k}{x^2}\right) \; = \; \sum_{k=1}^{10} k \; = \; \frac{10 \times 11}{2} \; = \; 55$.

questions.text: Let $x \; = \; 2$ be a root of the equation $x^2 \; + \; px \; + \; q \; = \; 0$ and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; \cos\left(x^2 \; - \; 4px \; + \; q^2 \; + \; 8q \; + \; 16\right)}{\left(x \; - \; 2p\right)^4}$ for $x \; \neq \; 2p$, and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; 0$ for $x \; = \; 2p$. Then $\lim_{x \to 2p^+} \left[f\left(x\right)\right]$, where $\left[\cdot\right]$ denotes greatest integer function, is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $4 \; + \; 2p \; + \; q \; = \; 0$ to express $q^2 \; + \; 8q \; + \; 16$ as $4p^2$, simplify the argument of cosine to $\left(x \; - \; 2p\right)^2$, and note that $\frac{1 \; - \; \cos\theta}{\theta^2} \; < \; \frac{1}{2}$ for small $\theta \; > \; 0$. // 📝 Solution: Since $x \; = \; 2$ is a root of $x^2 \; + \; px \; + \; q \; = \; 0$, we have $4 \; + \; 2p \; + \; q \; = \; 0 \implies q \; + \; 4 \; = \; -2p$. Squaring both sides gives $q^2 \; + \; 8q \; + \; 16 \; = \; 4p^2$. Thus, $x^2 \; - \; 4px \; + \; q^2 \; + \; 8q \; + \; 16 \; = \; x^2 \; - \; 4px \; + \; 4p^2 \; = \; \left(x \; - \; 2p\right)^2$. For $x \; \neq \; 2p$, let $\theta \; = \; \left(x \; - \; 2p\right)^2 \; > \; 0$. Then $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{1 \; - \; \cos\theta}{\theta^2}$. As $x \; \to \; 2p^+$, $\theta \; \to \; 0^+$, and since $1 \; - \; \cos\theta \; = \; \frac{\theta^2}{2} \; - \; \frac{\theta^4}{24} \; + \; \cdots \; < \; \frac{\theta^2}{2}$, $f\left(x\right)$ approaches $\frac{1}{2}$ from values strictly less than $\frac{1}{2}$ (i.e., $0 \; < \; f\left(x\right) \; < \; \frac{1}{2}$). Therefore, $\lim_{x \to 2p^+} \left[f\left(x\right)\right] \; = \; 0$.

questions.text: Let the slope of the line $45x \; + \; 5y \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0$ be $27r_1 \; + \; \frac{9r_2}{2}$ for some $r_1, \; r_2 \; \in \; \mathbb{R}$. Then $\lim_{x \to 3} \left(\int_{3}^{x} \frac{8t^2}{\frac{3r_2 x}{2} \; - \; r_2 x^2 \; - \; r_1 x^3 \; - \; 3x} \, dt\right)$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the relation between $r_1$ and $r_2$ using the slope of the line, pull the $x$-dependent denominator out of the $t$-integral, and apply L'Hôpital's rule. // 📝 Solution: The slope of the line $45x \; + \; 5y \; + \; 3 \; = \; 0$ is $-9$, so $27r_1 \; + \; \frac{9r_2}{2} \; = \; -9$. Since the denominator inside the integral is independent of $t$, we can rewrite the limit as $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\int_{3}^{x} 8t^2 \, dt}{\frac{3r_2 x}{2} \; - \; r_2 x^2 \; - \; r_1 x^3 \; - \; 3x}$. At $x \; = \; 3$, the denominator is $\frac{9r_2}{2} \; - \; 9r_2 \; - \; 27r_1 \; - \; 9 \; = \; -\left(27r_1 \; + \; \frac{9r_2}{2}\right) \; - \; 9 \; = \; 9 \; - \; 9 \; = \; 0$, making it a $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule and the Newton-Leibniz rule gives $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{8x^2}{\frac{3r_2}{2} \; - \; 2r_2 x \; - \; 3r_1 x^2 \; - \; 3} \; = \; \frac{8\left(9\right)}{\frac{3r_2}{2} \; - \; 6r_2 \; - \; 27r_1 \; - \; 3} \; = \; \frac{72}{-\left(27r_1 \; + \; \frac{9r_2}{2}\right) \; - \; 3} \; = \; \frac{72}{9 \; - \; 3} \; = \; 12$.
questions.topic: Limits with Definite Integrals & L'Hôpital's Rule

questions.text: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\left(1^2 \; - \; 1\right)\left(n \; - \; 1\right) \; + \; \left(2^2 \; - \; 2\right)\left(n \; - \; 2\right) \; + \; \cdots \; + \; \left(\left(n \; - \; 1\right)^2 \; - \; \left(n \; - \; 1\right)\right) \cdot 1}{\left(1^3 \; + \; 2^3 \; + \; \cdots \; + \; n^3\right) \; - \; \left(1^2 \; + \; 2^2 \; + \; \cdots \; + \; n^2\right)}$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express the numerator and denominator as summations of powers of $r$ and compare the coefficients of $n^4$. // 📝 Solution: The numerator is $\sum_{r=1}^{n-1} \left(r^2 \; - \; r\right)\left(n \; - \; r\right) \; = \; \sum_{r=1}^{n-1} \left(-r^3 \; + \; \left(n \; + \; 1\right)r^2 \; - \; nr\right)$. Using standard summation formulas and retaining the highest degree terms in $n$ (degree $4$), the numerator behaves as $-\frac{n^4}{4} \; + \; n \cdot \frac{n^3}{3} \; = \; \frac{n^4}{12}$. Similarly, the denominator is $\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^3 \; - \; \sum_{r=1}^{n} r^2$, whose leading term of degree $4$ is $\frac{n^4}{4}$. Therefore, the required limit as $n \; \to \; \infty$ is $\frac{1/12}{1/4} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: If $a \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{1 \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4}} \; - \; \sqrt{2}}{x^4}$ and $b \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin^2 x}{\sqrt{2} \; - \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; \cos x}}$, then the value of $ab^3$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Rationalize the numerator for $a$ and the denominator for $b$ to remove the radical expressions. // 📝 Solution: Rationalizing $a$ twice gives $a \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4} \; - \; 1}{x^4\left(\sqrt{1 \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4}} \; + \; \sqrt{2}\right)} \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^4}{x^4\left(\sqrt{1 \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4}} \; + \; \sqrt{2}\right)\left(\sqrt{1 \; + \; x^4} \; + \; 1\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{\left(2\sqrt{2}\right)\left(2\right)} \; = \; \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}$. Similarly, rationalizing the denominator of $b$ gives $b \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left(1 \; - \; \cos^2 x\right)\left(\sqrt{2} \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; \cos x}\right)}{1 \; - \; \cos x} \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \left(1 \; + \; \cos x\right)\left(\sqrt{2} \; + \; \sqrt{1 \; + \; \cos x}\right) \; = \; 2\left(2\sqrt{2}\right) \; = \; 4\sqrt{2}$. Therefore, $ab^3 \; = \; \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \times \left(4\sqrt{2}\right)^3 \; = \; \left(4\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \; = \; 32$.

questions.text: Let $f : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \; \to \; \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $f\left(0\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. If $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x \int_{0}^{x} f\left(t\right) \, dt}{e^{x^2} \; - \; 1} \; = \; \alpha$, then $8\alpha^2$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the standard limit $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x^2} \; - \; 1}{x^2} \; = \; 1$ and apply L'Hôpital's rule to $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\int_{0}^{x} f\left(t\right) \, dt}{x}$. // 📝 Solution: We can rewrite the given limit as $\alpha \; = \; \lim_{x \to 0} \left(\frac{x^2}{e^{x^2} \; - \; 1}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{\int_{0}^{x} f\left(t\right) \, dt}{x}\right)$. Since $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{e^{x^2} \; - \; 1} \; = \; 1$, applying L'Hôpital's rule and the Newton-Leibniz rule to the second factor gives $\alpha \; = \; 1 \cdot \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f\left(x\right)}{1} \; = \; f\left(0\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $8\alpha^2 \; = \; 8\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \; = \; 2$.

questions.text: Let $f, \; g$ and $h$ be the real valued functions defined on $\mathbb{R}$ as $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{x}{\left\lvert x \right\rvert}$ for $x \; \neq \; 0$ and $f\left(x\right) \; = \; 1$ for $x \; = \; 0$; $g\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{\sin\left(x \; + \; 1\right)}{\left(x \; + \; 1\right)}$ for $x \; \neq \; -1$ and $g\left(x\right) \; = \; 1$ for $x \; = \; -1$; and $h\left(x\right) \; = \; 2\left[x\right] \; - \; f\left(x\right)$, where $\left[x\right]$ is the greatest integer $\le \; x$. Then the value of $\lim_{x \to 1} g\left(h\left(x \; - \; 1\right)\right)$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate $h\left(x \; - \; 1\right)$ separately for $x \; \to \; 1^+$ and $x \; \to \; 1^-$ before applying the function $g$. // 📝 Solution: Let $x \; - \; 1 \; = \; t$, so $t \; \to \; 0$ as $x \; \to \; 1$. For the right-hand limit ($t \; \to \; 0^+$), we have $\left[t\right] \; = \; 0$ and $f\left(t\right) \; = \; 1$, which gives $h\left(t\right) \; = \; 2\left(0\right) \; - \; 1 \; = \; -1$. For the left-hand limit ($t \; \to \; 0^-$), we have $\left[t\right] \; = \; -1$ and $f\left(t\right) \; = \; -1$, which gives $h\left(t\right) \; = \; 2\left(-1\right) \; - \; \left(-1\right) \; = \; -1$. Thus, for all $x$ in the deleted neighborhood of $1$, $h\left(x \; - \; 1\right) \; = \; -1$ identically. Hence, $\lim_{x \to 1} g\left(h\left(x \; - \; 1\right)\right) \; = \; g\left(-1\right) \; = \; 1$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \; \to \; \left(0, \; \infty\right)$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f\left(3\right) \; = \; 18, \; f'\left(3\right) \; = \; 0$ and $f''\left(3\right) \; = \; 4$. Then $\lim_{x \to 1} \left(\log_e\left(\frac{f\left(2 \; + \; x\right)}{f\left(3\right)}\right)^{\frac{18}{\left(x \; - \; 1\right)^2}}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Bring the exponent $\frac{18}{\left(x \; - \; 1\right)^2}$ in front of the logarithm, use $\lim_{u \to 1} \frac{\log_e u}{u \; - \; 1} \; = \; 1$, and apply L'Hôpital's rule twice. // 📝 Solution: Using logarithm properties and $\lim_{u \to 1} \frac{\log_e u}{u \; - \; 1} \; = \; 1$, the given limit becomes $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{18}{\left(x \; - \; 1\right)^2} \log_e\left(1 \; + \; \frac{f\left(2 \; + \; x\right) \; - \; f\left(3\right)}{f\left(3\right)}\right) \; = \; \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{18}{\left(x \; - \; 1\right)^2} \cdot \frac{f\left(2 \; + \; x\right) \; - \; f\left(3\right)}{18} \; = \; \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{f\left(2 \; + \; x\right) \; - \; f\left(3\right)}{\left(x \; - \; 1\right)^2}$. Since this is in the $\frac{0}{0}$ form and $f'\left(3\right) \; = \; 0$, applying L'Hôpital's rule twice gives $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{f'\left(2 \; + \; x\right)}{2\left(x \; - \; 1\right)} \; = \; \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{f''\left(2 \; + \; x\right)}{2} \; = \; \frac{f''\left(3\right)}{2} \; = \; \frac{4}{2} \; = \; 2$.

questions.text: Let $a \; > \; 0$ be a root of the equation $2x^2 \; + \; x \; - \; 2 \; = \; 0$. If $\lim_{x \to \frac{1}{a}} \frac{16\left(1 \; - \; \cos\left(2 \; + \; x \; - \; 2x^2\right)\right)}{\left(1 \; - \; ax\right)^2} \; = \; \alpha \; + \; \beta\sqrt{17}$, where $\alpha, \; \beta \; \in \; \mathbb{Z}$, then $\alpha \; + \; \beta$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factorize $2x^2 \; - \; x \; - \; 2$ using the reciprocals of the roots of $2x^2 \; + \; x \; - \; 2 \; = \; 0$ and use $\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{1 \; - \; \cos \theta}{\theta^2} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a \; > \; 0$ and $b$ are the roots of $2x^2 \; + \; x \; - \; 2 \; = \; 0$, we have $a \; = \; \frac{-1 \; + \; \sqrt{17}}{4}$, and $\frac{1}{a}, \; \frac{1}{b}$ are the roots of $2x^2 \; - \; x \; - \; 2 \; = \; 0$. Thus, $2 \; + \; x \; - \; 2x^2 \; = \; -2\left(x \; - \; \frac{1}{a}\right)\left(x \; - \; \frac{1}{b}\right)$ with $\left(\frac{1}{a} \; - \; \frac{1}{b}\right)^2 \; = \; \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \; - \; 4\left(-1\right) \; = \; \frac{17}{4}$. Now, $\lim_{x \to \frac{1}{a}} \frac{16\left(1 \; - \; \cos\left(2\left(x \; - \; \frac{1}{a}\right)\left(x \; - \; \frac{1}{b}\right)\right)\right)}{a^2\left(x \; - \; \frac{1}{a}\right)^2} \; = \; \frac{16}{a^2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4\left(\frac{1}{a} \; - \; \frac{1}{b}\right)^2 \; = \; \frac{32}{a^2} \cdot \frac{17}{4} \; = \; \frac{136}{a^2}$. Substituting $a^2 \; = \; \frac{9 \; - \; \sqrt{17}}{8}$, the limit becomes $\frac{136 \times 8}{9 \; - \; \sqrt{17}} \; = \; \frac{136 \times 8\left(9 \; + \; \sqrt{17}\right)}{64} \; = \; 17\left(9 \; + \; \sqrt{17}\right) \; = \; 153 \; + \; 17\sqrt{17}$. Thus $\alpha \; = \; 153$ and $\beta \; = \; 17$, giving $\alpha \; + \; \beta \; = \; 170$.

questions.text: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \; \to \; \left(0, \; \infty\right)$ be a strictly increasing function such that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{f\left(7x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; = \; 1$. Then, the value of $\lim_{x \to \infty} \left[\frac{f\left(5x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; - \; 1\right]$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the inequality $f\left(x\right) \; < \; f\left(5x\right) \; < \; f\left(7x\right)$ for $x \; > \; 0$ and apply the Squeeze Theorem. // 📝 Solution: Since $f : \mathbb{R} \; \to \; \left(0, \; \infty\right)$ is a strictly increasing function, for any $x \; > \; 0$ we have $x \; < \; 5x \; < \; 7x \implies f\left(x\right) \; < \; f\left(5x\right) \; < \; f\left(7x\right)$. Since $f\left(x\right) \; > \; 0$, dividing throughout by $f\left(x\right)$ yields $1 \; < \; \frac{f\left(5x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; < \; \frac{f\left(7x\right)}{f\left(x\right)}$. Taking the limit as $x \; \to \; \infty$ and given $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{f\left(7x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; = \; 1$, by the Squeeze Theorem we get $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{f\left(5x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; = \; 1$. Therefore, $\lim_{x \to \infty} \left[\frac{f\left(5x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} \; - \; 1\right] \; = \; 1 \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0$.

questions.text: $\lim_{t \to 0} \left(1^{\frac{1}{\sin^2 t}} \; + \; 2^{\frac{1}{\sin^2 t}} \; + \; \cdots \; + \; n^{\frac{1}{\sin^2 t}}\right)^{\sin^2 t}$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Factor out the largest base $n^{\frac{1}{\sin^2 t}}$ from inside the parentheses and take the limit as $\sin^2 t \; \to \; 0^+$. // 📝 Solution: Factoring out $n^{\frac{1}{\sin^2 t}}$ from the bracket gives $\lim_{t \to 0} n \left[\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{\csc^2 t} \; + \; \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^{\csc^2 t} \; + \; \cdots \; + \; \left(\frac{n \; - \; 1}{n}\right)^{\csc^2 t} \; + \; 1\right]^{\sin^2 t}$. As $t \; \to \; 0$, $\csc^2 t \; \to \; \infty$ and $\sin^2 t \; \to \; 0$. Since $0 \; < \; \frac{k}{n} \; < \; 1$ for $1 \; \le \; k \; \le \; n \; - \; 1$, each term $\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^{\csc^2 t} \; \to \; 0$. Thus, the limit evaluates to $n\left(0 \; + \; 0 \; + \; \cdots \; + \; 1\right)^0 \; = \; n$.

questions.text: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{2\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert} \; - \; 2\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert \; - \; 1}{x^2}$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Multiply and divide by $\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert^2 \; = \; \sin^2 x$ and use the Maclaurin series expansion of $e^{2t}$ where $t \; = \; \left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert$. // 📝 Solution: Rewrite the limit as $\lim_{x \to 0} \left(\frac{e^{2\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert} \; - \; 2\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert \; - \; 1}{\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert^2}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}\right)$. Let $\left\lvert \sin x \right\rvert \; = \; t$, so $t \; \to \; 0^+$ as $x \; \to \; 0$. Using $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2} \; = \; 1$ and the Maclaurin expansion $e^{2t} \; = \; 1 \; + \; 2t \; + \; \frac{\left(2t\right)^2}{2!} \; + \; O\left(t^3\right)$, the limit becomes $\lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{\left(1 \; + \; 2t \; + \; 2t^2 \; + \; O\left(t^3\right)\right) \; - \; 2t \; - \; 1}{t^2} \cdot 1 \; = \; 2$.

questions.text: Let $f$ be a differentiable function in the interval $\left(0, \; \infty\right)$ such that $f\left(1\right) \; = \; 1$ and $\lim_{t \to x} \frac{t^2 f\left(x\right) \; - \; x^2 f\left(t\right)}{t \; - \; x} \; = \; 1$ for each $x \; > \; 0$. Then $2f\left(2\right) \; + \; 3f\left(3\right)$ is equal to _______
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Evaluate the limit with respect to $t$ using L'Hôpital's rule to form a first-order linear differential equation in $f\left(x\right)$. // 📝 Solution: Applying L'Hôpital's rule with respect to $t$ as $t \; \to \; x$, we get $\lim_{t \to x} \frac{2t f\left(x\right) \; - \; x^2 f'\left(t\right)}{1} \; = \; 1 \implies 2x f\left(x\right) \; - \; x^2 f'\left(x\right) \; = \; 1$. Let $y \; = \; f\left(x\right)$, then $\frac{dy}{dx} \; - \; \frac{2}{x}y \; = \; -\frac{1}{x^2}$. This is a linear differential equation with integrating factor $\text{I.F.} \; = \; e^{\int -\frac{2}{x} \, dx} \; = \; \frac{1}{x^2}$. Thus, $\frac{y}{x^2} \; = \; \int -\frac{1}{x^4} \, dx \; + \; C \implies \frac{y}{x^2} \; = \; \frac{1}{3x^3} \; + \; C$. Since $f\left(1\right) \; = \; 1$, we have $1 \; = \; \frac{1}{3} \; + \; C \implies C \; = \; \frac{2}{3}$. Therefore, $f\left(x\right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3x} \; + \; \frac{2x^2}{3}$. Now, $2f\left(2\right) \; + \; 3f\left(3\right) \; = \; 2\left(\frac{1}{6} \; + \; \frac{8}{3}\right) \; + \; 3\left(\frac{1}{9} \; + \; 6\right) \; = \; \frac{17}{3} \; + \; \frac{55}{3} \; = \; \frac{72}{3} \; = \; 24$.

questions.text: $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \left(\frac{\int_{x^3}^{\left(\pi/2\right)^3} \left(\sin\left(2t^{1/3}\right) \; + \; \cos\left(t^{1/3}\right)\right) \, dt}{\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply L'Hôpital's rule along with the Newton-Leibniz rule to differentiate the definite integral with respect to $x$. // 📝 Solution: As $x \; \to \; \frac{\pi}{2}$, the limit is of the $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule and the Leibniz rule, we get $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{-\left(\sin\left(2x\right) \; + \; \cos x\right) \cdot 3x^2}{2\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)} \; = \; \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{-3x^2 \cos x \left(2\sin x \; + \; 1\right)}{2\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)}$. Since $-\cos x \; = \; \sin\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sin\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}} \; = \; 1$, substituting $x \; = \; \frac{\pi}{2}$ gives $\frac{3\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 \left(2\sin\frac{\pi}{2} \; + \; 1\right)}{2} \cdot 1 \; = \; \frac{3 \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{4} \cdot 3}{2} \; = \; \frac{9\pi^2}{8}$.
questions.topic: Limits with Definite Integrals & Leibniz Rule

questions.text: If $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{3 \; + \; \alpha\sin x \; + \; \beta\cos x \; + \; \log_e\left(1 \; - \; x\right)}{3\tan^2 x} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$, then $2\alpha \; - \; \beta$ is equal to :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Expand $\sin x$, $\cos x$, and $\log_e\left(1 \; - \; x\right)$ using Maclaurin series up to $x^2$ and equate the constant and $x$ coefficients to zero. // 📝 Solution: Using Maclaurin expansions in the numerator and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan^2 x}{x^2} \; = \; 1$ in the denominator, we have $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{3 \; + \; \alpha\left(x \; - \; \frac{x^3}{6} \; + \; \cdots\right) \; + \; \beta\left(1 \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; + \; \cdots\right) \; + \; \left(-x \; - \; \frac{x^2}{2} \; - \; \cdots\right)}{3x^2} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. Grouping powers of $x$ gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left(3 \; + \; \beta\right) \; + \; \left(\alpha \; - \; 1\right)x \; - \; \left(\frac{\beta \; + \; 1}{2}\right)x^2 \; + \; O\left(x^3\right)}{3x^2} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$. For the limit to be finite, the constant and $x$ terms must vanish: $3 \; + \; \beta \; = \; 0 \implies \beta \; = \; -3$, and $\alpha \; - \; 1 \; = \; 0 \implies \alpha \; = \; 1$. Also, $-\frac{\beta \; + \; 1}{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{3}$, which is consistent. Thus, $2\alpha \; - \; \beta \; = \; 2\left(1\right) \; - \; \left(-3\right) \; = \; 5$.
questions.topic: Finding Unknown Constants Using Series Expansion

questions.text: $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \left(\frac{1}{\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2} \int_{x^3}^{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^3} \cos\left(\frac{1}{t^3}\right) \, dt\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply L'Hôpital's rule and the Newton-Leibniz rule to differentiate the numerator and denominator with respect to $x$. // 📝 Solution: Note: In the official question paper, the integrand is intended as $\cos\left(t^{1/3}\right)$. As $x \; \to \; \frac{\pi}{2}$, the limit is of the $\frac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule and the Newton-Leibniz rule, we get $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{0 \; - \; \cos\left(x\right) \cdot 3x^2}{2\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)} \; = \; \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{3x^2 \sin\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{2\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)}$. Using $\lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sin\left(x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{x \; - \; \frac{\pi}{2}} \; = \; 1$, the limit evaluates to $\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 \; = \; \frac{3\pi^2}{8}$.
questions.topic: Limits with Definite Integrals & Leibniz Rule

questions.text: The number of ways of getting a sum $16$ on throwing a dice four times is _____.
The number of words, with or without meaning, that can be formed using all the letters of the word ASSASSINATION so that the vowels occur together, is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Tie all $6$ vowels together as a single unit, permute the $8$ resulting units, and multiply by the internal arrangements of the vowels. // 📝 Solution: In the $13$-letter word ASSASSINATION, the vowels are A, A, A, I, I, O ($6$ vowels: $3$ A's, $2$ I's, $1$ O) and the consonants are S, S, S, S, N, N, T ($7$ consonants: $4$ S's, $2$ N's, $1$ T). Treating all $6$ vowels as $1$ single block, we have $7 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 8$ objects to arrange, which can be done in $\frac{8!}{4!\;2!}$ ways. The $6$ vowels inside the block can be arranged in $\frac{6!}{3!\;2!}$ ways. Total number of words $\;=\; \frac{8!}{4!\;2!} \;\times\; \frac{6!}{3!\;2!} \;=\; 840 \;\times\; 60 \;=\; 50400$.
questions.topic: String Method and Permutations with Repetition

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{(m, n) \;:\; m, n \;\in\; \left\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 50\right\}\right\}$. If the number of elements $(m, n)$ in $S$ such that $6^{m} \;+\; 9^{n}$ is a multiple of $5$ is $p$ and the number of elements $(m, n)$ in $S$ such that $m \;+\; n$ is a square of a prime number is $q$, then $p \;+\; q$ is equal to _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Reduce $6^{m} \;+\; 9^{n} \;\equiv\; 1^{m} \;+\; (-1)^{n} \pmod{5}$ to find $p$, and count pairs with $m \;+\; n \;\in\; \left\{4, 9, 25, 49\right\}$ to find $q$. // 📝 Solution: Modulo $5$, $6^{m} \;+\; 9^{n} \;\equiv\; 1^{m} \;+\; (-1)^{n} \;=\; 1 \;+\; (-1)^{n} \pmod{5}$, which is divisible by $5$ if and only if $n$ is odd. There are $50$ choices for $m$ and $25$ odd choices for $n$, so $p \;=\; 50 \;\times\; 25 \;=\; 1250$. Since $2 \;\le\; m \;+\; n \;\le\; 100$, the squares of primes in this range are $4, 9, 25, 49$. For $k \;\le\; 51$, the equation $m \;+\; n \;=\; k$ has $k \;-\; 1$ solutions in $\left\{1, \dots, 50\right\}^{2}$. Thus $q \;=\; (4 \;-\; 1) \;+\; (9 \;-\; 1) \;+\; (25 \;-\; 1) \;+\; (49 \;-\; 1) \;=\; 3 \;+\; 8 \;+\; 24 \;+\; 48 \;=\; 83$. Hence, $p \;+\; q \;=\; 1250 \;+\; 83 \;=\; 1333$.

questions.text: The number of ways of selecting two numbers $a$ and $b$, $a \;\in\; \left\{2, 4, 6, \dots, 100\right\}$ and $b \;\in\; \left\{1, 3, 5, \dots, 99\right\}$ such that $2$ is the remainder when $a \;+\; b$ is divided by $23$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since $a$ is even and $b$ is odd, $a \;+\; b$ is always an odd integer of the form $23k \;+\; 2$ between $3$ and $199$. // 📝 Solution: Since $a$ is even and $b$ is odd, $a \;+\; b$ is odd and $3 \;\le\; a \;+\; b \;\le\; 199$. Given $a \;+\; b \;=\; 23k \;+\; 2$, for $a \;+\; b$ to be odd, $k$ must be odd, so $a \;+\; b \;\in\; \left\{25, 71, 117, 163\right\}$. Case 1 ($a \;+\; b \;=\; 25$): $a \;\in\; \left\{2, 4, \dots, 24\right\}$ gives $12$ pairs. Case 2 ($a \;+\; b \;=\; 71$): $a \;\in\; \left\{2, 4, \dots, 70\right\}$ gives $35$ pairs. Case 3 ($a \;+\; b \;=\; 117$): $a \;\in\; \left\{18, 20, \dots, 100\right\}$ gives $\frac{100 \;-\; 18}{2} \;+\; 1 \;=\; 42$ pairs. Case 4 ($a \;+\; b \;=\; 163$): $a \;\in\; \left\{64, 66, \dots, 100\right\}$ gives $\frac{100 \;-\; 64}{2} \;+\; 1 \;=\; 19$ pairs. Total number of ways $\;=\; 12 \;+\; 35 \;+\; 42 \;+\; 19 \;=\; 108$.

questions.text: If all the words with or without meaning made using all the letters of the word "NAGPUR" are arranged as in a dictionary, then the word at $315^{\text{th}}$ position in this arrangement is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Arrange the letters of NAGPUR alphabetically as A, G, N, P, R, U and count words by prefix up to $315$. // 📝 Solution: The alphabetical order of the letters is A, G, N, P, R, U. Words starting with A: $5! \;=\; 120$. Words starting with G: $5! \;=\; 120$. Words starting with NA: $4! \;=\; 24$. Words starting with NG: $4! \;=\; 24$. Words starting with NP: $4! \;=\; 24$. Cumulative count up to prefix NP is $120 \;+\; 120 \;+\; 24 \;+\; 24 \;+\; 24 \;=\; 312$. Now list words starting with NR in alphabetical order: $313^{\text{th}}$ word is NRAGPU; $314^{\text{th}}$ word is NRAGUP; $315^{\text{th}}$ word is NRAPGU.

questions.text: The number of ways, in which $16$ oranges can be distributed to four children such that each child gets at least one orange, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the Stars and Bars formula ${}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$ for distributing $n$ identical objects among $r$ distinct recipients where each gets at least $1$. // 📝 Solution: Distributing $n \;=\; 16$ identical oranges among $r \;=\; 4$ children such that each child receives at least $1$ orange is equivalent to finding the number of positive integral solutions to $x_{1} \;+\; x_{2} \;+\; x_{3} \;+\; x_{4} \;=\; 16$, which is ${}^{16-1}C_{4-1} \;=\; {}^{15}C_{3} \;=\; \frac{15 \;\times\; 14 \;\times\; 13}{6} \;=\; 455$.
questions.topic: Distribution of Identical Objects (Stars and Bars)

questions.text: Let $S$ denote the set of $4$-digit numbers $abcd$ such that $a \;>\; b \;>\; c \;>\; d$ and $P$ denote the set of $5$-digit numbers having product of its digits equal to $20$. Then $n(S) \;+\; n(P)$ is equal to _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Any selection of $4$ distinct digits from $\left\{0, 1, \dots, 9\right\}$ gives a unique number in $S$, and factorize $20 \;=\; 2 \;\times\; 2 \;\times\; 5$ to find $n(P)$. // 📝 Solution: For $n(S)$: Choosing any $4$ distinct digits from $\left\{0, 1, 2, \dots, 9\right\}$ and arranging them in strictly decreasing order $a \;>\; b \;>\; c \;>\; d$ automatically ensures $a \;\ge\; 3 \;>\; 0$, so $n(S) \;=\; {}^{10}C_{4} \;=\; 210$. For $n(P)$: A $5$-digit number has digit product $20 \;=\; 2^{2} \;\times\; 5$ only if its digits are either $\left\{1, 1, 1, 4, 5\right\}$ (giving $\frac{5!}{3!} \;=\; 20$ numbers) or $\left\{1, 1, 2, 2, 5\right\}$ (giving $\frac{5!}{2!\;2!} \;=\; 30$ numbers). Thus $n(P) \;=\; 20 \;+\; 30 \;=\; 50$, and $n(S) \;+\; n(P) \;=\; 210 \;+\; 50 \;=\; 260$.

questions.text: The largest value of $n$, for which $40^{n}$ divides $60!$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Prime factorize $40^{n} \;=\; 2^{3n} \;\times\; 5^{n}$ and find the exponents of $2$ and $5$ in $60!$. // 📝 Solution: We have $40^{n} \;=\; \left(2^{3} \;\times\; 5\right)^{n} \;=\; 2^{3n} \;\times\; 5^{n}$. Exponent of $5$ in $60!$ is $E_{5}(60!) \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{5} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{25} \right\rfloor \;=\; 12 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 14$. Exponent of $2$ in $60!$ is $E_{2}(60!) \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{2} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{4} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{8} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{16} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{60}{32} \right\rfloor \;=\; 30 \;+\; 15 \;+\; 7 \;+\; 3 \;+\; 1 \;=\; 56$. For $40^{n}$ to divide $60!$, we require $n \;\le\; 14$ and $3n \;\le\; 56 \;\implies\; n \;\le\; 18$. Thus, the largest integer $n$ is $14$.

💡 Hint: Use the identity $\frac{{}^{n}C_{r}}{{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}} \;=\; \frac{n}{r}$ to form two linear equations in $n$ and $r$. // 📝 Solution: Using the ratio property $\frac{{}^{k}C_{m}}{{}^{k-1}C_{m-1}} \;=\; \frac{k}{m}$, we have $\frac{{}^{n+1}C_{r+1}}{{}^{n}C_{r}} \;=\; \frac{n \;+\; 1}{r \;+\; 1} \;=\; \frac{55}{35} \;=\; \frac{11}{7} \;\implies\; 7n \;-\; 11r \;=\; -4$, and $\frac{{}^{n}C_{r}}{{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}} \;=\; \frac{n}{r} \;=\; \frac{35}{21} \;=\; \frac{5}{3} \;\implies\; n \;=\; \frac{5}{3}r$. Substituting $n \;=\; \frac{5}{3}r$ into the first equation gives $7\left(\frac{5}{3}r\right) \;-\; 11r \;=\; -4 \;\implies\; \frac{2}{3}r \;=\; 4 \;\implies\; r \;=\; 6$, which gives $n \;=\; 10$. Therefore, $2n \;+\; 5r \;=\; 2(10) \;+\; 5(6) \;=\; 50$.

questions.text: The largest $n \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$, for which $7^{n}$ divides $101!$, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use Legendre's formula $E_{p}(m!) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left\lfloor \frac{m}{p^{k}} \right\rfloor$ to find the highest power of prime $7$ in $101!$. // 📝 Solution: Since $7$ is a prime number, the exponent of $7$ in $101!$ is given by Legendre's formula: $n \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{101}{7} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{101}{7^{2}} \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor \frac{101}{7^{3}} \right\rfloor \;=\; \left\lfloor 14.42 \right\rfloor \;+\; \left\lfloor 2.06 \right\rfloor \;+\; 0 \;=\; 14 \;+\; 2 \;=\; 16$.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 11\right\}$. The number of non-empty subsets of $S$ that have the sum of all elements a multiple of $3$, is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Group the elements of $S$ according to their remainders when divided by $3$, i.e., $3k$, $3k \;+\; 1$, and $3k \;+\; 2$. // 📝 Solution: Partition $S$ by remainders modulo $3$: Type $3k$: $A \;=\; \left\{3\right\}$ ($1$ element); Type $3k \;+\; 1$: $B \;=\; \left\{1, 7, 10\right\}$ ($3$ elements); Type $3k \;+\; 2$: $C \;=\; \left\{2, 5, 11\right\}$ ($3$ elements). A subset of $B \;\cup\; C$ has its sum divisible by $3$ if the number of elements chosen from $B$ and $C$ are either equal, or $3$ from one and $0$ from the other. Number of such subsets of $B \;\cup\; C$ is $\left({}^{3}C_{0}{}^{3}C_{0} \;+\; {}^{3}C_{1}{}^{3}C_{1} \;+\; {}^{3}C_{2}{}^{3}C_{2} \;+\; {}^{3}C_{3}{}^{3}C_{3}\right) \;+\; \left({}^{3}C_{3}{}^{3}C_{0} \;+\; {}^{3}C_{0}{}^{3}C_{3}\right) \;=\; \left(1 \;+\; 9 \;+\; 9 \;+\; 1\right) \;+\; \left(1 \;+\; 1\right) \;=\; 22$. The element $3 \;\in\; A$ can either be included or excluded in $2$ ways. Thus, total subsets including the empty set $\;=\; 22 \;\times\; 2 \;=\; 44$. Excluding the empty subset gives $44 \;-\; 1 \;=\; 43$.

questions.text: Number of ways of arranging $8$ identical books into $4$ identical shelves where any number of shelves may remain empty is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count the number of integer partitions of $8$ into at most $4$ positive parts. // 📝 Solution: Since both the $8$ books and the $4$ shelves are identical, we simply count the partitions of $8$ into at most $4$ parts: $3$ shelves empty: $(8, 0, 0, 0) \;\implies\; 1$ way. $2$ shelves empty: $(7, 1, 0, 0), (6, 2, 0, 0), (5, 3, 0, 0), (4, 4, 0, 0) \;\implies\; 4$ ways. $1$ shelf empty: $(6, 1, 1, 0), (5, 2, 1, 0), (4, 3, 1, 0), (4, 2, 2, 0), (3, 3, 2, 0) \;\implies\; 5$ ways. $0$ shelves empty: $(5, 1, 1, 1), (4, 2, 1, 1), (3, 3, 1, 1), (3, 2, 2, 1), (2, 2, 2, 2) \;\implies\; 5$ ways. Total number of ways $\;=\; 1 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 5 \;+\; 5 \;=\; 15$.

questions.text: The total number of words (with or without meaning) that can be formed out of the letters of the word 'DISTRIBUTION' taken four at a time, is equal to _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Group the $12$ letters by multiplicity—I(3), T(2), and $7$ singletons—and compute permutations for each $4$-letter pattern. // 📝 Solution: The word DISTRIBUTION has $9$ distinct letter types: I(3), T(2), D(1), S(1), R(1), B(1), U(1), O(1), N(1). Case 1 (All $4$ distinct): ${}^{9}C_{4} \;\times\; 4! \;=\; 126 \;\times\; 24 \;=\; 3024$. Case 2 ($2$ alike, $2$ distinct): ${}^{2}C_{1} \;\times\; {}^{8}C_{2} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{2!} \;=\; 2 \;\times\; 28 \;\times\; 12 \;=\; 672$. Case 3 ($2$ alike of one kind, $2$ alike of another kind): ${}^{2}C_{2} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{2!\;2!} \;=\; 1 \;\times\; 6 \;=\; 6$. Case 4 ($3$ alike, $1$ distinct): ${}^{1}C_{1} \;\times\; {}^{8}C_{1} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{3!} \;=\; 1 \;\times\; 8 \;\times\; 4 \;=\; 32$. Total $4$-letter words $\;=\; 3024 \;+\; 672 \;+\; 6 \;+\; 32 \;=\; 3734$.

questions.text: If $n$ is the number of ways five different employees can sit into four indistinguishable offices where any office may have any number of persons including zero, then $n$ is equal to:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Partition $5$ into at most $4$ parts and use the division into groups formula for each partition. // 📝 Solution: We distribute $5$ distinct employees into $4$ identical offices according to the possible group size partitions: $(5, 0, 0, 0) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{5!} \;=\; 1$; $(4, 1, 0, 0) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{4!\;1!} \;=\; 5$; $(3, 2, 0, 0) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{3!\;2!} \;=\; 10$; $(3, 1, 1, 0) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{3!\;(1!)^{2}\;2!} \;=\; 10$; $(2, 2, 1, 0) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{(2!)^{2}\;1!\;2!} \;=\; 15$; $(2, 1, 1, 1) \;\implies\; \frac{5!}{2!\;(1!)^{3}\;3!} \;=\; 10$. Total number of ways $n \;=\; 1 \;+\; 5 \;+\; 10 \;+\; 10 \;+\; 15 \;+\; 10 \;=\; 51$.

questions.text: In an examination of Mathematics paper, there are $20$ questions of equal marks and the question paper is divided into three sections: $A, B$ and $C$. A student is required to attempt total $15$ questions taking at least $4$ questions from each section. If section $A$ has $8$ questions, section $B$ has $6$ questions and section $C$ has $6$ questions, then the total number of ways a student can select $15$ questions is _____.
The total number of $4$-digit numbers whose greatest common divisor with $54$ is $2$, is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Since $54 \;=\; 2 \;\times\; 3^{3}$, a number has $\gcd(N, 54) \;=\; 2$ if and only if $N$ is divisible by $2$ but not divisible by $3$. // 📝 Solution: We have $54 \;=\; 2 \;\times\; 3^{3}$. For a $4$-digit number $N$ to satisfy $\gcd(N, 54) \;=\; 2$, $N$ must be a multiple of $2$ and not a multiple of $3$ (hence not a multiple of $6$). Out of $9000$ four-digit numbers ($1000$ to $9999$): Numbers divisible by $2$ $\;=\; \frac{9000}{2} \;=\; 4500$. Numbers divisible by $6$ $\;=\; \frac{9000}{6} \;=\; 1500$. Therefore, the required number of $4$-digit numbers is $4500 \;-\; 1500 \;=\; 3000$.

questions.text: Let $S \;=\; \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\right\}$. Let $x$ be the number of $9$-digit numbers formed using the digits of the set $S$ such that only one digit is repeated and it is repeated exactly twice. Let $y$ be the number of $9$-digit numbers formed using the digits of the set $S$ such that only two digits are repeated and each of these is repeated exactly twice. Then,
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $9!$ by choosing the repeated digits, the omitted digits, and permuting the $9$ positions. // 📝 Solution: For $x$: $1$ digit is repeated twice, $1$ digit is omitted, and $7$ digits appear once. Number of ways $x \;=\; {}^{9}C_{1} \;\times\; {}^{8}C_{1} \;\times\; \frac{9!}{2!} \;=\; 9 \;\times\; 8 \;\times\; \frac{9!}{2} \;=\; 36 \;\times\; 9!$. For $y$: $2$ digits are repeated twice each, $2$ digits are omitted, and $5$ digits appear once. Number of ways $y \;=\; {}^{9}C_{2} \;\times\; {}^{7}C_{2} \;\times\; \frac{9!}{2!\;2!} \;=\; 36 \;\times\; 21 \;\times\; \frac{9!}{4} \;=\; 189 \;\times\; 9!$. Taking the ratio gives $\frac{x}{y} \;=\; \frac{36}{189} \;=\; \frac{4}{21} \;\implies\; 21x \;=\; 4y$.

questions.text: There are $5$ points $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}, P_{5}$ on the side $AB$, excluding $A$ and $B$, of a triangle $ABC$. Similarly there are $6$ points $P_{6}, P_{7}, \dots, P_{11}$ on the side $BC$ and $7$ points $P_{12}, P_{13}, \dots, P_{18}$ on the side $CA$ of the triangle. The number of triangles, that can be formed using the points $P_{1}, P_{2}, \dots, P_{18}$ as vertices, is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Subtract the number of collinear triplets on each side of the triangle from the total ways of choosing $3$ points out of $18$. // 📝 Solution: Total number of given points on the three sides is $5 \;+\; 6 \;+\; 7 \;=\; 18$. A triangle is formed by selecting any $3$ non-collinear points. Therefore, the required number of triangles is ${}^{18}C_{3} \;-\; {}^{5}C_{3} \;-\; {}^{6}C_{3} \;-\; {}^{7}C_{3} \;=\; 816 \;-\; 10 \;-\; 20 \;-\; 35 \;=\; 751$.

questions.text: The number of $4$-letter words, with or without meaning, which can be formed using the letters PQRPQRSTUVP, is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Group the $11$ letters into frequencies P(3), Q(2), R(2), S(1), T(1), U(1), V(1) and count $4$-letter arrangements by multiplicity cases. // 📝 Solution: There are $7$ distinct letter types: P(3), Q(2), R(2), S(1), T(1), U(1), V(1). Case 1 (All $4$ distinct): ${}^{7}C_{4} \;\times\; 4! \;=\; 35 \;\times\; 24 \;=\; 840$. Case 2 ($2$ alike, $2$ distinct): ${}^{3}C_{1} \;\times\; {}^{6}C_{2} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{2!} \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 15 \;\times\; 12 \;=\; 540$. Case 3 ($2$ alike of one kind, $2$ alike of another kind): ${}^{3}C_{2} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{2!\;2!} \;=\; 3 \;\times\; 6 \;=\; 18$. Case 4 ($3$ alike, $1$ distinct): ${}^{1}C_{1} \;\times\; {}^{6}C_{1} \;\times\; \frac{4!}{3!} \;=\; 1 \;\times\; 6 \;\times\; 4 \;=\; 24$. Total $4$-letter words $\;=\; 840 \;+\; 540 \;+\; 18 \;+\; 24 \;=\; 1422$.

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Recall that the number of ways to distribute $m \;\cdot\; k$ distinct objects into $k$ distinct boxes of size $m$ each is $\frac{(mk)!}{(m!)^{k}} \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$. // 📝 Solution: We can write $\alpha \;=\; \frac{24!}{(4!)^{6}}$ and $\beta \;=\; \frac{120!}{(5!)^{24}}$. Since the number of ways of dividing $24$ distinct objects into $6$ ordered groups of $4$ objects each is $\frac{24!}{(4!)^{6}} \;=\; \alpha$, $\alpha$ must be a natural number. Similarly, the number of ways of dividing $120$ distinct objects into $24$ ordered groups of $5$ objects each is $\frac{120!}{(5!)^{24}} \;=\; \beta$, so $\beta$ is also a natural number. Hence, $\alpha \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$ and $\beta \;\in\; \mathbb{N}$.

questions.text: If all the six digit numbers $x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4}x_{5}x_{6}$ with $0 \;<\; x_{1} \;<\; x_{2} \;<\; x_{3} \;<\; x_{4} \;<\; x_{5} \;<\; x_{6}$ are arranged in the increasing order, then the sum of the digits in the $72^{\text{th}}$ number is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count how many strictly increasing $6$-digit numbers start with prefixes $12, 13, 14, 15,$ and $23$ to locate the $72^{\text{th}}$ number. // 📝 Solution: The digits are chosen from $\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\right\}$ and arranged in strictly increasing order. Count of numbers by prefix: Starting with $12$: ${}^{7}C_{4} \;=\; 35$. Starting with $13$: ${}^{6}C_{4} \;=\; 15$. Starting with $14$: ${}^{5}C_{4} \;=\; 5$. Starting with $15$: ${}^{4}C_{4} \;=\; 1$. Starting with $23$: ${}^{6}C_{4} \;=\; 15$. Cumulative count up to prefix $23$ is $35 \;+\; 15 \;+\; 5 \;+\; 1 \;+\; 15 \;=\; 71$. Therefore, the $72^{\text{th}}$ number is the very first number starting with $24$, which is $245678$. The sum of its digits is $2 \;+\; 4 \;+\; 5 \;+\; 6 \;+\; 7 \;+\; 8 \;=\; 32$.

questions.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Consider four points $p_{1}, p_{2}, p_{3}, p_{4}$ on the side $AB$, five points $p_{5}, p_{6}, p_{7}, p_{8}, p_{9}$ on the side $BC$, and four points $p_{10}, p_{11}, p_{12}, p_{13}$ on the side $AC$. None of these points is a vertex of the triangle $ABC$. Then the total number of pentagons, that can be formed by taking all the vertices from the points $p_{1}, p_{2}, \dots, p_{13}$, is _____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For a non-degenerate pentagon, no $3$ vertices can be collinear, so at most $2$ points can be chosen from each side of $\triangle ABC$. // 📝 Solution: We have $4$ points on $AB$, $5$ points on $BC$, and $4$ points on $AC$. Since no $3$ vertices of the pentagon can lie on the same side, we must select $2$ points from each of two sides and $1$ point from the remaining side, corresponding to permutations of $(1, 2, 2)$: Case 1 $(1, 2, 2)$: ${}^{4}C_{1} \;\cdot\; {}^{5}C_{2} \;\cdot\; {}^{4}C_{2} \;=\; 4 \;\times\; 10 \;\times\; 6 \;=\; 240$. Case 2 $(2, 1, 2)$: ${}^{4}C_{2} \;\cdot\; {}^{5}C_{1} \;\cdot\; {}^{4}C_{2} \;=\; 6 \;\times\; 5 \;\times\; 6 \;=\; 180$. Case 3 $(2, 2, 1)$: ${}^{4}C_{2} \;\cdot\; {}^{5}C_{2} \;\cdot\; {}^{4}C_{1} \;=\; 6 \;\times\; 10 \;\times\; 4 \;=\; 240$. Total number of pentagons $\;=\; 240 \;+\; 180 \;+\; 240 \;=\; 660$.
