questions.text: A person has been using spectacles of power $-1.0$ diopter for distant vision and a separate reading glass of power $+2.0$ diopters. What is the least distance of distinct vision for this person?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: A relaxed eye sees clearly when the lens forms the image at infinity, i.e. the object lies at the focal plane. // 📝 Solution: $P=+2\;\text{D}\implies f=\frac{1}{2}\;\text{m}=50\;\text{cm}$ $\implies u=-f=-50\;\text{cm}$ $\implies$ least distance $=50\;\text{cm}$
questions.topic: Power of lens, near point correction

questions.text: Two immiscible liquids of refractive indices $\frac{8}{5}$ and $\frac{3}{2}$ are put in a beaker as shown. The height of each column is $6\;\text{cm}$. A coin is placed at the bottom. For near normal vision, the apparent depth of the coin is $\frac{\alpha}{4}\;\text{cm}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For near-normal vision, apparent depth of stacked layers $=\sum\frac{h_i}{\mu_i}$. // 📝 Solution: $d_{\text{app}}=\frac{6}{8/5}+\frac{6}{3/2}=\frac{15}{4}+4=\frac{31}{4}\;\text{cm}\implies\alpha=31$

questions.text: A convex lens of refractive index $1.5$ and focal length $18\;\text{cm}$ in air is immersed in water of refractive index $\frac{4}{3}$. The change in its focal length is $\_\_\_\_\;\text{cm}$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the lensmaker's formula with $\frac{\mu_{\text{lens}}}{\mu_{\text{medium}}}-1$ in place of $\mu-1$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{1}{18}=\left(1.5-1\right)\frac{2}{R}\implies R=18\;\text{cm}$ $\implies \frac{1}{f_w}=\left(\frac{1.5}{4/3}-1\right)\frac{2}{R}=\frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{9}\implies f_w=72\;\text{cm}$ $\implies \Delta f=72-18=54\;\text{cm}$

questions.text: Two objects A and B are placed at $15\;\text{cm}$ and $25\;\text{cm}$ from the pole, in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature $40\;\text{cm}$. The distance between the images formed by the mirror is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$ with $f=\frac{R}{2}=-20\;\text{cm}$ for each object. // 📝 Solution: $u_A=-15\implies v_A=+60\;\text{cm}$ (virtual); $u_B=-25\implies v_B=-100\;\text{cm}$ (real) $\implies \left\lvert v_A-v_B\right\rvert=60+100=160\;\text{cm}$

questions.text: Three thin lenses are placed coaxially: $f_1=10\;\text{cm}$ at $30\;\text{cm}$ from an object, $f_2=-10\;\text{cm}$ at $5\;\text{cm}$ after the first lens, and $f_3=30\;\text{cm}$ at $10\;\text{cm}$ after the second lens. The position of the final image is: [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Solve lens by lens, using each image as the object for the next lens. // 📝 Solution: Lens 1: $u=-30$, $f=10\implies v_1=15\;\text{cm}$ $\implies$ for $L_2$ the object is virtual at $u_2=+10\;\text{cm}$ $\implies \frac{1}{v_2}=-\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}\implies v_2=\infty$ $\implies$ parallel rays to $L_3$ $\implies v_3=30\;\text{cm}$ right of $L_3$

questions.text: The critical angle of incidence for a pair of optical media is $45^\circ$. The refractive indices of the first and second media are in the ratio:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\sin\theta_c=\frac{\mu_{\text{rarer}}}{\mu_{\text{denser}}}$. // 📝 Solution: $\sin45^\circ=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\implies\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}=\sqrt{2}\implies\mu_1:\mu_2=\sqrt{2}:1$

questions.text: As shown in the figure, a thin plano-concave lens and a thin plano-convex lens are used to image an object placed at infinity. Both lenses have radius of curvature $30\;\text{cm}$ and refractive index $1.75$, and are placed $40\;\text{cm}$ apart. The image is formed at a distance $x\;=\;\_\_\_\;\text{cm}$ from the concave lens. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the lensmaker's formula to each lens, then treat the first image as the object for the second lens. // 📝 Solution: $f_1=-40\;\text{cm}$, $f_2=40\;\text{cm}$ $\implies$ image of $L_1$ lies $40\;\text{cm}$ left of $L_1$ $\implies$ object for $L_2$ is $80\;\text{cm}=2f_2$ away $\implies$ final image at $80\;\text{cm}$ right of $L_2$ $\implies$ $x=40+80=120\;\text{cm}$

questions.text: For a thin convex lens, the radii of curvature are $15\;\text{cm}$ and $30\;\text{cm}$ respectively. The focal length of the lens is $20\;\text{cm}$. The refractive index of the material of the lens is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the lensmaker's formula $\frac{1}{f}=\left(\mu-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{1}{20}=\left(\mu-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{15}+\frac{1}{30}\right)=\frac{\mu-1}{10}\implies\mu-1=\frac{1}{2}\implies\mu=1.5$

questions.text: A scientist observes bacteria through a compound microscope. To improve its resolving power he should (select the best option): (1) Increase the wavelength of the light (2) Increase the refractive index of the medium between the object and objective lens (3) Decrease the focal length of the eyepiece (4) Decrease the diameter of the objective lens.

options.text: (1) Increase the wavelength of the light
(2) Increase the refractive index of the medium between object and objective lens
(3) Decrease the focal length of the eyepiece
(4) Decrease the diameter of the objective lens

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Resolving power of a microscope is $P=\frac{2\mu\sin\theta}{1.22\lambda}$. // 📝 Solution: Official key marks option (1) $\implies$ Note: by the formula $P\propto\frac{\mu}{\lambda}$, option (2) is the physically expected choice, so verify the key.

questions.text: A convex lens of refractive index $1.5$ and focal length $18\;\text{cm}$ is immersed in water. The difference in focal lengths in water and in air is $\alpha\times f$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Refractive index of water $=\frac{4}{3}$)
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the lensmaker's formula with $\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_w}-1$ for water. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{1}{18}=0.5K\implies K=\frac{1}{9}\;\text{cm}^{-1}$ $\implies\frac{1}{f_w}=\left(\frac{1.5}{4/3}-1\right)K=\frac{1}{72}\implies f_w-f_a=72-18=54=3f$
questions.topic: Lens in water, focal length change

questions.text: The ratio of the magnitude of the kinetic energy to the potential energy of an electron in the $5^{\text{th}}$ excited state of a hydrogen atom is :
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: For any Bohr orbit, $\text{Kinetic Energy (KE)} = -\frac{1}{2} \text{Potential Energy (PE)}$.

📝 Step 1: The relation between kinetic energy and potential energy in a Bohr orbit is given by $\text{KE} = -\frac{1}{2} \text{PE}$.

Step 2: Therefore, the ratio of the magnitude of kinetic energy to potential energy is $\frac{\text{KE}}{\left\lvert \text{PE} \right\rvert} = \frac{1}{2}$, which is independent of the orbit number $n$.

questions.text: The ratio of the shortest wavelength of Balmer series to the shortest wavelength of Lyman series for hydrogen atom is:
questions.solution: Shortest wavelength occurs when $n_2 = \infty$. For Lyman: $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R(1)$. For Balmer: $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R(\frac{1}{4})$. Thus $\frac{\lambda_B}{\lambda_L} = 4:1$.

questions.text: An electron revolving in $n^{\text{th}}$ Bohr orbit has magnetic moment $\mu_{n}$. If $\mu_{n} \propto n^{x}$, the value of $x$ is:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Orbital magnetic moment is $\mu = i A$, where $i = \frac{e}{T}$ and $A = \pi r^{2}$.

📝 Step 1: The magnetic moment of an orbiting electron is $\mu = i A = \left( \frac{e}{T} \right) \left( \pi r^{2} \right) = \frac{e \omega r^{2}}{2} = \frac{evr}{2}$.

Step 2: From Bohr's quantization condition, $mvr = \frac{n h}{2\pi} \implies vr \propto n$.

Step 3: Thus, $\mu \propto \left( \text{v} \cdot r \right) \propto n$, which means $\mu_{n} \propto n^{1}$. Therefore, $x = 1$.

questions.text: According to Bohr's theory, the moment of momentum of an electron revolving in $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit of hydrogen atom is:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: The moment of momentum is the angular momentum $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Angular momentum is quantized according to Bohr's postulate: $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$.

Step 2: For the $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit, substitute $n = 4$.

Step 3: $L = \frac{4h}{2\pi} = \frac{2h}{\pi}$.

questions.text: An electron rotates in a circle around a nucleus having positive charge Ze. Correct relation between total energy (E) of electron to its potential energy (U) is:
questions.solution: Total energy $E = \frac{-KZe^2}{2r}$ and Potential Energy $U = \frac{-KZe^2}{r}$. Therefore, $E = \frac{U}{2} \implies 2E = U$.

questions.text: The angular momentum of an electron in a hydrogen atom is proportional to (where r is the radius of orbit of electron):
questions.solution: Centripetal force $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{Kq_1q_2}{r^2} \implies mv^2r = Kq_1q_2$. Angular momentum $L = mvr \implies L^2 = m^2v^2r^2 = m(mv^2r)r = m(Kq_1q_2)r \implies L \propto \sqrt{r}$.

questions.text: If an alpha particle with energy 7.7 MeV is bombarded on a thin gold foil, the closest distance from nucleus it can reach is: (Atomic number of gold 79 and $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^9$ in SI units)
questions.solution: At closest approach, $KE = PE \implies 7.7 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2e)(79e)}{r_{min}} \implies r_{min} = 2.95 \times 10^{-14}$ m.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Most of the mass of the atom and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus and the electrons revolve around it, is Rutherford's model.

Statement II : An atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it, is a special case of Rutherford's model.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate from the options given below.

options.text: Both statement I and statement II are false
Statement I is false but statement II is true
Statement I is true but statement II is false
Both statement I and statement II are true

questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Statement I describes Rutherford's atomic model, while Statement II describes Thomson's atomic model.

📝 Step 1: According to Rutherford's atomic model, most of the mass of the atom and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus and electrons revolve around it. Hence, Statement I is true.

Step 2: According to Thomson's atomic model, an atom is a spherical cloud of positive charge with electrons embedded in it (plum pudding model), which is completely different from Rutherford's model. Hence, Statement II is false.

questions.text: Two electrons are moving in orbits of two hydrogen like atoms with speeds $3\times10^5$ m/s and $2.5\times10^5$ m/s respectively. If the radii of these orbits are nearly same then the possible order of energy states are respectively:
questions.solution: Velocity $v \propto \frac{Z}{n}$ and radius $r \propto \frac{n^2}{Z} \implies r \propto \frac{n}{v}$. Since radii are same, $\frac{n_1}{v_1} = \frac{n_2}{v_2} \implies \frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{3}{2.5} = \frac{6}{5}$.

questions.text: A hydrogen atom in ground state is given an energy of $10.2 \; \text{eV}$. How many spectral lines will be emitted due to transition of electrons?
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Energy of $10.2 \; \text{eV}$ excites the hydrogen atom from $n = 1$ to $n = 2$ (first excited state).

📝 Solution:

Step 1: The energy given to the hydrogen atom is $10.2 \; \text{eV}$, which corresponds to the excitation state $n = 2$.

Step 2: When the electron returns from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$, only one spectral line is emitted.

Step 3: Number of spectral lines = $1$.

questions.text: The ratio of the magnitude of the kinetic energy to the potential energy of an electron in the 5th excited state of a hydrogen atom is:
questions.solution: For any Bohr orbit, Kinetic Energy $KE = \frac{1}{2}|PE|$. Therefore, the ratio $\frac{KE}{|PE|} = \frac{1}{2}$.

questions.text: The longest wavelength associated with Paschen series is: (Given $R_H = 1.097 \times 10^7$ SI unit)
questions.solution: For longest wavelength in Paschen series, transition is from $n=4$ to $n=3$. $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}) = R(\frac{7}{144}) \implies \lambda = \frac{144}{7R} = 1.876 \times 10^{-6}$ m.

questions.text: If Rydberg's constant is $R$, the longest wavelength of radiation in Paschen series will be $\frac{\alpha}{7R}$, where $\alpha = \dots\dots$
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: The longest wavelength in any spectral series corresponds to the transition from the nearest higher energy level ($n_{i} = n_{f} + 1$). For Paschen series, $n_{f} = 3$ and $n_{i} = 4$.

📝 Step 1: Using the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^{2} \left( \frac{1}{n_{f}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{i}^{2}} \right)$.

Step 2: For Paschen series and $Z = 1$: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{3^{2}} - \frac{1}{4^{2}} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = \frac{7R}{9 \times 16} = \frac{7R}{144}$.

Step 3: $\lambda = \frac{144}{7R}$, giving $\alpha = 144$.

questions.text: If the binding energy of ground state electron in a hydrogen atom is $13.6 \text{ eV}$, then the energy required to remove the electron from the second excited state of $\text{Li}^{2+}$ will be: $x \times 10^{-1} \text{ eV}$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Binding energy $E_n = 13.6 \times \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For $\text{Li}^{2+}$, atomic number $Z = 3$.

Step 2: Second excited state corresponds to principal quantum number $n = 3$.

Step 3: $E_3 = 13.6 \times \frac{3^2}{3^2} = 13.6 \text{ eV} = 136 \times 10^{-1} \text{ eV}$. Thus $x = 136$.

questions.text: A photon is emitted in transition from $n=4$ to $n=1$ level in hydrogen atom. The corresponding wavelength for this transition is (given, $h=4\times10^{-15}$ eVs):
questions.solution: $\Delta E = 13.6(1 - \frac{1}{16}) = 12.75$ eV. Wavelength $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{1242 \text{ eV nm}}{12.75 \text{ eV}} \approx 94.1$ nm.

questions.text: In an alpha particle scattering experiment distance of closest approach for the $\alpha$ particle is $4.5 \times 10^{-14} \; \text{m}$. If target nucleus has atomic number $80$, then maximum velocity of $\alpha$-particle is _______ $\times 10^5 \; \text{m/s}$ approximately. \; ($\frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \; \text{SI unit}$, mass of $\alpha$ particle $= 6.72 \times 10^{-27} \; \text{kg}$)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: At the distance of closest approach, kinetic energy is completely converted into electrostatic potential energy.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \frac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_{\text{min}}}$.

Step 2: Rearranging for velocity: $v = \sqrt{\frac{4 K Z e^2}{m \, r_{\text{min}}}}$.

Step 3: Substituting values: $v = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 80 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{6.72 \times 10^{-27} \times 4.5 \times 10^{-14}}} = 156 \times 10^5 \; \text{m/s}$.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Most of the mass of the atom and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus and the electrons revolve around it, is Rutherford's model.
Statement II: An atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it, is a special case of Rutherford's model.

options.text: Both statement I and statement II are false
Statement I is false but statement II is true
Statement I is true but statement II is false
Both statement I and statement II are true

questions.solution: Statement I describes Rutherford's model and is true. Statement II describes Thomson's plum pudding model, not a special case of Rutherford's model, so it is false.

questions.text: A hydrogen atom changes its state from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$. Due to recoil, the percentage change in the wavelength of emitted light is approximately $1 \times 10^{-n}$. The value of $n$ is _____. \; [Given $R_{\text{hc}} = 13.6 \; \text{eV}, \; hc = 1242 \; \text{eVnm}, \; h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \; \text{J s}, \; m = 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \; \text{kg}$]
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use conservation of momentum and energy during transition considering the recoil of the hydrogen atom.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Energy change for $n = 3$ to $n = 2$ is given by $\Delta E = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right) = 1.9 \; \text{eV}$.

Step 2: Using recoil velocity and energy conservation, the shift in wavelength is related by $\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta E}{2 \, m \, c^2}$.

Step 3: Substituting the values gives $\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx 10^{-7}$, hence $n = 7$.

questions.text: The longest wavelength associated with Paschen series is : (Given $R_{\text{H}} = 1.097 \times 10^7 \; \text{SI unit}$)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: For Paschen series, longest wavelength corresponds to transition from $n_2 = 4$ to $n_1 = 3$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Rydberg formula for Paschen series longest wavelength: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_{\text{H}} \left( \frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} \right)$.

Step 2: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_{\text{H}} \left( \frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = R_{\text{H}} \left( \frac{16 - 9}{144} \right) = \frac{7 R_{\text{H}}}{144}$.

Step 3: $\lambda = \frac{144}{7 \times 1.097 \times 10^7} = 1.876 \times 10^{-6} \; \text{m}$.

questions.text: Speed of an electron in Bohr's 7th orbit for Hydrogen atom is $3.6 \times 10^6$ m/s. The corresponding speed of the electron in 3rd orbit, in m/s is:
questions.solution: Speed $v \propto \frac{1}{n} \implies \frac{v_3}{v_7} = \frac{7}{3} \implies v_3 = \frac{7}{3} \times 3.6 \times 10^6 = 8.4 \times 10^6$ m/s.

questions.text: Speed of an electron in Bohr's $7^{\text{th}}$ orbit for Hydrogen atom is $3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$. The corresponding speed of the electron in $3^{\text{rd}}$ orbit, in $\text{m/s}$ is:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Speed of electron in Bohr's orbit is inversely proportional to $n$ ($v \propto \frac{Z}{n}$).

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For Hydrogen, $Z = 1$, so $v_n \propto \frac{1}{n}$.

$\frac{v_3}{v_7} = \frac{7}{3}$

Step 2: $v_3 = \frac{7}{3} v_7 = \frac{7}{3} \times 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s} = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.text: In Franck-Hertz experiment, the first dip in the current-voltage graph for hydrogen is observed at $10.2 \; \text{V}$. The wavelength of light emitted by hydrogen atom when excited to the first excitation level is _________ nm. \; (Given $hc = 1245 \; \text{eVnm}, \; e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \; \text{C}$).
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: First excitation energy corresponds to transition from $n = 1$ to $n = 2$, which is $10.2 \; \text{eV}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: The energy of emitted light is equal to the excitation energy $\Delta E = 10.2 \; \text{eV}$.

Step 2: Wavelength $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{1245 \; \text{eV-nm}}{10.2 \; \text{eV}}$.

Step 3: $\lambda \approx 122.06 \; \text{nm}$.

questions.text: An electron of hydrogen atom on an excited state is having energy $E_{n} = -0.85 \; \text{eV}$. The maximum number of allowed transitions to lower energy level is ...... .
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: First find the principal quantum number $n$ using $E_{n} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}} \; \text{eV}$, then use $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ for the number of transitions.

📝 Step 1: Given $E_{n} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}} = -0.85 \; \text{eV} \implies n^{2} = \frac{13.6}{0.85} = 16 \implies n = 4$.

Step 2: The maximum number of allowed transitions from level $n$ to lower energy levels is given by $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Step 3: Substituting $n = 4$: $\frac{4(4-1)}{2} = \frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$.

questions.text:
In hydrogen atom spectrum, (R -> Rydberg's constant):
A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3R}$
B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum
C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$
D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4R}$
Choose the correct answer:
questions.solution: A is true ($\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(1 - \frac{1}{4}) = \frac{3R}{4}$). B is true. C is true ($\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(\frac{1}{3^2}) = \frac{R}{9}$). D is false (minimum Lyman is $\frac{1}{R}$). Thus A, B, and C are correct.

questions.text: The radius of third stationary orbit of electron for Bohr's atom is R. The radius of fourth stationary orbit will be:
questions.solution: Radius $r \propto n^2$. Thus $\frac{r_4}{r_3} = \frac{4^2}{3^2} = \frac{16}{9} \implies r_4 = \frac{16}{9}R$.

questions.text: According to Bohr's theory, the moment of momentum of an electron revolving in 4th orbit of hydrogen atom is:
questions.solution: Angular momentum $L = mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$. For $n=4$, $L = \frac{4h}{2\pi} = \frac{2h}{\pi}$.

questions.text: Nucleus A having $Z = 17$ and equal number of protons and neutrons has $1.2 \text{ MeV}$ binding energy per nucleon. Another nucleus B of $Z = 12$ has total 26 nucleons and $1.8 \text{ MeV}$ binding energy per nucleon. The difference of binding energy of B and A will be $\underline{\quad\quad\quad}$ MeV.
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: $\text{Total Binding Energy} = (\text{Binding Energy per nucleon}) \times \text{Mass number}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For nucleus A, $Z = 17$, equal number of protons and neutrons means $A = 17 + 17 = 34$. Total binding energy of A $= 1.2 \times 34 = 40.8 \text{ MeV}$.

Step 2: For nucleus B, mass number $= 26$. Total binding energy of B $= 1.8 \times 26 = 46.8 \text{ MeV}$.

Step 3: Difference $= 46.8 - 40.8 = 6 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.text: An electron rotates in a circle around a nucleus having positive charge $Ze$. Correct relation between total energy ($E$) of electron to its potential energy ($U$) is:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Total energy is half of the potential energy in magnitude and negative of kinetic energy.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Potential energy of the system is given by $U = -\frac{K \, Z \, e^2}{r}$.

Step 2: Total energy is $E = -\frac{K \, Z \, e^2}{2r}$.

Step 3: Comparing both equations, we get $2E = U$.

questions.text:
For hydrogen atom, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the wavelengths corresponding to the transitions $1$ and $2$ respectively as shown in [FIGURE]. The ratio of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ is $\frac{x}{32}$. The value of $x$ is

[FIGURE]
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use the Rydberg formula for wavelength $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For transition 1 ($n=1$ to $n=3$): $\frac{1}{\lambda_1} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{8}{9} \right) \dots \text{(1)}$

Step 2: For transition 2 ($n=1$ to $n=2$): $\frac{1}{\lambda_2} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{3}{4} \right) \dots \text{(2)}$

Step 3: Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{9}{8} = \frac{27}{32}$. Thus $x = 27$.

questions.text: The wavelength of the radiation emitted is $\lambda_0$ when an electron jumps from the second excited state to the first excited state of hydrogen atom. If the electron jumps from the third excited state to the second orbit of the hydrogen atom, the wavelength of the radiation emitted will be $\frac{20}{x} \lambda_0$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Second excited state to first excited state means $n = 3 \to n = 2$.

$\frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right) \implies \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 13.6 \left( \frac{5}{36} \right) \dots \text{(i)}$

Step 2: Third excited state to second orbit means $n = 4 \to n = 2$.

$\frac{hc}{\left( \frac{20\lambda_0}{x} \right)} = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} \right) \implies \frac{hc}{\left( \frac{20\lambda_0}{x} \right)} = 13.6 \left( \frac{3}{16} \right) \dots \text{(ii)}$

Step 3: Dividing (ii) by (i) gives $\frac{x}{20} = \frac{3}{16} \times \frac{36}{5} \implies x = 27$.

questions.text: A light of energy $12.75 \text{ eV}$ is incident on hydrogen atom in its ground state. The atom absorbs the radiation and reaches to one of its excited states. The angular momentum of the atom in the excited state is $\frac{x}{\pi} \times 10^{-17} \text{ eVs}$. The value of $x$ is (use $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15} \text{ eVs}, c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ ms}^{-1}$):
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Energy of state $E_n = E_1 + \Delta E$. Angular momentum $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Ground state energy is $-13.6 \text{ eV}$. Energy of excited state $E_n = -13.6 + 12.75 = -0.85 \text{ eV}$.

Step 2: Using $E_n = \frac{-13.6}{n^2} \implies -0.85 = \frac{-13.6}{n^2} \implies n^2 = 16 \implies n = 4$.

Step 3: $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi} = \frac{4 \times 4.14 \times 10^{-15}}{2\pi} = \frac{8.28 \times 10^{-15}}{\pi} = \frac{828 \times 10^{-17}}{\pi} \text{ eVs}$. Hence $x = 828$.

questions.text: A photon is emitted in transition from $n = 4$ to $n = 1$ level in hydrogen atom. The corresponding wavelength for this transition is (given, $h = 4 \times 10^{-15} \text{ eVs}$):
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use Rydberg's formula $\frac{hc}{\lambda} = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right) \text{ eV}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} = \left( 1 - \frac{1}{16} \right) \left( 13.6 \text{ eV} \right)$

Step 2: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{15}{16} \times 13.6$

Step 3: Solving for $\lambda$ gives $\lambda = 94.1 \text{ nm}$.

questions.text: When a hydrogen atom going from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$ emits a photon, its recoil speed is $\frac{x}{5} \; \text{m/s}$. Where $x = \dots\dots$ (Use : mass of hydrogen atom $= 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \; \text{kg}$)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: By conservation of linear momentum, the momentum of the emitted photon equals the recoil momentum of the hydrogen atom ($p_{\text{photon}} = p_{\text{atom}}$).

📝 Step 1: Energy of the emitted photon for transition from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$ is $\Delta E = 13.6 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) = 10.2 \; \text{eV} = 10.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \; \text{J}$.

Step 2: Momentum of the photon is $p = \frac{\Delta E}{c} = \frac{10.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{3 \times 10^{8}}$.

Step 3: Recoil speed $v = \frac{p}{m} = \frac{10.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-27} \times 3 \times 10^{8}} = \frac{10.2}{3 \times 10^{-2}} = 3.4 \; \text{m/s} = \frac{17}{5} \; \text{m/s}$.

Step 4: Therefore, $x = 17$.
questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum in Atomic Transitions

questions.text: Hydrogen atom is bombarded with electrons accelerated through a potential difference of $V$, which causes excitation of hydrogen atoms. If the experiment is being formed at $T = 0 \; \text{K}$, the minimum potential difference needed to observe any Balmer series lines in the emission spectra will be $\frac{\alpha}{10} \; \text{V}$, where $\alpha = \dots\dots$
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: To observe Balmer series lines in emission, electrons must at least be excited to the $n = 3$ state from the ground state ($n = 1$).

📝 Step 1: For the minimum potential difference, the bombarding electron must supply enough energy to excite the hydrogen atom from $n = 1$ to $n = 3$.

Step 2: $\Delta E = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{1^{2}} - \frac{1}{3^{2}} \right) \; \text{eV} = 13.6 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{9} \right) = 13.6 \times \frac{8}{9} \approx 12.088 \; \text{eV}$.

Step 3: Therefore, the minimum potential difference $V = 12.09 \; \text{V}$, which gives $\alpha = 121$.

questions.text:
The energy levels of an atom is shown in figure. Which one of these transitions will result in the emission of a photon of wavelength 124.1 nm? (Given $h=6.62\times10^{-34}$ Js)
Level 1: 0.0 eV, Level 2: -2.2 eV, Level 3: -5.2 eV, Level 4: -10.0 eV
Transitions: A (1 to 3), B (2 to 4), C (1 to 4), D (3 to 4)
questions.solution: Energy of photon $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1241 \text{ eV nm}}{124.1 \text{ nm}} = 10$ eV. The energy difference between Level 1 (0.0 eV) and Level 4 (-10.0 eV) is exactly 10 eV, which corresponds to transition D.

questions.text: The smallest wavelength of Lyman series is $91 \text{ nm}$. The difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly $\ldots\ldots\ldots \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use the Rydberg formula to find the Rydberg constant from the smallest wavelength of Lyman series, then calculate the largest wavelengths for Balmer and Paschen series.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For the smallest wavelength of Lyman series ($n_{1} = 1 \text{ to } n_{2} = \infty$), we have $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^{2}} - \frac{1}{\infty^{2}} \right) \implies R = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{91} \text{ nm}^{-1}$.

Step 2: For the largest wavelength of Balmer series ($n_{1} = 2 \text{ to } n_{2} = 3$), $\frac{1}{\lambda_{B}} = R \left( \frac{1}{2^{2}} - \frac{1}{3^{2}} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9} \right) = \frac{5 R}{36}$. Substituting $R = \frac{1}{91}$, we get $\lambda_{B} = \frac{91 \times 36}{5} = 655.2 \text{ nm}$.

Step 3: For the largest wavelength of Paschen series ($n_{1} = 3 \text{ to } n_{2} = 4$), $\frac{1}{\lambda_{p}} = R \left( \frac{1}{3^{2}} - \frac{1}{4^{2}} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = \frac{7 R}{144}$. Thus, $\lambda_{p} = \frac{91 \times 144}{7} = 1872 \text{ nm}$.

Step 4: The difference between the two wavelengths is $\Delta \lambda = \lambda_{p} - \lambda_{B} = 1872 - 655.2 = 1216.8 \text{ nm} \approx 1217 \text{ nm}$. Hence, option B is correct.

questions.text: Two electrons are moving in orbits of two hydrogen like atoms with speeds $3 \times 10^{5} \text{ m/s}$ and $2.5 \times 10^{5} \text{ m/s}$ respectively. If the radii of these orbits are nearly same then the possible order of energy states are respectively.
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use the proportionalities for hydrogen-like atoms: velocity $V \propto \frac{Z}{n}$ and radius $r \propto \frac{n^{2}}{Z}$, which gives $r \propto \frac{n}{V}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Since the radii of the two orbits are nearly the same ($r_{1} \approx r_{2}$), we have:
$\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}} = 1 \implies \frac{n_{1} / V_{1}}{n_{2} / V_{2}} = 1 \implies \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}$.

Step 2: Substituting the given speeds:
$\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{5}}{2.5 \times 10^{5}} = \frac{6}{5}$.

Step 3: Thus, the possible order of energy states ($n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$) are 6 and 5 respectively. Hence, the correct option is D.

questions.text: A particular hydrogen-like ion emits the radiation of frequency $3 \times 10^{15} \; \text{Hz}$ when it makes transition from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$. The frequency of radiation emitted in transition from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$ is $\frac{x}{9} \times 10^{15} \; \text{Hz}$, when $x = \dots\dots$

The mass defect in a particular reaction is $0.4 \; \text{g}$. The amount of energy liberated is $n \times 10^{7} \; \text{kWh}$, where $n = \dots\dots$ (speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^{8} \; \text{m/s}$)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use mass-energy equivalence $E = \Delta m c^{2}$ and convert Joules or Watt-seconds to kWh.

📝 Step 1: Given mass defect $\Delta m = 0.4 \; \text{g} = 0.4 \times 10^{-3} \; \text{kg}$.

Step 2: Energy liberated $E = \Delta m c^{2} = 0.4 \times 10^{-3} \times \left( 3 \times 10^{8} \right)^{2} = 0.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 9 \times 10^{16} = 3.6 \times 10^{13} \; \text{J}$ (or $\text{Ws}$).

Step 3: Convert to $\text{kWh}$: $E = \frac{3.6 \times 10^{13} \; \text{Ws}}{3.6 \times 10^{6} \; \text{Ws/kWh}} = 10^{7} \; \text{kWh}$.

Step 4: Comparing with $n \times 10^{7} \; \text{kWh}$, we get $n = 1$.

questions.text: The smallest wavelength of Lyman series is 91 nm. The difference between the largest wavelengths of Paschen and Balmer series is nearly:
questions.solution: Smallest Lyman $\implies R = \frac{1}{91}$ nm$^{-1}$. Largest Balmer ($3 \to 2$): $\lambda_B = \frac{36}{5R} = 655.2$ nm. Largest Paschen ($4 \to 3$): $\lambda_P = \frac{144}{7R} = 1872$ nm. Difference $\Delta \lambda = 1872 - 655.2 = 1216.8 \approx 1217$ nm.

questions.text: The shortest wavelength of the spectral lines in the Lyman series of hydrogen spectrum is $915 \; \text{\AA}$. The longest wavelength of spectral lines in the Balmer series will be _____ $\text{\AA}$.
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use Rydberg formula for shortest wavelength in Lyman and longest in Balmer series.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Shortest wavelength of Lyman series corresponds to $n_1 = 1$ and $n_2 = \infty$, so $\frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 13.6 \; \text{eV} \implies \lambda_0 = 915 \; \text{\AA}$.

Step 2: Longest wavelength of Balmer series corresponds to $n_1 = 2$ and $n_2 = 3$, so $\frac{hc}{\lambda_1} = 13.6 \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right) = 13.6 \left( \frac{5}{36} \right)$.

Step 3: Solving for $\lambda_1$, we get $\lambda_1 = \frac{36 \lambda_0}{5} = \frac{36 \times 915}{5} = 6588 \; \text{\AA}$.

questions.text: An electron revolving in $n^{th}$ Bohr orbit has magnetic moment $\mu_n$. If $\mu_n \propto n^x$, the value of x is:
questions.solution: Magnetic moment $\mu = \frac{evr}{2}$. Since $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$, we have $vr = \frac{nh}{2\pi m}$. Thus $\mu = \frac{e}{2m}(\frac{nh}{2\pi}) \propto n^1$. So $x=1$.

questions.text: The radius of third stationary orbit of electron for Bohr's atom is $R$. The radius of fourth stationary orbit will be:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: The radius of the $n^{\text{th}}$ Bohr orbit is proportional to $n^{2}$ ($r \propto n^{2}$).

📝 Step 1: The formula for the radius of a Bohr orbit is $r_{n} = r_{0} \frac{n^{2}}{Z}$.

Step 2: Therefore, $r \propto n^{2}$, which means $\frac{r_{4}}{r_{3}} = \frac{4^{2}}{3^{2}} = \frac{16}{9}$.

Step 3: Given $r_{3} = R$, we get $r_{4} = \frac{16}{9} R$.

questions.text: The angular momentum of an electron in a hydrogen atom is proportional to: \; (Where $r$ is the radius of orbit of electron)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use the centripetal force equation and angular momentum quantization.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Centripetal force balance gives $\frac{m v^2}{r} = \frac{K q_1 q_2}{r^2}$, which implies $m v^2 r = K q_1 q_2$.

Step 2: Angular momentum $L = mvr$, squaring it gives $L^2 = m^2 v^2 r^2 = m (m v^2 r) r = m K q_1 q_2 r$.

Step 3: Therefore, $L \propto \sqrt{r}$.

questions.text: The energy of an electron in an orbit of the Bohr's atom is $-0.04E_0$ eV where $E_0$ is the ground state energy. If L is the angular momentum of the electron in this orbit and h is the Planck's constant, then $\frac{2\pi L}{h}$ is:
questions.solution: Energy $E_n = -\frac{E_0}{n^2} = -0.04E_0 \implies n^2 = 25 \implies n=5$. Angular momentum $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi} \implies \frac{2\pi L}{h} = n = 5$.

questions.text: If an alpha particle with energy $7.7 \text{ MeV}$ is bombarded on a thin gold foil, the closest distance from nucleus it can reach is $\ldots\ldots\ldots \text{ m}$. (Atomic number of gold $Z = 79$ and $\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} = 9 \times 10^{9}$ in SI units)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: At the distance of closest approach, the initial kinetic energy of the alpha particle is completely converted into electrostatic potential energy.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Equating kinetic energy to potential energy at closest approach $r_{\min}$: $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_{\min}}$.

Step 2: Rearranging for $r_{\min}$:
$r_{\min} = \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{2 Z e^{2}}{\text{KE}} = \frac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^{2}}{7.7 \times 10^{6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$.

Step 3: Simplifying the expression:
$r_{\min} = \frac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 79 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{7.7 \times 10^{6}} = \frac{2275.2 \times 10^{-10}}{7.7 \times 10^{6}} = 2.95 \times 10^{-14} \text{ m}$.

Step 4: Therefore, option D is the correct answer.

questions.text:
The energy levels of an atom is shown in [FIGURE]. Which one of these transitions will result in the emission of a photon of wavelength $124.1 \text{ nm}$? Given ($h = 6.62 \times 10^{-34} \text{ Js}$):

[FIGURE]
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Energy of emitted photon is $\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: $\Delta E = \frac{6.62 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{124.1 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \text{ eV} = 10 \text{ eV}$.

Step 2: Check the energy difference for transitions from the energy level diagram. Transition D corresponds to an energy change of $-10.0 \text{ eV} - 0 \text{ eV} = 10 \text{ eV}$.

Step 3: Therefore, transition D results in the desired photon emission.

questions.text: The radius of electron's second stationary orbit in Bohr's atom is R. The radius of 3rd orbit will be:
questions.solution: Radius $r \propto n^2 \implies \frac{r_3}{r_2} = \frac{3^2}{2^2} = \frac{9}{4} = 2.25 \implies r_3 = 2.25R$.

questions.text: The minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in ground state to emit radiation in Balmer series is nearly:
questions.solution: To emit in Balmer series, the electron must first be excited from $n=1$ to at least $n=3$. $\Delta E = E_3 - E_1 = -1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09 \approx 12.1$ eV.

questions.text: A hydrogen atom in ground state is given an energy of 10.2eV. How many spectral lines will be emitted due to transition of electrons?
questions.solution: The electron is excited to $n=2$ state because $\Delta E = 13.6(1 - \frac{1}{4}) = 10.2$ eV. From $n=2$, only 1 spectral line is emitted in transitioning back to $n=1$.

questions.text: The mass of proton, neutron and helium nucleus are respectively $1.0073 \text{ u}$, $1.0087 \text{ u}$ and $4.0015 \text{ u}$. The binding energy of helium nucleus is:
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: $\text{B.E.} = \left[ \left( Z m_p + (A-Z) m_n \right) - m_{\text{nucleus}} \right] \times 931.5 \text{ MeV}$ (or equivalent conversion factor).

📝 Solution:

Step 1: $\text{B.E.} = \left( 2 \times 1.0073 + 2 \times 1.0087 - 4.0015 \right) c^2$

Step 2: Mass defect $\Delta m = (2.0146 + 2.0174) - 4.0015 = 4.0320 - 4.0015 = 0.0305 \text{ u}$.

Step 3: $\text{B.E.} = 0.0305 \times 931.5 \approx 28.4 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.text: Assume that protons and neutrons have equal masses. Mass of a nucleon is $1.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and radius of nucleus is $1.5 \times 10^{-15} \; A^{1/3} \text{ m}$. The approximate ratio of the nuclear density and water density is $n \times 10^{13}$. The value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Nuclear density is given by $\rho = \frac{\text{Mass of nuclei}}{\text{Volume of nuclei}}$ and is independent of mass number $A$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: $\rho = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-27} A}{\frac{4}{3} \pi \left( 1.5 \times 10^{-15} \right)^{3} A} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-27}}{14.14 \times 10^{-45}} = 0.113 \times 10^{18}$

Step 2: Density of water is $\rho_w = 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3$.

Step 3: Ratio $\frac{\rho}{\rho_w} = 11.31 \times 10^{13} \approx 11 \times 10^{13}$. Hence $n = 11$.

questions.text:
In hydrogen atom spectrum, ($R \rightarrow \text{Rydberg's constant}$)
A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3 R}$
B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum
C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$
D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4 R}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Check each statement individually using Rydberg's formula for spectral series of hydrogen atom: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}} \right)$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: For maximum wavelength of Lyman series ($n_{1} = 1 \text{ to } n_{2} = 2$), $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^{2}} - \frac{1}{2^{2}} \right) = \frac{3 R}{4} \implies \lambda = \frac{4}{3 R}$. (Statement A is TRUE)

Step 2: The Balmer series corresponds to transitions ending at $n_{1} = 2$ and falls within the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum. (Statement B is TRUE)

Step 3: For minimum wavelength of Paschen series ($n_{1} = 3 \text{ to } n_{2} = \infty$), $\frac{1}{\lambda'} = R \left( \frac{1}{3^{2}} - \frac{1}{\infty^{2}} \right) = \frac{R}{9} \implies \lambda' = \frac{9}{R}$. (Statement C is TRUE)

Step 4: For minimum wavelength of Lyman series ($n_{1} = 1 \text{ to } n_{2} = \infty$), $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{1^{2}} - \frac{1}{\infty^{2}} \right) = R \implies \lambda = \frac{1}{R}$ (Statement D is FALSE, as it stated $\frac{5}{4 R}$).

Step 5: Hence, statements A, B and C are correct, making option B the right choice.

questions.text: The energy of an electron in an orbit of the Bohr's atom is $E_{n} = - \frac{E_{0}}{n^{2}} \text{ eV}$ where $E_{0}$ is the ground state energy. If $L$ is the angular momentum of the electron in this orbit and $h$ is the Planck's constant, then $\frac{2 \pi L}{h}$ is :
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Use the given energy expression to find the principal quantum number $n$ and substitute it into the angular momentum quantization condition $L = \frac{n h}{2 \pi}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Given energy of the electron is $E = - 0.04 E_{0}$. Comparing this with $E_{n} = - \frac{E_{0}}{n^{2}}$, we get $\frac{E_{0}}{n^{2}} = 0.04 E_{0} \implies n^{2} = \frac{1}{0.04} = 25 \implies n = 5$.

Step 2: The angular momentum in Bohr's model is given by $L = n \hbar = n \frac{h}{2 \pi}$.

Step 3: Rearranging the terms, we get $\frac{2 \pi L}{h} = n = 5$. Therefore, the correct option is A.

questions.text: An electron of a hydrogen like atom, having $Z = 4$, jumps from $4^{\text{th}}$ energy state to $2^{\text{nd}}$ energy state, The energy released in this process, will be: (Given $Rch = 13.6 \text{ eV}$ where $R = \text{Rydberg constant}$, $c = \text{Speed of light in vacuum}$, $h = \text{Planck's constant}$)
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: $\Delta E = 13.6 Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right) \text{ eV}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: $\Delta E = 13.6 \times (4)^2 \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} \right)$

Step 2: $\Delta E = 13.6 \times 16 \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16} \right) = 13.6 \times 16 \left( \frac{3}{16} \right)$

Step 3: $\Delta E = 13.6 \times 3 = 40.8 \text{ eV}$.

questions.text: The radius of electron's secondary stationary orbit in Bohr's atom is $R$. The radius of $3^{\text{rd}}$ orbit will be
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Radius of Bohr's orbit is proportional to $n^2$ ($r_n \propto n^2$).

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Secondary orbit means $n = 2$. So $r_2 = k (2^2) = 4k = R$.

Step 2: Radius of $3^{\text{rd}}$ orbit is $r_3 = k (3^2) = 9k$.

Step 3: $\frac{r_3}{R} = \frac{9}{4} = 2.25 \implies r_3 = 2.25R$.

questions.text: Radius of a certain orbit of hydrogen atom is $8.48 \; \text{\AA}$. If energy of electron in this orbit is $\frac{E}{x}$, then $x = $ _____ \; (Given $a_0 = 0.529 \; \text{\AA}$, $E = $ energy of electron in ground state).
questions.solution:
💡 Hint: Radius $r = a_0 n^2$ and Energy $E_n = \frac{E}{n^2}$.

📝 Solution:

Step 1: Radius formula is $r = 0.529 \, n^2$. Substituting values: $8.48 = 0.529 \, n^2 \implies n^2 = 16 \implies n = 4$.

Step 2: Energy in the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit is given by $E_n = \frac{E}{n^2} = \frac{E}{16}$.

Step 3: Comparing with $\frac{E}{x}$, we get $x = 16$.

questions.text: Match List-I with List-II. List-I (Number): (A) $1001$, (B) $010.1$, (C) $100.100$, (D) $0.0010010$. List-II (Significant figures): (I) $3$, (II) $4$, (III) $5$, (IV) $6$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Count non-zero digits, zeros between non-zero digits, and trailing zeros after a decimal point. // 📝 Solution: $1001\to4$, $010.1\to3$, $100.100\to6$, $0.0010010\to5$ $\;\implies\;$ (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.text: In an expression $a\times10^{b}$:

options.text: $b$ is the order of magnitude for $a\ge5$
$b$ is the order of magnitude for $a\le5$
$a$ is the order of magnitude for $b\le5$
$b$ is the order of magnitude for $5<a\le10$

questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Order of magnitude is the power of 10 after rounding the mantissa to the nearest power of 10, with threshold 5. // 📝 Solution: For $a\le5$, $a\times10^{b}$ rounds to $10^{b}\;\implies\;$ order $=b$; for $a>5$, it rounds to $10^{b+1}$.

questions.text: In an experiment of measuring the refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope, a student measures the real thickness of the slab as $5.25\;\mathrm{mm}$ and apparent thickness as $5.00\;\mathrm{mm}$. The microscope has 20 divisions per cm on the main scale and 50 Vernier divisions equal 49 main scale divisions. The estimated uncertainty in the refractive index is $\frac{x}{10}\times10^{-3}$, where $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Vernier least count is one main scale division divided by the number of Vernier divisions; use $\frac{\Delta\mu}{\mu}=\frac{\Delta h}{h}+\frac{\Delta h'}{h'}$. // 📝 Solution: $\mathrm{LC}=\frac{1}{20}\;\mathrm{cm}-\frac{49}{50}\cdot\frac{1}{20}\;\mathrm{cm}=\frac{1}{50}\cdot\frac{1}{20}\;\mathrm{cm}=0.01\;\mathrm{mm}$ $\;\implies\;\Delta\mu=\frac{5.25}{5.00}\left[\frac{0.01}{5.25}+\frac{0.01}{5.00}\right]=\frac{41}{10}\times10^{-3}$
questions.topic: Vernier least count and error propagation

questions.text: The focal length $(f)$ of a convex lens is measured. The least counts of the scales for object position $(u)$ and image position $(v)$ are $\Delta u$ and $\Delta v$, respectively. The error in the measurement of the focal length will be:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Differentiate the lens formula $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}$ and take maximum errors. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta f}{f^{2}}=\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}+\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}\;\implies\;\Delta f=f^{2}\left[\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}+\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}\right]$

questions.text: In an experiment the values of two spring constants were measured as $k_{1}=(10\pm0.2)\;\mathrm{N/m}$ and $k_{2}=(20\pm0.3)\;\mathrm{N/m}$. If these springs are connected in parallel, the percentage error in the equivalent spring constant is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For parallel springs $k_{eq}=k_{1}+k_{2}$, so absolute errors add. // 📝 Solution: $k_{eq}=30\;\mathrm{N/m}$, $\Delta k_{eq}=0.2+0.3=0.5\;\mathrm{N/m}$ $\;\implies\;\frac{\Delta k_{eq}}{k_{eq}}\times100=\frac{0.5}{30}\times100\approx1.67\%$

questions.text: The resistance $R=\frac{V}{I}$ where $V=(200\pm5)\;\mathrm{V}$ and $I=(20\pm0.2)\;\mathrm{A}$. The percentage error in the measurement of $R$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For a quotient, the fractional errors add. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta R}{R}=\frac{\Delta V}{V}+\frac{\Delta I}{I}=\frac{5}{200}+\frac{0.2}{20}=0.025+0.01=0.035\;\implies\;3.5\%$

questions.text: Four persons measure the length of a rod as $20.00\;\mathrm{cm}$, $19.75\;\mathrm{cm}$, $17.01\;\mathrm{cm}$ and $18.25\;\mathrm{cm}$. The relative error in the measurement of the average length of the rod is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Relative error equals mean absolute error divided by mean value. // 📝 Solution: $\bar{l}=\frac{75.01}{4}=18.7525\;\mathrm{cm}$ $\;\implies\;\overline{\Delta l}=\frac{1.2475+0.9975+1.7425+0.5025}{4}=1.1225$ $\;\implies\;\frac{\overline{\Delta l}}{\bar{l}}=\frac{1.1225}{18.7525}\approx0.06$
questions.topic: Mean absolute error and relative error

questions.text: To find the spring constant $(k)$ of a spring experimentally, a student commits $2\%$ positive error in the measurement of time and $1\%$ negative error in the measurement of mass. The percentage error in determining $k$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: From $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$, use $\frac{\Delta k}{k}=\frac{\Delta m}{m}-2\frac{\Delta T}{T}$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta k}{k}\times100=(-1)-2(2)=-5\%\;\implies\;\left\lvert\frac{\Delta k}{k}\right\rvert\times100=5\%$

questions.text: Time periods of oscillation of the same simple pendulum measured using four different clocks were recorded as $4.62\;\mathrm{s}$, $4.632\;\mathrm{s}$, $4.6\;\mathrm{s}$ and $4.64\;\mathrm{s}$. The arithmetic mean of these readings in correct significant figures is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Round each reading to the least number of significant figures in the data before averaging. // 📝 Solution: $\text{Sum}=4.6+4.6+4.6+4.6=18.4\;\implies\;\text{Mean}=\frac{18.4}{4}=4.6\;\mathrm{s}$

questions.text: The radius $(r)$, length $(l)$ and resistance $(R)$ of a metal wire were measured as $r=(0.35\pm0.05)\;\mathrm{cm}$, $R=(100\pm10)\;\Omega$, $l=(15\pm0.2)\;\mathrm{cm}$. The percentage error in the resistivity of the material of the wire is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\rho=\frac{\pi r^{2}R}{l}$ so that $\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\frac{\Delta R}{R}+2\frac{\Delta r}{r}+\frac{\Delta l}{l}$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\frac{10}{100}+2\times\frac{0.05}{0.35}+\frac{0.2}{15}\approx0.1+0.2857+0.0133=0.399\;\implies\;39.9\%$

questions.text: If the percentage errors in measuring the length and the diameter of a wire are $0.1\%$ each, the percentage error in measuring its resistance will be:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $R=\frac{\rho L}{\pi d^{2}/4}$, use $\frac{\Delta R}{R}=\frac{\Delta L}{L}+2\frac{\Delta d}{d}$. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta R}{R}\times100=0.1+2(0.1)=0.3\%$

questions.text: Young's modulus is given by $Y=49000\,\frac{M}{l}\;\frac{\mathrm{dyn}}{\mathrm{cm}^{2}}$, where $M$ is the mass and $l$ is the extension of the wire. Error in $Y$ is estimated from an $M-l$ plot. The smallest scale divisions are $5\;\mathrm{g}$ along the load axis and $0.02\;\mathrm{cm}$ along the extension axis. If $M=500\;\mathrm{g}$ and $l=2\;\mathrm{cm}$, the percentage error in $Y$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For $Y\propto M/l$, the fractional errors add. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=\frac{5}{500}+\frac{0.02}{2}=0.01+0.01=0.02\;\implies\;\%\,\frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=2\%$

questions.text: A physical quantity $Q$ depends on $a,b,c$ by the relation $Q=\frac{a^{4}b^{3}}{c^{2}}$. The percentage errors in $a,b$ and $c$ are $3\%$, $4\%$ and $5\%$, respectively. The percentage error in $Q$ is:
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For a power-law relation, the percentage error is the sum of each power times its percentage error. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{\Delta Q}{Q}\times100=4(3)+3(4)+2(5)=12+12+10=34\%$

questions.text: A solid sphere and a hollow cylinder roll up without slipping on the same inclined plane with the same initial speed $v$. The sphere and the cylinder reach up to maximum heights $h_1$ and $h_2$ respectively, above the initial level. The ratio $h_1 : h_2$ is $\frac{n}{10}$. The value of $n$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Energy conservation: $gh \; = \; \frac{v^2}{2}\left( 1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2} \right)$. // 📝 Solution: $h \; \propto \; 1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2} \implies \frac{h_1}{h_2} \; = \; \frac{1 + \frac{2}{5}}{1 + 1} \; = \; \frac{7}{10} \implies n \; = \; 7$

questions.text: A uniform solid cylinder with radius $R$ and length $L$ has moment of inertia $I_1$ about the axis of the cylinder. A concentric solid cylinder of radius $R' \; = \; \frac{R}{2}$ and length $L' \; = \; \frac{L}{2}$ is carved out of the original cylinder. If $I_2$ is the moment of inertia of the carved out portion, then $\frac{I_1}{I_2} \; = \;$ ______. (Both $I_1$ and $I_2$ are about the axis of the cylinder)
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Mass is proportional to volume, and $I \; = \; \frac{1}{2}mr^2$ for a solid cylinder about its axis. // 📝 Solution: $m_2 \; = \; \frac{m_1}{8} \implies I_2 \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{m_1}{8} \right)\left( \frac{R}{2} \right)^2 \; = \; \frac{m_1 R^2}{64}$ and $I_1 \; = \; \frac{m_1 R^2}{2} \implies \frac{I_1}{I_2} \; = \; 32$
questions.topic: Moment of Inertia of Solid Cylinder

questions.text: Two cars $A$ and $B$ each of mass $10^3 \text{ kg}$ are moving on parallel tracks separated by a distance of $10 \text{ m}$, in same direction with speeds $72 \text{ km/h}$ and $36 \text{ km/h}$. The magnitude of angular momentum of car $A$ with respect to car $B$ is ____ $\text{J s}$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $L \; = \; m\,v_{rel}\,d$ with $d$ the perpendicular separation. // 📝 Solution: $v_{rel} \; = \; 20 - 10 \; = \; 10 \text{ m/s} \implies L \; = \; 10^3 \times 10 \times 10 \; = \; 10^5 \text{ J s}$

questions.text: Two masses $400 \text{ g}$ and $350 \text{ g}$ are suspended from the ends of a light string passing over a heavy pulley of radius $2 \text{ cm}$. When released from rest the heavier mass is observed to fall $81 \text{ cm}$ in $9 \text{ s}$. The rotational inertia of the pulley is ____ $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2$. $\left( g \; = \; 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 \right)$
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find $a$ from kinematics, then $\left( m_1 - m_2 \right)g - \left( m_1 + m_2 \right)a \; = \; \frac{Ia}{R^2}$. // 📝 Solution: $a \; = \; \frac{2 \times 0.81}{81} \; = \; 0.02 \text{ m/s}^2 \implies 0.05 \times 9.8 - 0.75 \times 0.02 \; = \; I \times \frac{0.02}{0.0004} \implies 0.475 \; = \; 50I \implies I \; = \; 9.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^2$

questions.text: A thin uniform rod $\left( X \right)$ of mass $M$ and length $L$ is pivoted at a height $\left( \frac{L}{3} \right)$ as shown in the figure. The rod is allowed to fall from a vertical position and lie horizontally on the table. The angular velocity of this rod when it hits the table top, is ____. $\left( g \; = \; \text{gravitational acceleration} \right)$ [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The centre of mass lies $\frac{L}{6}$ from the pivot; use energy conservation about the pivot. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; \frac{ML^2}{12} + M\left( \frac{L}{6} \right)^2 \; = \; \frac{ML^2}{9};\; Mg\frac{L}{6} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{ML^2}{9}\omega^2 \implies \omega^2 \; = \; \frac{3g}{L} \implies \omega \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}$

questions.text: A solid sphere of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ is making pure rolling on a horizontal surface with kinetic energy $2240 \text{ J}$. The velocity of centre of mass of the sphere will be ______ $\text{ms}^{-1}$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Total KE in pure rolling is $\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ for a solid sphere. // 📝 Solution: $2240 \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left( 2 \right)v^2 \; + \; \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{5}\left( 2 \right)v^2 \; = \; \frac{7}{5}v^2 \implies v^2 \; = \; 1600 \implies v \; = \; 40 \text{ m/s}$

questions.text: A skater spinning with arms outstretched pulls her arms in so that her moment of inertia becomes half. Her angular speed becomes
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Angular momentum is conserved when no external torque acts. // 📝 Solution: $I\omega \; = \; \dfrac{I}{2}\omega' \implies \omega' \; = \; 2\omega$

questions.text: For a solid sphere rolling without slipping on a horizontal surface, the ratio of rotational kinetic energy to total kinetic energy is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Write both KE terms using $v \; = \; \omega R$. // 📝 Solution: $K_{rot} \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}\left( \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 \right)\omega^2 \; = \; \dfrac{1}{5}Mv^2, \; K_{tot} \; = \; \dfrac{7}{10}Mv^2 \implies \dfrac{K_{rot}}{K_{tot}} \; = \; \dfrac{2}{7}$

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass $2\;\text{kg}$ and radius $4\;\text{m}$ about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is ______ $\text{kg m}^2$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: For a disc, $I \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; \dfrac{1}{2}\left( 2 \right)\left( 4 \right)^2 \; = \; 16\;\text{kg m}^2$
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a disc

questions.text: A string is wrapped around the rim of a wheel of moment of inertia $0.40 \text{ kgm}^2$ and radius $10 \text{ cm}$. The wheel is free to rotate about its axis. Initially the wheel is at rest. The string is now pulled by a force of $40 \text{ N}$. The angular velocity of the wheel after $10 \text{ s}$ is $x \text{ rad/s}$, where $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\tau \; = \; FR \; = \; I\alpha$ and $\omega \; = \; \alpha t$. // 📝 Solution: $40 \times 0.1 \; = \; 0.4\alpha \implies \alpha \; = \; 10 \text{ rad/s}^2 \implies \omega \; = \; 10 \times 10 \; = \; 100 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.text: Two small balls with masses $m$ and $2m$ are attached to both ends of a rigid rod of length $d$ and negligible mass. If angular momentum of this system is $L$ about an axis $\left( A \right)$ passing through its centre of mass and perpendicular to the rod then angular velocity of the system about $A$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Locate the centre of mass, find $I_{cm}$, then $\omega \; = \; \frac{L}{I}$. // 📝 Solution: $r_m \; = \; \frac{2d}{3},\; r_{2m} \; = \; \frac{d}{3} \implies I \; = \; m\frac{4d^2}{9} + 2m\frac{d^2}{9} \; = \; \frac{2md^2}{3} \implies \omega \; = \; \frac{3L}{2md^2}$
questions.topic: Angular Momentum about Centre of Mass

questions.text: A car is moving on a circular path of radius $600 \text{ m}$ such that the magnitudes of the tangential acceleration and centripetal acceleration are equal. The time taken by the car to complete the first quarter of revolution, if it is moving with an initial speed of $54 \text{ km/hr}$, is $t\left( 1 - e^{-\pi/2} \right) \text{ s}$. The value of $t$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $a_t \; = \; v\frac{dv}{dx} \; = \; \frac{v^2}{R}$ and integrate. // 📝 Solution: $v \; = \; v_0 e^{x/R},\; v_0 \; = \; 15 \text{ m/s} \implies \int_0^{\pi R/2} e^{-x/R}dx \; = \; v_0 t_0 \implies t_0 \; = \; \frac{R}{v_0}\left( 1 - e^{-\pi/2} \right) \; = \; 40\left( 1 - e^{-\pi/2} \right) \implies t \; = \; 40$

questions.text: A ring and a disc of the same mass and radius are released from rest at the top of an inclined plane and roll down without slipping. Which one reaches the bottom first?
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Acceleration is $a \; = \; \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 \; + \; I/MR^2}$, so smaller $I/MR^2$ gives larger $a$. // 📝 Solution: $\dfrac{I}{MR^2} \; = \; 1 \text{ (ring)}, \; \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ (disc)} \implies a_{disc} \; > \; a_{ring} \implies \text{disc reaches first}$

questions.text: Three balls of masses $2 \text{ kg},\; 4 \text{ kg}$ and $6 \text{ kg}$ respectively are arranged at centre of the edges of an equilateral triangle of side $2 \text{ m}$. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through the centroid and perpendicular to the plane of triangle, will be ______ $\text{kgm}^2$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Each edge midpoint is at the inradius $r \; = \; \frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}}$ from the centroid. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $r \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies I \; = \; r^2\left( 2 + 4 + 6 \right) \; = \; \frac{1}{3} \times 12 \; = \; 4 \text{ kg m}^2$
questions.topic: Moment of Inertia of Point Masses

questions.text: The pulley shown in figure is made using a thin rim and two rods of length equal to diameter of the rim. The rim and each rod have a mass of $M$. Two blocks of mass of $M$ and $m$ are attached to two ends of a light string passing over the pulley, which is hinged to rotate freely in vertical plane about its center. The magnitudes of the acceleration experienced by the blocks is ____ (assume no slipping of string on pulley). [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the pulley's $I$ as rim plus two rods about the centre, then use $\left( M - m \right)g \; = \; \left( M + m + \frac{I}{R^2} \right)a$. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; MR^2 + 2\cdot\frac{M\left( 2R \right)^2}{12} \; = \; \frac{5MR^2}{3} \implies \left( M - m \right)g \; = \; \left( M + m + \frac{5M}{3} \right)a \implies a \; = \; \frac{\left( M - m \right)g}{\frac{8}{3}M + m}$

questions.text: Moment of inertia of a disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about any of its diameter is $\frac{MR^2}{4}$. The moment of inertia of this disc about an axis normal to the disc and passing through a point on its edge will be $\frac{x}{2}MR^2$. The value of $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Perpendicular axis theorem gives $I_{cm} \; = \; \frac{MR^2}{2}$, then use the parallel axis theorem. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $I \; = \; \frac{MR^2}{2} \; + \; MR^2 \; = \; \frac{3}{2}MR^2 \implies x \; = \; 3$

questions.text: A car is moving on a horizontal curved road with radius $50 \text{ m}$. The approximate maximum speed of the car will be, if the friction between tyres and road is $0.34$. [Take $g \; = \; 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Maximum static friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu mg \; = \; \frac{mv^2}{r}$. // 📝 Solution: $v_{max} \; = \; \sqrt{\mu r g} \; = \; \sqrt{0.34 \times 50 \times 10} \; = \; \sqrt{170} \; \approx \; 13 \text{ m/s}$
questions.topic: Banking and Friction on Curved Road

questions.text: If a solid sphere of mass $5 \text{ kg}$ and a disc of mass $4 \text{ kg}$ have the same radius, then the ratio of the moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane to the moment of inertia of the sphere about its tangent will be $\frac{x}{7}$. The value of $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the parallel axis theorem for both bodies about a tangent, with $I_{disc,\,diameter} \; = \; \frac{1}{4}mR^2$. // 📝 Solution: $I_{sphere} \; = \; \frac{2}{5}\left( 5 \right)R^2 \; + \; 5R^2 \; = \; 7R^2$ and $I_{disc} \; = \; \frac{4R^2}{4} \; + \; 4R^2 \; = \; 5R^2 \implies \frac{I_{disc}}{I_{sphere}} \; = \; \frac{5}{7} \implies x \; = \; 5$

questions.text: Consider a Disc of mass $5 \text{ kg}$, radius $2 \text{ m}$, rotating with angular velocity of $10 \text{ rad/s}$ about an axis perpendicular to the plane of rotation. An identical disc is kept gently over the rotating disc along the same axis. The energy dissipated so that both the discs continue to rotate together without slipping is ______ J. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Conserve angular momentum, then find the kinetic energy loss. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; 10,\; L \; = \; 100 \implies 100 \; = \; 20\omega_f \implies \omega_f \; = \; 5;\; E_i \; = \; 500,\; E_f \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left( 20 \right)\left( 25 \right) \; = \; 250 \implies \Delta E \; = \; 250 \text{ J}$

questions.text: The condition for pure rolling (rolling without slipping) of a body of radius $R$ is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: The contact point must have zero velocity. // 📝 Solution: $v_{contact} \; = \; v_{cm} \; - \; R\omega \; = \; 0 \implies v_{cm} \; = \; R\omega$

questions.text: Solid sphere $A$ of radius $5 \text{ cm}$ is rotating about an axis $PQ$ which is at a distance $10 \text{ cm}$ from its centre. [FIGURE] Its radius of gyration about $PQ$ will be $\sqrt{x} \text{ cm}$. The value of $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the parallel axis theorem $I \; = \; I_{cm} \; + \; md^2$ and $I \; = \; mk^2$. // 📝 Solution: $k^2 \; = \; \frac{2}{5}R^2 \; + \; d^2 \; = \; \frac{2}{5}\left( 25 \right) \; + \; 100 \; = \; 110 \implies x \; = \; 110$
questions.topic: Parallel Axis Theorem and Radius of Gyration

questions.text: Two circular discs of radius each $10 \text{ cm}$ are joined at their centres by a rod of length $30 \text{ cm}$ and mass $600 \text{ gm}$ as shown in figure. If the mass of each disc is $600 \text{ gm}$ and applied torque between two discs is $43 \times 10^5 \text{ dyne. cm}$, the angular acceleration of the discs about the given axis $AB$ is ____ $\text{rad/s}^2$. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Add $I$ of the rod and both discs about $AB$ (parallel axis theorem), then $\alpha \; = \; \frac{\tau}{I}$. // 📝 Solution: $I_{rod} \; = \; 600\left( \frac{900}{12} + 25 \right) \; = \; 6 \times 10^4;\; I_1 \; = \; 15000 + 60000;\; I_2 \; = \; 15000 + 240000 \implies I \; = \; 39 \times 10^4 \text{ g cm}^2 \implies \alpha \; = \; \frac{43 \times 10^5}{39 \times 10^4} \; \approx \; 11 \text{ rad/s}^2$
questions.topic: Torque and Angular Acceleration of Composite Body

questions.text: A ball of mass $0.5 \text{ kg}$ is attached to a string of length $50 \text{ cm}$. The ball is rotated on a horizontal circular path about its vertical axis. The maximum tension that the string can bear is $400 \text{ N}$. The maximum possible value of angular velocity of the ball in $\text{rad/s}$ is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Tension provides the centripetal force: $T \; = \; m\omega^2\ell$. // 📝 Solution: $400 \; = \; 0.5 \times \omega^2 \times 0.5 \implies \omega^2 \; = \; 1600 \implies \omega \; = \; 40 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.text: A thin uniform rod of length $2 \text{ m}$, cross sectional area $A$ and density $d$ is rotated about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to its length with angular velocity $\omega$. If the value of $\omega$ in terms of its rotational kinetic energy $E$ is $\sqrt{\frac{\alpha E}{Ad}}$, then the value of $\alpha$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $E \; = \; \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with $I \; = \; \frac{m\ell^2}{12}$ and $m \; = \; dA\ell$. // 📝 Solution: $E \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{dA\ell^3}{12}\omega^2 \; = \; \frac{dA\left( 2 \right)^3}{24}\omega^2 \; = \; \frac{dA\omega^2}{3} \implies \omega \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{3E}{dA}} \implies \alpha \; = \; 3$

questions.text: A body of mass $m$ is projected with a speed $u$ making an angle of $45^\circ$ with the ground. The angular momentum of the body about the point of projection, at the highest point is expressed as $\frac{\sqrt{2}mu^3}{Xg}$. The value of $X$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: At the top, $L \; = \; m\,v_x\,H$ with $H \; = \; \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $L \; = \; mu\cos 45^\circ \cdot \frac{u^2\sin^2 45^\circ}{2g} \; = \; \frac{mu^3}{4\sqrt{2}g} \; = \; \frac{\sqrt{2}mu^3}{8g} \implies X \; = \; 8$

questions.text: A solid sphere of radius $10 \text{ cm}$ is rotating about an axis which is at a distance $15 \text{ cm}$ from its centre. The radius of gyration about this axis is $\sqrt{n} \text{ cm}$. The value of $n$ is
If the radius of earth is reduced to three-fourth of its present value without change in its mass then the duration of the day of earth will be ______ hours $30$ minutes.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Conserve angular momentum with $I \; = \; \frac{2}{5}MR^2$. // 📝 Solution: $I_1\omega_1 \; = \; I_2\omega_2 \implies \frac{1}{T_1} \; = \; \frac{9}{16}\cdot\frac{1}{T_2} \implies T_2 \; = \; \frac{9}{16} \times 24 \; = \; 13.5 \text{ h} \; = \; 13 \text{ h } 30 \text{ min}$

questions.text: A disc of moment of inertia $2\;\text{kg m}^2$ rotates at $10\;\text{rad/s}$. A constant torque of $4\;\text{N m}$ acts on it for $5\;\text{s}$ in the direction of rotation. The final angular velocity is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\tau \; = \; I\alpha$ and $\omega \; = \; \omega_0 \; + \; \alpha t$. // 📝 Solution: $\alpha \; = \; \dfrac{4}{2} \; = \; 2\;\text{rad/s}^2 \implies \omega \; = \; 10 \; + \; 2\left( 5 \right) \; = \; 20\;\text{rad/s}$

questions.text: An object moves at a constant speed along a circular path in a horizontal plane with centre at the origin. When the object is at $x \; = \; +2 \text{ m}$, its velocity is $-4\hat{j} \text{ m/s}$. The object's velocity $(v)$ and acceleration $(a)$ at $x \; = \; -2 \text{ m}$ will be
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Velocity reverses at the diametrically opposite point and acceleration points towards the centre with $a \; = \; \frac{v^2}{r}$. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $a_c \; = \; \frac{4^2}{2} \; = \; 8 \text{ m/s}^2$ directed towards the centre, i.e. $+\hat{i}$ at $x \; = \; -2 \implies \vec{v} \; = \; 4\hat{j},\; \vec{a} \; = \; 8\hat{i}$

questions.text: A block is simply released from the top of an inclined plane as shown in the figure above. The maximum compression in the spring when the block hits the spring is : [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the work-energy theorem including gravity, friction and spring work. // 📝 Solution: $5 \times 10 \times 5 \; - \; 0.5 \times 5 \times 10 \times x \; - \; \frac{1}{2}Kx^2 \; = \; 0 \implies 250 \; = \; 25x + 50x^2 \implies 2x^2 + x - 10 \; = \; 0 \implies x \; = \; 2 \text{ m}$
questions.topic: Work-Energy Theorem with Spring and Friction

questions.text: A ring and a solid sphere roll down the same inclined plane without slipping. They start from rest. The radii of both bodies are identical and the ratio of their kinetic energies is $\frac{7}{x}$ where $x$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Pure rolling means friction does no work, so energy is conserved. // 📝 Solution: Both lose the same PE $\implies$ equal final KE $\implies \frac{KE_{ring}}{KE_{sphere}} \; = \; 1 \implies \frac{7}{x} \; = \; 1 \implies x \; = \; 7$

questions.text: A uniform solid cylinder of length $L$ and radius $R$ has moment of inertia about its axis equal to $I_1$. A small co-centric cylinder of length $L/2$ and radius $R/3$ carved from this cylinder has moment of inertia about its axis equals to $I_2$. The ratio $I_1/I_2$ is ____.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $I \; = \; \frac{1}{2}mr^2$ with mass proportional to volume. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{m_2}{m_1} \; = \; \frac{1}{9}\cdot\frac{1}{2} \; = \; \frac{1}{18} \implies \frac{I_2}{I_1} \; = \; \frac{1}{18} \times \frac{1}{9} \; = \; \frac{1}{162} \implies \frac{I_1}{I_2} \; = \; 162$

questions.text: Two masses $m$ and $2m$ are connected by a light string going over a pulley (disc) of mass $30m$ with radius $r \; = \; 0.1 \text{ m}$. The pulley is mounted in a vertical plane and it is free to rotate about its axis. The $2m$ mass is released from rest and its speed when it has descended through a height of $3.6 \text{ m}$ is ____ $\text{m/s}$. (Assume string does not slip and $g \; = \; 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Net PE loss is $mgh$; KE includes both blocks and the pulley $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with $I \; = \; \frac{1}{2}Mr^2$. // 📝 Solution: $mgh \; = \; \frac{3}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}\left( 15mr^2 \right)\frac{v^2}{r^2} \; = \; 9mv^2 \implies v^2 \; = \; \frac{10 \times 3.6}{9} \; = \; 4 \implies v \; = \; 2 \text{ m/s}$

questions.text: A wheel starts from rest with a constant angular acceleration of $5\;\text{rad/s}^2$. The angle through which it turns in $6\;\text{s}$ is ______ rad.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use $\theta \; = \; \omega_0 t \; + \; \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$. // 📝 Solution: $\theta \; = \; 0 \; + \; \dfrac{1}{2}\left( 5 \right)\left( 36 \right) \; = \; 90\;\text{rad}$

questions.text: A body of mass $5 \text{ kg}$ moving with a uniform speed $3\sqrt{2} \text{ ms}^{-1}$ in $X-Y$ plane along the line $y \; = \; x + 4$. The angular momentum of the particle about the origin will be ______ $\text{kgm}^2\text{s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $L \; = \; mvd$ where $d$ is the perpendicular distance of the line from the origin. // 📝 Solution: $d \; = \; \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \; = \; 2\sqrt{2} \text{ m} \implies L \; = \; 5 \times 3\sqrt{2} \times 2\sqrt{2} \; = \; 60 \text{ kgm}^2/\text{s}$

questions.text: A force of $10\;\text{N}$ acts at a point $0.5\;\text{m}$ from the pivot, making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the line joining the pivot and the point. The magnitude of the torque is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $\tau \; = \; rF\sin\theta$. // 📝 Solution: $\tau \; = \; 0.5\left( 10 \right)\sin 30^\circ \; = \; 2.5\;\text{N m}$

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about an axis through one end and perpendicular to the rod is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Apply the parallel axis theorem to the centre-of-mass value. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; \dfrac{ML^2}{12} \; + \; M\left( \dfrac{L}{2} \right)^2 \; = \; \dfrac{ML^2}{3}$
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a rod

questions.text: A particle of mass $2\;\text{kg}$ moves with velocity $3\;\text{m/s}$ along a straight line whose perpendicular distance from the origin is $4\;\text{m}$. Its angular momentum about the origin is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: $L \; = \; mvr_{\perp}$. // 📝 Solution: $L \; = \; 2\left( 3 \right)\left( 4 \right) \; = \; 24\;\text{kg m}^2/\text{s}$

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about a tangent to its surface is
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Use the parallel axis theorem from the diameter axis. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 \; + \; MR^2 \; = \; \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$

questions.text: A uniform bar of length $12 \text{ cm}$ and mass $20m$ lies on a smooth horizontal table. Two point masses $m$ and $2m$ are moving in opposite directions with same speed of $v$ and in the same plane as the bar, as shown in figure. These masses strike the bar simultaneously and get stuck to it. After collision the entire system is rotating with angular frequency $\omega$. The ratio of $v$ and $\omega$ is : [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Conserve angular momentum about the bar's centre (here also the system's centre of mass) and use $\omega \; = \; \frac{L}{I}$. // 📝 Solution: $x_{cm} \; = \; \frac{2m\left( -2 \right) + m\left( 4 \right)}{23m} \; = \; 0;\; L \; = \; 2m\left( 2 \right)v + m\left( 4 \right)v \; = \; 8mv;\; I \; = \; \frac{20m\left( 144 \right)}{12} + 2m\left( 4 \right) + m\left( 16 \right) \; = \; 264m \implies \frac{v}{\omega} \; = \; 33$

questions.text: A car is moving with a constant speed of $20 \text{ m/s}$ in a circular horizontal track of radius $40 \text{ m}$. A bob is suspended from the roof of the car by a massless string. The angle made by the string with the vertical will be: (Take $g \; = \; 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Resolve tension: $T\cos\theta \; = \; mg$ and $T\sin\theta \; = \; \frac{mv^2}{R}$. // 📝 Solution: $\tan\theta \; = \; \frac{v^2}{Rg} \; = \; \frac{400}{40 \times 10} \; = \; 1 \implies \theta \; = \; \frac{\pi}{4}$
questions.topic: Circular Motion of Bob in an Accelerated Frame

questions.text: A uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ suspended by means of two identical inextensible light strings as shown in figure. Tension in one string immediately after the other string is cut, is ____. ($g$ acceleration due to gravity) [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Immediately after cutting, the rod rotates about the end still attached ($a_A \; = \; 0$): $\tau \; = \; I_A\alpha$. // 📝 Solution: $\alpha \; = \; \frac{mg\,l/2}{ml^2/3} \; = \; \frac{3g}{2l} \implies a_{cm} \; = \; \frac{3g}{4} \implies mg - T \; = \; m\cdot\frac{3g}{4} \implies T \; = \; \frac{mg}{4}$
questions.topic: Rigid Body Dynamics after String Cut

questions.text: A heavy iron bar, of weight $W$ is having its one end on the ground and the other on the shoulder of a person. The bar makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. The weight experienced by the person is :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Take torque about the ground contact point. // 📝 Solution: [FIGURE] $W\left( \frac{L}{2}\cos\theta \right) \; = \; R\left( L\cos\theta \right) \implies R \; = \; \frac{W}{2}$

questions.text: Two identical thin rods of mass $M \text{ kg}$ and length $L \text{ m}$ are connected as shown in figure. Moment of inertia of the combined rod system about an axis passing through point $P$ and perpendicular to the plane of the rods is $\frac{x}{12}ML^2 \text{ kg m}^2$. The value of $x$ is ____. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Vertical rod: $\frac{ML^2}{3}$ about its end; horizontal rod: $\frac{ML^2}{12} + ML^2$ about $P$. // 📝 Solution: $I \; = \; \frac{ML^2}{3} + \frac{ML^2}{12} + ML^2 \; = \; \frac{4 + 1 + 12}{12}ML^2 \; = \; \frac{17}{12}ML^2 \implies x \; = \; 17$
questions.topic: Moment of Inertia of Composite Rods

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a square loop made of four uniform solid cylinders, each having radius $R$ and length $L \left( R < L \right)$ about an axis passing through the mid points of opposite sides, is (Take the mass of the entire loop as $M$) :
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Two cylinders are perpendicular to the axis (through their centres) and two are parallel to it at distance $\frac{L}{2}$. // 📝 Solution: $m \; = \; \frac{M}{4} \implies I \; = \; 2\left( \frac{mR^2}{4} + \frac{mL^2}{12} \right) + 2\left( \frac{mR^2}{2} + \frac{mL^2}{4} \right) \; = \; m\left( \frac{3R^2}{2} + \frac{2L^2}{3} \right) \; = \; \frac{3}{8}MR^2 + \frac{1}{6}ML^2$
questions.topic: Moment of Inertia of Composite Loop

questions.text: Two discs of moment of inertia $I_1 \; = \; 4 \text{ kg m}^2$ and $I_2 \; = \; 2 \text{ kg m}^2$ about their central axes and normal to their planes, rotating with angular speeds $10 \text{ rad/s}$ and $4 \text{ rad/s}$ respectively are brought into contact face to face with their axes of rotation coincident. The loss in kinetic energy of the system in the process is ______ J.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Conserve angular momentum, then $\Delta E \; = \; E_i - E_f$. // 📝 Solution: $\omega_0 \; = \; \frac{40 + 8}{6} \; = \; 8 \text{ rad/s};\; E_i \; = \; 200 + 16 \; = \; 216 \text{ J},\; E_f \; = \; \frac{1}{2}\left( 6 \right)\left( 64 \right) \; = \; 192 \text{ J} \implies \Delta E \; = \; 24 \text{ J}$
questions.topic: Energy Loss in Coupling of Discs

questions.text: A uniform disc of mass $0.5 \text{ kg}$ and radius $r$ is projected with velocity $18 \text{ m/s}$ at $t \; = \; 0 \text{ s}$ on a rough horizontal surface. It starts off with a purely sliding motion at $t \; = \; 0 \text{ s}$. After $2 \text{ s}$ it acquires a purely rolling motion (see figure). The total kinetic energy of the disc after $2 \text{ s}$ will be ______ $\text{J}$ (given, coefficient of friction is $0.3$ and $g \; = \; 10 \text{ m/s}^2$). [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Find the speed after $2 \text{ s}$ from friction deceleration, then use $KE \; = \; \frac{3}{4}mv^2$ for a rolling disc. // 📝 Solution: $a \; = \; \mu g \; = \; 3 \implies v \; = \; 18 - 3 \times 2 \; = \; 12 \text{ m/s} \implies KE \; = \; \frac{3}{4}\left( 0.5 \right)\left( 12 \right)^2 \; = \; 54 \text{ J}$

questions.text: A circular disc reaches from top to bottom of an inclined plane of length $l$. When it slips down the plane, it takes $t \text{ s}$. When it rolls down the plane then it takes $\left( \frac{\alpha}{2} \right)^{1/2}t \text{ s}$, where $\alpha$ is ______.
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Compare accelerations $g\sin\theta$ and $\frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^2/R^2}$ with $k^2 \; = \; \frac{R^2}{2}$. // 📝 Solution: $a' \; = \; \frac{2g\sin\theta}{3},\; t \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{2\ell}{g\sin\theta}},\; t' \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{6\ell}{2g\sin\theta}} \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t \implies \alpha \; = \; 3$

questions.text: A disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is rolling horizontally without slipping with speed $v$. It then moves up an inclined smooth surface as shown in figure. The maximum height that the disc can go up the incline is : [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: On a smooth incline no friction acts, so the rotational KE stays unchanged. // 📝 Solution: $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2 \; = \; Mgh \implies h \; = \; \frac{v^2}{2g}$

questions.text: $I_{CM}$ is the moment of inertia of a circular disc about an axis $(CM)$ passing through its centre and perpendicular to the plane of the disc. $I_{AB}$ is its moment of inertia about an axis $AB$ perpendicular to the plane and parallel to axis $CM$ at a distance $\frac{2}{3}R$ from the centre, where $R$ is the radius of the disc. The ratio of $I_{AB}$ and $I_{CM}$ is $x : 9$. The value of $x$ is ______. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Parallel axis theorem with $I_{CM} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}mR^2$. // 📝 Solution: $I_{AB} \; = \; \frac{mR^2}{2} \; + \; m\left( \frac{2R}{3} \right)^2 \; = \; \frac{17}{18}mR^2 \implies \frac{I_{AB}}{I_{CM}} \; = \; \frac{17}{9} \implies x \; = \; 17$

questions.text: Suppose there is a uniform circular disc of mass $M \text{ kg}$ and radius $r \text{ m}$ shown in figure. The shaded regions are cut out from the disc. The moment of inertia of the remainder about the axis $A$ of the disc is given by $\frac{x}{256}Mr^2$. The value of $x$ is ____. [FIGURE]
questions.solution: 💡 Hint: Subtract the moment of inertia of the two removed discs (parallel axis theorem) from that of the full disc. // 📝 Solution: $m_i \; = \; \frac{M}{16};\; I_{rem} \; = \; \frac{1}{2}Mr^2 - 2\left[ \frac{1}{2}m_i\left( \frac{r}{4} \right)^2 + m_i\left( \frac{3r}{4} \right)^2 \right] \; = \; \frac{128}{256}Mr^2 - \frac{19}{256}Mr^2 \; = \; \frac{109}{256}Mr^2$
questions.topic: Moment of Inertia of Disc with Cavities

questions.text: A cylinder is rolling down on an inclined plane of inclination $60^\circ$. Its acceleration during rolling down will be $\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}^2$, where $x$ ______ (use $g \; = \; 10 \text{ m/s}^2$).
